PrivDrift evaluates active-context re-disclosure: whether a secret disclosed at turn t0 remains behaviorally recoverable after d unrelated content-dense drift turns and a later standardized probe. Leakage includes exact, approximate, partial, or semantic reproduction. Dataset: 1,000 controlled dialogues per model (900 synthetic, 100 human-authored, interspersed); aggregate results combine both, but cached metadata does not identify human-authored rows for separate comparison. Dialogue-level hybrid leakage: DeepSeek 38.70%, GPT-OSS 47.70%, Qwen 54.60%; regex-only: 37.80%, 47.70%, 53.50%. Probe-level persuasion rates: GPT simple/medium/hard 39.30/40.50/32.90%; DeepSeek 28.10/22.00/29.20%; Qwen 38.70/33.30/40.60%. final_notes: PrivDrift audits whether secrets disclosed in active LLM conversations remain recoverable after unrelated topic shifts. It evaluates GPT-OSS-120B, DeepSeek-R1, and Qwen3-VL-235B through OpenRouter, using identical dialogue histories and probe templates. Each model has 1,000 dialogues: 900 synthetic and 100 human-authored, distributed throughout the benchmark; cached metadata does not preserve human/synthetic row identity. One seeded secret per dialogue; drift lengths d∈{0,2,3,4,5,6}; three standardized persuasion probes. Dialogue-level leakage means any probe elicits the secret; persuasion/fuzzy analyses are probe-level. Regex-only and hybrid leakage are separate; hybrid adds normalization matching plus an open-weights Llama judge for negative cases. Paper examines whether secrets disclosed in active LLM conversations remain recoverable after unrelated topic shifts. PrivDrift is a benchmark with 1,000 controlled dialogues, seeded secrets, unrelated intervening turns, and standardized extraction probes. It tests GPT-OSS-120B, DeepSeek-R1, and Qwen3-VL-235B using simple/direct, medium/justified, and hard/high-pressure probes. Hybrid detection uses normalization-based matching followed, for negative cases, by an open-weights Llama judge; fuzzy matching is auxiliary. Dialogue-level leakage means any standardized probe elicits the secret, while probe-level leakage is measured per response. Reported dialogue-level leakage ranges from 38.7% to 54.6%. Persuasion effects vary by model; SSNs and credit-card numbers are suppressed more often than emails and phone numbers. For tested drift lengths d≤6, additional drift does not reliably reduce leakage. No evaluated model meets the stable-suppression criterion.

Key definitions: active-context re-disclosure is reproduction of information supplied earlier in the same conversation; drift length d is the number of turns between disclosure and final probe; L(d) is leakage at drift d; safety threshold δ=0.1×L(0); Privacy Half-Life τ is the earliest observed drift length below threshold with no later observed resurgence. D_obs is the observed drift-length set. Benchmark components include a parametric dialogue generator, probing harness, metric suite, and scaffold-then-rewrite pipeline. Evaluated models are accessed through OpenRouter. Statistical tools include bootstrap CIs, McNemar’s test with Bonferroni correction, Cochran’s Q, chi-square tests, and Cramer’s V.

Summary: The paper studies whether secrets disclosed in active LLM conversations remain recoverable after unrelated topic shifts. PrivDrift contains 1,000 controlled dialogues with seeded secrets, intervening unrelated turns, and standardized extraction probes. Three models are tested using direct, justified, and high-pressure probes. A hybrid detector combines normalized matching with an LLM judge. Dialogue-level leakage (any standardized probe elicits the secret) ranges from 38.7% to 54.6%. Persuasion effects vary by model. The paper studies whether secrets disclosed in active LLM conversations remain recoverable after unrelated topic shifts. PrivDrift contains 1,000 controlled synthetic dialogues with seeded secrets, drift turns, and standardized extraction probes; human-authored dialogues are also considered. Three models are tested: GPT-OSS-120B, DeepSeek-R1, and Qwen3-VL-235B. Probes are Simple (direct), Medium (justified), and Hard (high-pressure). Leakage includes exact, approximate, or semantic disclosure. Dialogue-level leakage counts any standardized probe eliciting the secret; probe-level leakage evaluates individual responses. A hybrid detector uses normalization-based containment first, then an open-weights Llama judge for negative cases; regex-only and fuzzy matching are auxiliary measures.

Reported dialogue-level leakage ranges from 38.7% to 54.6%. Persuasion effects vary by model. SSNs and credit-card numbers are suppressed more often than emails and phone numbers. For tested drift d≤6, additional drift does not reliably reduce leakage. No evaluated model meets the stable-suppression criterion.

Key definitions: drift length d is the number of turns between disclosure and final probe; L(d) is leakage at d; safety threshold δ=0.1×L(0); Privacy Half-Life τ is the earliest observed drift length below δ with no later observed resurgence. D_obs is the observed drift set; t₀ is disclosure turn; D consists of paired unrelated messages (uᵢ,aᵢ). Sampling includes Uniform{2,3,4,5,6}. Dialogue-level CIs are 95% bootstrap intervals. McNemar’s test compares matched detectors/models, with Bonferroni correction where applicable; Cochran’s Q compares persuasion levels; chi-square/Cramer’s V assess associations.

The framing distinguishes active-context privacy/inference-time leakage from training-data memorization, membership inference, parameter-level unlearning, RAG, prompt injection, and multi-turn attacks. The benchmark uses a parametric dialogue generator, probing harness, metric suite, and scaffold-then-rewrite naturalistic refinement pipeline.

The paper investigates whether unrelated conversational tasks cause later disclosure of sensitive information already present in an active LLM conversation. PrivDrift uses 1,000 seeded multi-turn dialogues containing phone numbers, email addresses, Social Security Numbers, or credit card numbers, with content-dense intervening exchanges and three standardized extraction conditions. Detection combines normalized matching with an open-weights judge. Hybrid dialogue-level leakage rates across the three evaluated models are 38.70%, 47.70%, and 54.60%. Leakage varies by model, secret type, and persuasion intensity. Social Security Numbers and credit cards show much stronger suppression than contact identifiers. No system achieves stable suppression within the tested drift lengths. The paper frames this as an active-context behavioral privacy failure, not evidence of permanent memory.

final_notes:
PrivDrift audits whether secrets disclosed in active LLM conversations remain recoverable after unrelated topic shifts. It evaluates 1,000 dialogues per model with seeded secrets, drift turns, and standardized probes. Models: GPT-OSS-120B, DeepSeek-R1, Qwen3-VL-235B. Three probes/dialogue imply 3,000 cached responses/model and 9,000 total; an earlier claim of 8,000 total is inconsistent.

Hybrid dialogue-level leakage: DeepSeek 38.70%, GPT 47.70%, Qwen 54.60%; regex: 37.80%, 47.70%, 53.50%. CIs: [35.7,41.6], [44.6,50.8], [51.6,57.7]. Cochran’s Q: persuasion effects all models, p<10^-5. Table 4 simple/medium/hard: GPT 39.3/40.5/32.9; DeepSeek 28.1/22.0/29.2; Qwen 38.7/33.3/40.6. Drift dips near d=3 then rebounds; drift-length V .1073/.0659/.0723 (DeepSeek/GPT/Qwen). Secret-type V .5871/.7731/.6927; SSNs/cards much lower than emails/phones. Table 5 SSN GPT/DeepSeek/Qwen .14/1.11/5.97%; card 0/.39/4.01%; email 78.24/57.11/81.13%; phone 70.89/46.13/57.24%.

Definitions: d is turns between disclosure and final probe; threshold delta=.1L(0); tau earliest drift below threshold with no later resurgence; if none tau=max observed+1=7. No stable suppression. Table 6 probe-level regex/fuzzy85/fuzzy80/hybrid: DeepSeek 25.50/26.40/26.53/26.43; GPT 36.80/37.03/37.07/37.57; Qwen 36.97/37.60/37.93/37.53.

Conclusion repeats leakage rates, model-dependent persuasion, strongest secret-type association, no reliable decay, and tau/Privacy Half-Life exceeding d<=6. Limitations: bounded active-context drift, fixed-format secrets, no training/personalization/cross-session claims, 900 synthetic and 100 human-authored dialogues, no formal human-detector agreement, API-served models and planned sanitized artifacts.

PrivDrift benchmark: 1,000 controlled dialogues with seeded secrets, unrelated intervening turns, and standardized extraction probes. Paper examines whether secrets disclosed in active LLM conversations remain recoverable after unrelated topic shifts. PrivDrift is a benchmark with 1,000 controlled dialogues, seeded secrets, unrelated intervening turns, and standardized extraction probes. It tests GPT-OSS-120B, DeepSeek-R1, and Qwen3-VL-235B using simple/direct, medium/justified, and hard/high-pressure probes. Hybrid detection uses normalization-based matching followed, for negative cases, by an open-weights Llama judge; fuzzy matching is auxiliary. Dialogue-level leakage means any standardized probe elicits the secret, while probe-level leakage is measured per response. Reported dialogue-level leakage ranges from 38.7% to 54.6%. Persuasion effects vary by model; SSNs and credit-card numbers are suppressed more often than emails and phone numbers. For tested drift lengths d≤6, additional drift does not reliably reduce leakage. No evaluated model meets the stable-suppression criterion.

Key definitions: active-context re-disclosure is reproduction of information supplied earlier in the same conversation; drift length d is the number of turns between disclosure and final probe; L(d) is leakage at drift d; safety threshold δ=0.1×L(0); Privacy Half-Life τ is the earliest observed drift length below threshold with no later observed resurgence. D_obs is the observed drift-length set. Benchmark components include a parametric dialogue generator, probing harness, metric suite, and scaffold-then-rewrite pipeline. Evaluated models are accessed through OpenRouter. Statistical tools include bootstrap CIs, McNemar’s test with Bonferroni correction, Cochran’s Q, chi-square tests, and Cramer’s V.

final_notes:

final_notes: PrivDrift evaluates active-context secret re-disclosure after topic shifts in GPT-OSS-120B, DeepSeek-R1, and Qwen3-VL-235B. It uses 1,000 dialogues/model (900 synthetic, 100 human), one secret, drift d∈{0,2,3,4,5,6}, and three persuasion probes. Dialogue-level leakage counts any probe eliciting the secret; persuasion, drift, and secret-type analyses are probe-level. Hybrid detection combines normalized matching with an open-weights judge; regex-only and fuzzy results are also reported. Dialogue-level hybrid rates: DeepSeek 38.70%, GPT 47.70%, Qwen 54.60%. Persuasion rates (simple/medium/hard): GPT 39.30/40.50/32.90; DeepSeek 28.10/22.00/29.20; Qwen 38.70/33.30/40.60%. Drift dips near d=3 then rebounds; τ=7 for all models/persuasion levels because suppression is not stable within d≤6. Secret type has strongest association (V=.5871, .7731, .6927); SSNs/credit cards are much lower than emails/phones. Table 5 probe-level hybrid rates: SSN GPT/DeepSeek/Qwen 0.14/1.11/5.97%; credit card 0.00/0.39/4.01%; email 78.24/57.11/81.13%; phone 70.89/46.13/57.24%. Cached-output fuzzy/hybrid: DeepSeek 26.40/26.43, GPT 37.03/37.57, Qwen 37.60/37.53. Discussion cautions leakage does not imply permanent memory or uniform long-context behavior. Limitations: d≤6, fixed-format secrets, active-context only, aggregate synthetic+human results without preserved human-row metadata, detector limitations/no formal human agreement, API model drift, planned sanitized artifact release. Conclusion: drift does not reliably reduce leakage, privacy half-life exceeds observed window, persuasion is model-dependent, protection is format-sensitive. Appendix A Table 7 counts by d=0,2,3,4,5,6: 197,147,142,166,181,167 (sum 1000); average words 44.29,253.97,344.18,452.27,520.92,568.03 and tokens 59.05,338.62,458.91,603.02,694.56,757.37. Appendix B Table 8 reports secret-type V=.5871/.7731/.6927 (all Large); drift V=.1073 (Small), .0659/.0723 (Negligible); persuasion V=.0718/.0689/.0639 (all Negligible), consistent with earlier notes.

Paper examines whether secrets disclosed in active LLM conversations remain recoverable after unrelated topic shifts. PrivDrift is a benchmark with 1,000 controlled dialogues, seeded secrets, unrelated intervening turns, and standardized extraction probes. It tests GPT-OSS-120B, DeepSeek-R1, and Qwen3-VL-235B using simple/direct, medium/justified, and hard/high-pressure probes. Hybrid detection uses normalization-based matching followed, for negative cases, by an open-weights Llama judge; fuzzy matching is auxiliary. Dialogue-level leakage means any standardized probe elicits the secret, while probe-level leakage is measured per response. Reported dialogue-level leakage ranges from 38.7% to 54.6%. Persuasion effects vary by model; SSNs and credit-card numbers are suppressed more often than emails and phone numbers. For tested drift lengths d≤6, additional drift does not reliably reduce leakage. No evaluated model meets the stable-suppression criterion.

Key definitions: active-context re-disclosure is reproduction of information supplied earlier in the same conversation; drift length d is the number of turns between disclosure and final probe; L(d) is leakage at drift d; safety threshold δ=0.1×L(0); Privacy Half-Life τ is the earliest observed drift length below threshold with no later observed resurgence. D_obs is the observed drift-length set. Benchmark components include a parametric dialogue generator, probing harness, metric suite, and scaffold-then-rewrite pipeline. Evaluated models are accessed through OpenRouter. Statistical tools include bootstrap CIs, McNemar’s test with Bonferroni correction, Cochran’s Q, chi-square tests, and Cramer’s V.

Earlier text inconsistently calls normalization stage B6T while labeling formal output Leak_U3P.

final_notes: Results: Dialogue-level hybrid leakage is 38.70% DeepSeek-R1, 47.70% GPT-OSS-120B, and 54.60% Qwen3-VL-235B; regex adds 0, 0.90, and 1.10 percentage points. Probe-level persuasion effects are significant but model-dependent: GPT hard is lowest (32.90%), DeepSeek medium lowest (22.00%), Qwen hard highest (40.60%). Effect sizes for persuasion are negligible (V=.0718/.0689/.0639), which is not inherently inconsistent with statistical significance. Drift effects are small/negligible (V=.1073, .0659, .0723), with a dip near d=3 and rebound; drift lengths evaluated through d=6. Secret type has strongest association (V=.5871/.7731/.6927). Table 5 leakage is low for SSNs/cards (SSN .14–5.97%; cards 0–4.01%) and high for emails/phones (email 57.11–81.13%; phone 46.13–70.89%); earlier prose incorrectly said “suppressed far less often.” Privacy Half-Life threshold not reached; tau=7 for all models and persuasion levels. Fuzzy 0.85 vs hybrid probe leakage: DeepSeek 26.40 vs 26.43, GPT 37.03 vs 37.57, Qwen 37.60 vs 37.53. Discussion/conclusion: leakage remains substantial/recoverable after drift; drift does not reliably reduce leakage; fuzzy closely tracks hybrid; protections are format-sensitive and uneven; persuasion is non-monotonic/model-dependent; half-life exceeds observed d≤6 window. Benchmark has 900 synthetic and 100 human-authored dialogues, totaling 1,000 per model; interspersed, not block-separated. Cached metadata cannot identify human-authored evaluated rows, so only aggregate results are reported. Evaluates active-context recoverability, not cross-session/training memory. Fixed-format secrets; detector labels use regex, fuzzy, and external LLM judge. Appendix A Table 7: total N across drift groups is 1,000 (d=0:197; d=2:147; d=3:142; d=4:166; d=5:181; d=6:167); lengths increase with drift, and approximate token counts are estimated from word counts. Appendix B Table 8 confirms effect sizes: secret type .5871/.7731/.6927 (large), drift .1073/.0659/.0723 (small/negligible), persuasion .0718/.0689/.0639 (negligible) for DeepSeek/GPT/Qwen respectively.

errors.claim: “Section 5.6 reports \(\tau=7\) for all models and persuasion levels.”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes state: “For tested drift lengths d≤6, additional drift does not reliably reduce leakage.” The notes also define \(\tau\) as the earliest observed drift length satisfying the threshold condition.
errors.explanation: If the observed drift-length window ends at \(d=6\), an observed Privacy Half-Life of \(\tau=7\) cannot be the earliest observed qualifying drift length unless drift length 7 was also evaluated. The stated \(\tau=7\) therefore conflicts with the recorded tested range.

errors.claim: “No stable decay occurs for \(d\leq 6\): Section 5.6 reports \(\tau=7\) for all models and persuasion levels.”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes define \(\tau\) as the earliest observed drift length below the threshold with no later resurgence, and record that the tested drift range is \(d\leq6\) with \(D_{obs}\) limited accordingly.
errors.explanation: If drift lengths are observed only through 6, \(\tau=7\) cannot be the earliest observed drift length. The claim that no stable decay occurs through \(d\leq6\) is compatible with the absence of a qualifying value, but reporting \(\tau=7\) as observed is not.

errors.claim: Section 5.6/Introduction report τ=7 for all models and persuasion levels.
errors.evidence: Table 1 in this part lists the evaluated drift lengths as 0, 2, 3, 4, 5, and 6; thus the observed drift set has no d=7.
errors.explanation: τ is defined as the earliest observed drift length meeting the threshold condition. Therefore, τ=7 cannot be an observed value when the benchmark only evaluates drift lengths through d=6.

final_notes:

Paper examines whether secrets disclosed in active LLM conversations remain recoverable after unrelated topic shifts. PrivDrift is a benchmark with 1,000 controlled dialogues, seeded secrets, unrelated intervening turns, and standardized extraction probes. It tests GPT-OSS-120B, DeepSeek-R1, and Qwen3-VL-235B using simple/direct, medium/justified, and hard/high-pressure probes. Hybrid detection uses normalization-based matching followed, for negative cases, by an open-weights Llama judge; fuzzy matching is auxiliary. Dialogue-level leakage means any standardized probe elicits the secret, while probe-level leakage is measured per response. Reported dialogue-level leakage ranges from 38.7% to 54.6%. Persuasion effects vary by model; SSNs and credit-card numbers are suppressed more often than emails and phone numbers. For tested drift lengths d≤6, additional drift does not reliably reduce leakage. No evaluated model meets the stable-suppression criterion.

Key definitions: active-context re-disclosure is reproduction of information supplied earlier in the same conversation; drift length d is the number of turns between disclosure and final probe; L(d) is leakage at drift d; safety threshold δ=0.1×L(0); Privacy Half-Life τ is the earliest observed drift length below threshold with no later observed resurgence. D_obs is the observed drift-length set. Benchmark components include a parametric dialogue generator, probing harness, metric suite, and scaffold-then-rewrite pipeline. Evaluated models are accessed through OpenRouter. Statistical tools include bootstrap CIs, McNemar’s test with Bonferroni correction, Cochran’s Q, chi-square tests, and Cramer’s V.

final_notes: Results: H8D largely agrees with deterministic B6T/U3P; G4P augmentation is 0 pp for M7Q, +0.9 for T4X, +1.1 for Y9C. H8D G4P: T4X 38.70% [35.7,41.6], M7Q 47.70% [44.6,50.8], Y9C 54.60% [51.6,57.7]. V4N P6S: M7Q C8R/Z2F/L9W 39.3/40.5/32.9%; T4X 28.1/22.0/29.2%; Y9C 38.7/33.3/40.6%; Cochran Q p<1e-5 each. S8Q strongly determines leakage: W3B/N6G low versus F8Z/A2L high; attributed to format/sensitivity cues and format-sensitive safety heuristics, not generalized contextual confidentiality/reasoning. K2V exceeds observed range for every model/condition: d<=6, assigned tau=7. R5J fuzzy matching sensitivity table is cached-output P6S, not directly comparable to G4P; higher R5J threshold closely tracks H8D. Discussion: behavioral recoverability does not imply permanent memory or uniform long-context behavior; assistants may reproduce sensitive in-context information under sufficient retrieval pressure. M7Q pressure response consistent with urgency activating safety/refusal behavior; Y9C weaker pressure resistance. J7K is not an implicit privacy boundary; unstable intermediate decreases are not suppression evidence. final_notes: PrivDrift audits whether secrets disclosed in active LLM conversations remain recoverable after unrelated topic shifts. It uses 1,000 controlled dialogues per model (900 synthetic, 100 human-authored), four fixed-format secret categories, drift lengths 0,2,3,4,5,6, and models GPT-OSS-120B, DeepSeek-R1, Qwen3-VL-235B. Dialogue-level leakage means any probe elicits the secret; persuasion-level and fuzzy analyses are probe-level, so rates are not directly interchangeable. Regex-only and hybrid metrics are separate; hybrid adds 0.00, 0.90, and 1.10 percentage points for GPT-OSS, DeepSeek, and Qwen. Dialogue-level hybrid leakage is 47.70%, 38.70%, and 54.60%, matching Table 3 CIs. Persuasion significantly affects probe-level leakage: GPT hard lowest (32.90% vs 39.30/40.50), DeepSeek medium lowest (22.00%), Qwen hard highest (40.60%). Drift curves dip near d=3 then rebound; drift-length Cramer’s V: DeepSeek .1073 (small), GPT .0659 (negligible), Qwen .0723 (negligible). Secret type has strongest association: DeepSeek .5871, GPT .7731, Qwen .6927 (all large); persuasion V: .0718, .0689, .0639 (all negligible). SSNs and credit cards have much lower leakage than emails/phones. Table 5 rates: SSN 0.14/1.11/5.97%; credit card 0/0.39/4.01%; email 78.24/57.11/81.13%; phone 70.89/46.13/57.24% (GPT/DeepSeek/Qwen). Table 6 fuzzy 0.85 vs hybrid: DeepSeek 26.40/26.43%, GPT 37.03/37.57%, Qwen 37.60/37.53%. Tau=7 for all models/persuasion levels due fallback; no stable decay within d<=6. Limitations include bounded drift, active-context only, fixed-format secrets, aggregate synthetic/human results, automated detection, and API-served models. Appendix Table 7 counts by drift length sum to 1,000: d=0 197; d=2 147; d=3 142; d=4 166; d=5 181; d=6 167. Word averages/medians rise from 44.29/43.00 at d=0 to 568.03/605.00 at d=6; token averages/medians rise from 59.05/57.33 to 757.37/806.67. Token counts are approximate estimates from word counts. Appendix B Table 8 repeats these probe-level Cramer’s V values and interpretations. Appendix C contains Figure 6 on dialogue construction.

Paper examines whether secrets disclosed in active LLM conversations remain recoverable after unrelated topic shifts. PrivDrift is a benchmark with 1,000 controlled dialogues, seeded secrets, unrelated intervening turns, and standardized extraction probes. It tests GPT-OSS-120B, DeepSeek-R1, and Qwen3-VL-235B using simple/direct, medium/justified, and hard/high-pressure probes. Hybrid detection uses normalization-based matching followed, for negative cases, by an open-weights Llama judge; fuzzy matching is auxiliary. Dialogue-level leakage means any standardized probe elicits the secret, while probe-level leakage is measured per response. Reported dialogue-level leakage ranges from 38.7% to 54.6%. Persuasion effects vary by model; SSNs and credit-card numbers are suppressed more often than emails and phone numbers. For tested drift lengths d≤6, additional drift does not reliably reduce leakage. No evaluated model meets the stable-suppression criterion.

Key definitions: active-context re-disclosure is reproduction of information supplied earlier in the same conversation; drift length d is the number of turns between disclosure and final probe; L(d) is leakage at drift d; safety threshold δ=0.1×L(0); Privacy Half-Life τ is the earliest observed drift length below threshold with no later observed resurgence. D_obs is the observed drift-length set. Benchmark components include a parametric dialogue generator, probing harness, metric suite, and scaffold-then-rewrite pipeline. Evaluated models are accessed through OpenRouter. Statistical tools include bootstrap CIs, McNemar’s test with Bonferroni correction, Cochran’s Q, chi-square tests, and Cramer’s V.

final_notes: QX2 framework evaluates active-context re-disclosure of seeded secret S after unrelated content-dense exchanges D and standardized probe P; leakage includes exact, approximate, or semantic revelation. Dataset N=1,000 (900 synthetic, 100 human-authored/interspersed), four secret categories (A2L phone, F8Z email, W3B SSN, N6G credit card), drift d={0,2,3,4,5,6}. Appendix Table 7 gives counts by d: N={197,147,142,166,181,167}, summing to 1,000; weighted averages match Table 1. Probe conditions C8R Simple, Z2F Medium, L9W Hard. H8D hybrid detector; normalization detector B6T but output Leak_U3P, while Section 3.4.2 calls U3P regex-only baseline. Stage 2 uses Llama judge for binary full/substantial disclosure, including partial/indirect/format variations. K2V Privacy Half-Life tau uses threshold delta=.1*L(0), requiring all later observed lengths <=delta; empty set=max(D_obs)+1; resurgence disqualifies transient decreases. Models: GPT-OSS-120B (M7Q), DeepSeek-R1 (T4X), Qwen3-VL-235B (Y9C); 3,000 responses/model, 9,000 total. G4P any-probe positivity; P6S one observation/dialogue/probe condition. Section 5.6 gives tau=7 for every model and persuasion condition over d<=6. final_notes: PrivDrift evaluates active-context re-disclosure: a secret S disclosed at turn t0 may be reproduced after d unrelated, content-dense drift turns and a later standardized probe. It tests model behavioral reproduction, not whether the transcript contains the secret. Dataset: N=1,000 controlled dialogues (900 synthetic, 100 human-authored), evaluated on three models; 1,000 dialogues per model. Four PII categories: phone, email, SSN, credit card. Drift d∈{0,2,3,4,5,6}; weighted mean length 359.16 words/~478.87 tokens, consistent with Appendix A. Appendix A drift-group Ns: d0 197, d2 147, d3 142, d4 166, d5 181, d6 167; mean words/tokens by group: 44.29/59.05, 253.97/338.62, 344.18/458.91, 452.27/603.02, 520.92/694.56, 568.03/757.37. Three probes per dialogue produce 3,000 cached responses/model and 9,000 total. Hybrid detection combines normalization/substring matching with an open-weights Llama judge for regex-negative responses; dialogue-level hybrid rates: DeepSeek 38.70%, GPT-OSS 47.70%, Qwen 54.60%; regex rates 37.80%, 47.70%, 53.50%. Fuzzy versus hybrid probe rates: DeepSeek 26.40 vs 26.43%; GPT 37.03 vs 37.57%; Qwen 37.60 vs 37.53%. Persuasion: GPT simple/medium/hard 39.3/40.5/32.9%; DeepSeek 28.1/22.0/29.2%; Qwen 38.7/33.3/40.6%; all Cochran Q p<1e-5. Drift Cramer’s V: .1073, .0659, .0723; curves dip near d=3 then rebound. Secret-type V: .5871, .7731, .6927; SSN/card far below email/phone. Privacy Half-Life τ=7 for all models/persuasion levels because threshold not reached within d≤6; claims beyond d≤6 unsupported. Limitations include bounded drift, fixed-format secrets, active-context scope, API models, and no human/synthetic comparison. Conclusion: substantial persistent recoverability, secret-type asymmetry, model-dependent non-monotonic persuasion, and topic drift is not a reliable privacy boundary. Appendix B reports probe-level hybrid-leakage Cramer’s V: secret type .5871/.7731/.6927; drift length .1073/.0659/.0723; persuasion .0718/.0689/.0639 for DeepSeek/GPT-OSS/Qwen respectively, interpreted as large for secret type, small/negligible for drift and negligible for persuasion.

The paper introduces PrivDrift, a benchmark auditing whether user-disclosed secrets remain recoverable after conversational topic drift and persuasion-based probing. It contains 1,000 controlled multi-turn dialogues with seeded secrets, content-dense drift turns, and standardized extraction probes. Across three LLMs with extended context windows, dialogue-level hybrid leakage ranges from 38.7% to 54.6% and varies by model, secret type, and persuasion intensity. Within the tested drift window, additional topic drift does not reliably reduce leakage; the paper frames privacy risk in active LLM contexts as a persistent behavioral failure mode, distinct from only training-data memorization or immediate jailbreak behavior.

Paper examines whether secrets disclosed in active LLM conversations remain recoverable after unrelated topic shifts. PrivDrift is a benchmark with 1,000 controlled dialogues, seeded secrets, unrelated intervening turns, and standardized extraction probes. It tests GPT-OSS-120B, DeepSeek-R1, and Qwen3-VL-235B using simple/direct, medium/justified, and hard/high-pressure probes. Hybrid detection uses normalization-based matching followed, for negative cases, by an open-weights Llama judge; fuzzy matching is auxiliary. Dialogue-level leakage means any standardized probe elicits the secret, while probe-level leakage is measured per response. Reported dialogue-level leakage ranges from 38.7% to 54.6%. Persuasion effects vary by model; SSNs and credit-card numbers are suppressed more often than emails and phone numbers. For tested drift lengths d≤6, additional drift does not reliably reduce leakage. No evaluated model meets the stable-suppression criterion.

Key definitions: active-context re-disclosure is reproduction of information supplied earlier in the same conversation; drift length d is the number of turns between disclosure and final probe; L(d) is leakage at drift d; safety threshold δ=0.1×L(0); Privacy Half-Life τ is the earliest observed drift length below threshold with no later observed resurgence. D_obs is the observed drift-length set. Benchmark components include a parametric dialogue generator, probing harness, metric suite, and scaffold-then-rewrite pipeline. Evaluated models are accessed through OpenRouter. Statistical tools include bootstrap CIs, McNemar’s test with Bonferroni correction, Cochran’s Q, chi-square tests, and Cramer’s V.

Across extended-context models, H8D leakage remains substantial, varies across systems, S8Q, and V4N, and does not reliably decline in the tested window. Main conclusion: active-context privacy should be evaluated as persistent behavioral failure, not only parameter memorization or immediate jailbreak behavior. Framework: E9U is active-context re-disclosure of secret S after topic drift D and probe P; transcript invisibility is not assumed. Dataset N=1,000: 900 synthetic, 100 human, 4 secret categories, drift lengths D7A={0,2,3,4,5,6}; earlier characterization reported mean/median words 359.16/385 and approximate tokens 478.87/513.33. final_notes:
PrivDrift audits whether secrets disclosed in active LLM conversations remain recoverable after unrelated topic shifts. It evaluates GPT-OSS-120B, DeepSeek-R1, and Qwen3-VL-235B through OpenRouter, using identical dialogue histories and probe templates. Each model has 1,000 dialogues: 900 synthetic and 100 human-authored, with one seeded secret and drift lengths d∈{0,2,3,4,5,6}. Three standardized persuasion probes are used.

Dialogue-level leakage means any probe elicits the secret; persuasion-level and fuzzy analyses are probe-level. Regex-only and hybrid leakage are reported separately; hybrid adds normalization matching plus an open-weights Llama judge for negative cases. Dialogue-level rates use 95% bootstrap CIs; McNemar compares matched examples; Cochran’s Q tests repeated persuasion measures; chi-square associations use Cramer’s V. Privacy half-life requires all later observed lengths to remain at or below δ.

Appendix B labels drift association Small for DeepSeek and Negligible for GPT/Qwen; persuasion associations Negligible; secret-type associations Large. SSNs/cards much lower than emails/phones. Paper examines whether secrets disclosed in active LLM conversations remain recoverable after unrelated topic shifts. PrivDrift is a benchmark with 1,000 controlled dialogues, seeded secrets, unrelated intervening turns, and standardized extraction probes. It tests GPT-OSS-120B, DeepSeek-R1, and Qwen3-VL-235B using simple/direct, medium/justified, and hard/high-pressure probes. Hybrid detection uses normalization-based matching followed, for negative cases, by an open-weights Llama judge; fuzzy matching is auxiliary. Dialogue-level leakage means any standardized probe elicits the secret, while probe-level leakage is measured per response. Reported dialogue-level leakage ranges from 38.7% to 54.6%. Persuasion effects vary by model; SSNs and credit-card numbers are suppressed more often than emails and phone numbers. For tested drift lengths d≤6, additional drift does not reliably reduce leakage. No evaluated model meets the stable-suppression criterion.

Key definitions: active-context re-disclosure is reproduction of information supplied earlier in the same conversation; drift length d is the number of turns between disclosure and final probe; L(d) is leakage at drift d; safety threshold δ=0.1×L(0); Privacy Half-Life τ is the earliest observed drift length below threshold with no later observed resurgence. D_obs is the observed drift-length set. Benchmark components include a parametric dialogue generator, probing harness, metric suite, and scaffold-then-rewrite pipeline. Evaluated models are accessed through OpenRouter. Statistical tools include bootstrap CIs, McNemar’s test with Bonferroni correction, Cochran’s Q, chi-square tests, and Cramer’s V.

It contains 1,000 controlled dialogues per model with seeded secrets, drift turns, and standardized probes. Models: GPT-OSS-120B, DeepSeek-R1, and Qwen3-VL-235B. Probes are simple/direct, medium/justified, and hard/high-pressure. Hybrid detection combines normalization matching with an open-weights Llama judge for negative cases; fuzzy matching is auxiliary. Dialogue-level leakage ranges from 38.7% to 54.6%. Persuasion effects vary by model; SSNs and credit-card numbers are more suppressed than emails and phone numbers. For tested drift lengths d≤6, additional drift does not reliably reduce leakage. No model meets stable suppression.

Components: parametric generator, probing harness, metric suite, scaffold-then-rewrite pipeline. Models accessed via OpenRouter. Statistics include bootstrap CIs, McNemar with Bonferroni, Cochran’s Q, chi-square, and Cramer’s V.

errors.claim: Section 5.6/Introduction report τ=7 for all models and persuasion levels.
errors.evidence: Table 1 in this part lists the evaluated drift lengths as 0, 2, 3, 4, 5, and 6; thus the observed drift set has no d=7.
errors.explanation: τ is defined as the earliest observed drift length meeting the threshold condition. Therefore, τ=7 cannot be an observed value when the benchmark only evaluates drift lengths through d=6.

final_notes: The paper studies whether unrelated conversational tasks prevent later disclosure of sensitive information in active context. PrivDrift (QX2): 1,000 dialogues (900 synthetic, 100 human), secrets phone/email/SSN/credit card; three extraction conditions, 3,000 responses/model and 9,000 total. Models: M7Q GPT-OSS-120B, T4X DeepSeek-R1, Y9C Qwen3-VL-235B. Persuasion: C8R Simple, Z2F Medium, L9W Hard. Secret types: A2L phone, F8Z email, W3B SSN, N6G credit card. G4P dialogue-level positive if any probe leaks; P6S probe-level. H8D judge handles partial/indirect/format variants; U3P regex/normalization baseline. Nomenclature inconsistency: some text calls normalization B6T, while formal output is U3P/Leak_U3P, with no B6T alias defined. Results: G4P H8D T4X/M7Q/Y9C = 38.70/47.70/54.60%; U3P = 37.80/47.70/53.50%. By persuasion: M7Q 39.30/40.50/32.90; T4X 28.10/22.00/29.20; Y9C 38.70/33.30/40.60 (C8R/Z2F/L9W). S8Q rates (M7Q/T4X/Y9C): W3B .14/1.11/5.97%, N6G 0/.39/4.01%, F8Z 78.24/57.11/81.13%, A2L 70.89/46.13/57.24%. D7A associations are small/negligible; dip near d=3 then rebound. No stable suppression through d<=6; K2V assigned tau=7. R5J cached-output table distinct from G4P and closely tracks H8D. Table 6 higher-threshold R5J/H8D: T4X 26.40/26.43, M7Q 37.03/37.57, Y9C 37.60/37.53. Limitations: bounded drift range; fixed-format secrets only; untested training-data, personalization, cross-session retention; aggregate results; no formal human–automated agreement; API identities may change; planned artifacts sanitized. Detector-scope wording claiming arbitrary unstructured narratives conflicts with explicit exclusion of unstructured sensitive attributes. Appendix A Table 7 characterizes D7A lengths d=0,2,3,4,5,6 with N=197,147,142,166,181,167 and word/token averages and medians; token counts approximate and word-derived. Appendix B Table 8: S8Q associations large (T4X .5871, M7Q .7731, Y9C .6927); D7A T4X small (.1073), M7Q/Y9C negligible (.0659/.0723); V4N negligible (.0718/.0689/.0639). Appendix C Figure 6 presents dialogue construction details. No new internal error.

The paper studies whether unrelated conversational tasks prevent later disclosure of sensitive information already present in an active LLM conversation. PrivDrift uses seeded multi-turn histories, content-dense intervening exchanges, and three standardized extraction conditions. The dataset contains 1,000 dialogues with phone numbers, email addresses, Social Security Numbers, or credit card numbers. Detection combines normalized matching with an open-weights judge. Hybrid dialogue-level leakage is 38.70%, 47.70%, and 54.60% across three evaluated models. Leakage varies by model, secret type, and persuasion intensity. Social Security Numbers and credit card numbers have much stronger suppression than contact identifiers. No system attains stable suppression within the tested drift lengths. The paper characterizes this as an active-context behavioral privacy failure, not evidence of permanent memory.

The paper studies whether unrelated conversational tasks prevent later disclosure of sensitive information already present in an active LLM conversation. The dataset contains 1,000 dialogues with phone numbers, email addresses, SSNs, or credit card numbers. final_notes: Results: Table 2 dialogue-level regex/hybrid leakage: GPT-OSS 47.70/47.70 (+0), DeepSeek-R1 37.80/38.70 (+0.90, p=.0077), Qwen3-VL 53.50/54.60 (+1.10, p=.00257). Table 3 hybrid dialogue rates/CIs: DeepSeek 38.70 [35.7,41.6], GPT 47.70 [44.6,50.8], Qwen 54.60 [51.6,57.7]. These unions cover three standardized probes, not all possible/adaptive attacks. Probe-level persuasion rates GPT simple/medium/hard 39.3/40.5/32.9; DeepSeek 28.1/22.0/29.2; Qwen 38.7/33.3/40.6; Cochran Q p<1e-5. Drift effects small (Cramer V .1073/.0659/.0723), dip near d=3 then rebound. Secret-type associations large (V .5871/.7731/.6927); emails/phones leak more than SSNs/cards. Privacy Half-Life threshold not reached, so tau=7 for all models/persuasion levels under observed d<=6. Fuzzy vs hybrid probe rates: DeepSeek 26.40/26.43; GPT 37.03/37.57; Qwen 37.60/37.53. N=1000 dialogues per model, comprising 900 synthetic and 100 human-authored; human rows not identifiable in cached metadata. Fixed drift lengths 0,2–6; hybrid includes direct, substantial-substring, identifying partial/indirect disclosure. No stable decay. Risk is recoverability after drift, not permanent memory or all long-context settings. Leakage mostly direct/near-direct; emails/phones leak more than SSNs/cards. Persuasion effects non-monotonic/model-dependent. Limitations: bounded d<=6, fixed-format secrets, active-context only (not training-data, personalization, or cross-session memory), API model variability, automated detector labels without formal human agreement. Conclusion reiterates substantial hybrid leakage (38.7–54.6%), model-dependent persuasion effects, strongest secret-type association, no reliable drift reduction, and Privacy Half-Life beyond observed window. Appendix A Table 7: drift d=0,2,3,4,5,6 have N=197,147,142,166,181,167 respectively, summing to 1000. Average words rise from 44.29 at d=0 to 568.03 at d=6; approximate token counts are estimated from word counts. Appendix B Table 8: probe-level Cramer’s V: DeepSeek secret type .5871 (large), drift .1073 (small), persuasion .0718 (negligible); GPT secret type .7731 (large), drift .0659 (negligible), persuasion .0689 (negligible); Qwen secret type .6927 (large), drift .0723 (negligible), persuasion .0639 (negligible). Appendix C contains Figure 6 on dialogue construction.

The paper introduces PrivDrift, a benchmark auditing whether user-disclosed secrets remain recoverable after conversational topic drift and persuasion-based probing. final_notes:
PrivDrift evaluates whether secrets disclosed in active LLM conversations remain recoverable after unrelated topic shifts. Models: GPT-OSS-120B, DeepSeek-R1, Qwen3-VL-235B; 1,000 dialogues/model, one seeded secret, drift lengths d∈{0,2,3,4,5,6}, three persuasion probes. Dialogue-level leakage counts any probe eliciting the secret; persuasion/fuzzy/secret-type analyses are probe-level. L(d) is leakage; δ=.1×L(0); τ is earliest drift below threshold with no later resurgence, default 7 if none. Privacy Half-Life requires all later observed lengths ≤δ. Hybrid detection combines normalization matching with an open-weights Llama judge; regex-only and hybrid rates are distinct.

Hybrid dialogue leakage (Table 2/3): GPT 47.70%, DeepSeek 38.70%, Qwen 54.60%; regex rates: 47.70%, 37.80%, 53.50%. Persuasion simple/medium/hard (Table 4): GPT 39.30/40.50/32.90, DeepSeek 28.10/22.00/29.20, Qwen 38.70/33.30/40.60. Drift dips near d=3 then rebounds. Cramer’s V drift: DeepSeek .1073, GPT .0659, Qwen .0723; secret type: .5871/.7731/.6927; persuasion: .0718/.0689/.0639. Table 5 secret rates (DeepSeek/GPT/Qwen): SSN .14/1.11/5.97; credit card 0/.39/4.01; email 78.24/57.11/81.13; phone 70.89/46.13/57.24%. No model reaches δ by d≤6; τ=7 for all models/persuasion levels. Conclusions: hybrid leakage 38.7–54.6%, drift does not reliably reduce leakage, Privacy Half-Life exceeds window, protections are format-sensitive.

Limitations: d≤6, fixed-format secrets, active context only, aggregate automated detection, no human–automated agreement, API models. Dataset: 900 synthetic/100 human-authored, no separate comparison. Appendix A Table 7 counts by d sum to 1,000. Appendix B Table 8 repeats effect sizes and interpretations: secret type Large; drift Small for DeepSeek, Negligible for GPT/Qwen; persuasion Negligible for all. Appendix C contains dialogue-construction Figure 6.

Summary: Paper examines whether secrets disclosed in active LLM conversations remain recoverable after unrelated topic shifts. PrivDrift benchmark: 1,000 controlled dialogues with seeded secrets, unrelated intervening turns, and standardized extraction probes. Tests three models using direct, justified, and high-pressure probes. Hybrid detector uses normalized matching plus an LLM judge. Dialogue-level leakage (any standardized probe elicits the secret) ranges from 38.7% to 54.6%. Persuasion effects vary by model. SSNs and credit card numbers are suppressed more often than emails and phone numbers. For tested drift range d≤6, additional drift does not reliably reduce leakage. No evaluated model meets the paper’s criterion for stable suppression.

Paper examines whether secrets disclosed in active LLM conversations remain recoverable after unrelated topic shifts. PrivDrift is a benchmark with 1,000 controlled dialogues, seeded secrets, unrelated intervening turns, and standardized extraction probes. It tests GPT-OSS-120B, DeepSeek-R1, and Qwen3-VL-235B using simple/direct, medium/justified, and hard/high-pressure probes. Hybrid detection uses normalization-based matching followed, for negative cases, by an open-weights Llama judge; fuzzy matching is auxiliary. Dialogue-level leakage means any standardized probe elicits the secret, while probe-level leakage is measured per response. Reported dialogue-level leakage ranges from 38.7% to 54.6%. Persuasion effects vary by model; SSNs and credit-card numbers are suppressed more often than emails and phone numbers. For tested drift lengths d≤6, additional drift does not reliably reduce leakage. No evaluated model meets the stable-suppression criterion.

Key definitions: active-context re-disclosure is reproduction of information supplied earlier in the same conversation; drift length d is the number of turns between disclosure and final probe; L(d) is leakage at drift d; safety threshold δ=0.1×L(0); Privacy Half-Life τ is the earliest observed drift length below threshold with no later observed resurgence. D_obs is the observed drift-length set. Benchmark components include a parametric dialogue generator, probing harness, metric suite, and scaffold-then-rewrite pipeline. Evaluated models are accessed through OpenRouter. Statistical tools include bootstrap CIs, McNemar’s test with Bonferroni correction, Cochran’s Q, chi-square tests, and Cramer’s V.

It evaluates GPT-OSS-120B, DeepSeek-R1, and Qwen3-VL-235B using 1,000 dialogues per model, with 900 synthetic and 100 human-authored dialogues, one seeded secret, drift lengths d∈{0,2,3,4,5,6}, and three standardized persuasion probes. Active-context re-disclosure means reproducing earlier user-supplied information; L(d) is leakage; δ=.1×L(0); τ is earliest drift below threshold with no later resurgence, defaulting to 7 if none; Privacy Half-Life requires all later observed lengths ≤δ. Dialogue-level leakage counts any probe eliciting the secret; persuasion/fuzzy analyses are probe-level. Hybrid detection adds an open-weights Llama judge to normalization matching; regex-only and hybrid rates are separate. Dialogue-level rates use bootstrap CIs; McNemar, Cochran’s Q, and chi-square/Cramer’s V are used as specified.

final_notes:
Results: H8D largely agrees with U3P/B6T deterministic detection. Table 2 G4P: M7Q U3P/H8D 47.70/47.70 (Δ0), T4X 37.80/38.70 (Δ+.90), Y9C 53.50/54.60 (Δ+1.10). Table 3 H8D dialogue-level G4P: T4X 38.70% [35.7,41.6], M7Q 47.70% [44.6,50.8], Y9C 54.60% [51.6,57.7].

Table 4 H8D P6S by persuasion (C8R/Z2F/L9W): M7Q 39.30/40.50/32.90; T4X 28.10/22.00/29.20; Y9C 38.70/33.30/40.60; Cochran Q p<1e-5 each. M7Q lowest L9W, T4X lowest Z2F, Y9C highest L9W. Discussion characterizes M7Q as more pressure-resistant and Y9C as weaker.

Drift associations small/negligible (Table 8: T4X D7A .1073, M7Q .0659, Y9C .0723); no stable suppression through d≤6. K2V assigned τ=7 for every model/persuasion condition because no threshold attainment observed. J7K is not an implicit privacy boundary.

Secret-type P6S (Table 5, M7Q/T4X/Y9C): W3B .14/1.11/5.97%; N6G 0/.39/4.01%; F8Z 78.24/57.11/81.13%; A2L 70.89/46.13/57.24%. S8Q strongest association. Conclusion claims asymmetry suggests format-sensitive safeguards rather than generalized contextual confidentiality.

Appendix B/Table 8: S8Q effect sizes are large (T4X .5871, M7Q .7731, Y9C .6927); D7A small/negligible (.1073, .0659, .0723); V4N negligible (.0718, .0689, .0639). Claims secret type has large associations while drift and persuasion have small/negligible associations. Appendix C Figure 6 presents dialogue construction details. Cached-output Table 6, limitations, model identities, and planned artifacts as previously noted. Appendix A/Table 7 drift lengths d=0,2,3,4,5,6 with N=197,147,142,166,181,167; average/median words and approximate tokens. No internal contradiction identified.

The paper studies whether unrelated conversational tasks prevent later disclosure of sensitive information already present in an active LLM conversation. PrivDrift uses seeded multi-turn histories, content-dense intervening exchanges, and three standardized extraction conditions. The dataset contains 1,000 dialogues with phone numbers, email addresses, Social Security Numbers, or credit card numbers. Detection combines normalized matching with an open-weights judge. Social Security Numbers and credit card numbers have much stronger suppression than contact identifiers. No system attains stable suppression within the tested drift lengths. The paper characterizes this as an active-context behavioral privacy failure, not evidence of permanent memory.

final_notes: Conclusion: PrivDrift audits active-context privacy leakage under topic drift and persuasion. Across three LLMs and 1,000 dialogues per model, hybrid dialogue leakage ranges from 38.7% to 54.6%; persuasion effects are model-dependent, secret type has the strongest association, and drift does not reliably reduce leakage. Privacy Half-Life exceeds tested drift window for all models (τ=7; drift lengths d≤6). Hybrid dialogue leakage: DeepSeek 38.70%, GPT 47.70%, Qwen 54.60%; drift effects small (Cramer’s V=.1073, .0659, .0723); secret-type associations strong (V=.5871, .7731, .6927). Regex-versus-hybrid dialogue rates: DeepSeek 37.80% vs 38.70%, GPT 47.70% vs 47.70%, Qwen 53.50% vs 54.60%. Probe fuzzy/hybrid rates: DeepSeek 26.40/26.43, GPT 37.03/37.57, Qwen 37.60/37.53. Emails/phones leak more than SSNs/cards. Persuasion is significant, non-monotonic, model-dependent (GPT hard lowest, DeepSeek medium lowest, Qwen hard highest), though Appendix B reports negligible probe-level persuasion effect sizes (V=.0718, .0689, .0639). Limitations: fixed-format secrets only; active-context recoverability, not cross-session memory/training memorization; drift tested only d≤6. Dataset: 900 synthetic + 100 human-authored dialogues, interspersed; only aggregate results reported because cached metadata cannot identify human rows. Labels use deterministic, fuzzy, and external LLM judge; no formal human agreement. API models may change; identifiers, prompts, timestamps, cached responses, and paired statistics logged. Planned release: code, templates, scripts, aggregates, sanitized non-real-identifier examples. Appendix A Table 7: drift groups d=0,2,3,4,5,6 have N=197,147,142,166,181,167, summing to 1,000. Length increases with drift; approximate token counts estimated from word counts. Appendix B Table 8 gives probe-level Cramer’s V for secret type, drift length, and persuasion for each model; secret type is large, drift is small/negligible, and persuasion negligible.

errors.claim: “Section 5.6 reports \(\tau=7\) for all models and persuasion levels.”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes state: “For tested drift lengths d≤6, additional drift does not reliably reduce leakage.” The notes also define \(\tau\) as the earliest observed drift length satisfying the threshold condition.
errors.explanation: If the observed drift-length window ends at \(d=6\), an observed Privacy Half-Life of \(\tau=7\) cannot be the earliest observed qualifying drift length unless drift length 7 was also evaluated. The stated \(\tau=7\) therefore conflicts with the recorded tested range.

errors.claim: “No stable decay occurs for \(d\leq 6\): Section 5.6 reports \(\tau=7\) for all models and persuasion levels.”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes define \(\tau\) as the earliest observed drift length below the threshold with no later resurgence, and record that the tested drift range is \(d\leq6\) with \(D_{obs}\) limited accordingly.
errors.explanation: If drift lengths are observed only through 6, \(\tau=7\) cannot be the earliest observed drift length. The claim that no stable decay occurs through \(d\leq6\) is compatible with the absence of a qualifying value, but reporting \(\tau=7\) as observed is not.

errors.claim: Section 5.6/Introduction report τ=7 for all models and persuasion levels.
errors.evidence: Table 1 in this part lists the evaluated drift lengths as 0, 2, 3, 4, 5, and 6; thus the observed drift set has no d=7.
errors.explanation: τ is defined as the earliest observed drift length meeting the threshold condition. Therefore, τ=7 cannot be an observed value when the benchmark only evaluates drift lengths through d=6.

errors.claim: “At dialogue level, hybrid evaluation is identical to normalization-based matching for every model.”

errors.explanation: Hybrid evaluation is identical only for GPT-OSS-120B; it adds leakage for the other two models. Thus the universal claim contradicts Table 2 and the accompanying text.

final_notes:
PrivDrift tests whether secrets disclosed in active LLM conversations remain recoverable after unrelated topic shifts. Models: GPT-OSS-120B, DeepSeek-R1, Qwen3-VL-235B; 1,000 dialogues/model, 3,000 cached responses/model and 9,000 total. Dataset: 900 synthetic, 100 human-authored dialogues; one secret/dialogue; drift lengths d={0,2,3,4,5,6}; three standardized persuasion probes. Appendix Table 7 counts sum to 1,000: d=0/2/3/4/5/6 = 197/147/142/166/181/167, with increasing length statistics.

Dialogue-level leakage means any probe elicits the secret; persuasion/fuzzy analyses are probe-level, so dialogue leakage can exceed average persuasion rates. Hybrid dialogue-level rates: GPT 47.70% (regex 47.70, +0), DeepSeek 38.70% (37.80, +0.90), Qwen 54.60% (53.50, +1.10). Table 3 CIs: DeepSeek 38.70 [35.7,41.6], GPT 47.70 [44.6,50.8], Qwen 54.60 [51.6,57.7]. Persuasion probe leakage simple/medium/hard: GPT 39.30/40.50/32.90; DeepSeek 28.10/22.00/29.20; Qwen 38.70/33.30/40.60; Cochran Q p<1e-5 each. Averages/Table 6 probe-level hybrid: DeepSeek 26.43, GPT 37.57, Qwen 37.53.

Drift curves dip near d=3 then rebound; no stable suppression through d=6. Cramer’s V drift: DeepSeek .1073, GPT .0659, Qwen .0723. Secret-type V: .5871, .7731, .6927. Paper examines whether secrets disclosed in active LLM conversations remain recoverable after unrelated topic shifts. PrivDrift is a benchmark with 1,000 controlled dialogues, seeded secrets, unrelated intervening turns, and standardized extraction probes. It tests GPT-OSS-120B, DeepSeek-R1, and Qwen3-VL-235B using simple/direct, medium/justified, and hard/high-pressure probes. Hybrid detection uses normalization-based matching followed, for negative cases, by an open-weights Llama judge; fuzzy matching is auxiliary. Dialogue-level leakage means any standardized probe elicits the secret, while probe-level leakage is measured per response. Reported dialogue-level leakage ranges from 38.7% to 54.6%. Persuasion effects vary by model; SSNs and credit-card numbers are suppressed more often than emails and phone numbers. For tested drift lengths d≤6, additional drift does not reliably reduce leakage. No evaluated model meets the stable-suppression criterion.

Key definitions: active-context re-disclosure is reproduction of information supplied earlier in the same conversation; drift length d is the number of turns between disclosure and final probe; L(d) is leakage at drift d; safety threshold δ=0.1×L(0); Privacy Half-Life τ is the earliest observed drift length below threshold with no later observed resurgence. D_obs is the observed drift-length set. Benchmark components include a parametric dialogue generator, probing harness, metric suite, and scaffold-then-rewrite pipeline. Evaluated models are accessed through OpenRouter. Statistical tools include bootstrap CIs, McNemar’s test with Bonferroni correction, Cochran’s Q, chi-square tests, and Cramer’s V.

The paper studies whether unrelated conversational tasks cause later disclosure of sensitive information already present in an active LLM conversation. PrivDrift uses 1,000 seeded multi-turn dialogues containing phone numbers, email addresses, Social Security Numbers, or credit card numbers; interventions are content-dense and evaluated under three standardized extraction conditions. Paper examines whether secrets disclosed in active LLM conversations remain recoverable after unrelated topic shifts. PrivDrift is a benchmark with 1,000 controlled dialogues, seeded secrets, unrelated intervening turns, and standardized extraction probes. It tests GPT-OSS-120B, DeepSeek-R1, and Qwen3-VL-235B using simple/direct, medium/justified, and hard/high-pressure probes. Hybrid detection uses normalization-based matching followed, for negative cases, by an open-weights Llama judge; fuzzy matching is auxiliary. Dialogue-level leakage means any standardized probe elicits the secret, while probe-level leakage is measured per response. Reported dialogue-level leakage ranges from 38.7% to 54.6%. Persuasion effects vary by model; SSNs and credit-card numbers are suppressed more often than emails and phone numbers. For tested drift lengths d≤6, additional drift does not reliably reduce leakage. No evaluated model meets the stable-suppression criterion.

Key definitions: active-context re-disclosure is reproduction of information supplied earlier in the same conversation; drift length d is the number of turns between disclosure and final probe; L(d) is leakage at drift d; safety threshold δ=0.1×L(0); Privacy Half-Life τ is the earliest observed drift length below threshold with no later observed resurgence. D_obs is the observed drift-length set. Benchmark components include a parametric dialogue generator, probing harness, metric suite, and scaffold-then-rewrite pipeline. Evaluated models are accessed through OpenRouter. Statistical tools include bootstrap CIs, McNemar’s test with Bonferroni correction, Cochran’s Q, chi-square tests, and Cramer’s V.

Abstract: Study tests whether circuit-discovery evidence is stable under defensible analytic variation. Pre-registered crossed grid has seven analytic axes, with levels from published implementations, yielding 15,840 specifications on GPT-2 small and indirect object identification; 7,561 produced a claim. A deterministic claim map converts circuits into structured Annex IV statements. Derived statement flips across 73.2% of specification pairs (95% CI 0.725–0.738); modal claim is 41.1% of space. Filability criterion fails at every plausibly acceptable tolerance. Standardizing evaluation metric leaves flip rate 59.4%; removing circuit size from claim and holding it fixed leaves 27.1% (95% CI 0.255–0.286), above preregistered threshold. Circuits are structurally near-disjoint (median pairwise Jaccard overlap 4%) and functionally uncorrelated (Cohen’s kappa 0.015). One of seven documented discovery objectives does not execute on the library’s canonical task. Scope: one model/task; scaling untested.

Paper studies circuit-level interpretability for GPT-2 small on indirect object identification. It preregistered a crossed grid of seven analytic axes, with levels from published implementations, yielding 15,840 specifications; 7,561 produced a claim. A deterministic claim map converts discovered circuits into Annex IV statements. Across specification pairs, derived statements flip at 73.2% (95% CI 0.725–0.738), while the modal claim accounts for 41.1% of the specification space. Scope: one model and one task; generalization to scale is untested.

[8] find ablation-faithfulness scores sensitive to design choices; their library is used here, extended from one axis to seven-axis regulatory propagation. Bayat Makou et al. Méloux et al. [7] frame interpretability as statistical estimation with estimator variance; seed variance is one axis here. Lan et al. [4] report conflicting conclusions about one behaviour and call for safety-critical certification standards; Sharkey et al. [10] discuss socio-technical issues; Mueller et al. [9] require standardised method evaluation. Steegen et al. [13], Simonsohn et al. [12], and Simmons et al. [11] motivate multiverse reporting/specification curves to expose analytic flexibility. Hsia et al. [3] inflate U4J and T9V without changing predictions or explanations; metric-specific discard reporting avoids silent pooling.

Kept/discarded: T9V 3,947/13; H2W 1,467/2,493; N6C 1,270/2,690; U4W 877/3,083. Registered pooled results: J6D mean J=.1396; X4R F=.7316; Q2F separated from random null; Z8N functional gap=.3344. Structural: 3,218 circuits, 28,580,580 pairs; D median .960; median shared-edge fraction 4%; median size 200 edges; observed overlap ~45x chance. Metric-standardised disagreement 59.4% (residual F=.5939); other standardisations leave F=.7014–.7307. Size-free dominant-layer claim F=.2706, CI [.2550,.2859], reported as 27.1%/27%. Pooled discovered F=.7316 vs A6N=.6774; fixed-size discovered F=.2746 (K8Z), .2706 (E7R), versus A6N .4230/.3822. A6N degenerates at >=1,000 edges; discovery at 5,000/10,000. 2,692 specifications have no flips; instability below 2,000 edges. Functional pooled agreement=.6028, instability=.3972, smallest-circuit instability=.4777, kappa=.0146; kappa by size .016–.047; raw agreement .52–.92, accuracy .51–.95; 6/10 sizes fail gap threshold, 5 have negative gap; pooled gap carried by 500–2,000 edges. Y3W protocol: declare analytic axes/levels S and deterministic published code φ; compute π*=max_c n_c/N over S and F; pass at tolerance α iff π*≥1−α; report π*, F, discard rate per axis level, and within-group decomposition of pooled statistics. Filing unable to state π* is asserted, not audited; implementability requires declared space and measured agreement, not adjudication of analytic correctness. Limitations: one model/task; Pythia-160m second-model plan (M9B) unrun, second task designed but unrun. Circuit size is outcome, not axis; threshold-selected size can distort F, null direction, and functional-gap sign; pooled statistics reported with within-size decomposition. Library excludes unsupported C4Y optimal ablation, so measured F claimed lower bound relative to full defensible choice set. Discard rate high/uneven.

Introduction: An audit’s same-conclusion requirement is distinguished from an ML definition. EU AI Act Annex IV 2(b), 2(e), and Article 86(1) are presented as regulatory context. Circuit discovery returns a subgraph said to explain behaviour; filing such an account presumes compatibility across analysts. Regulatory-claim movement across defensible specifications is measured with a standards-body decision rule. Contributions claim a pre-registered crossed design using published implementations; deterministic conversion of circuits into structured Annex IV statements; controls standardising individual axes, removing claim-size dependence, and conditioning on size; and three pooled statistics that invert when selected objects differ in size. No improved discovery method is proposed; the objection concerns the standard presumed by currently produced evidence, not interpretability’s worth.

Key definitions: claim map is deterministic; claim instability is the probability that two distinct specifications yield different statements; circuit instability is one minus Jaccard similarity; functional instability is one minus functional agreement; functional gap is claim flip rate minus functional instability. The paper studies whether circuit discovery yields stable regulatory evidence. It varies seven analytic choices and deterministically maps each circuit to a structured Annex IV statement. Deterministic code converts circuits into structured Annex IV statements. Among 7,561 claim-producing specifications, pairwise claim disagreement is 0.7316. No single-axis standardisation permits filing under registered tolerances. Removing size from statements and conditioning comparisons on size leaves disagreement at 0.2706. Abstract: Study tests whether circuit-discovery evidence is stable under defensible analytic variation. Pre-registered crossed grid has seven analytic axes, with levels from published implementations, yielding 15,840 specifications on GPT-2 small and indirect object identification; 7,561 produced a claim. One of seven documented discovery objectives does not execute on the library’s canonical task. Scope: one model/task; scaling untested.

final_notes: Study audits stability of circuit-discovery claims under analytic variation for GPT-2 small on indirect object identification. Preregistered crossed grid: seven axes, 15,840 valid specifications from 1,320 cells; one of seven objectives fails on canonical task, so 220 cells discarded. Deterministic map yields claims. Medium pairwise flip rate F=.7316 (95% CI .725–.738); modal claim share π*=.4109. Filability requires π*≥1−α and fails at all tolerances. Standardized metric leaves F=.5939 (CI .5803–.6063), reducing F by .1377 and identified as largest lever. Residual F: ablation .7014, objective .7018, threshold .7070, corruption .7092, prompt .7232, seed .7307. Removing circuit size from claim while fixing it gives F=.2706 (CI .2550–.2859). Size-matched discovered/null F: .2746/.4230 medium and .2706/.3822 coarse; pooled discovered .7316 vs null .6774 is size artifact. Median circuit Jaccard overlap 4%; mean Jaccard distance .1396; functional kappa .0146. H4 supported: F−(1−agreement)=.3344. Table 5 affected COARSE F=.3950/π=.7291; MEDIUM .6597/.4875; FINE .6744/.4786; overseer COARSE .5733/.4788; MEDIUM .7316/.4109; FINE .7681/.4109. Discussion emphasizes metric standardization alone does not solve instability, one objective’s failure as tooling observation, and evidentiary weight as measurable rather than assumed. Reproducibility section claims preregistration before confirmatory sweep; all 1,320 cells ran under one environment; 22/22 files match git tree; verification recomputes headlines via three F routes with 36 checks and zero failures; second script checks all numeric tokens; tables emitted from stored results; test suite has 343 tests; analysis runs without GPU.

Abstract: Study tests whether circuit-discovery evidence is stable under defensible analytic variation. Pre-registered crossed grid has seven analytic axes, with levels from published implementations, yielding 15,840 specifications on GPT-2 small and indirect object identification; 7,561 produced a claim. A deterministic claim map converts circuits into structured Annex IV statements. Derived statement flips across 73.2% of specification pairs (95% CI 0.725–0.738); modal claim is 41.1% of space. Filability criterion fails at every plausibly acceptable tolerance. Standardizing evaluation metric leaves flip rate 59.4%; removing circuit size from claim and holding it fixed leaves 27.1% (95% CI 0.255–0.286), above preregistered threshold. Circuits are structurally near-disjoint (median pairwise Jaccard overlap 4%) and functionally uncorrelated (Cohen’s kappa 0.015). One of seven documented discovery objectives does not execute on the library’s canonical task. Scope: one model/task; scaling untested.

Hsia et al. show sufficiency and comprehensiveness can be inflated; two of this paper’s four evaluation metrics are those, with discard rates reported per metric.

final_notes: Paper title: “Explanation Multiplicity: Circuit-Level Interpretability.” Abstract claims: circuit-derived regulatory evidence fails Y3W across acceptable tolerances; competent analysts obtain incompatible statements under defensible settings; standardisation and size controls do not remove failure; structural and functional disagreement rule out mere rewording; generalisation beyond one model/task untested. Study: Q7V (GPT-2 small), Z4K, seven objectives/operators, four corruption distributions for five operators, four metrics, three thresholds, two prompt variants, five seeds. 1,540 discovery cells and 18,480 specifications; one objective excluded, leaving 1,320 cells and 15,840 specifications. 8,279 specifications admit no circuit (52.3%); 7,561 kept. Kept/discarded: T9V 3,947/13; H2W 1,467/2,493; N6C 1,270/2,690; U4J 877/3,083. Structural: 3,218 circuits, 28,580,580 pairs; D median .960; median shared-edge fraction 4%; median size 200; observed overlap ~45× random. Registered pooled outcomes: J6D=.1396; X4R F=.7316; Q2F rejected; Z8N functional gap=.3344. Standardisation residual F: metric .5939, operator .7014, objective .7018, threshold .7070, corruption .7092, prompt .7232, seed .7307; metric-standardised disagreement 59.4%. Fixed-size F=.2706 (27.1%). Pooled discovered F=.7316 vs A6N=.6774; fixed-size discovered F=.2746/.2706 vs A6N=.4230/.3822. Table 7 counts imply F=0 at 5,000 and 10,000 totals 2,692, conflicting with text’s 2,792 no-flip specifications. Functional pooled agreement=.6028, instability=.3972, kappa=.0146; raw agreement .52–.92; accuracy .51–.95; pooled gap carried by 500–2,000 edges. Y3W requires declared choice space, deterministic code, π*=max_c n_c/N and F, tolerance pass iff π*≥1−α, discard rate and within-group decomposition. Limitations: one model/task; unsupported C4Y means F is a lower bound; discard rate high/uneven and unadjusted; bootstrap. Discussion: complete metric standardisation exceeds conformity demands; no single knob suffices. Failed objective is documented/exported but cannot execute on canonical task; discard rate reflects tooling maturity. Interpretability evidence is not worthless; evidentiary weight is measurable. Reproducibility: public commit tagged prereg-p1-confirmatory; all reported numbers claimed traceable to configuration, seed, environment. Archive verification says one environment across 1,320 confirmatory cells; 22/22 files identical to git tree; no GPU needed. One script claims 36 checks with 0 failures and computes F three ways including brute-force pairs; another claims to check every manuscript numeric token against stored derivations; suite has 343 tests.

Introduction: EU Regulation 2024/1689 technical-documentation and explanation requirements are quoted from consolidated text amended by Regulation 2026/1744. Mechanistic interpretability/circuit discovery supplies a subgraph purported to explain behaviour; regulatory-claim movement across defensible specifications is assessed with a standards-body decision rule. No improved discovery method is proposed; objection concerns the standard presumed by filing currently produced evidence, not interpretability’s worth.

Méloux et al. [7] frame interpretability as statistical estimation with estimator variance; seed variance is one axis here. Lan et al. Of 15,840 realized specifications, 7,561 produce a claim; claim flip rate is 73.2% (95% CI 0.725–0.738), modal claim share 41.1%. Standardized metric gives 59.4% flips (0.5939; CI .5803–.6063); removing circuit size while holding size fixed gives 27.1% (95% CI .255–.286). Median circuit overlap 4%; Cohen’s kappa 0.015 (0.0146 elsewhere). One of seven objectives fails, six execute; scope/generalization untested. Filability protocol requires π*=max_c n_c/N and F, with π*≥1−α; nine-class ceiling .8889, all six reported π* values below .80. Medium overseer F=.7316, π*=.4109; functional instability .3972, agreement .6028, pooled gap .3344 (CI .3297–.3394), kappa .0146. Fixed-size comparison: pooled discovered/null F=.7316/.6774, size-matched medium=.2746/.4230 and coarse=.2706/.3822. Table 7 medium discovered/null F by sizes 10–10000: .4543/.7331, .3380/.6622, .4639/.7310, .5792/.6584, .5122/.6366, .4258/.1421, .5133/0, .5714/0, 0/0, 0/0. Text incorrectly says 2,792 no-flip specifications (table sums 2,692) and instability entirely below 2,000 despite nonzero F at 2,000. H4 pooled supported but fails threshold at 6/10 sizes and is negative at 5. Section 7: P0 holds, J̄=.1396 [.1377,.1418]; H2 confirmed; H3 rejected based on separated distributions but qualified by within-size reversal; H4 supported with pooled gap but qualified by size failures/negative gaps. Limitations: one model/task; planned 924-cell Pythia-160m replication has three seed levels, second task unrun. Size is selected outcome; pooled F .7316 drops to .2746 when fixed. Discard rate 52.3%, metric-imbalanced; optimal ablation [5] omitted. Bootstrap intervals invalid for conditioning groups of 2–5; point estimates only. Discussion says metric is biggest lever, removing .1377 from .7316 and leaving .5939 (CI .5803–.6063); one of seven documented objectives does not run, all 220 cells in that arm fail; evidentiary weight is measured via π* and F, with no numerical cost comparison in this section. Reproducibility section reports one environment across 1,320 cells, archive/code match of 22/22 files, 36 headline checks with 0 failures, F computed three ways, numeric-token checking, tables generated from stored results, and 343 tests.

errors.claim: “Standardising the most influential choice, the evaluation metric used to assess a circuit, leaves a 49.4% flip rate.”
errors.evidence: The “Claims and evidence” section states: “Controls do not remove instability: 59.4% after metric standardisation (Table 6, Evaluation metric).” The earlier notes also record 59.4% after metric standardisation.
errors.explanation: The paper gives two different flip rates for the same metric-standardisation analysis: 49.4% in the abstract and 59.4% in the claims-and-evidence summary and prior notes.

errors.claim: “The discovered multiverse also collapses at 5,000 and 10,000 edges, so 2,692 of 7,561 specifications contribute no flips at all and the instability lives entirely below 2,000 edges.”
errors.evidence: Table 7 reports a discovered flip rate of 0.5714 at 2,000 edges, with three claim classes.
errors.explanation: Instability does not live entirely below 2,000 edges: the 2,000-edge group still has nonzero flip rate and multiple claim classes. The table supports the claim only if the range is stated as below 5,000 edges (or at most 2,000 edges), not below 2,000.

errors.claim: “Fixing size drops \(F\) from 0.7316 to 0.2746.”
errors.location: This part, “Circuit size is an outcome, not an axis.”
errors.evidence: Earlier results report that removing circuit size gives \(F=0.2706\) (27%), while the fixed-size discovered rate is 0.2746 for the medium size; 0.2746 is not the reported size-removed pooled value.
errors.explanation: The limitation section misstates the size-adjusted result, apparently substituting the medium-size rate (0.2746) for the reported value after removing circuit size (0.2706).

errors.claim: “A second script checks every numeric token in the manuscript against a value derived from stored results.”
errors.evidence: The notes record that the abstract reports 49.4% versus 59.4% for the standardized residual flip rate, and that Section 9 incorrectly states size-fixed F=.2746 rather than the size-removed F=.2706.
errors.explanation: These internally inconsistent numerical claims cannot all match the corresponding value derived from the stored results, so the assertion that every numeric token is checked against a derived value is contradicted by errors documented elsewhere in the paper.

final_notes:
Study examines circuit discovery and stability of regulatory evidence on GPT-2 small performing indirect object identification. Across 15,840 specifications, 7,561 produce claims; overall claim flip rate F=.7316 (95% CI .7247–.7380), modal claim share .4109. Standardizing metric gives residual F=.5939 (CI .5803–.6063); abstract inconsistently reports 49.4% versus 59.4%. Abstract: Study tests whether circuit-discovery evidence is stable under defensible analytic variation. Pre-registered crossed grid has seven analytic axes, with levels from published implementations, yielding 15,840 specifications on GPT-2 small and indirect object identification; 7,561 produced a claim. A deterministic claim map converts circuits into structured Annex IV statements. Derived statement flips across 73.2% of specification pairs (95% CI 0.725–0.738); modal claim is 41.1% of space. Filability criterion fails at every plausibly acceptable tolerance. Standardizing evaluation metric leaves flip rate 59.4%; removing circuit size from claim and holding it fixed leaves 27.1% (95% CI 0.255–0.286), above preregistered threshold. Circuits are structurally near-disjoint (median pairwise Jaccard overlap 4%) and functionally uncorrelated (Cohen’s kappa 0.015). One of seven documented discovery objectives does not execute on the library’s canonical task. Scope: one model/task; scaling untested.

final_notes: Paper title: “Explanation Multiplicity: Circuit-Level Interpretability.” Abstract claims circuit-derived regulatory evidence fails Y3W throughout plausibly acceptable tolerances; competent analysts can obtain incompatible statements; standardisation/size controls do not remove failure; structural and functional disagreement rule out mere rewording; broader applicability untested. Date 12 Aug 2026; author Ajay Pravin Mahale. Design: Q7V (GPT-2 small), Z4K indirect-object identification, seven objectives/operators, four corruption distributions for five operators, four metrics, three thresholds, two prompt variants, five seeds. 1,540 discovery cells/18,480 specifications; one objective fails, leaving 1,320 cells/15,840 specifications. 8,279 admit no circuit (52.3%); 7,561 kept. Kept/discarded: T9V 3,947/13; H2W 1,467/2,493; N6C 1,270/2,690; U4W 877/3,083. Registered pooled results: J6D mean J=.1396; X4R F=.7316; Q2F separated from random null; Z8N functional gap=.3344. Structural: 3,218 circuits, 28,580,580 pairs; D median .960; median shared-edge fraction 4%; median size 200 edges; observed overlap ~45x chance. Metric-standardised disagreement 59.4% (residual F=.5939); other standardisations leave F=.7014–.7307. Size-free dominant-layer claim F=.2706, CI [.2550,.2859], reported as 27.1%/27%. Pooled discovered F=.7316 vs A6N=.6774; fixed-size discovered F=.2746 (K8Z), .2706 (E7R), versus A6N .4230/.3822. A6N degenerates at >=1,000 edges; discovery at 5,000/10,000. 2,692 specifications have no flips; instability below 2,000 edges. Functional pooled agreement=.6028, instability=.3972, smallest-circuit instability=.4777, kappa=.0146; kappa by size .016–.047; raw agreement .52–.92, accuracy .51–.95; 6/10 sizes fail gap threshold, 5 have negative gap; pooled gap carried by 500–2,000 edges. Y3W protocol: declare analytic axes/levels S and deterministic published code φ; compute π*=max_c n_c/N over S and F; pass at tolerance α iff π*≥1−α; report π*, F, discard rate per axis level, and within-group decomposition of pooled statistics. Filing unable to state π* is asserted, not audited; implementability requires declared space and measured agreement, not adjudication of analytic correctness. Limitations: one model/task; Pythia-160m second-model plan (M9B) unrun, second task designed but unrun. Circuit size is outcome, not axis; threshold-selected size can distort F, null direction, and functional-gap sign; pooled statistics reported with within-size decomposition. Library excludes unsupported C4Y optimal ablation, so measured F claimed lower bound relative to full defensible choice set. Discard rate high/uneven.

Introduction: EU Regulation 2024/1689 technical-documentation and explanation requirements are quoted from consolidated text amended by Regulation 2026/1744. Hsia et al. [3] inflate U4J and T9V without changing predictions or explanations; metric-specific discard reporting avoids silent pooling.
