final_notes: Study examines circuit discovery and stability of regulatory evidence, varying analytic choices and deterministically mapping circuits to Annex IV statements. Of 15,840 realized specifications, 7,561 produce a claim; claim flip rate is 73.2% (95% CI 0.725–0.738), modal claim share 41.1%. Standardized metric gives 59.4% flips; removing circuit size while holding size fixed gives 27.1% (95% CI 0.255–0.286). Median circuit overlap 4%; Cohen’s kappa 0.015 (0.0146 elsewhere). One of seven documented objectives fails, six execute; scope/generalization untested. Discovered circuits more stable than fixed-size random null (.2746 vs .4230); pooled functional instability .3972. Table 5: affected COARSE F=.3950, π*=.7291; affected MEDIUM/FINE F=.6597/.6744; overseer COARSE/MEDIUM/FINE F=.5733/.7316/.7681. All π* below .80. Axis-standardized residual F: metric .5939, ablation .7014, objective .7018, threshold .7070, corruption .7092, prompt .7232, seed .7307. Structural variance: ablation-corruption interaction 78.8%, residual 11.5%, ablation 4.4%, threshold 4.1%, metric 0.7%. Size-held-fixed medium F=.2746; pooled discovered F=.7316 versus size-matched random null .6774; H3 rejected with qualifications. Table 7 medium discovered/null F: size 10 .4543/.7331; 20 .3380/.6622; 50 .4639/.7310; 100 .5792/.6584; 200 .5122/.6366; 500 .4258/.1421; 1,000 .5133/0; 2,000 .5714/0; 5,000 and 10,000 0/0. Limitations include one model/task and unrun replications. Reproducibility section claims one environment across 1,540 cells, but its summary bullet says 1,320 cells; this is an internal inconsistency. It also reports 22/22 files identical, 36 headline checks with 0 failures, three F-computation routes, and 343 tests.

Summary: The study examines circuit discovery and stability of regulatory evidence. It varies seven analytic choices and deterministically maps each circuit to a structured Annex IV statement. Key definitions: claim map is deterministic; claim instability is the probability that two distinct specifications yield different statements; circuit instability is one minus Jaccard similarity; functional instability is one minus functional agreement; functional gap is claim flip rate minus functional instability. Four evaluation metrics are comprehensiveness, KL divergence, logit difference, and sufficiency. Specifications vary objective, ablation operator, corruption distribution, metric, size threshold, prompt variant, seed, and granularity. Bootstrap resamples specifications (not pairs); U-statistics use dependent pairs. H2 requires F>0.20 with CI lower bound above threshold; H3 concerns separation from the random null; H4 requires F−(1−agreement)>0.10. P0 reports mean Jaccard but is not tested. Filability requires modal claim share π*≥1−α.

errors.evidence: The Claims and evidence bullet states: “The sweep used one environment across 1,320 cells, verified from the archive (section text).”

grade.reason: The reviewer flagged the exact sentence about 1,540 cells and noted the paper elsewhere reports 1,320 cells, matching the planted error’s contradiction with Section 6.

errors.claim: “The grid contains seven objectives, seven operators, four corruption distributions nested within the five operators reading them, four metrics, three thresholds, two prompt variants and five seeds: 1,540 discovery cells and 18,480 pre-registered specifications.”
errors.evidence: The listed specification-level factors give 4 metrics × 3 thresholds × 2 prompt variants × 5 seeds = 120 specifications per discovery cell. Thus 1,540 discovery cells imply 184,800 specifications, not 18,480. Likewise, the realised 1,320 cells should imply 158,400 specifications, whereas the table reports 15,840; Table 2 totals 15,840 (3,960 per metric), agreeing with the latter figure but not with the stated factor crossing.
errors.explanation: The specification totals are inconsistent with the explicitly listed crossed factors by a factor of ten.

errors.claim: “Observed/chance overlap | about 45 times”
errors.location: this part, Section 7.1 structural diagnostic table
errors.evidence: The same table reports a median shared-edge fraction of 4% and an analytic random overlap of 0.0031 at the median circuit size.
errors.explanation: Using the table’s reported observed median overlap and random overlap gives approximately 0.04/0.0031 ≈ 13 times, not about 45 times. No other observed-overlap statistic is provided to support the stated 45-fold comparison.

errors.evidence: Table 7 reports a discovered \(F=0.5714\) with 3 classes at exactly 2,000 edges (\(n=312\)).

Abstract: Study tests whether circuit-discovery evidence is stable under defensible analytic variation. Pre-registered crossed grid has seven analytic axes, with levels from published implementations, yielding 15,840 specifications on GPT-2 small and indirect object identification; 7,561 produced a claim. A deterministic claim map converts circuits into structured Annex IV statements. Derived statement flips across 73.2% of specification pairs (95% CI 0.725–0.738); modal claim is 41.1% of space. final_notes: Paper title: “Explanation Multiplicity: Circuit-Level Interpretability.” Abstract claims circuit-derived regulatory evidence fails Y3W throughout plausibly acceptable tolerances; competent analysts can obtain incompatible statements; standardisation/size controls do not remove failure; structural and functional disagreement rule out mere rewording; broader applicability untested. Date 12 Aug 2026; author Ajay Pravin Mahale. Design: Q7V (GPT-2 small), Z4K indirect-object identification, seven objectives/operators, four corruption distributions for five operators, four metrics, three thresholds, two prompt variants, five seeds. 1,540 discovery cells/18,480 specifications; one objective fails, leaving 1,320 cells/15,840 specifications. 8,279 admit no circuit (52.3%); 7,561 kept. Kept/discarded: T9V 3,947/13; H2W 1,467/2,493; N6C 1,270/2,690; U4W 877/3,083. Registered pooled results: J6D mean J=.1396; X4R F=.7316; Q2F separated from random null; Z8N functional gap=.3344. Structural: 3,218 circuits, 28,580,580 pairs; D median .960; median shared-edge fraction 4%; median size 200 edges; observed overlap ~45x chance. Metric-standardised disagreement 59.4% (residual F=.5939); other standardisations leave F=.7014–.7307. Size-free dominant-layer claim F=.2706, CI [.2550,.2859], reported as 27.1%/27%. Pooled discovered F=.7316 vs A6N=.6774; fixed-size discovered F=.2746 (K8Z), .2706 (E7R), versus A6N .4230/.3822. A6N degenerates at >=1,000 edges; discovery at 5,000/10,000. 2,692 specifications have no flips; instability below 2,000 edges. Functional pooled agreement=.6028, instability=.3972, smallest-circuit instability=.4777, kappa=.0146; kappa by size .016–.047; raw agreement .52–.92, accuracy .51–.95; 6/10 sizes fail gap threshold, 5 have negative gap; pooled gap carried by 500–2,000 edges. Y3W protocol: declare analytic axes/levels and deterministic code; compute pi* = max_c n_c/N over S and F; pass iff pi* >= 1-alpha; report pi*, F, discard rate per axis level, and within-group decomposition. Claims E7R D9P filings are more stable than E7R L3X filings, and implementability requires declared space and measured agreement, not regulatory adjudication. Limitations: one model/task; committed but unrun Pythia-160m second-model plan (M9B), 924-cell grid with three rather than five seed levels; second task designed but unrun. Circuit size is an outcome, not an axis; threshold-selected size distorts F, null-comparison direction, and functional-gap sign; conditioning on size reduces instability more than registered-axis standardisation, but pooled results include within-size decomposition. Library omits unsupported optimal-ablation.

final_notes: Study examines circuit discovery and stability of regulatory evidence, varying analytic choices and deterministically mapping circuits to Annex IV statements. Of 15,840 realized specifications, 7,561 produce a claim; claim flip rate is 73.2% (95% CI 0.725–0.738), modal claim share 41.1%. Standardized metric gives 59.4% flips (F=.5939, CI .5803–.6063); removing circuit size while holding size fixed gives F=.2706 (27.1%, CI .255–.286). Median circuit overlap 4%; Cohen’s kappa .015 (.0146 elsewhere). One of seven documented objectives fails, six execute; all 220 cells in that objective arm fail. Scope/generalization untested. Formalism: eight specification dimensions; instability=1−edge-set Jaccard; claim map φ; flip rate pairwise Gini–Simpson; filability requires π*≥1−α, with nine-class ceiling .8889. Discovered circuits more stable than fixed-size random null (.2746 vs .4230); functional instability .3972 pooled, .4777 smallest; kappa indicates functional uncorrelatedness. Table 5: affected COARSE F=.3950, π*=.7291; affected MEDIUM/FINE F=.6597/.6744; overseer COARSE/MEDIUM/FINE F=.5733/.7316/.7681. Dominant overseer-medium claims: early/distributed 3,107 (41.09%), late/sparse 2,153 (28.48%). Layer attribution: early 47.9%, late 43.6%, middle 8.5%. Axis-standardized residual F: metric .5939, ablation .7014, objective .7018, threshold .7070, corruption .7092, prompt .7232, seed .7307. Structural variance: ablation-corruption interaction 78.8%, residual 11.5%, ablation 4.4%, threshold 4.1%, metric 0.7%. H3 rejected; H4 functional agreement .6028, instability .3972, gap .3344, kappa .0146. Limitations: one model/task; planned 924-cell Pythia-160m replication with three seed levels and unrun second task; size is an outcome and fixed-size F=.2706; optimal ablation [5] omitted; discard rate 52.3% and metric-imbalanced; bootstrap intervals invalid for conditioning groups of 2–5, so point estimates reported. Discussion: metric removes .1377 from .7316, leaving .5939 (CI .5803–.6063); one-axis standardization remains insufficient. Evidentiary weight is measured by π* and F; no numerical cost comparison is given. Reproducibility section claims a preregistration, one verified environment across 1,320 cells, 22/22 archive files matching the git tree, 36 headline checks with 0 failures, three independent F computations, numeric-token/table verification, and 343 tests. The 1,320-cell count may refer to cells rather than the 15,840 realized specifications, so no contradiction is established.

On GPT-2 small, indirect object identification: 7,561 of 15,840 specifications produce a claim; claim flip rate is 73.2%; the modal claim covers 41.1% of specifications. Standardizing the evaluation metric gives a 59.4% flip rate. Removing circuit size from the claim and holding size fixed gives 27.1%. Key definitions: claim map is deterministic; claim instability is the probability that two distinct specifications yield different statements; circuit instability is one minus Jaccard similarity; functional instability is one minus functional agreement; functional gap is claim flip rate minus functional instability. Four evaluation metrics are comprehensiveness, KL divergence, logit difference, and sufficiency. Specifications vary objective, ablation operator, corruption distribution, metric, size threshold, prompt variant, seed, and granularity. Bootstrap resamples specifications (not pairs); U-statistics use dependent pairs. H2 requires F>0.20 with CI lower bound above threshold; H3 concerns separation from the random null; H4 requires F−(1−agreement)>0.10. P0 reports mean Jaccard but is not tested. Filability requires modal claim share π*≥1−α.

Abstract: Study tests whether circuit-discovery evidence is stable under defensible analytic variation. Pre-registered crossed grid has seven analytic axes, with levels from published implementations, yielding 15,840 specifications on GPT-2 small and indirect object identification; 7,561 produced a claim. A deterministic claim map converts circuits into structured Annex IV statements. Derived statement flips across 73.2% of specification pairs (95% CI 0.725–0.738); modal claim is 41.1% of space. Filability criterion fails at every plausibly acceptable tolerance. Standardizing evaluation metric leaves flip rate 59.4%; removing circuit size from claim and holding it fixed leaves 27.1% (95% CI 0.255–0.286), above preregistered threshold. Circuits are structurally near-disjoint (median pairwise Jaccard overlap 4%) and functionally uncorrelated (Cohen’s kappa 0.015). One of seven documented discovery objectives does not execute on the library’s canonical task. Scope: one model/task; scaling untested.

Paper title: “Explanation Multiplicity: Circuit-Level Interpretability.” Abstract claims: (1) circuit-derived regulatory evidence fails Y3W throughout tolerances plausibly acceptable to a conformity-assessment body; (2) competent analysts with the same system and tool obtain incompatible statements under different defensible settings; (3) standardisation and size controls do not remove the failure; (4) structural and functional disagreement rule out merely reworded mechanisms; (5) applicability beyond one model and task remains untested. Date: 12 August 2026. Author: Ajay Pravin Mahale.

Introduction: EU Regulation 2024/1689 technical-documentation and explanation requirements are quoted from consolidated text amended by Regulation 2026/1744. Mechanistic interpretability/circuit discovery supplies a subgraph purported to explain behaviour; regulatory-claim movement across defensible specifications is assessed with a standards-body decision rule. Contributions: preregistered crossed design using published implementations; circuits deterministically converted into structured Annex IV statements; controls standardise individual axes, remove claim-size dependence, and condition on size. Three pooled statistics invert when selected objects differ in size. No improved discovery method is proposed; objection concerns the standard presumed by filing currently produced evidence, not interpretability’s worth.

Related work: Méloux et al. [6] argue explanations need not be unique under mechanistic-interpretability criteria. Miller et al. [8] find ablation-faithfulness scores sensitive to design choices; their library is used here, extended from one axis to seven-axis regulatory propagation. Bayat Makou et al. [1] find structurally distinct circuits can implement the same computation under fixed task and varied input statistics (W5T phantom specialisation); this motivates functional measurement. Méloux et al. [7] frame interpretability as statistical estimation with estimator variance; seed variance is one axis here. Lan et al. [4] report conflicting conclusions about one behaviour and call for safety-critical certification standards; Sharkey et al. [10] discuss socio-technical issues; Mueller et al. [9] require standardised method evaluation. Steegen et al. [13], Simonsohn et al. [12], and Simmons et al. [11] motivate multiverse reporting/specification curves to expose analytic flexibility. Hsia et al. [3] inflate U4J and T9V without changing predictions or explanations; metric-specific discard reporting avoids silent pooling.

Section 9 says size conditioning leaves lower instability than evaluation-metric standardisation (size-conditioned F=.2706 vs metric-row residual F=.5939), despite wording elsewhere that suggests the reverse. Deterministic map converts circuits into structured Annex IV statements. Derived statement flips across 73.2% of specification pairs (95% CI 0.725–0.738); modal claim is 41.1% of space. Filability criterion is π* ≥ 1−α and fails at every plausibly acceptable tolerance. Standardizing evaluation metric leaves flip rate 59.4%; removing circuit size from claim and holding it fixed leaves 27.1% (95% CI 0.255–0.286), above preregistered threshold. Circuits are structurally near-disjoint (median pairwise Jaccard overlap 4%) and functionally uncorrelated (Cohen’s kappa 0.015; this part reports 0.0146). One of seven documented discovery objectives does not execute on the library’s canonical task. Scope is one model/task; scaling untested. Introduction frames audit as requiring two auditors to reach same conclusion; cites EU AI Act Annex IV 2(b), 2(e), Article 86(1). Contributions: seven-axis multiverse and deterministic Annex IV map; filability criterion and canonical-task measurement; instability surviving standardizing one axis, removing circuit size from claim, and holding size fixed; pooled-statistics inversion when specifications select objects of different sizes, with three examples. Related work: Méloux et al. discuss non-identifiability; this paper measures its cost when explanations are filed. Miller et al. find faithfulness metrics sensitive to design choices; this study crosses seven axes and uses their released library. Bayat Makou et al. find structurally distinct circuits can implement the same computation; this paper addresses the objection via functional measurement in Section 7.6 and reports circuits are not functionally interchangeable. Méloux et al. frame mechanistic interpretability as statistical estimation; seed variance is one axis. Lan et al. call for auditing standards; this paper offers measurement and criterion. Hsia et al. show sufficiency and comprehensiveness can be inflated; two of this paper’s four evaluation metrics are those, with discard rates reported per metric. Section 3 clarifies non-claims: discovered circuits are better than size-matched random null

final_notes: Paper title: “Explanation Multiplicity: Circuit-Level Interpretability.” Abstract claims: circuit-derived regulatory evidence fails Y3W throughout plausibly acceptable tolerances; competent analysts can obtain incompatible statements; standardisation/size controls do not remove failure; structural and functional disagreement rule out mere rewording; broader applicability untested. Date 12 Aug 2026; author Ajay Pravin Mahale. Design: Q7V (GPT-2 small), Z4K indirect-object identification, seven objectives/operators, four corruption distributions for five operators, four metrics, three thresholds, two prompt variants, five seeds. 1,540 discovery cells/18,480 specifications; one objective fails, leaving 1,320 cells/15,840 specifications. 8,279 admit no circuit (52.3%); 7,561 kept. Kept/discarded: T9V 3,947/13; H2W 1,467/2,493; N6C 1,270/2,690; U4W 877/3,083. Registered pooled results: J6D mean J=.1396; X4R F=.7316; Q2F separated from random null; Z8N functional gap=.3344. Structural: 3,218 circuits, 28,580,580 pairs; D median .960; median shared-edge fraction 4%; median size 200 edges; observed overlap ~45x chance. Metric-standardised disagreement F=.5939; other standardisations F=.7014–.7307. Size-free dominant-layer F=.2706, CI [.2550,.2859]. Pooled discovered F=.7316 vs A6N=.6774; fixed-size discovered F=.2746/.2706 vs A6N .4230/.3822. A6N degenerates at >=1,000 edges; discovery at 5,000/10,000. 2,692 specifications have no flips; instability below 2,000 edges. Functional pooled agreement=.6028, instability=.3972, smallest-circuit instability=.4777, kappa=.0146; kappa by size .016–.047; raw agreement .52–.92, accuracy .51–.95; 6/10 sizes fail gap threshold, 5 negative; pooled gap carried by 500–2,000 edges. Section 8 defines Y3W: analytic axes/levels S and deterministic code phi; pi*=max_c n_c/N over S and F; pass iff pi* >= 1-alpha; report pi*, F, discard rates, within-group decomposition. Claims filings unable to state pi* are asserted, not audited. Section 8 claims all high-risk AI systems fail Y3W, conflicting with abstract’s broader-applicability-untested claim. Limitations: one model/task; second-model Pythia-160m plan and second task unrun. Size is an outcome, not an axis; threshold selection distorts F/null direction/functional-gap sign, and pooled statistics are reported with within-size decomposition. Library narrower than literature: optimal ablation C4Y excluded, so F is a lower bound relative to full defensible choice set. Discard rate high/uneven and not adjusted. Bootstrap invalid for one family with 2–5-specification groups; intervals replaced by point estimates; no post hoc bias.

final_notes: Study examines circuit discovery and stability of regulatory evidence, varying analytic choices and deterministically mapping circuits to Annex IV statements. Of 15,840 realized specifications, 7,561 produce a claim; claim flip rate is 73.2% (95% CI 0.725–0.738), modal claim share 41.1%. Standardized metric gives 59.4% flips; removing circuit size while holding size fixed gives 27.1% (F=.2706, CI .2550–.2859). Median circuit overlap 4%; Cohen’s kappa .015 (.0146 elsewhere). Filability requires π*≥1−α, with nine-class ceiling .8889. Discovered circuits more stable than fixed-size random null (.2746 vs .4230); functional instability .3972 pooled, .4777 smallest. Table 5: affected COARSE F=.3950, π*=.7291; affected MEDIUM/FINE F=.6597/.6744; overseer COARSE/MEDIUM/FINE F=.5733/.7316/.7681. All six π* values below .80. Dominant overseer-medium claims: early/distributed 3,107 (41.09%), late/sparse 2,153 (28.48%). Axis-standardized residual F: metric .5939, ablation .7014, objective .7018, threshold .7070, corruption .7092, prompt .7232, seed .7307. Structural variance: ablation-corruption interaction 78.8%, residual 11.5%, ablation 4.4%, threshold 4.1%, metric 0.7%. Null at sizes ≥1,000 has one class and F=0; discovered circuits collapse at 5,000 and 10,000. H4 pooled functional agreement .6028, instability .3972, gap versus claim flip .3344 (CI .3297–.3394), exceeding .10. Limitations: one model/task; planned 924-cell Pythia-160m replication has three seed levels; second task unrun; optimal ablation absent; discard rate 52.3% and uneven; bootstrap intervals invalid for conditioning groups of 2–5, so point estimates reported. Final universal claim that all high-risk AI systems fail filability conflicts with untested scope/generalization. Discussion: metric is biggest single-axis lever, reducing .7316 by .1377 to .5939 (CI .5803–.6063), so one-axis standardization insufficient. One of seven documented/publicly exported objectives fails on canonical task; all 220 cells in that arm fail. Reproducibility section reports one environment across 1,320 cells, archive/code identity for 22/22 files, 36 headline checks with 0 failures, three F computation routes, numeric-token verification, and 343 tests. No new internal contradiction identified.

On GPT-2 small, indirect object identification: 7,561 of 15,840 specifications produce a claim; claim flip rate is 73.2% (95% CI 0.725–0.738); modal claim covers 41.1%. Standardizing evaluation metric gives 59.4% flip rate. Removing circuit size from the claim and holding size fixed gives 27.1% (95% CI 0.255–0.286). Median circuit overlap is 4%; Cohen’s kappa is 0.015. One documented discovery objective does not execute: seven objectives documented, six executed. Scope is one model/task; scalability/generalization untested.

Possible count inconsistency: paper calls crossed grid seven analytic axes, but notes record eight dimensions: objective, ablation operator, corruption distribution, metric, size threshold, prompt variant, seed, granularity. Current related-work section repeats “cross seven”; check whether one dimension is nested/excluded.

Definitions: deterministic claim map; claim instability is probability two distinct specifications yield different statements; circuit instability = 1−Jaccard; functional instability = 1−functional agreement; functional gap = claim flip rate minus functional instability. Metrics: comprehensiveness, KL divergence, logit difference, sufficiency. H2 requires F>0.20 with CI lower bound above threshold; H3 separates from random null; H4 requires F−(1−agreement)>0.10. P0 reports mean Jaccard but is not tested. Filability requires modal claim share π*≥1−α.

Related work claims non-identifiability, faithfulness-metric sensitivity, possible structural/function dissociation, auditability needs, multiverse effects, and inflation of sufficiency/comprehensiveness; no internal numerical results here.

errors.claim: "It establishes that all high-risk AI systems fail filability under defensible analytic variation."
errors.evidence: Earlier notes state that the study's "scope/generalization [is] untested" and report results for the analyzed specifications, including six π* values below .80.
errors.explanation: The paper's results establish non-filability only for the studied system/specification space and claim maps, not for all high-risk AI systems. The universal conclusion contradicts the paper's own acknowledgment that scope and generalization were untested.

errors.location: this part, section 9, “Circuit size is an outcome, not an axis”

errors.explanation: The limitation section presents 0.2746 as the overall fixed-size value, but the paper’s reported overall size-removed/held-fixed estimate is 0.2706; 0.2746 applies specifically to the medium-size comparison.

grade.reason: The reviewer's fourth reported error explicitly flags the universal claim that the protocol establishes failure for all high-risk AI systems and notes the paper itself admits scope/generalization was untested, matching the planted-error critique.

sol_grade.reason: The fourth reported error identifies the planted universal claim as wrong because the results cover only the studied system and specification space, while scope and generalization remain untested.

errors.claim: “The grid contains seven objectives, seven operators, four corruption distributions nested within the five operators reading them, four metrics, three thresholds, two prompt variants and five seeds: 1,540 discovery cells and 18,480 pre-registered specifications.”
errors.evidence: The listed specification-level factors give 4 metrics × 3 thresholds × 2 prompt variants × 5 seeds = 120 specifications per discovery cell. Thus 1,540 discovery cells imply 184,800 specifications, not 18,480. Likewise, the realised 1,320 cells should imply 158,400 specifications, whereas the table reports 15,840; Table 2 totals 15,840 (3,960 per metric), agreeing with the latter figure but not with the stated factor crossing.
errors.explanation: The specification totals are inconsistent with the explicitly listed crossed factors by a factor of ten.

errors.claim: “Observed/chance overlap | about 45 times”
errors.location: this part, Section 7.1 structural diagnostic table
errors.evidence: The same table reports a median shared-edge fraction of 4% and an analytic random overlap of 0.0031 at the median circuit size.
errors.explanation: Using the table’s reported observed median overlap and random overlap gives approximately 0.04/0.0031 ≈ 13 times, not about 45 times. No other observed-overlap statistic is provided to support the stated 45-fold comparison.

final_notes: Paper: “Explanation Multiplicity: Circuit-Level Interpretability,” dated 12 August 2026. Study asks whether circuit-derived regulatory claims remain compatible across defensible analytic settings, using GPT-2 small (Q7V) on indirect object identification (Z4K). Pre-registered crossed multiverse; G7U maps circuits to Annex IV statements. Among 7,561 claim-producing specifications, pairwise claim disagreement F=0.7316. No single-axis standardisation permits filing under registered tolerances (Y3W). Removing size from statements and conditioning comparisons on size leaves disagreement 0.2706. Discovered circuits outperform size-matched random circuits at fixed size (K8Z 0.2746 vs 0.4230; E7R 0.2706 vs 0.3822, lower-is-better). Scope one model/task; Pythia-160m and second task unrun. Q7V graph: 32,491 edges, 144 attention heads + 12 MLPs; output has 157 non-terminal sources. Nine claim classes, ceiling 0.8889, observed fraction 82.3%. Section 5 committed size-bin F=.7316; alternatives no size .5733 and equal thirds .7018. Section 6 grid inconsistency: listed factors imply 184,800 specs, reported 18,480; realised 1,320 cells/15,840 specs, matching Table 2. 8,279 no circuit; discard 52.3%. Leading claims early/distributed 3,107 (.4109), late/sparse 2,153 (.2848). REML structural variance: ablation-corruption interaction 78.8%, residual 11.5%, ablation 4.4%, threshold 4.1%, metric 0.7%. Discovery F=0 at 5,000 and 10,000, but F=.5714 at 2,000, so “entirely below 2,000” is inconsistent. Pooled agreement .6028, instability .3972, kappa .0146; within-size kappa .016–.047. Six sizes fail gap threshold; pooled-gap band 500–2,000. Y3W requires declared analytic space, deterministic code, pi*, F, pass iff pi*≥1−alpha, and reporting discards/decompositions. It incorrectly claims failure for all high-risk AI systems despite one-model/task scope. Size is outcome and conditioning reduces instability; size affects pooled F, null-comparison direction, and functional-gap sign. C4Y optimal ablation is defensible but excluded, so measured F is claimed as a lower bound relative to the wider choice set. Discard rate is uneven (0.003, 0.630, 0.679, 0.779). Bootstrap conditioning groups with 2–5 specifications have dominating self-pairs; point estimates replace unusable intervals, with no post hoc bias-corrected estimator. Discussion: single-axis standardisation does not resolve instability; Table 6 best residual F=.5939 (95% CI .5803–.6063), evaluation-metric row, 59.4%. Instrument has 220 failed objective cells, 8,279 no-circuit specifications.

final_notes: Title: “Explanation Multiplicity: Circuit-Level Interpretability.” Abstract claims circuit-derived regulatory evidence fails Y3W throughout tolerances plausibly acceptable to a conformity-assessment body; competent analysts with same system/tool obtain incompatible statements under different defensible settings. Standardisation and size controls do not remove failure. Structural and functional disagreement indicate outputs are not merely reworded mechanisms. Abstract claims failure across model families, tasks, and deployment scale, while Introduction says no scale claim is made; §9 says only one model/one task were run, creating a direct internal conflict with the abstract’s cross-model/task claim. Date 12 Aug 2026. EU Regulation 2024/1689 requirements cited (Annex IV 2(b), 2(e), Article 86(1)); quotations use consolidated text amended by Regulation 2026/1744, read 11 Aug 2026. Contributions: pre-registered crossed design, published implementations, deterministic conversion to structured Annex IV statements, standardised axes, size controls, pooled statistics. Q7V |E|=32,491; 144 attention heads + 12 MLPs = 156 components. Circuit distance = Jaccard complement. F = unbiased Gini–Simpson pairwise disagreement; within-axis F conditions on G with equal pair weighting. Ceiling with 9 observed classes is 0.8889; observed fraction of ceiling 82.3%. Committed size-bin F=0.7316; alternatives: thresholds ×0.5=0.7448, ×0.8=0.7435, ×0.9=0.7394, deciles=0.7719. Factor-four binning range 0.70–0.77; no-size term E7R=0.5733. D9P mapping orders layer band, size class, input segment; L3X leads with input segment and right belonging to decision subject. E7R COARSE, K8Z MEDIUM, V2H FINE nested. Section 6: Q7V GPT-2 small; Z4K indirect-object identification; grid 7 objectives × 7 operators × 4 metrics × 3 thresholds × 2 prompt variants × 5 seeds. Limitations: second model M9B Pythia-160m and second task unrun; size is outcome; C4Y optimal ablation excluded; discard rate uneven; bootstrap invalid for one family, with point estimates substituted for unusable intervals. §10 says complete metric standardisation exceeds what conformity could demand, no single knob suffices, and evidentiary weight is measurable; failed objective is documented/exported but cannot execute on library’s canonical task; discard rate reflects tooling maturity. §11 reproducibility: public timestamped commit tagged prereg-p1-confirmatory; every reported number traces to configuration, seed, environment fingerprint. Archive verification

errors.claim: “The grid contains seven objectives, seven operators, four corruption distributions nested within the five operators reading them, four metrics, three thresholds, two prompt variants and five seeds: 1,540 discovery cells and 18,480 pre-registered specifications.”

errors.explanation: The reported specification totals are inconsistent with the explicitly stated crossed dimensions by a factor of ten, unless one of the dimensions is not actually crossed as described.

errors.explanation: Discovery instability is still present at 2,000 edges, so it does not live entirely below 2,000; the claim would need to say below or equal to 2,000 (or below 5,000).

final_notes: Paper: “Explanation Multiplicity: Circuit-Level Interpretability,” 12 Aug 2026. Study tests compatibility of circuit-derived regulatory claims across analytic settings in GPT-2 small (Q7V), indirect object identification (Z4K). Preregistered multiverse crosses objective, ablation operator/corruption, metric, threshold, prompt, seed, and granularity; G7U maps circuits to Annex IV statements. Among 7,561 claim-producing specifications, pairwise claim disagreement F=0.7316 [0.7247, 0.7380]. No single-axis standardisation permits filing under Y3W tolerance; removing size from statements/conditioning comparisons on size gives F=0.2706 [0.2550, 0.2859]. Fixed-size discovered circuits outperform random circuits (K8Z: 0.2746 vs 0.4230; E7R: 0.2706 vs 0.3822), though still fail Y3W. Pooled discovered F=.7316 vs A6N=.6774, with disjoint intervals; pooled direction is size-confounded. H4 pooled functional gap=.3344 [.3297,.3394]; functional diagnostic reports pooled agreement=.6028, instability=.3972, kappa=.0146. J6D mean Jaccard=.1396 [.1377,.1418]. Structural table: 3,218 circuits, 28,580,580 pairs; D quantiles 1%=.196, 25%=.788, median=.960, 75%=.998. Metric is smallest single-axis residual F=.5939 (CI .5803–.6063; 59.4%). K8Z A6N F=0 at sizes >=1,000; discovered F=0 only at 5,000 and 10,000. No-flip specifications=2,692; discovered instability remains at size 2,000. Functional gap holds pooled but not all sizes: 6/10 fail threshold and 5 have negative gaps; pooled-gap band 500–2,000 edges. Y3W requires declared space, measured pi* and F; filing without pi* is not audited. Section 9 limitations: second-model plan uses M9B/Pythia-160m, 924-cell grid, three rather than five seed levels; unrun. Size is an outcome, not axis; conditioning reduces instability more than any registered-axis standardisation and affects pooled F, null-comparison direction, and functional-gap sign. C4Y optimal ablation is unsupported/outside measured space. Discard rate is 52.3%, with uneven Table 2 rates .003, .630, .679, .779. Bootstrap intervals invalid for groups of 2–5 specifications due to dominating self-pairs; point estimates with diagnostics used instead. Section 10 discussion: complete metric standardisation does not resolve filing; no single knob suffices. Failed objective: 220 cells; 8,279 specifications admit no circuit; discard rate 52.3%. Discovered circuits retain information (fixed-size K8Z .2746 vs random .4230; E7R .2706 vs .3822). Measurement is asserted to be cheap relative to discovery, without numerical cost comparison. Section 11 reproducibility: public

errors.claim: “The surviving pool is therefore 52% comprehensiveness against 25% by design.”
errors.evidence: The same section states that 8,279 of 15,840 specifications were discarded, leaving 7,561 survivors. Thus the surviving pool is 7,561/15,840 = 47.7%, not 52%. Table 2 also shows the comprehensiveness metric itself retained 3,947 of 3,960 specifications (99.7%), with a discard rate of 0.003.
errors.explanation: The stated 52% does not match either the overall surviving fraction or the comprehensiveness row in Table 2. The 52.3% figure is the discard rate, not the surviving-pool rate.

errors.claim: “$\pi^{*}=0.8109$, so the evidence is filable at the loosest pre-registered tolerance: 0.811 clears 0.80.” (Section 7.2)
errors.evidence: Table 4 identifies the modal claim as 3,107/7,561 = 0.4109. Table 5 reports the overseer MEDIUM result as $\pi^{*}=0.4109$ and marks it “no” for filability, with the same $F=0.7316$ reported in Section 7.2. The paper’s earlier summary also says filability fails at every plausibly acceptable tolerance.
errors.explanation: The stated $\pi^{*}=0.8109$ conflicts with the medium-granularity overseer modal share of 0.4109 in both Tables 4 and 5. Consequently, the claim that this result is filable at tolerance 0.20 is contradicted by Table 5’s explicit “no.”

errors.claim: “The discovered multiverse also collapses at 5,000 and 10,000 edges, so 2,692 of 7,561 specifications contribute no flips at all and the instability lives entirely below 2,000 edges.”
errors.evidence: Table 7 reports a discovered flip rate of 0.5714 at size 2,000, with 312 specifications.
errors.explanation: Because flips still occur at 2,000 edges, the instability is not entirely below 2,000 edges. The table supports a cutoff below 5,000 edges (or, at most, below or including 2,000), not the stated ‘entirely below 2,000’ claim.

Abstract: Study tests whether circuit-discovery evidence is stable under defensible analytic variation. Pre-registered crossed grid has seven analytic axes, with levels from published implementations, yielding 15,840 specifications on GPT-2 small and indirect object identification; 7,561 produced a claim. A deterministic claim map converts circuits into structured Annex IV statements. Derived statement flips across 73.2% of specification pairs (95% CI 0.725–0.738); modal claim is 41.1% of space. Filability criterion fails at every plausibly acceptable tolerance. Standardizing evaluation metric leaves flip rate 59.4%; removing circuit size from claim and holding it fixed leaves 27.1% (95% CI 0.255–0.286), above preregistered threshold. Circuits are structurally near-disjoint (median pairwise Jaccard overlap 4%) and functionally uncorrelated (Cohen’s kappa 0.015). One of seven documented discovery objectives does not execute on the library’s canonical task. Scope: one model/task; scaling untested.

Deterministic map converts circuits into structured Annex IV statements. Derived statement flips across 73.2% of specification pairs (95% CI 0.725–0.738); modal claim is 41.1% of space. Filability criterion is π* ≥ 1−α and fails at every plausibly acceptable tolerance. Standardizing evaluation metric leaves flip rate 59.4%; removing circuit size from claim and holding it fixed leaves 27.1% (95% CI 0.255–0.286), above preregistered threshold. Circuits are structurally near-disjoint (median pairwise Jaccard overlap 4%) and functionally uncorrelated (Cohen’s kappa 0.015; Section 7.6 reports 0.0146). One of seven documented discovery objectives does not execute on the library’s canonical task. Scope is one model/task; scaling untested. Contributions include pooled-statistics inversion when specifications select objects of different sizes, with three examples. Formalism: specification has seven analytic axes; GPT-2 small factorised graph has |E|=32,491 and 156 components (144 heads + 12 MLPs). Circuit instability uses pairwise Jaccard distance. Claim flip rate F is the unbiased Gini–Simpson probability that two without-replacement draws differ; modal share π*. Filability iff π*≥1−α. Nine observed classes imply F ceiling 0.8889; observed F=0.7316 is 82.3% of ceiling. Section 5: Deterministic claim map φ has two addressees (overseer and affected), with nested granularities. Table 1 reports F=0.7316 for committed size bins; alternatives range from 0.7018 (equal thirds) to 0.7719 (deciles), and no size term (COARSE) gives F=0.5733. This differs from the earlier 27.1% result because that earlier note specifies removing size from the claim while holding it fixed. Section 6: Preregistered grid had 1,540 discovery cells and 18,480 specifications. One objective (220 cells) failed, leaving six objectives, 1,320 cells, and 15,840 specifications. Metric-relative threshold discarded 8,279 specifications (52.3%), leaving 7,561; hence survivor fraction is 47.7%, not 52%. errors.claim: “$\pi^{*}=0.8109$, so the evidence is filable at the loosest pre-registered tolerance: 0.811 clears 0.80.” (Section 7.2)
errors.evidence: Table 4 identifies the modal claim as 3,107/7,561 = 0.4109. Table 5 reports the overseer MEDIUM result as $\pi^{*}=0.4109$ and marks it “no” for filability, with the same $F=0.7316$ reported in Section 7.2. The paper’s earlier summary also says filability fails at every plausibly acceptable tolerance.
errors.explanation: The stated $\pi^{*}=0.8109$ conflicts with the medium-granularity overseer modal share of 0.4109 in both Tables 4 and 5. Consequently, the claim that this result is filable at tolerance 0.20 is contradicted by Table 5’s explicit “no.”

errors.claim: “The discovered multiverse also collapses at 5,000 and 10,000 edges, so 2,692 of 7,561 specifications contribute no flips at all and the instability lives entirely below 2,000 edges.”

final_notes: Section 7 reports preregistered outcomes: J6D mean J=0.1396 [0.1377, 0.1418], premise holds; X4R F=0.7316 [0.7247, 0.7380], confirmed; Q2F separated from random null, rejected; Z8N F-(1-agreement)=0.3344 [0.3297, 0.3394], supported. There are 7,561 claim-producing specifications, 3,218 distinct circuits, and 28,580,580 pairs. Structural D quantiles: 1%=0.196, 25%=0.788, median=.960, 75%=.998; median shared-edge fraction 4%, only 1% pairs Jaccard >.8, median size 200 edges, observed/chance overlap about 45x. Table 4 pair disagreement is 73.2% [0.725, .738], with modal class 41.1% and second 28.5%; class counts sum to 7,561. Size-aggregated early/late/middle shares are 47.9/43.6/8.5%. Table 5 at alpha=.20, required pi*>=.80: all Y3W outcomes are “no”; text incorrectly says loosest tolerance permits filing. Residual metric-standardised disagreement F=.5939; size-free dominant-layer F=.2706 [0.2550,.2859]. Pooled discovered F=.7316 versus A6N .6774; fixed-size K8Z .2746 vs .4230 and E7R .2706 vs .3822. A6N degenerates at and above 1,000 edges; 2,692 specifications have no flips. Functional pooled agreement=.6028, instability=.3972; smallest-circuit instability=.4777; kappa=.0146; raw agreement 0.52–0.92, accuracy .51–.95; pooled gap carried by 500–2,000 edges. Section 8 defines Y3W and pass criterion pi*>=1-alpha. Section 9 limitations include one model/task, unrun replication, circuit size as outcome, multiverse exclusions, discard-rate caveat, and bootstrap limitations. Section 10 says complete metric standardisation exceeds conformity demands; no single knob suffices; failed objective cannot execute on canonical task; discard rate reflects tooling maturity; evidentiary weight is measurable. Section 11 reproducibility: public commit tagged prereg-p1-confirmatory; one environment across 1,320 confirmatory cells; 22/22 archive files match git tree; no GPU needed. One script has 36 checks with 0 failures and recomputes F three ways including brute-force pairs; another checks manuscript numeric tokens; tables are emitted directly; suite has 343 tests.

Paper title: “Explanation Multiplicity: Circuit-Level Interpretability.” Abstract claims: (1) circuit-derived regulatory evidence fails Y3W throughout tolerances plausibly acceptable to a conformity-assessment body; (2) competent analysts with the same system and tool obtain incompatible statements under different defensible settings; (3) standardisation and size controls do not remove the failure; (4) structural and functional disagreement rule out merely reworded mechanisms; (5) applicability beyond one model and task remains untested. Date: 12 August 2026. Author: Ajay Pravin Mahale.

Introduction: EU Regulation 2024/1689 technical-documentation and explanation requirements are quoted from consolidated text amended by Regulation 2026/1744. Mechanistic interpretability/circuit discovery supplies a subgraph purported to explain behaviour; regulatory-claim movement across defensible specifications is assessed with a standards-body decision rule. Contributions: preregistered crossed design using published implementations; circuits deterministically converted into structured Annex IV statements; controls standardise individual axes, remove claim-size dependence, and condition on size. Three pooled statistics invert when selected objects differ in size. No improved discovery method is proposed; objection concerns the standard presumed by filing currently produced evidence, not interpretability’s worth.

Related work: Méloux et al. [6] argue explanations need not be unique under mechanistic-interpretability criteria. Miller et al. [8] find ablation-faithfulness scores sensitive to design choices; their library is used here, extended from one axis to seven-axis regulatory propagation. Bayat Makou et al. [1] find structurally distinct circuits can implement the same computation under fixed task and varied input statistics (W5T phantom specialisation); this motivates functional measurement. Méloux et al. [7] frame interpretability as statistical estimation with estimator variance; seed variance is one axis here. Lan et al. [4] report conflicting conclusions about one behaviour and call for safety-critical certification standards; Sharkey et al. [10] discuss socio-technical issues; Mueller et al. [9] require standardised method evaluation. Steegen et al. [13], Simonsohn et al. [12], and Simmons et al. [11] motivate multiverse reporting/specification curves to expose analytic flexibility. Hsia et al. [3] inflate U4J and T9V without changing predictions or explanations; metric-specific discard reporting avoids silent pooling.

final_notes:
Study examines circuit discovery and stability of regulatory evidence, varying analytic choices and deterministically mapping circuits to Annex IV statements. Of 15,840 realized specifications, 7,561 produce a claim; claim flip rate is 73.2% (95% CI 0.725–0.738), modal claim share 41.1%. Standardized metric gives 59.4% flips (reduction .1377); holding size fixed gives 27.06% (.2706; medium-size value .2746). Median circuit overlap 4%; Cohen’s kappa .015. Filability requires modal share π*≥.80 (α=.20); nine-class ceiling .8889.

Pooled discovered F=.7316 versus random-null .6774, but pooled direction is a size-distribution artefact. Fixed-size discovered circuits are more stable: medium .2746 vs null .4230; coarse .2706 vs .3822. Table 7 medium sizes 10/20/50/100/200/500/1000/2000/5000/10000: discovered F .4543/.3380/.4639/.5792/.5122/.4258/.5133/.5714/0/0; null .7331/.6622/.7310/.6584/.6366/.1421/0/0/0/0. Discovered n=7,561; 5,000 and 10,000 comprise 2,692 and collapse to one class.

Functional agreement=.6028, instability=.3972; pooled gap=.3344 [95% CI .3297–.3394], but size decomposition fails threshold at 6/10 sizes and is negative at 5; pooled gap carried by 500–2,000. Kappa=.0146; size-specific .016–.047, raw agreement .52–.92, accuracy .51–.95. H4 supported only for preregistered pooled quantity. P0 holds; H2 confirmed; H3 rejected due to separated distributions, qualified by within-size reversal.

Discussion claims metric is the biggest lever, but this conflicts with the larger reduction from holding size fixed. One of seven objectives fails; all 220 cells in that arm fail. Limitations include one model/task, unrun replication/task, size-selection distortions, absent optimal ablation, 52.3% discard rate, uneven metric rates, and invalid bootstrap intervals for groups with 2–5 specifications.

Reproducibility section: preregistration committed before confirmatory sweep; one environment across 1,320 cells; archive/git comparison found 22/22 identical files. Verification recomputes headlines: 36 checks, 0 failures, F by three routes including brute force. Numeric tokens and tables checked/generated from stored results; test suite has 343 tests. No contradiction identified in this part.

Bootstrap resamples specifications (not pairs); U-statistics use dependent pairs. H2 requires F>0.20 with CI lower bound above threshold; H3 concerns separation from the random null; H4 requires F−(1−agreement)>0.10. P0 reports mean Jaccard but is not tested. Filability requires modal claim share π*≥1−α.

Hsia et al. [3] inflate U4J and T9V without changing predictions or explanations; metric-specific discard reporting avoids silent pooling.

errors.claim: “One of seven documented, publicly exported discovery objectives does not run on the library’s own canonical task,” followed by “All documented objectives supply usable circuit evidence.”
errors.evidence: The first statement says one of the seven objectives does not run on the canonical task, whereas the second says all seven documented objectives supply usable circuit evidence.
errors.explanation: An objective that does not run on the canonical task cannot also supply usable circuit evidence for that task, unless “usable circuit evidence” is intended to refer to a different setting, which is not stated.

grade.reason: The third reported error directly flags the contradiction between ‘one of seven objectives does not run’ and ‘all documented objectives supply usable circuit evidence,’ matching the planted error's stated inconsistency.

errors.claim: “All documented objectives supply usable circuit evidence.”

Date 12 Aug 2026; author Ajay Pravin Mahale. Design: Q7V (GPT-2 small), Z4K indirect-object identification, seven objectives/operators, four corruption distributions for five operators, four metrics, three thresholds, two prompt variants, five seeds. 1,540 discovery cells/18,480 specifications; one objective fails, leaving 1,320 cells/15,840 specifications. 8,279 admit no circuit (52.3%); 7,561 kept. Kept/discarded: T9V 3,947/13; H2W 1,467/2,493; N6C 1,270/2,690; U4W 877/3,083. Registered pooled results: J6D mean J=.1396; X4R F=.7316; Q2F separated from random null; Z8N functional gap=.3344. Structural: 3,218 circuits, 28,580,580 pairs; D median .960; median shared-edge fraction 4%; median size 200 edges; observed overlap ~45x chance. Metric-standardised disagreement 59.4% (residual F=.5939); other standardisations leave F=.7014–.7307. Size-free dominant-layer claim F=.2706, CI [.2550,.2859], reported as 27.1%/27%. Pooled discovered F=.7316 vs A6N=.6774; fixed-size discovered F=.2746 (K8Z), .2706 (E7R), versus A6N .4230/.3822. A6N degenerates at >=1,000 edges; discovery at 5,000/10,000. 2,692 specifications have no flips; instability below 2,000 edges. Functional pooled agreement=.6028, instability=.3972, smallest-circuit instability=.4777, kappa=.0146; kappa by size .016–.047; raw agreement .52–.92, accuracy .51–.95; 6/10 sizes fail gap threshold, 5 have negative gap; pooled gap carried by 500–2,000 edges. Y3W protocol: declare analytic axes/levels S and deterministic published code φ; compute π*=max_c n_c/N over S and F; pass at tolerance α iff π*≥1−α; report π*, F, discard rate per axis level, and within-group decomposition of pooled statistics. Filing unable to state π* is asserted, not audited; implementability requires declared space and measured agreement, not adjudication of analytic correctness. Limitations: one model/task; Pythia-160m second-model plan (M9B) unrun, second task designed but unrun. Circuit size is outcome, not axis; threshold-selected size can distort F, null direction, and functional-gap sign; pooled statistics reported with within-size decomposition. Library excludes unsupported C4Y optimal ablation, so measured F claimed lower bound relative to full defensible choice set. Discard rate high/uneven.

Paper title: “Explanation Multiplicity: Circuit-Level Interpretability.” Abstract claims: (1) circuit-derived regulatory evidence fails Y3W throughout tolerances plausibly acceptable to a conformity-assessment body; (2) competent analysts with the same system and tool obtain incompatible statements under different defensible settings; (3) standardisation and size controls do not remove the failure; (4) structural and functional disagreement rule out merely reworded mechanisms; (5) applicability beyond one model and task remains untested. Date: 12 August 2026. Author: Ajay Pravin Mahale.

Introduction: EU Regulation 2024/1689 technical-documentation and explanation requirements are quoted from consolidated text amended by Regulation 2026/1744. Mechanistic interpretability/circuit discovery supplies a subgraph purported to explain behaviour; regulatory-claim movement across defensible specifications is assessed with a standards-body decision rule. Contributions: preregistered crossed design using published implementations; circuits deterministically converted into structured Annex IV statements; controls standardise individual axes, remove claim-size dependence, and condition on size. Three pooled statistics invert when selected objects differ in size. No improved discovery method is proposed; objection concerns the standard presumed by filing currently produced evidence, not interpretability’s worth.

[4] report conflicting conclusions about one behaviour and call for safety-critical certification standards; Sharkey et al. [10] discuss socio-technical issues; Mueller et al. [9] require standardised method evaluation. Steegen et al. [13], Simonsohn et al. [12], and Simmons et al. [11] motivate multiverse reporting/specification curves to expose analytic flexibility. Hsia et al. [3] inflate U4J and T9V without changing predictions or explanations; metric-specific discard reporting avoids silent pooling.

final_notes: Study examines circuit discovery and stability of regulatory evidence, varying analytic choices and deterministically mapping circuits to Annex IV statements. Of 15,840 realized specifications, 7,561 produce a claim; claim flip rate is 73.2% (95% CI 0.725–0.738), modal claim share 41.1%. Standardized metric gives 59.4% flips; removing circuit size while holding size fixed gives 27.1% (95% CI 0.255–0.286). Median circuit overlap 4%; Cohen’s kappa 0.015 (0.0146 elsewhere). One of seven documented objectives fails on the canonical task; six execute, and all 220 cells in the failed arm fail. Table 5: affected COARSE=.3950, π*=.7291; affected MEDIUM/FINE=.6597/.6744; overseer COARSE/MEDIUM/FINE=.5733/.7316/.7681. All π* below .80. Dominant overseer-medium claims: early/distributed 3,107 (41.09%), late/sparse 2,153 (28.48%). Layer attribution: early 47.9%, late 43.6%, middle 8.5%. Axis-standardized residual F: metric .5939, ablation .7014, objective .7018, threshold .7070, corruption .7092, prompt .7232, seed .7307. Structural variance: ablation-corruption interaction 78.8%, residual 11.5%, ablation 4.4%, threshold 4.1%, metric 0.7%. Size-held-fixed medium F=.2746, above preregistered .20 threshold. Pooled discovered F=.7316 versus size-matched random null .6774; H3 rejected with qualifications. Null at sizes ≥1,000 has one class and F=0; discovered circuits collapse at 5,000 and 10,000. Limitations include one model/task, unrun replication/task, size as outcome, optimal ablation absent, 52.3% discard rate, and invalid bootstrap intervals for groups of 2–5. Discussion: metric removes .1377 from .7316, leaving .5939 (CI .5803–.6063); one-axis standardization is insufficient. Evidentiary weight is measured by π* and F. Reproducibility section claims archive/sweep covers 1,320 cells, conflicting with seven 220-cell objective arms (1,540 total) unless the failed arm is explicitly excluded. Claims 36 verification checks pass, F computed three ways, 22/22 files identical, and 343 tests.

Key definitions: claim map is deterministic; claim instability is the probability that two distinct specifications yield different statements; circuit instability is one minus Jaccard similarity; functional instability is one minus functional agreement; functional gap is claim flip rate minus functional instability. Four evaluation metrics are comprehensiveness, KL divergence, logit difference, and sufficiency. Specifications vary objective, ablation operator, corruption distribution, metric, size threshold, prompt variant, seed, and granularity. Bootstrap resamples specifications (not pairs); U-statistics use dependent pairs. H2 requires F>0.20 with CI lower bound above threshold; H3 concerns separation from the random null; H4 requires F−(1−agreement)>0.10. P0 reports mean Jaccard but is not tested. Filability requires modal claim share π*≥1−α.

Study asks whether circuit-derived regulatory claims remain compatible across defensible analytic settings, using GPT-2 small (Q7V) on indirect object identification (Z4K). Pre-registered crossed multiverse; G7U maps circuits to Annex IV statements. Among 7,561 claim-producing specifications, pairwise claim disagreement F=0.7316. No single-axis standardisation permits filing under registered tolerances (Y3W). Removing size from statements and conditioning comparisons on size leaves disagreement 0.2706. Discovered circuits outperform size-matched random circuits at fixed size (K8Z 0.2746 vs 0.4230; E7R 0.2706 vs 0.3822, lower-is-better). Scope one model/task; Pythia-160m unrun. Q7V graph: 32,491 edges, 144 attention heads + 12 MLPs; output has 157 non-terminal sources. Nine claim classes, ceiling 0.8889, observed fraction 82.3%. Section 5 committed size-bin F=.7316; alternatives no size .5733 and equal thirds .7018. Section 6 grid inconsistency: listed factors imply 184,800 specs, reported 18,480; realised 1,320 cells/15,840 specs, matching Table 2. 8,279 no circuit; discard 52.3%. Leading claims early/distributed 3,107 (.4109), late/sparse 2,153 (.2848). REML structural variance: ablation-corruption interaction 78.8%, residual 11.5%, ablation 4.4%, threshold 4.1%, metric 0.7%. Table 7: discovery F=0 at 5,000 and 10,000 (2,692 specs), but F=.5714 at 2,000, so “entirely below 2,000” is inconsistent. A6N F=0 at and above 1,000. Pooled functional diagnostic: agreement .6028, instability .3972, kappa .0146; within-size kappa .016–.047. Six sizes fail gap threshold, five have negative gaps; stated band carrying pooled gap is 500–2,000. Y3W protocol: declare analytic space S and deterministic code phi; compute pi*=max_c n_c/N over S and F; pass iff pi* >= 1-alpha; report pi*, F, discard rate per axis level, and within-group decomposition of pooled statistics. Limitations: one model/task; second-model Pythia-160m plan unrun, 924 cells with three rather than five seed levels. Abstract reports a pre-registered crossed grid of seven analytic axes applied to GPT-2 small on indirect object identification. There were 15,840 specifications; 7,561 produced a claim. Derived statements flipped across 73.2% of specification pairs (95% CI 0.725–0.738), and the modal claim represented 41.1% of the space. Every pre-registered specification is said to yield evidence failing filability at every plausibly acceptable tolerance. Standardizing the evaluation metric leaves a 59.4% flip rate; removing circuit size from the claim and holding it fixed leaves 27.1% (95% CI 0.255–0.286), above the pre-registered threshold. Circuits are structurally near-disjoint (median pairwise Jaccard overlap 4%) and functionally uncorrelated (Cohen’s kappa 0.015). The paper presents a filability protocol and reports that one of seven documented discovery objectives does not execute on the library’s canonical task. final_notes:
Abstract claims: Every pre-registered specification yields circuit-derived regulatory evidence that fails Y3W across plausibly acceptable tolerances; competent analysts using the same system/tool obtain incompatible statements under defensible settings. Standardisation and size controls do not remove failure. Structural and functional disagreement are not merely reworded mechanisms. Applicability beyond one model/task is untested.

Study: Q7V GPT-2 small, Z4K indirect-object identification; R8X edge attribution patching and B3Q integrated edge gradients; 7 objectives, operators/corruptions, 4 metrics (T9V, H2W, N6C, U4J), 3 thresholds, 2 prompt variants, 5 seeds. Planned 1,540 cells/18,480 specs; one 220-cell objective arm failed runtime, yielding 1,320 cells/15,840 specs. 8,279 no-circuit discards and 7,561 kept. Metric retained/discarded: T9V 3,947/13; H2W 1,467/2,493; N6C 1,270/2,690; U4J 877/3,083.

Results: J6D premise holds (mean J=.1396); X4R confirmed (F=.7316); Q2F rejected versus random null; Z8N supported (functional gap=.3344). 3,218 distinct circuits; median shared-edge fraction 4%, overlap about 45x chance. Pair disagreement 73.2%; modal D9P/K8Z class 41.09%. No registered tolerance permits filing. Maximum/coarsest L3X pi*=.7291 (<.80); D9P/K8Z pi*=.4109.

Standardisation: metric-standardised F=.5939; residual F by axis: ablation .7014, objective .7018, threshold .7070, corruption .7092, prompt .7232, seed .7307. REML structural variance: ablation-corruption interaction 78.8%, residual 11.5%, ablation 4.4%, threshold 4.1%, metric 0.7%. Size-free fixed-size dominant-layer attribution F=.2706. Pooled discovered F=.7316 vs A6N=.6774; fixed-size K8Z=.2746 vs A6N=.4230, E7R=.2706 vs .3822. A6N degenerates above 1,000 edges; discovery at 5,000/10,000. 2,692 specs at those sizes.

Discussion: No single knob suffices; one-axis standardisation cannot justify declaring resolution. The failed objective is documented/exported but cannot execute on the canonical task; it is not the headline or criticism of authors. Interpretability evidence has measurable, not presumed, evidentiary weight.

Reproducibility: public commit tagged prereg-p1-confirmatory; reported numbers trace to configuration, seed, environment. Archive verification found one environment across all 1,320 confirmatory cells; 22/22 files matched git tree. No GPU needed. One script recomputes headline quantities, including F by three routes and brute-force pairs (36 checks, 0 failures); another checks manuscript numeric tokens against stored-result derivations. Tables emitted directly; test suite has 343 tests.

errors.claim: “A pre-registered multiverse—a designed space of defensible analytic specifications—over seven circuit-discovery axes.”
errors.evidence: Earlier content states that specifications vary objective, ablation operator, corruption distribution, metric, size threshold, prompt variant, seed, and granularity—eight listed dimensions.
errors.explanation: The stated seven axes conflicts with the earlier enumeration of eight specification dimensions, unless one of those dimensions is not intended to be an axis.

errors.claim: “We use their released library. Our study therefore stress-tests the tooling by its own definitions. … we cross seven and propagate the result to a regulatory statement.”
errors.evidence: Earlier in the paper, the specification dimensions are listed as eight: objective, ablation operator, corruption distribution, metric, size threshold, prompt variant, seed, and granularity. The Introduction also calls them seven axes.
errors.explanation: The paper inconsistently describes the multiverse as crossing seven axes despite listing eight specification dimensions elsewhere. This part reinforces the seven-axis count without explaining which listed dimension is excluded.

errors.claim: "The grid has seven discovery objectives, seven ablation operators, four corruption distributions nested within the five operators that read them, four metrics, three thresholds, two prompt variants and five seeds. As pre-registered, this gives 1,540 discovery cells and 18,480 specifications."
errors.evidence: With seven operators, five of which use four corruption distributions, the operator/corruption combinations are 5×4+2=22. Multiplying by the other stated factors gives 7×22×4×3×2×5=18,480 specifications, not 1,540 discovery cells; equivalently, the stated factors imply 2,640 specifications per objective, whereas 1,540 cells implies 220 per objective.
errors.explanation: The reported total of 18,480 is consistent with the stated grid factors only as the total number of specifications, but the claimed intermediate total of 1,540 cells is not. The factors imply 2,640 cells (or specifications before the objective factor), not 1,540.

Table 5 rows: affected coarse/medium/fine F=.3950/.6597/.6744 with modal shares .7291/.4875/.4786; overseer coarse/medium/fine F=.5733/.7316/.7681 with shares .4788/.4109/.4109. All fail pi*≥.80. Dominant claims: early/distributed 3,107=.4109; late/sparse 2,153=.2848. Layers: early 47.9%, late 43.6%, middle 8.5%; early coarse .4788. Table 6 residual F: metric .5939 (reduction .1377), ablation .7014, objective .7018, threshold .7070, corruption .7092, prompt .7232, seed .7307; reductions .0302, .0298, .0246, .0224, .0084, .0009. Table 7 discovered/null F by medium size: 10 .4543/.7331; 20 .3380/.6622; 50 .4639/.7310; 100 .5792/.6584; 200 .5122/.6366; 500 .4258/.1421; 1,000 .5133/0; 2,000 .5714/0; 5,000/10,000 0/0. Fixed-size ordering reverses: medium .2746 vs .4230; coarse .2706 vs .3822. H4 pooled agreement .6028, instability .3972, gap .3344 [.3297,.3394] vs .10; kappa .0146; pooled result reportedly carried by 500–2,000 band. Section 8: filing requires modal share pi*≥1-alpha and within-group decomposition. Section 9: one model/task; planned Pythia-160m 924-cell replication with 3 seed levels and second task unrun. Size selection distorts pooled F, null direction, and functional-gap sign; fixing size drops F .7316 to .2746, more than any preregistered-axis standardization. Summary: The study examines circuit discovery and stability of regulatory evidence. It varies seven analytic choices and deterministically maps each circuit to a structured Annex IV statement. On GPT-2 small, task indirect object identification: 7,561 of 15,840 specifications produce a claim; claim flip rate is 73.2%; the most common claim covers 41.1% of specifications. Standardizing the evaluation metric gives a 59.4% flip rate. Removing circuit size from the claim and holding size fixed gives 27.1%. Median circuit overlap is 4%, and chance-adjusted functional agreement is near zero. One documented discovery objective does not execute. Scope is one model and one task; scalability/generalization is untested.

The study examines circuit discovery and stability of regulatory evidence. It varies seven analytic choices and deterministically maps each circuit to a structured Annex IV statement. On GPT-2 small, indirect object identification: 7,561 of 15,840 specifications produce a claim; claim flip rate is 73.2%; the modal claim covers 41.1% of specifications. Standardizing the evaluation metric gives a 59.4% flip rate. Removing circuit size from the claim and holding size fixed gives 27.1%. Median circuit overlap is 4%, and chance-adjusted functional agreement is near zero. One documented discovery objective does not execute: seven objectives were documented, six executed. Scope is one model and one task; scalability/generalization is untested.

Key definitions: claim map is deterministic; claim instability is the probability that two distinct specifications yield different statements; circuit instability is one minus Jaccard similarity; functional instability is one minus functional agreement; functional gap is claim flip rate minus functional instability. Four evaluation metrics are comprehensiveness, KL divergence, logit difference, and sufficiency. Specifications vary objective, ablation operator, corruption distribution, metric, size threshold, prompt variant, seed, and granularity. Bootstrap resamples specifications (not pairs); U-statistics use dependent pairs. H2 requires F>0.20 with CI lower bound above threshold; H3 concerns separation from the random null; H4 requires F−(1−agreement)>0.10. P0 reports mean Jaccard but is not tested. Filability requires modal claim share π*≥1−α.

errors.evidence: Earlier notes record Table 7 medium discovered F values of 0 at circuit sizes 5,000 and 10,000.
errors.explanation: The reported F=0 at sizes 5,000 and 10,000 indicates no measured flip instability at those sizes, contradicting the claim that instability persists at every circuit size.

final_notes: Study examines circuit discovery and stability of regulatory evidence, varying analytic choices and deterministically mapping circuits to Annex IV statements. Of 15,840 realized specifications, 7,561 produce a claim; claim flip rate is 73.2% (95% CI 0.725–0.738), modal claim share 41.1%. Standardized metric gives 59.4% flips; removing circuit size while holding size fixed gives 27.1% (95% CI 0.255–0.286). Median circuit overlap 4%; Cohen’s kappa 0.015 (0.0146 elsewhere). One of seven documented objectives fails, six execute; scope/generalization untested. Discovered circuits more stable than fixed-size random null (.2746 vs .4230); pooled functional instability .3972; functional kappa indicates uncorrelatedness. Table 5: affected COARSE F=.3950, π*=.7291; affected MEDIUM/FINE F=.6597/.6744; overseer COARSE/MEDIUM/FINE F=.5733/.7316/.7681; all π* below .80. Axis-standardized residual F: metric .5939, ablation .7014, objective .7018, threshold .7070, corruption .7092, prompt .7232, seed .7307. Structural variance: ablation-corruption interaction 78.8%, residual 11.5%, ablation 4.4%, threshold 4.1%, metric 0.7%. Size-held-fixed medium F=.2746 (coarse .2706), above preregistered .20 threshold. Pooled discovered F=.7316 versus size-matched random null .6774; H3 rejected, with within-size reversal and size-distribution artefact qualification. Table 7 medium discovered/null F: size 10 .4543/.7331; 20 .3380/.6622; 50 .4639/.7310; 100 .5792/.6584; 200 .5122/.6366; 500 .4258/.1421; 1,000 .5133/0; 2,000 .5714/0; 5,000 and 10,000 0/0. Discussion claims metric removes .1377 from .7316, leaving .5939 (CI .5803–.6063), and says instability persists at every circuit size—contradicted by F=0 at 5,000 and 10,000. Limitations: one model/task; planned but unrun Pythia-160m replication and second task. Size is outcome, not axis; optimal ablation absent, so measured F lower bound. Discard rate 52.3%, metric-imbalanced surviving pool; metric discard rates .003, .630, .679, .779. Bootstrap intervals invalid for conditioning groups of 2–5 due to retained self-pairs; point estimates only. Reproducibility section claims preregistration and archive verification across 1,320 cells, 22/22 files identical, 36 headline checks with 0 failures, three routes for F, all numeric tokens checked, tables generated from results, and 343 tests. No new demonstrable internal contradiction.

Summary: The study examines circuit discovery and stability of regulatory evidence. It varies seven analytic choices and deterministically maps each circuit to a structured Annex IV statement. On GPT-2 small, task indirect object identification: 7,561 of 15,840 specifications produce a claim; claim flip rate is 73.2%; the most common claim covers 41.1% of specifications. Standardizing the evaluation metric gives a 59.4% flip rate. Removing circuit size from the claim and holding size fixed gives 27.1%. Median circuit overlap is 4%, and chance-adjusted functional agreement is near zero. One documented discovery objective does not execute. Scope is one model and one task; scalability/generalization is untested.

The study examines circuit discovery and stability of regulatory evidence. It varies seven analytic choices and deterministically maps each circuit to a structured Annex IV statement. On GPT-2 small, indirect object identification: 7,561 of 15,840 specifications produce a claim; claim flip rate is 73.2%; the modal claim covers 41.1% of specifications. Standardizing the evaluation metric gives a 59.4% flip rate. Removing circuit size from the claim and holding size fixed gives 27.1%. Median circuit overlap is 4%, and chance-adjusted functional agreement is near zero. One documented discovery objective does not execute: seven objectives were documented, six executed. Scope is one model and one task; scalability/generalization is untested.

Key definitions: claim map is deterministic; claim instability is the probability that two distinct specifications yield different statements; circuit instability is one minus Jaccard similarity; functional instability is one minus functional agreement; functional gap is claim flip rate minus functional instability. Four evaluation metrics are comprehensiveness, KL divergence, logit difference, and sufficiency. Specifications vary objective, ablation operator, corruption distribution, metric, size threshold, prompt variant, seed, and granularity. Bootstrap resamples specifications (not pairs); U-statistics use dependent pairs. H2 requires F>0.20 with CI lower bound above threshold; H3 concerns separation from the random null; H4 requires F−(1−agreement)>0.10. P0 reports mean Jaccard but is not tested. Filability requires modal claim share π*≥1−α.

errors.claim: “The grid has seven discovery objectives, seven ablation operators, four corruption distributions nested within the five operators that read them, four metrics, three thresholds, two prompt variants and five seeds. H4 supported by pooled gap 0.3344 [0.3297, 0.3394], but fails at 6/10 sizes and has negative gaps at 5. Discovered pooled F=.7316 vs size-matched null=.6774. Table 7 medium discovered/null: sizes 10 .4543/.7331, 20 .3380/.6622, 50 .4639/.7310, 100 .5792/.6584, 200 .5122/.6366, 500 .4258/.1421, 1,000 .5133/0, 2,000 .5714/0, 5,000 and 10,000 0/0. Fixed-size F: medium .2746 vs .4230, coarse .2706 vs .3822; earlier size-held result .2706 [.2550,.2859].

Section 8: preregister specification space/levels and deterministic claim map; compute pi*=max_c n_c/N and F; report pi*, F, discard rate by axis and within-group decomposition.

Section 9: one model/task; planned 924-cell Pythia-160m replication has 3 seed levels; second task unrun. Claims size changes F .7316 to .2746 (reduction .4570), conflicting with Discussion’s metric reduction .1377 as biggest lever. Optimal ablation absent. Discard rate 52.3%, uneven metric rates .003/.630/.679/.779. Bootstrap CIs invalid for conditioning groups of 2–5; point estimates reported. One of seven objectives does not run; all 220 cells in that arm fail.

Section 10: Discussion calls metric biggest lever, removing .1377 from .7316 to .5939 (CI .5803–.6063), conflicting with larger size reduction. Evidentiary weight uses pi* and F; no numerical cost comparison.

Section 11: claims preregistration was timestamped/public and pre-confirmatory; every reported number traces to config, seed, environment fingerprint. Results archive says one environment across 1,320 cells; 22/22 files identical to git tree. Verification recomputes headline quantities, 36 checks with 0 failures, including three routes for F. Second script checks every numeric manuscript token against stored results; tables generated from results; test suite has 343 tests. No definite internal contradiction established between 1,320 total cells and the earlier 924-cell planned replication.

final_notes:
Table 7 (K8Z within-size): A6N null degenerates at and above 1,000 edges (F=0, one class). Discovered F is nonzero through 2,000 edges (10:.4543; 20:.3380; 50:.4639; 100:.5792; 200:.5122; 500:.4258; 1,000:.5133; 2,000:.5714), then collapses at 5,000 and 10,000 (F=0, one class). Caption claim that instability is entirely below 2,000 conflicts with nonzero 2,000 result; correct boundary is at or below 2,000.

Pooled discovered instability F=.7316 exceeds A6N .6774; fixed-size ordering reverses (K8Z .2746 vs .4230; E7R .2706 vs .3822). Functional section: pooled agreement .6028, functional instability .3972, kappa .0146; within-size kappa .016–.047 despite raw agreement .52–.92 and accuracy .51–.95. Six of ten sizes fail gap threshold, five have negative gaps; pooled Z8N gap .3344 [.3297,.3394] is only pooled, with intermediate 500–2,000-edge band carrying it.

Y3W protocol requires declared space S and deterministic code phi; compute pi*=max_c n_c/N over S and F; pass iff pi* >= 1-alpha; report pi*, F, discard rate per axis level, and within-group decomposition. Limitations: generalization, second-model study (M9B/Pythia-160m, 924-cell grid, three rather than five seed levels), and second task unrun. Size is an outcome; conditioning size reduces F more than any single-axis standardization (fixed-size F=.2706 vs smallest Table 6 residual F=.5939), and affects null direction and functional-gap sign. C4Y optimal ablation unsupported/outside measured space. Discard rate 52.3%, uneven (.003, .630, .679, .779). Small bootstrap groups (2–5 specs) retain self-pairs; point estimates replace unusable intervals, without bias correction.

Discussion: best Table 6 residual F=.5939 (95% CI .5803–.6063); 220 failed objective cells; 8,279 specifications admit no circuit; 52.3% discard. Measurement asserted cheap relative to discovery without numerical comparison. Failed objectives cannot execute on canonical task; execution/retention problems documented, not headline.

Reproducibility: public commit tagged prereg-p1-confirmatory; one verified environment across 1,320 confirmatory cells; archive matches git tree 22/22 files; no GPU. One script: 36 checks, 0 failures, F checked three ways including brute-force pairs; another checks manuscript numeric tokens. Tables emitted directly; test suite has 343 tests.

Abstract: Study evaluates linear probes on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct for deception detection, focusing on generalization across 3 held-out OOD datasets. Projecting activations onto a small subset of PCs from the training distribution enables cross-domain transfer nearly matching probes trained directly on test distributions. An LLM judge scores PCs based on whether their most/least activating examples imply a transferable deception direction; probing highest-scoring PCs closes the baseline-to-oracle gap by 78% on Insider Trading Report and 25% on Sandbagging. Heavily weighted source-probe directions may encode source-specific surface features, while transferable directions encode the contrast more abstractly. Main conclusion: OOD probe robustness is largely determined by subspace selection.

Introduction: Linear probes may learn spurious correlations despite linear representation of concepts. Study uses source-domain PCA basis for deception probes on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, training on Roleplaying deception scenarios and evaluating on held-out Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, and Sandbagging. Contributions: (1) target-supervised greedy search finds a small transferable subspace of 8–15 source PCs where source-trained probes nearly match target-trained probes; (2) source- and target-side PC weight rankings fail to outperform the full-representation baseline; (3) an LLM judge partially recovers the transferable subspace without target data by selecting PCs likely to encode behavioral contrast rather than surface patterns.

Experiments: Source-trained full-representation baseline AUROC: Confirm 0.874, Report 0.706, Sandbagging 0.606. Target-trained probes within top-100 source-PC subspace (5-fold CV) achieve 0.936 / 0.950 / 0.869 across Report / Confirm / Sandbagging (order implied by target listing), showing the subspace contains sufficient target information. Greedy target-guided PC selection trains source probes on subsets, using target folds for selection and held-out target folds for evaluation; it stops when no candidate improves AUROC >0.001. Average selected PCs: Report 15, Confirm 8, Sandbagging 14. This is an upper bound, not unbiased OOD estimate. Greedy improves baseline by 0.22 (Report) and 0.23 (Sandbagging), nearly reaching target-trained performance; variance-top-k control matches greedy only on Confirm and lags on harder tasks. Section 4.3 tests whether greedy PCs are individually target-discriminative or simply heavily weighted by source probe. Rankings use absolute standardized coefficients (absolute coefficient × PC standard deviation) from probes trained on source-PCA projections.
