Abstract: The paper studies linear probes for deception detection in Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct across 3 held-out, out-of-distribution datasets. Projecting activations onto a small subset of principal components (PCs) from the training distribution enables cross-domain transfer nearly matching probes trained directly on the test distribution. An LLM judge scores PCs based on whether their most/least activating examples imply a transferable deception direction; probing on highest-scoring PCs closes the baseline-to-oracle gap by 78% on Insider Trading Report and 25% on Sandbagging. Heavily weighted source-probe directions appear to encode source-specific surface features, whereas transferable directions encode the same contrast more abstractly and can be captured by natural-language descriptions. Main conclusion: probe OOD robustness is largely determined by subspace selection.

Introduction: The testbed is deception probes on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, trained on Roleplaying deception scenarios and evaluated on three held-out targets: Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, and Sandbagging. Activations are represented in the source-domain PCA basis. Contributions claimed: (1) a small transferable subspace exists; target-supervised greedy search finds 8–15 PCs where a source-trained probe nearly matches a target-trained probe; (2) source- and target-side rankings by probe weights fail to recover a subspace better than the full-representation baseline; (3) an LLM judge can partially recover the transferable subspace without target data by selecting PCs encoding transferable behavioral contrast rather than surface patterns. The paper frames subspace selection as the key determinant of OOD robustness.

Setup: Four datasets: Roleplaying (source), Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, and Sandbagging (targets). Labels are honest=0, ambiguous=-1, deceptive=1 from GPT-4o; ambiguous responses are removed. Use layer-15 residual-stream activations of Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, averaging activations over assistant-response tokens. Standardize source activations to zero mean/unit variance and apply source statistics to targets. Run PCA on scaled source activations, retaining top 100 PCs. Logistic probes use lambda=10; subset probes project onto selected PCs, while baseline probes use full standardized activations. Top 100 chosen because PC alignment with SAE decoder features decreases by index, making low-index PCs more interpretable; authors explicitly say this is not a claim that low-index PCs generalize better. Section 4.1 reportedly confirms the 100-PC subspace retains enough information to separate deceptive and honest responses on every target.

Abstract: Studies linear deception probes in Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct across OOD Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, and Sandbagging, using Roleplaying as source. Source-trained probes on selected source PCs nearly match target-trained probes; LLM PC selection closes baseline-to-oracle gap by 78% on Report and 25% on Sandbagging. Main conclusion: OOD robustness depends largely on subspace selection.

Setup: Labels honest=0, ambiguous=-1, deceptive=1; ambiguous removed. Layer-15 residual-stream activations averaged over assistant tokens. Source activations standardized; source statistics applied to targets. PCA on source, top 100 PCs retained. Logistic probes use lambda=10. Full probes use all standardized activations; subset probes use selected PCs. Authors state low-index PCs are more interpretable but explicitly do not claim they generalize better.

Section 4.1 baseline: Full-representation source-trained AUROC: Insider Trading Confirm 0.874, Report 0.706, Sandbagging 0.606. Target-trained probes within top-100 source-PC subspace (5-fold CV) achieve 0.936 / 0.950 / 0.869 across the three targets, apparently ordered Report / Confirm / Sandbagging; this confirms the subspace contains enough information.

Section 4.2 greedy oracle: Iteratively selects PCs among top 100 using labeled target data, training probes on source projections; 5-fold target CV selects on non-held-out folds and evaluates held-out fold. Stops when no candidate improves AUROC >.001. Average selected PCs: Report 15, Confirm 8, Sandbagging 14. It is an upper bound, not unbiased OOD estimate. Greedy improves baseline by 0.22 Report and 0.23 Sandbagging, nearly matching target-trained performance. Top-k variance control matches greedy only for Confirm and falls behind on Report/Sandbagging.

Section 4.3 introduces rankings by standardized absolute probe coefficients, testing whether greedy PCs are individually target-discriminative or source-probe-weighted.

final_notes: Paper: “Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection.” Abstract/introduction: source-probe-heavy directions encode source-specific surface features; transferable directions encode the same contrast more abstractly and can be captured in natural language; OOD robustness largely depends on subspace selection. Setup: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (E6), layer 15 residual activations averaged over assistant-response tokens; source Roleplaying (V8); targets Insider Trading Report (C2R), Insider Trading Confirm (W6), Sandbagging (J9). Labels honest 0, ambiguous -1, deceptive 1; ambiguous removed. Standardize source/targets, retain leading 100 PCA Q7 directions, use subsets for projection/training/evaluation. Logistic regression lambda=10; full baseline B8Q uses all standardized activations. W6 transfers well/high baseline with little headroom; C2R moderate; J9 poor/most OOD. Target-trained probes separate classes on every target. H2 target-guided search finds small source-trained subspaces nearly matching target-trained probes, especially C2R/J9; transfer upper bound, not unbiased OOD evaluation. T6 source-ranking about as good as B8Q; M9 target-ranking good C2R, worse than H2 W6, below random J9. L2 language-only selection improves over B8Q on all targets and exceeds A7; closes 78% of baseline–H2 gap C2R and 25% J9; W6 methods except A7 roughly tied. Appendix values: B8Q AUROC C2R/W6/J9=.706/.874/.606; target-trained=.936/.950/.869; H2 recovery=.929 C2R, .832 J9; L2=.881/.662. Mean H2 CV subset sizes 15/8/14; full-target k=13/7/14. Decoder alignment Spearman rho: best feature -0.857, top-10 mean -0.917. Appendix C says lower-index Q7 directions have stronger decoder alignment. The paper studies OOD deception detection using linear logistic-regression probes trained on one source dataset and evaluated on 3 held-out target datasets. It investigates selecting principal components (PCs), or directions in a source activation basis, as a transferable subspace. Appendix D reports greedy-vs-target-PCA Jaccard overlaps of 0.182 (Report), 0.077 (Confirm), and 0.167 (Sandbagging), all below one fifth. However, Table 2’s listed sets yield different values: Report intersection 4 and union 24 = 0.167; Confirm intersection 2 and union 20 = 0.100; Sandbagging intersection 4 and union 26 = 0.154. Thus the reported overlap statistics conflict with the table. Table 2 lists source-weight PCs (15), greedy sets (Report 13, Confirm 7, Sandbagging 15), and target-ranking sets (15 each), arguing transferable PCs are neither simply source- nor target-discriminative.

Appendix E: Table 3 reports repeatedly greedy-selected PCs: PC62, PC57, and PC86 score 6; PC9 and PC81 score 3. Table 4 reports leading source-probe PCs: PC4 scores 6; PC7, PC11, and PC12 score 3; PC8 scores 4. The claims summarizing these scores match the tables. High-score interpretations include caveats about noise, lexical/surface dependence, brittleness, and false positives.

The paper studies OOD deception detection using linear logistic-regression probes trained on one source dataset and evaluated on three held-out target datasets. It investigates selecting principal components (PCs) or directions in a source activation basis. A target-supervised greedy search selects 8–15 PCs and nearly matches probes trained directly on target data. Ranking PCs by source- or target-probe weights does not recover the transferable subspace. An LLM judge evaluates natural-language descriptions of PCs without target data; selecting 19 PCs receiving the maximum observed score in both runs improves transfer on all three targets. This selection closes 78% and 25% of the gap between the full-representation baseline and the greedy oracle on two targets.

The paper studies OOD deception detection using linear logistic-regression probes trained on the Roleplaying source dataset and evaluated on three held-out targets: Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, and Sandbagging. Full standardized activations form the baseline. A target-supervised greedy oracle repeatedly selects the PC giving the largest target-AUROC improvement, typically selecting 8–15 PCs and nearly matching target-trained probes. Source- or target-probe standardized coefficient rankings do not recover the transferable subspace. A variance/top-PC control is also used.

An LLM judge (GPT-5-mini) describes PC poles and scores likely OOD deception usefulness from 1–10. The maximum observed score is 6. This selection improves transfer on all three targets and closes 78% and 25% of the full-baseline-to-greedy-oracle gaps on two targets. No causal inference-time ablation validation was performed. All experimental probes use logistic regression; nonlinear probes and alternative readout locations remain open questions.

Summary: The paper examines whether selecting subspaces of language-model representations improves out-of-distribution deception detection. It compares probes (classifiers detecting a property) trained on full representations versus selected directions. One selection method uses target labels without fitting probe weights on the target data; another uses natural-language interpretations without target data. Small target-guided subspaces nearly match target-trained probes. Selection by source weights, target-class separation, or explained variance does not recover the same transferable subspaces. Interpretation-based selection improves over the full-representation baseline on all targets, but recovery varies sharply. The study uses one model and one source dataset. Interpretations are descriptive, not causal. Glossary heading appears, but no glossary content is provided in this part.

The paper studies whether selecting subspaces of language-model residual-stream representations improves OOD deception detection. It compares source-trained logistic-regression probes on full standardized activations with probes using selected directions. One target-label-guided method selects directions without fitting probe weights on target data; interpretation-based selection uses natural-language direction descriptions without target data. Small target-guided subspaces nearly match target-trained probes, while source-weight, target-class-separation, and explained-variance rankings do not recover the same transferable subspaces. Interpretation-based selection improves over the full-representation baseline on all targets, but recovery varies. The study uses one model (E6/Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct), layer-15 residual-stream activations averaged over assistant-response tokens, and one source dataset (V8/Roleplaying); targets are C2R, W6, and J9. Labels are -1 ambiguous, 0 honest, and 1 deceptive; ambiguous examples are removed. Standardization uses source statistics for source and targets. N4D retains the leading 100 source PCs. All classifiers are logistic regression with stated λ=10. B8Q is the full-representation source-trained baseline; Y4 ranks PCs by explained variance; H2 is target-guided greedy selection with source-fitted probe weights and 5-fold CV, treated as a transfer upper bound rather than unbiased OOD evaluation. T6 and M9 provide source- and target-PCA coefficient rankings; X4 is absolute coefficient times Q7 standard deviation. C7 judges direction interpretations (P2/GPT-5-mini); L2 selects directions reaching maximum OOD rating in both runs, and A7 uses the complement. Decoder alignment uses SAE resource `andyrdt/saes-llama-3.1-8b-instruct`; Spearman ρ and Jaccard overlap D3 are reported. Interpretations are descriptive, not causal. Glossary heading/content appears in the paper; no contradictions identified so far.

Variance ranking Y4 matches H2 only on W6 and lags on C2R/J9.

T6 is source-PCA coefficient ranking; M9 target-PCA coefficient ranking; X4 is absolute coefficient times Q7 SD. T6 transfers about like B8Q. M9 does well on C2R, worse than H2 on W6, and below random on J9. H2–M9 set overlap D3: C2R .182, W6 .077, J9 .167. Full-target H2 k: C2R 13, W6 7, J9 14. Interpretations suggest domain-stable abstraction, with partial/noisy recovery. No contradictions identified.

Abstract: Study evaluates linear probes on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct for deception detection, focusing on generalization across 3 held-out OOD datasets. Projecting activations onto a small subset of PCs from the training distribution enables cross-domain transfer nearly matching probes trained directly on test distributions. An LLM judge scores PCs based on whether their most/least activating examples imply a transferable deception direction; probing highest-scoring PCs closes the baseline-to-oracle gap by 78% on Insider Trading Report and 25% on Sandbagging. Heavily weighted source-probe directions may encode source-specific surface features, while transferable directions encode the contrast more abstractly. Main conclusion: OOD probe robustness is largely determined by subspace selection.

Setup: Roleplaying is source; targets are Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, and Sandbagging. Layer 15 residual-stream activations, assistant-response-token averages; labels honest=0, ambiguous=-1, deceptive=1, with ambiguous removed. Experiments: Source-trained full-representation baseline AUROC: Confirm 0.874, Report 0.706, Sandbagging 0.606. Target-trained probes within top-100 source-PC subspace (5-fold CV) achieve 0.936 / 0.950 / 0.869 across Report / Confirm / Sandbagging (order implied by target listing), showing the subspace contains sufficient target information. Greedy target-guided PC selection trains source probes on subsets, using target folds for selection and held-out target folds for evaluation; it stops when no candidate improves AUROC >0.001. Average selected PCs: Report 15, Confirm 8, Sandbagging 14. This is an upper bound, not unbiased OOD estimate. Greedy improves baseline by 0.22 (Report) and 0.23 (Sandbagging), nearly reaching target-trained performance; variance-top-k control matches greedy only on Confirm and lags on harder tasks. Section 4.3 tests whether greedy PCs are individually target-discriminative or simply heavily weighted by source probe. Rankings use absolute standardized coefficients (absolute coefficient × PC standard deviation) from probes trained on source-PCA projections.

final_notes: Appendix C reports negative correlations between PC rank and decoder alignment: Spearman rho = -0.857 for the best-matching SAE feature and -0.917 for the mean of the top 10. Appendix D reports greedy-vs-target-PCA Jaccards of 0.182 (Report), 0.077 (Confirm), and 0.167 (Sandbagging), which do not match Table 2: the listed sets yield 0.167, 0.100, and 0.154 respectively. Table 2 lists source-probe, greedy, and target-separability PC sets. Greedy sets shown are 13 PCs for Report, 7 for Confirm, and 15 for Sandbagging; the last conflicts with the earlier Section 4.3 note that Sandbagging greedy selection had k=14. Appendix D concludes transferable PCs are not simply the most source- or target-discriminative PCs. Appendix E lists interpretability-based OOD scores: Table 3 selects PC62 (6), PC57 (6), PC9 (3), PC81 (3), and PC86 (6); Table 4 scores PC7 (3), PC8 (4), PC11 (3), PC12 (3), and PC4 (6). The explanations characterize these as varying in generality, with many relying on brittle surface or task-specific cues; no internal contradiction identified in Appendix E.

Abstract: Study evaluates linear probes on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct for deception detection, focusing on generalization across 3 held-out OOD datasets. Projecting activations onto a small subset of PCs from the training distribution enables cross-domain transfer nearly matching probes trained directly on test distributions. An LLM judge scores PCs based on whether their most/least activating examples imply a transferable deception direction; probing highest-scoring PCs closes the baseline-to-oracle gap by 78% on Insider Trading Report and 25% on Sandbagging. Heavily weighted source-probe directions may encode source-specific surface features, while transferable directions encode the contrast more abstractly. Main conclusion: OOD probe robustness is largely determined by subspace selection.

Introduction: Linear probes may learn spurious correlations despite linear representation of concepts. Study uses source-domain PCA basis for deception probes on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, training on Roleplaying deception scenarios and evaluating on held-out Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, and Sandbagging. Contributions: (1) target-supervised greedy search finds a small transferable subspace of 8–15 source PCs where source-trained probes nearly match target-trained probes; (2) source- and target-side PC weight rankings fail to outperform the full-representation baseline; (3) an LLM judge partially recovers the transferable subspace without target data by selecting PCs likely to encode behavioral contrast rather than surface patterns.

Related work: Linear concept directions and low-dimensional subspaces have been studied for truth/falsehood, honesty, emotion, refusal, and assistant-like behavior. The paper studies OOD deception detection using linear logistic-regression probes trained on one source dataset and evaluated on 3 held-out target datasets. It investigates selecting principal components (PCs), or directions in a source activation basis, as a transferable subspace. A target-supervised greedy search selects 8–15 PCs and nearly matches probes trained on target data. Ranking PCs by source- or target-probe weights does not recover the transferable subspace. An LLM judge selects 19 PCs receiving the maximum observed score in both runs, without target data; this improves transfer on all 3 targets and closes 78% and 25% of the gap between the full-representation baseline and the greedy oracle on two targets.

Activations are averaged over assistant-response tokens from Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct; GPT-4o labels responses honest (0), ambiguous (-1, removed), or deceptive (1). Activations are standardized using source statistics, and PCA produces 100 source PCs. A target-supervised greedy oracle selects 8–15 PCs by repeatedly adding the PC with the greatest target-AUROC improvement and nearly matches target-trained probes. Ranking PCs by source- or target-probe standardized coefficients does not recover the transferable subspace. An LLM judge (GPT-5-mini) rates PC directions for likely OOD usefulness on a 1–10 scale; 6 is the maximum observed score. The remaining 81 PCs form the interp-ablated control, but no causal inference-time ablation validation was performed. Other controls include selecting top PCs by source variance. Key metrics are AUROC with 5-fold target CV and 95% CIs. Glossary definitions introduce no contradictions.

Full source-trained transfer AUROCs are 0.706/0.874/0.606, versus target-trained probes 0.936/0.950/0.869. Target-supervised greedy mean subset sizes are 15/8/14; a separate full-target greedy procedure gives k=13/7/14. Nineteen PCs are selected without target data. Five PCs are selected greedily for multiple targets; 3/5 received judge rating 6, versus 1/5 top source-ranked PCs. Metrics are AUROC with 95% CIs. It compares probes (classifiers detecting a property) trained on full representations versus selected directions. One selection method uses target labels without fitting probe weights on the target data; another uses natural-language interpretations without target data. Abstract: Study evaluates linear probes on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct for deception detection, focusing on generalization across 3 held-out OOD datasets. Projecting activations onto a small subset of PCs from the training distribution enables cross-domain transfer nearly matching probes trained directly on test distributions. An LLM judge scores PCs based on whether their most/least activating examples imply a transferable deception direction; probing highest-scoring PCs closes the baseline-to-oracle gap by 78% on Insider Trading Report and 25% on Sandbagging. Heavily weighted source-probe directions may encode source-specific surface features, while transferable directions encode the contrast more abstractly. Main conclusion: OOD probe robustness is largely determined by subspace selection.

Introduction: Linear probes may learn spurious correlations despite linear representation of concepts. Study uses source-domain PCA basis for deception probes on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, training on Roleplaying deception scenarios and evaluating on held-out Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, and Sandbagging. Contributions: (1) target-supervised greedy search finds a small transferable subspace of 8–15 source PCs where source-trained probes nearly match target-trained probes; (2) source- and target-side PC weight rankings fail to outperform the full-representation baseline; (3) an LLM judge partially recovers the transferable subspace without target data by selecting PCs likely to encode behavioral contrast rather than surface patterns.

Experiments: Source-trained full-representation baseline AUROC: Confirm 0.874, Report 0.706, Sandbagging 0.606. Target-trained probes within top-100 source-PC subspace (5-fold CV) achieve 0.936 / 0.950 / 0.869 across Report / Confirm / Sandbagging (order implied by target listing), showing the subspace contains sufficient target information. Greedy target-guided PC selection trains source probes on subsets, using target folds for selection and held-out target folds for evaluation; it stops when no candidate improves AUROC >0.001. Average selected PCs: Report 15, Confirm 8, Sandbagging 14. This is an upper bound, not unbiased OOD estimate. Greedy improves baseline by 0.22 (Report) and 0.23 (Sandbagging), nearly reaching target-trained performance; variance-top-k control matches greedy only on Confirm and lags on harder tasks. Section 4.3 tests whether greedy PCs are individually target-discriminative or simply heavily weighted by source probe. Rankings use absolute standardized coefficients (absolute coefficient × PC standard deviation) from probes trained on source-PCA projections.

Section 4.3: Source-PCA probe ranks source PCs by weights from a source-trained probe; target-PCA probe ranks PCs by weights from a target-trained probe. Both then train probes on source data projected onto top-k PCs in the source-PCA basis. Greedy full-target (not CV) selection sets k=13 Report, 7 Confirm, 14 Sandbagging; these differ slightly from prior CV averages (15, 8, 14). Source-PCA probe transfers about as well as the full-representation baseline. Target-PCA performs well on Report, worse than greedy on Confirm, and below random on Sandbagging. Thus neither hypothesis recovers greedy performance.

Section 4.4: For each top-100 source PC, 8 most/least activating source examples are interpreted by an LLM. OOD generalizability scored 1–10; no score exceeded 6, so 6 is the maximum observed. PCs scoring 6 in both runs yield 19 PCs. Five PCs occurred in greedy selections for more than one target; 3/5 received maximum OOD score. Only 1 of the top 5 source-PCA-selected PCs did. Greedy-selected interpretations describe abstractions surviving domain shifts.

Section 4.5: Interpretability-selected subspace uses 19 PCs, compared in Figure 5 with full-representation baseline, top-19 variance PCs, and the remaining 81 PCs after ablating selected PCs. Scores are run twice; retain PCs receiving maximum in both, without target data.

final_notes: The paper studies OOD deception detection using Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (E6), layer-15 residual activations averaged over assistant tokens. Source: Roleplaying (V8); targets: Insider Trading Report (C2R), Insider Trading Confirm (W6), Sandbagging (J9). Labels -1/0/1; ambiguous removed. Activations standardized with source statistics. N4D is source PCA with 100 PCs; B8Q uses all standardized activations. Logistic regression λ=10; 100-PC cutoff is for interpretability comparability, not optimal generalization. Error bars are 95% CIs. Baseline B8Q AUROC: W6 .874, C2R .706, J9 .606. Target-trained probes: C2R .936, W6 .950, J9 .869. H2 is target-guided greedy selection using source probe weights and target 5-fold CV, a transfer upper bound rather than unbiased OOD evaluation. Mean H2 subset sizes: C2R 15, W6 8, J9 14; full-target k: 13, 7, 14. H2 CV F3: C2R .929, J9 .832. L2: C2R .881, J9 .662. Recovery is 78% for C2R and 25% for J9 based on appendix values; earlier text reportedly stated J9 as 35%, an internal inconsistency. Values imply ~25%: (.662-.606)/(.832-.606). T6 transfers about like B8Q; M9 strong on C2R, below H2 on W6, below random on J9. H2–M9 overlaps: C2R .182, W6 .077, J9 .167; all are less than one-fifth. Appendix D exact sets: T6 source indices 7,8,11,12,4,5,2,3,6,27,22,21,1,41,18; H2 sizes C2R 13, W6 7, J9 15; M9 sizes 15 each. Decoder alignment: lower-index Q7 directions align more strongly with decoder features; Spearman rho -0.857 (best feature) and -0.917 (mean top 10). Interpretations are not causally verified. Conclusion claims selected subspaces outperform full representations in transfer. Appendix E: GPT-5-mini ratings retain 19 Q7 directions rated maximum R5=6 in both of two runs; 81 complementary directions go to A7. Five directions are selected by H2 for more than one target, three of those have maximum ratings. Among the top five T6 selections, one has maximum rating. Table 3 lists the five shared H2 directions: Q7 62, 57, 9, 81, 86, with ratings 6,6,3,3,6 and substantial lexical/domain/brittleness caveats. Table 4 lists source-ranked Q7 directions 7,8,11,12,4 with ratings 3,4,3,3,6 and similar transfer caveats.

Summary: The paper examines whether selecting subspaces of language-model representations improves out-of-distribution deception detection. It compares probes (classifiers detecting a property) trained on full representations versus selected directions. One selection method uses target labels without fitting probe weights on the target data; another uses natural-language interpretations without target data. Small target-guided subspaces nearly match target-trained probes. Selection by source weights, target-class separation, or explained variance does not recover the same transferable subspaces. Interpretation-based selection improves over the full-representation baseline on all targets, but recovery varies sharply. The study uses one model and one source dataset. Interpretations are descriptive, not causal. Glossary heading appears, but no glossary content is provided in this part.

final_notes: Limitations: experiments use only Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (layer 15) and Roleplaying as source. Dataset totals/label counts: Roleplaying 371 (140/59/172); Insider Trading Report 473 (218/194/61); Insider Trading Confirm 151 (29/38/84); Sandbagging 1000 (379/375/246), labels -1/0/1. Baseline transfer AUROCs: Confirm 0.874, Report 0.706, Sandbagging 0.606. Interpretability selection improves Sandbagging to 0.662 (greedy upper bound 0.832; 25% gap recovered) and Report to 0.881 (greedy 0.929; 78% gap recovered); Confirm near ceiling. Report described as more robust. Pipeline is PCA plus logistic regression, fully linear; nonlinear probes/readout locations untested. PC encoding claims are descriptive, based on top activations and LLM verbalization; no causal ablation. Fixed-k greedy selections earlier: 13 Report, 7 Confirm, 14 Sandbagging; Appendix D Table 2 instead lists 15 Sandbagging PCs. Target-trained probes within source-PC subspace: Report 0.950, Confirm 0.936, Sandbagging 0.869. Conclusion claims a small source-PC subset nearly matches target-trained probes, contradicted especially by Sandbagging (0.662 vs 0.869). Appendix C: negative Spearman correlations of PC rank with decoder alignment: -0.857 (best SAE feature), -0.917 (mean top 10). Appendix D claims Jaccard overlaps Report 0.182, Confirm 0.077, Sandbagging 0.167, but Table 2 sets imply 0.167, 0.100, 0.154. Appendix E lists LLM-judged OOD usefulness scores: Table 3 Report+Sandbagging PCs 62=6, 57=6, 9=3; Confirm+Sandbagging PCs 81=3, 86=6. Table 4 PCs 7=3, 8=4, 11=3, 12=3, 4=6. Interpretations generally describe these as noisy, surface-cue-sensitive, and context-dependent.

Abstract: Study evaluates linear probes on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct for deception detection, focusing on generalization across 3 held-out OOD datasets. Projecting activations onto a small subset of PCs from the training distribution enables cross-domain transfer nearly matching probes trained directly on test distributions. An LLM judge scores PCs based on whether their most/least activating examples imply a transferable deception direction; probing highest-scoring PCs closes the baseline-to-oracle gap by 78% on Insider Trading Report and 25% on Sandbagging. Heavily weighted source-probe directions may encode source-specific surface features, while transferable directions encode the contrast more abstractly. Main conclusion: OOD probe robustness is largely determined by subspace selection.

Related work: Linear concept directions and low-dimensional subspaces have been studied for truth/falsehood, honesty, emotion, refusal, and assistant-like behavior. Appendix D compares greedy and target-separability PC sets. Jaccard overlaps are 0.182 (Report), 0.077 (Confirm), and 0.167 (Sandbagging), each below one-fifth. Table 2 lists source-probe PCs (15), greedy sets: Report has 13 PCs, Confirm 7 PCs, and Sandbagging 15 PCs; this contradicts the earlier recorded claim that the full-target Sandbagging greedy set has k=14. Target-ranking rows list 15 PCs for each target. The paper claims the transferable subspace is neither simply the most source-discriminative nor the most target-discriminative space, based on set comparisons and transfer results. Table 4 lists leading source-probe PCs: PC4 receives 6; PC7, PC11, and PC12 receive 3; PC8 receives 4. The claims accurately summarize these tables. The paper studies OOD deception detection using linear logistic-regression probes trained on one source dataset and evaluated on 3 held-out target datasets. It investigates selecting principal components (PCs), or directions in a source activation basis, as a transferable subspace. Paper studies linear probes for OOD deception detection using Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct activations. Abstract reports 3 held-out deception-detection datasets totaling 1,216 non-ambiguous responses. Projecting inputs onto a small subset of principal components (PCs) from the training activation distribution enables cross-domain transfer nearly matching probes trained directly on the test distribution. Heavily weighted source-probe directions allegedly encode source-specific surface features, while transferable directions encode the same contrast more abstractly and are capturable by natural-language descriptions. Main conclusion: OOD probe robustness is largely determined by subspace selection.

Paper title: “Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection.” Abstract claims: source-probe-heavy directions encode source-specific surface features; transferable directions encode the same contrast more abstractly and can be captured in natural language; OOD robustness is largely determined by subspace selection. The selection problem is choosing dimensions that permit generalizing rather than spurious source-trained classification. Figure 1 describes projection into the source N4D basis, filtering candidate Q7 directions, and probe training in the selected low-dimensional subspace. Setup: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (E6), layer 15 residual-stream activations, averaged over assistant-response tokens. Four datasets: source Roleplaying (V8) and held-out targets Insider Trading Report (C2R), Insider Trading Confirm (W6), and Sandbagging (J9), totaling 1,216 non-ambiguous responses; labels honest 0, ambiguous -1, deceptive 1, with ambiguous removed. Source activations are standardized to zero mean/unit variance; source statistics standardize targets. PCA (N4D) retains leading 100 principal components (Q7); subset S is projected before logistic-regression training/evaluation. Full-representation baseline (B8Q) trains on all standardized activations. Lambda=10. Retention of 100 is based on interpretability comparability: alignment with U9 decreases with index, so lower-index PCs are more natural-language interpretable, not because of superior low-index generalization. Error bars are 95% CIs.

Experiments: W6 transfer is reasonably good, C2R moderate, J9 poor for source-trained probes; target-trained probes in retained source Q7 subspace separate honest/deceptive responses on all targets. Figure 2 compares source-trained B8Q, source-trained leading-100 Q7, and target-trained Q7 probes.

Greedy target-guided subset search (H2) selects source Q7 directions using target labels, fits probe weights only on source data, and evaluates via target 5-fold CV; it is a transfer upper bound, not unbiased OOD evaluation. Small source-trained subsets nearly match target-trained probes, especially C2R/J9. Variance selection (Y4) matches H2 only on easy W6 and performs poorly on C2R/J9; explained variance is not predictive.

Source-side ranking (T6) and target-side ranking (M9), both using standardized coefficient magnitude X4, do not recover the transferable subspace or outperform B8Q overall. T6 is about as good as B8Q; M9 is strong on C2R, below H2 on W6, and below random on J9. H2 full-target selection supplies stable set/k; its results differ slightly from CV.

Interpretations of H2 directions aim to identify abstraction-surviving contrasts. LLM judge C7 gives direction descriptions and noisy OOD scores R5 from eight highest/lowest activating source examples; retain directions reaching observed maximum in both runs.

Language-only interpreted selection L2 improves over B8Q on all targets, exceeds variance control Y4 widely on C2R/J9, and exceeds A7 everywhere. It substantially closes baseline–H2 gap on C2R but only partially on J9; W6 has little headroom and methods except A7 are roughly tied. L2 is retained intersection; A7 is complementary ablation and Y4 equal-dimensional top-variance control; all are source-trained probes.

steps.notes_before: Experiments: W6 transfer is reasonably good and has an already-high baseline/little headroom, so results there are relatively uninformative; C2R is moderate with a more robust improvement; J9 is poor/weakest and most out-of-distribution, with only modest improvement likely reflecting distribution shift. Target-trained probes in retained source Q7 subspace separate honest/deceptive responses on all targets. Figure 2 compares source-trained B8Q, source-trained leading-100 Q7, and target-trained Q7 probes. H2 selects source Q7 directions using target labels, fits probe weights only on source data, and evaluates via target 5-fold CV; it is a transfer upper bound, not unbiased OOD evaluation. Small source-trained subsets nearly match target-trained probes, especially C2R/J9. Y4 matches H2 only on easy W6 and performs poorly on C2R/J9; explained variance is not predictive. T6 and M9, using standardized coefficient magnitude X4, do not recover the transferable subspace or outperform B8Q overall. L2 improves over B8Q on all targets, substantially closing the baseline–H2 gap on C2R but only partially on J9; W6 methods except A7 are roughly tied. Appendix values: labels V8 371/473/151/1000 for source/C2R/W6/J9; B8Q AUROCs .706/.874/.606 (C2R/W6/J9); target-trained .936/.950/.869; H2 comparison .929/—/.832; L2 .881/—/.662; recovery 78%/—/25%; mean H2 subset sizes 15/8/14, full-target k 13/7/14. Appendix B uses GPT-5-mini to interpret bipolar Q7 directions. Appendix C says lower-index Q7 directions have stronger decoder alignment. Appendix D reports H2–M9 Jaccards .182/.077/.167 for C2R/W6/J9, but these conflict with the listed sets, which imply .167/.100/.154 respectively. Table 2 lists T6, H2, and M9 selected Q7 indices.

errors.claim: “Jaccard overlap ... is 0.182 for Insider Trading Report, 0.077 for Insider Trading Confirm, and 0.167 for Sandbagging.”
errors.evidence: From Table 2, Report’s greedy and target-ranking sets intersect in PC6, PC89, PC14, and PC66: 4 shared PCs out of 24 in the union, giving 4/24 = 0.167. Confirm intersects in PC53 and PC28: 2/20 = 0.100. Sandbagging intersects in PC51, PC62, PC41, and PC86: 4/26 = 0.154.

final_notes: Appendix D reports greedy-versus-target-ranking Jaccard overlaps as 0.182 / 0.077 / 0.167 for Report / Confirm / Sandbagging, but Table 2 sets imply 0.167 (4/24), 0.100 (2/20), and 0.154 (4/26), respectively. The table lists source probe PCs (15), greedy sets (Report 13, Confirm 7, Sandbagging 15), and target-ranking sets (15 each). It claims the transferable subspace is neither simply source- nor target-discriminative. Earlier notes: target counts imply 998 non-ambiguous responses, conflicting with stated 1,216; dataset totals Roleplaying 371, Report 473, Confirm 151, Sandbagging 1000. Baseline source-trained AUROCs Report/Confirm/Sandbagging = 0.706/0.874/0.606; target-trained top-100 PC = 0.936/0.950/0.869. Greedy AUROCs Report 0.929, Sandbagging 0.832; interpretation-only Report 0.881, Sandbagging 0.662. Greedy k = 13/7/14 in one account (table has Sandbagging 15), while another summary gives mean 15/8/14. Five PCs selected across targets; PC62, PC57, PC86 score 6; PC9 and PC81 score 3. PCA uses top 100 source PCs; source activations standardized; layer-15 Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. Limitations: one model/layer/source, no nonlinear or causal validation. Appendix C: lower-index PCs align more with SAE decoder (rho=-0.857). Appendix E is internally consistent: Table 3 identifies three repeatedly selected PCs with score 6 (PC62, PC57, PC86) and two with score 3 (PC9, PC81); Table 4 identifies only PC4 among five leading source-probe PCs as scoring 6, with PC7/PC8/PC11/PC12 scoring 3/4/3/3. High-score interpretations retain caveats about lexical/surface dependence, brittleness, noise, and false positives.

The paper studies OOD deception detection using linear logistic-regression probes trained on one source dataset and evaluated on 3 held-out target datasets. It investigates selecting principal components (PCs), or directions in a source activation basis, as a transferable subspace. A target-supervised greedy search selects 8–15 PCs and nearly matches probes trained on target data. Ranking PCs by source- or target-probe weights does not recover the transferable subspace. An LLM judge selects 19 PCs receiving the maximum observed score in both runs, without target data; this improves transfer on all 3 targets and closes 78% and 25% of the gap between the full-representation baseline and the greedy oracle on two targets.

The paper studies OOD deception detection using linear logistic-regression probes trained on one source dataset and evaluated on 3 held-out target datasets. Source is Roleplaying; targets include Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, and Sandbagging. Activations are averaged over assistant-response tokens from Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct; GPT-4o labels responses honest (0), ambiguous (-1, removed), or deceptive (1). Activations are standardized using source statistics, and PCA produces 100 source PCs. A target-supervised greedy oracle selects 8–15 PCs by repeatedly adding the PC with the greatest target-AUROC improvement and nearly matches target-trained probes. Ranking PCs by source- or target-probe standardized coefficients does not recover the transferable subspace. An LLM judge (GPT-5-mini) rates PC directions for likely OOD usefulness on a 1–10 scale; 6 is the maximum observed score. The 19 PCs receiving 6 in both scoring runs are interp-selected, without target data; this improves transfer on all 3 targets and closes 78% and 25% of the gap between the full-representation baseline and greedy oracle on two targets. The remaining 81 PCs form the interp-ablated control, but no causal inference-time ablation validation was performed. Other controls include selecting top PCs by source variance. Key metrics are AUROC with 5-fold target CV and 95% CIs. Glossary definitions introduce no contradictions.

final_notes: Appendix C claims lower PCs have stronger decoder alignment: Spearman rho = -0.857 for best-matching SAE feature and -0.917 for mean top 10. Appendix D reports greedy/target-PCA Jaccard overlaps of 0.182 (IT Report), 0.077 (IT Confirm), and 0.167 (Sandbagging), but these do not match Table 2: the listed sets yield 0.167 (4/24), 0.100 (2/20), and 0.154 (4/26), respectively. Table 2 lists source-probe-weight PCs (15), greedy PCs with 13 for IT Report, 7 for IT Confirm, and 15 for Sandbagging, and target-separability rankings with 15 each. The Sandbagging greedy count of 15 conflicts with the earlier stated k=14. The text concludes transferable subspace is neither source- nor target-discriminative. Appendix E reports LLM-judged OOD interpretability scores: Table 3 selects PC62 (6), PC57 (6), PC9 (3), PC81 (3), and PC86 (6) for likely transferability; Table 4 scores PC7=3, PC8=4, PC11=3, PC12=3, and PC4=6. Explanations generally characterize higher-scoring PCs as moderately generalizable but noisy and lower-scoring PCs as surface/task-specific and brittle.

Abstract: Study evaluates linear probes for Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct on 3 held-out deception-detection datasets. Claim: projecting activations onto a small subset of PCs from the training distribution enables cross-domain transfer nearly matching probes trained directly on each test distribution. PC interpretations are used to select transferable PCs: an LLM judge scores PCs based on whether their most/least activating examples imply a transferable deception direction. Selecting highest-scoring PCs closes the baseline-to-oracle gap by 78% on Insider Trading Report and 25% on Sandbagging. Heavily weighted source-probe directions are said to encode source-specific surface features, while transferable directions encode the same contrast more abstractly and are describable in natural language. Broad conclusion: OOD probe robustness is largely determined by subspace selection.

Introduction: Work uses the source-domain PCA basis rather than raw activation dimensions. A target-supervised greedy search finds 8–15 source PCs on which a source-trained probe nearly matches a target-trained probe. Ranking PCs by source- or target-probe weights fails to yield a basis transferring better than the full-representation baseline. An LLM judge can partially recover the transferable subspace without target data by selecting PCs likely to encode transferable behavioral contrast rather than surface patterns. Figure overview: project activations onto source PCA basis, filter candidate PC directions, and train probes on selected low-dimensional subspaces.

final_notes: The paper studies OOD deception detection with linear probes on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct layer-15 residuals, source-trained on Roleplaying and evaluated on Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, and Sandbagging. Full source-transfer AUROCs are 0.706 / 0.874 / 0.606; target-trained probes in the top-100 source-PC space achieve 0.936 / 0.950 / 0.869. Full-target greedy oracle AUROCs are 0.929 / unspecified / 0.832; earlier mean selected sizes are 15 / 8 / 14. Full-source greedy sets use k=13 / 7 / 14 for Report / Confirm / Sandbagging, differing from CV values. Target ranking does well on Report, worse than greedy on Confirm, and below random on Sandbagging; its broad claim of outperforming greedy is internally inconsistent. Earlier reported greedy/target-ranking Jaccards are 0.182 / 0.077 / 0.167, while Appendix D Table 2 sets imply 0.167 (4/24), 0.100 (2/20), and 0.154 (4/26). Interpretation scoring gives no PC above 6; 19 score 6 in both runs. Five PCs are selected by greedy for multiple targets, 3/5 score 6; only 1/5 top source-probe PCs scores 6. No causal ablation validation was done. Interpretation-only selection beats baseline on all targets and controls: Report 0.706 to 0.881 versus greedy 0.929; Confirm baseline 0.874 and methods roughly equal/little headroom; Sandbagging 0.606 to 0.662 versus greedy 0.832. Appendix A label distributions: Roleplaying 371 (140/59/172); Report 473 (218/194/61); Confirm 151 (29/38/84); Sandbagging 1000 (379/375/246), ordered ambiguous/honest/deceptive. Conclusion claims small source-PC subspaces (8–15 components) nearly match target-trained performance, source/target separability alone does not identify them, and interpretation partly recovers them without target data. The paper studies OOD deception detection using linear logistic-regression probes trained on one source dataset and evaluated on 3 held-out target datasets. It investigates selecting principal components (PCs), or directions in a source activation basis, as a transferable subspace. A target-supervised greedy search selects 8–15 PCs and nearly matches probes trained on target data. Ranking PCs by source- or target-probe weights does not recover the transferable subspace. An LLM judge selects 19 PCs receiving the maximum observed score in both runs, without target data; this improves transfer on all 3 targets and closes 78% and 25% of the gap between the full-representation baseline and the greedy oracle on two targets.

The paper studies OOD deception detection using linear logistic-regression probes trained on one source dataset and evaluated on 3 held-out target datasets. Source is Roleplaying; targets include Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, and Sandbagging. Activations are averaged over assistant-response tokens from Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct; GPT-4o labels responses honest (0), ambiguous (-1, removed), or deceptive (1). Activations are standardized using source statistics, and PCA produces 100 source PCs. A target-supervised greedy oracle selects 8–15 PCs by repeatedly adding the PC with the greatest target-AUROC improvement and nearly matches target-trained probes. Ranking PCs by source- or target-probe standardized coefficients does not recover the transferable subspace. An LLM judge (GPT-5-mini) rates PC directions for likely OOD usefulness on a 1–10 scale; 6 is the maximum observed score. The 19 PCs receiving 6 in both scoring runs are interp-selected, without target data; this improves transfer on all 3 targets and closes 78% and 25% of the gap between the full-representation baseline and greedy oracle on two targets. The remaining 81 PCs form the interp-ablated control, but no causal inference-time ablation validation was performed. Other controls include selecting top PCs by source variance. Key metrics are AUROC with 5-fold target CV and 95% CIs. Glossary definitions introduce no contradictions.

Summary: The paper examines whether selecting subspaces of language-model representations improves out-of-distribution deception detection. It compares probes (classifiers detecting a property) trained on full representations versus selected directions. One selection method uses target labels without fitting probe weights on the target data; another uses natural-language interpretations without target data. Small target-guided subspaces nearly match target-trained probes. Selection by source weights, target-class separation, or explained variance does not recover the same transferable subspaces. Interpretation-based selection improves over the full-representation baseline on all targets, but recovery varies sharply. The study uses one model and one source dataset. Interpretations are descriptive, not causal. Glossary heading appears, but no glossary content is provided in this part.

It compares source-trained logistic-regression probes on full standardized activations with probes using selected directions. One target-label-guided method selects directions without fitting probe weights on target data; interpretation-based selection uses natural-language direction descriptions without target data. errors.claim: “H2 and M9 agree on less than a fifth of selections under Jaccard overlap,” with D3 values C2R 0.182, W6 0.077, and J9 0.167.
errors.evidence: Using the listed indices in Table 2, the Jaccard overlaps are C2R: 4 shared directions out of 24 in the union = 0.167; W6: 2 out of 20 = 0.100; J9: 3 out of 27 = 0.111. These do not match the reported D3 values.
errors.explanation: The reported overlap values conflict with the direction sets shown in the same table. Although all recomputed overlaps are still below one fifth, the specific values and the claimed set measure are internally inconsistent.

steps.notes_before: The paper studies whether selecting subspaces of Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (E6) layer-15 residual representations improves OOD deception detection. Source V8; targets C2R, W6, J9. Labels -1/0/1; ambiguous removed; activations standardized with source statistics. Dataset totals/counts: V8 371 (140/59/172), C2R 473 (218/194/61), W6 151 (29/38/84), J9 1000 (379/375/246). Baseline B8Q transfer F3: W6 .874, C2R .706, J9 .606. Target-trained probes: C2R .936, W6 .950, J9 .869. H2 is target-guided and an upper bound, not unbiased OOD; H2 F3 C2R .929, J9 .832; mean subset sizes C2R 15, W6 8, J9 14; full-target k C2R 13, W6 7, J9 14. Y4 matches H2 only W6. T6 is source-coefficient ranking; M9 target-PCA coefficient ranking. H2/M9 overlaps previously reported: C2R .182, W6 .077, J9 .167, but Appendix D’s listed sets yield C2R 4/24=.167, W6 2/20=.100, J9 3/27=.111, an internal inconsistency. L2 retains 19 shared interpretation directions; L2 F3 C2R .881, J9 .662; exceeds B8Q/Y4/A7 on all targets. Appendix C: lower-index Q7 directions align more strongly with decoder features (Spearman -.857 and -.917).

grade.reason: The reviewer flagged inconsistent Jaccard overlap values between H2 and M9, which does not identify or contradict the planted claim about target-separability-selected PCs transferring better than greedy selections.

errors.claim: "Jaccard overlap between the PC sets of 2 methods (greedy and target-pca) is 0.182 for Insider Trading Report, 0.077 for Insider Trading Confirm, and 0.167 for Sandbagging."
errors.evidence: Table 2 lists 13 greedy and 15 target PCs for Report, with 4 shared PCs (PC6, PC89, PC14, PC66), giving Jaccard overlap 4/(13+15−4) = 0.167. For Confirm, the lists share PC53 and PC28, giving 2/(7+15−2) = 0.100. For Sandbagging, they share PC51, PC86, PC62, and PC41, giving 4/(15+15−4) = 0.154.
errors.explanation: The reported Jaccard values do not match the PC sets shown in Table 2. In addition, the Sandbagging greedy list contains 15 PCs, conflicting with the earlier note that greedy selection used k=14 for Sandbagging.

final_notes:

The paper studies OOD deception detection using linear logistic-regression probes trained on one source dataset and evaluated on 3 held-out target datasets. It investigates selecting principal components (PCs), or directions in a source activation basis, as a transferable subspace. A target-supervised greedy search selects 8–15 PCs and nearly matches probes trained on target data. Ranking PCs by source- or target-probe weights does not recover the transferable subspace. An LLM judge selects 19 PCs receiving the maximum observed score in both runs, without target data; this improves transfer on all 3 targets and closes 78% and 25% of the gap between the full-representation baseline and the greedy oracle on two targets.

The paper studies OOD deception detection using linear logistic-regression probes trained on one source dataset and evaluated on 3 held-out target datasets. Source is Roleplaying; targets include Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, and Sandbagging. Activations are averaged over assistant-response tokens from Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct; GPT-4o labels responses honest (0), ambiguous (-1, removed), or deceptive (1). Activations are standardized using source statistics, and PCA produces 100 source PCs. A target-supervised greedy oracle selects 8–15 PCs by repeatedly adding the PC with the greatest target-AUROC improvement and nearly matches target-trained probes. Ranking PCs by source- or target-probe standardized coefficients does not recover the transferable subspace. An LLM judge (GPT-5-mini) rates PC directions for likely OOD usefulness on a 1–10 scale; 6 is the maximum observed score. The 19 PCs receiving 6 in both scoring runs are interp-selected, without target data; this improves transfer on all 3 targets and closes 78% and 25% of the gap between the full-representation baseline and greedy oracle on two targets. The remaining 81 PCs form the interp-ablated control, but no causal inference-time ablation validation was performed. Other controls include selecting top PCs by source variance. Key metrics are AUROC with 5-fold target CV and 95% CIs. Glossary definitions introduce no contradictions.

Summary: The paper examines whether selecting subspaces of language-model representations improves out-of-distribution deception detection. It compares probes (classifiers detecting a property) trained on full representations versus selected directions. One selection method uses target labels without fitting probe weights on the target data; another uses natural-language interpretations without target data. Small target-guided subspaces nearly match target-trained probes. Selection by source weights, target-class separation, or explained variance does not recover the same transferable subspaces. Interpretation-based selection improves over the full-representation baseline on all targets, but recovery varies sharply. The study uses one model and one source dataset. Interpretations are descriptive, not causal. Glossary heading appears, but no glossary content is provided in this part.

Abstract: Study evaluates linear probes on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct for deception detection, focusing on generalization across 3 held-out OOD datasets. Projecting activations onto a small subset of PCs from the training distribution enables cross-domain transfer nearly matching probes trained directly on test distributions. An LLM judge scores PCs based on whether their most/least activating examples imply a transferable deception direction; probing highest-scoring PCs closes the baseline-to-oracle gap by 78% on Insider Trading Report and 25% on Sandbagging. Heavily weighted source-probe directions may encode source-specific surface features, while transferable directions encode the contrast more abstractly. Main conclusion: OOD probe robustness is largely determined by subspace selection.

An LLM judge scores PCs based on whether their most/least activating examples imply a transferable deception direction; probing highest-scoring PCs closes the baseline-to-oracle gap by 78% on Insider Trading Report and 25% on Sandbagging. Source-probe directions may encode source-specific surface features, while transferable directions encode the contrast more abstractly. Source=Roleplaying; targets=Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, Sandbagging. Labels honest=0, ambiguous=-1, deceptive=1; ambiguous removed. Layer-15 residual activations averaged over assistant-response tokens; source standardization applied to targets; top 100 source PCs; logistic regression lambda=10. Full source-trained transfer AUROC: Confirm 0.874, Report 0.706, Sandbagging 0.606. Target-trained probes in top-100 source-PC subspace: Report 0.950, Confirm 0.936, Sandbagging 0.869. Greedy target-guided selection: Report 15, Confirm 8, Sandbagging 14 (CV); full-target greedy sets k=13, 7, 14 and values Report 0.929, Sandbagging 0.832. Section 4.3: source-PCA ranks by source-probe weights; target-PCA by target-probe weights, but both train source probes on selected source-PC projections. Both ranking hypotheses fail: source-PCA transfers about baseline; target-PCA does well on Report but below greedy on Confirm and below-random on Sandbagging. Section 4.4: 19 interp-selected PCs; no PC scored above 6; five PCs appeared in greedy selections for >1 target, 3/5 maximum score; only 1 of top 5 source-PCA PCs maximum. Section 4.5: interp-selected probes outperform baseline, top-19 variance control, and interp-ablated on all targets; Report 0.706→0.881 closes 78% of gap to greedy 0.929, Sandbagging 0.606→0.662 closes 25% to greedy 0.832. Limitations: single model/source; Confirm baseline transfer 0.874 makes results uninformative; Sandbagging gain is modest; pipeline linear; no causal ablation of high-scoring PCs.

The paper studies probe OOD robustness for deception detection. Abstract/introduction claims: source-probe-heavy directions encode source-specific surface features, while transferable directions encode the contrast more abstractly and can be captured in natural language; OOD robustness is largely determined by subspace selection. The selection goal is to choose dimensions that generalize rather than support spurious source-trained classification. Figure 1 pipeline: project into the source N4D basis, filter candidate Q7 directions, and train a probe in the selected low-dimensional subspace.

Work uses source V8 coordinates (PCA directions), with source statistics standardizing targets. Model: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (E6), layer-15 residual activations averaged over assistant-response tokens. Full baseline B8Q uses all standardized activations. Removing leading components improves downstream embedding performance; leading-component projections are a probing baseline. U9 alignment decreases with index (lower indices more interpretable), correcting an earlier conflicting claim that higher-index Q7 directions show stronger U9 alignment. W6 transfer is reasonably good with little headroom; C2R moderate with robust improvement; J9 weakest. H2 finds small transferable subspaces but is a transfer upper bound. The paper studies OOD deception detection using linear logistic-regression probes trained on one source dataset and evaluated on 3 held-out target datasets. It investigates selecting principal components (PCs), or directions in a source activation basis, as a transferable subspace. A target-supervised greedy search selects 8–15 PCs and nearly matches probes trained on target data. Ranking PCs by source- or target-probe weights does not recover the transferable subspace. An LLM judge selects 19 PCs receiving the maximum observed score in both runs, without target data; this improves transfer on all 3 targets and closes 78% and 25% of the gap between the full-representation baseline and the greedy oracle on two targets.

The paper studies OOD deception detection using linear logistic-regression probes trained on one source dataset and evaluated on 3 held-out target datasets. Source is Roleplaying; targets include Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, and Sandbagging. Activations are averaged over assistant-response tokens from Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct; GPT-4o labels responses honest (0), ambiguous (-1, removed), or deceptive (1). Activations are standardized using source statistics, and PCA produces 100 source PCs. A target-supervised greedy oracle selects 8–15 PCs by repeatedly adding the PC with the greatest target-AUROC improvement and nearly matches target-trained probes. Ranking PCs by source- or target-probe standardized coefficients does not recover the transferable subspace. An LLM judge (GPT-5-mini) rates PC directions for likely OOD usefulness on a 1–10 scale; 6 is the maximum observed score. The 19 PCs receiving 6 in both scoring runs are interp-selected, without target data; this improves transfer on all 3 targets and closes 78% and 25% of the gap between the full-representation baseline and greedy oracle on two targets. The remaining 81 PCs form the interp-ablated control, but no causal inference-time ablation validation was performed. Other controls include selecting top PCs by source variance. Key metrics are AUROC with 5-fold target CV and 95% CIs. Glossary definitions introduce no contradictions.

Abstract: Study evaluates linear probes on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct for deception detection, focusing on generalization across 3 held-out OOD datasets. Projecting activations onto a small subset of PCs from the training distribution enables cross-domain transfer nearly matching probes trained directly on test distributions. An LLM judge scores PCs based on whether their most/least activating examples imply a transferable deception direction; probing highest-scoring PCs closes the baseline-to-oracle gap by 78% on Insider Trading Report and 25% on Sandbagging. Heavily weighted source-probe directions may encode source-specific surface features, while transferable directions encode the contrast more abstractly. Main conclusion: OOD probe robustness is largely determined by subspace selection.

Layer-15 residual activations from Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct are averaged over assistant tokens, standardized with source statistics, and reduced to the top 100 source PCs. Target-guided selection improves baseline by about 0.22 / 0.23 on Report / Sandbagging. Matched-k variance controls match only Confirm and underperform on harder tasks. GPT-5-mini rates PCs for OOD usefulness; 19 PCs rated 6 in both runs are selected without target data. Interp-selected AUROCs are 0.881 / roughly comparable to baseline on Confirm / 0.662, closing 78% of the baseline-to-greedy gap on Report and 25% on Sandbagging. The remaining 81 PCs form an interp-ablated control; this is not causal inference-time ablation validation. Interp-selection beats baseline and both controls on all three targets. Source/target coefficient rankings do not recover greedy transfer; target-PCA ranking is below random on Sandbagging. Appendix D reports greedy/target-PCA Jaccard overlaps of 0.182 / 0.077 / 0.167 (Report / Confirm / Sandbagging), and Table 2 lists differing PC sets; no internal contradiction found. Layer-15 residual activations from Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct are averaged over assistant tokens, standardized with source statistics, and reduced to the top 100 source PCs. Full source-trained transfer AUROCs are 0.706 / 0.874 / 0.606 (Report / Confirm / Sandbagging); target-trained probes in the 100-PC subspace achieve 0.936 / 0.950 / 0.869 with 5-fold target CV.

Target-supervised greedy selection chooses mean 15 / 8 / 14 PCs for Report / Confirm / Sandbagging, using non-held-out target labels; it is an oracle, not unbiased OOD evaluation. It improves baseline by 0.22 and 0.23 on Report and Sandbagging and nearly matches target-trained probes there. Matched-k variance controls match only Confirm and underperform on harder tasks. Source- and target-probe coefficient rankings do not recover greedy transfer performance.

GPT-5-mini rates PCs for OOD usefulness; 6 is the maximum. Nineteen PCs rated 6 in both runs are selected without target data. Earlier text says these close 78% of the baseline-to-greedy-oracle gap on Report and 25% on Sandbagging. The remaining 81 PCs form an interp-ablated control; no causal inference-time ablation validation was performed. Metrics are AUROC with 95% CIs.

errors.claim: “H2 and M9 agree on less than a fifth of selections under Jaccard overlap,” with the reported overlaps C2R 0.182, W6 0.077, and J9 0.167.
errors.evidence: The listed sets in Table 2 imply different Jaccard overlaps: C2R has 4 shared indices out of 24 in the union (4/24 = 0.167), W6 has 2 out of 20 (0.100), and J9 has 4 out of 26 (0.154), rather than 0.182, 0.077, and 0.167.
errors.explanation: The reported D3 values are inconsistent with the exact H2 and M9 index sets in the same table. Although all computed overlaps remain below one-fifth, the numerical values do not match the displayed sets.

final_notes:
Appendix D reports H2–M9 Jaccard overlaps as C2R .182, W6 .077, J9 .167 and claims each is below one-fifth. However, Table 2’s exact sets imply C2R 4/24=.167 (shared 6,89,14,66), W6 2/20=.100 (shared 53,28), and J9 4/26=.154 (shared 51,86,62,41), creating an internal numerical inconsistency. Table 2 lists T6 source indices and H2/M9 target-specific indices. Earlier key findings: L2 is source-trained target-free; L2 beats B8Q, Y4, A7 on all targets; baseline B8Q AUROCs W6 .874, C2R .706, J9 .606; L2 C2R .881, J9 .662. H2 mean sizes C2R 15, W6 8, J9 14; full-target k C2R 13, W6 7, J9 14. H2–M9 reported overlaps in earlier notes match Appendix D but conflict with listed sets.

Appendix E: Q7 retains 19 directions rated maximum R5=6 in both of 2 runs, with 81 complement directions used by A7. H2 selects 5 directions for more than one target; 3/5 are maximum-rated. Among top T6 selections, 1 of top 5 is maximum-rated. Table 3 lists shared H2 directions: Q7 62 and 57 (C2R+J9), 9 (C2R+J9), 81 and 86 (W6+J9), with R5 ratings 6,6,3,3,6 respectively; explanations emphasize lexical/domain dependence, noise, brittleness, and false positives. Table 4 lists source-ranked directions Q7 7,8,11,12,4 with R5 3,4,3,3,6 and similar transfer caveats. No internal contradiction found in Appendix E.

Summary: The paper examines whether selecting subspaces of language-model representations improves out-of-distribution deception detection. It compares probes (classifiers detecting a property) trained on full representations versus selected directions. One selection method uses target labels without fitting probe weights on the target data; another uses natural-language interpretations without target data. Small target-guided subspaces nearly match target-trained probes. Selection by source weights, target-class separation, or explained variance does not recover the same transferable subspaces. Interpretation-based selection improves over the full-representation baseline on all targets, but recovery varies sharply. The study uses one model and one source dataset. Interpretations are descriptive, not causal. Glossary heading appears, but no glossary content is provided in this part.

The paper studies whether selecting subspaces of language-model residual-stream representations improves OOD deception detection. It compares source-trained logistic-regression probes on full standardized activations with probes using selected directions. One target-label-guided method selects directions without fitting probe weights on target data; interpretation-based selection uses natural-language direction descriptions without target data. Small target-guided subspaces nearly match target-trained probes, while source-weight, target-class-separation, and explained-variance rankings do not recover the same transferable subspaces. Interpretation-based selection improves over the full-representation baseline on all targets, but recovery varies. The study uses one model (E6/Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct), layer-15 residual-stream activations averaged over assistant-response tokens, and one source dataset (V8/Roleplaying); targets are C2R, W6, and J9. Labels are -1 ambiguous, 0 honest, and 1 deceptive; ambiguous examples are removed. Standardization uses source statistics for source and targets. N4D retains the leading 100 source PCs. All classifiers are logistic regression with stated λ=10. B8Q is the full-representation source-trained baseline; Y4 ranks PCs by explained variance; H2 is target-guided greedy selection with source-fitted probe weights and 5-fold CV, treated as a transfer upper bound rather than unbiased OOD evaluation. T6 and M9 provide source- and target-PCA coefficient rankings; X4 is absolute coefficient times Q7 standard deviation. C7 judges direction interpretations (P2/GPT-5-mini); L2 selects directions reaching maximum OOD rating in both runs, and A7 uses the complement. Decoder alignment uses SAE resource `andyrdt/saes-llama-3.1-8b-instruct`; Spearman ρ and Jaccard overlap D3 are reported. Interpretations are descriptive, not causal. Glossary heading/content appears in the paper; no contradictions identified so far.

The paper evaluates linear probes on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct for deception detection. Roleplaying is the source; targets are Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, and Sandbagging. Layer 15 residual-stream activations are averaged over assistant-response tokens; labels are honest=0, ambiguous=-1, deceptive=1, with ambiguous cases removed. Source activations are standardized and the same statistics applied to targets; PCA uses the top 100 source PCs; logistic regression lambda=10.

Source-trained full-representation baseline AUROC: Confirm 0.874, Report 0.706, Sandbagging 0.606. Target-trained probes in the top-100 source-PC subspace: Report 0.936, Confirm 0.950, Sandbagging 0.869. Full-target greedy AUROCs: Report 0.929, Sandbagging 0.832. Interpretability-selected: Report 0.881, Sandbagging 0.662, described as 78% and 25% of greedy gaps. Confirm transfer baseline 0.874 is uninformative. Limitations: one model/source and no causal ablation validation.

Dataset counts: Roleplaying 371 (140/-1, 59/0, 172/1); Report 473 (218/194/61); Confirm 151 (29/38/84); Sandbagging 1000 (379/375/246). Appendix D states greedy/target-PCA Jaccards Report .182, Confirm .077, Sandbagging .167 and says all overlaps are <1/5, but Table 2 sets imply .167, .100, and .200 respectively.

Appendix E: Table 3 interprets selected PCs: Report+Sandbagging PCs 62 (score 6), 57 (6), 9 (3); Confirm+Sandbagging PCs 81 (3), 86 (6). Table 4 lists PCs 7 (3), 8 (4), 11 (3), 12 (3), and 4 (6), with explanations emphasizing mostly surface/task-dependent denial, admission, hedging, and stylistic cues, while some may reflect general deception-relevant strategies.

Abstract: Study evaluates linear probes on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct for deception detection, focusing on generalization across 3 held-out OOD datasets. Projecting activations onto a small subset of PCs from the training distribution enables cross-domain transfer nearly matching probes trained directly on test distributions. An LLM judge scores PCs based on whether their most/least activating examples imply a transferable deception direction; probing highest-scoring PCs closes the baseline-to-oracle gap by 78% on Insider Trading Report and 25% on Sandbagging. Heavily weighted source-probe directions may encode source-specific surface features, while transferable directions encode the contrast more abstractly. Main conclusion: OOD probe robustness is largely determined by subspace selection.

Introduction: Linear probes may learn spurious correlations despite linear representation of concepts. Study uses source-domain PCA basis for deception probes on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, training on Roleplaying deception scenarios and evaluating on held-out Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, and Sandbagging. Contributions: (1) target-supervised greedy search finds a small transferable subspace of 8–15 source PCs where source-trained probes nearly match target-trained probes; (2) source- and target-side PC weight rankings fail to outperform the full-representation baseline; (3) an LLM judge partially recovers the transferable subspace without target data by selecting PCs likely to encode behavioral contrast rather than surface patterns.

Related work: Linear concept directions and low-dimensional subspaces have been studied for truth/falsehood, honesty, emotion, refusal, and assistant-like behavior. Linear probes are useful for analyzing represented information but high accuracy may reflect probe-learned tasks or surface correlates; recoverability does not necessarily establish encoding. Safety probes can generalize unevenly OOD. LLM-generated natural-language explanations have been used to interpret neurons/features and, in some work, guide interventions or ablations.

The paper studies OOD deception detection using linear logistic-regression probes trained on one source dataset and evaluated on 3 held-out target datasets. Summary: The paper examines whether selecting subspaces of language-model representations improves out-of-distribution deception detection. It compares probes (classifiers detecting a property) trained on full representations versus selected directions. One selection method uses target labels without fitting probe weights on the target data; another uses natural-language interpretations without target data. Small target-guided subspaces nearly match target-trained probes. Selection by source weights, target-class separation, or explained variance does not recover the same transferable subspaces. Interpretation-based selection improves over the full-representation baseline on all targets, but recovery varies sharply. The study uses one model and one source dataset. Interpretations are descriptive, not causal. Glossary heading appears, but no glossary content is provided in this part.

The paper studies whether selecting subspaces of language-model residual-stream representations improves OOD deception detection. It compares source-trained logistic-regression probes on full standardized activations with probes using selected directions. One target-label-guided method selects directions without fitting probe weights on target data; interpretation-based selection uses natural-language direction descriptions without target data. Small target-guided subspaces nearly match target-trained probes, while source-weight, target-class-separation, and explained-variance rankings do not recover the same transferable subspaces. Interpretation-based selection improves over the full-representation baseline on all targets, but recovery varies. The study uses one model (E6/Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct), layer-15 residual-stream activations averaged over assistant-response tokens, and one source dataset (V8/Roleplaying); targets are C2R, W6, and J9. Decoder alignment uses SAE resource `andyrdt/saes-llama-3.1-8b-instruct`; Spearman ρ and Jaccard overlap D3 are reported. Interpretations are descriptive, not causal. Abstract: Study evaluates linear probes on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct for deception detection, focusing on generalization across 3 held-out OOD datasets. Projecting activations onto a small subset of PCs from the training distribution enables cross-domain transfer nearly matching probes trained directly on test distributions. An LLM judge scores PCs based on whether their most/least activating examples imply a transferable deception direction; probing highest-scoring PCs closes the baseline-to-oracle gap by 78% on Insider Trading Report and 25% on Sandbagging. Heavily weighted source-probe directions may encode source-specific surface features, while transferable directions encode the contrast more abstractly. Main conclusion: OOD probe robustness is largely determined by subspace selection.

Introduction: Linear probes may learn spurious correlations despite linear representation of concepts. Study uses source-domain PCA basis for deception probes on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, training on Roleplaying deception scenarios and evaluating on held-out Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, and Sandbagging. Contributions: (1) target-supervised greedy search finds a small transferable subspace of 8–15 source PCs where source-trained probes nearly match target-trained probes; (2) source- and target-side PC weight rankings fail to outperform the full-representation baseline; (3) an LLM judge partially recovers the transferable subspace without target data by selecting PCs likely to encode behavioral contrast rather than surface patterns.

Abstract/introduction: Study evaluates linear probes on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct for deception detection, using Roleplaying as source and Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, and Sandbagging as held-out targets. Source-PCA subspaces can enable transfer; target-supervised greedy selection finds 8–15 transferable PCs, nearly matching target-trained probes. Transferable directions may encode an abstract behavioral contrast, whereas heavily weighted source directions may reflect source-specific surface features.

Setup: Layer-15 residual-stream activations, averaged over assistant-response tokens; labels honest=0, ambiguous=-1, deceptive=1, with ambiguous removed. Source activations standardized; same source statistics applied to targets. PCA on source, top 100 PCs retained. Logistic probes use lambda=10. Full-representation source baselines: Insider Trading Confirm 0.874 AUROC, Insider Trading Report 0.706, Sandbagging 0.606. Target-trained probes within top-100 source-PC subspace achieve, respectively, 0.936 / 0.950 / 0.869 AUROC (ordering: Report / Confirm / Sandbagging in the text’s ‘three targets’ statement is potentially ambiguous; figure/context should clarify).

Greedy oracle selects PCs using target labels with 5-fold target CV, while fitting probe weights on source data; stops when improvement <=.001. Average selected PCs: Report 15, Confirm 8, Sandbagging 14. It improves baseline by 0.22 AUROC on Report and 0.23 on Sandbagging, and nearly reaches target-trained performance. Variance-matched top-k PCs only matches greedy on Confirm and lags on harder targets. Section 4.3 tests whether greedy PCs are individually target-discriminative or simply heavily weighted by the source probe, using standardized coefficient magnitude (absolute coefficient times PC standard deviation).

Section 4.1 says source probe favored directions “causally increase” target deception, conflicting with Section 5’s claim that interpretations are descriptive rather than causal and no causal inference-time ablation was performed.
