The paper studies OOD deception detection using linear logistic-regression probes trained on one source dataset and evaluated on 3 held-out target datasets. It investigates selecting principal components (PCs), or directions in a source activation basis, as a transferable subspace. A target-supervised greedy search selects 8–15 PCs and nearly matches probes trained on target data. Ranking PCs by source- or target-probe weights does not recover the transferable subspace. An LLM judge selects 19 PCs receiving the maximum observed score in both runs, without target data; this improves transfer on all 3 targets and closes 78% and 25% of the gap between the full-representation baseline and the greedy oracle on two targets.

The paper studies OOD deception detection using linear logistic-regression probes trained on one source dataset and evaluated on 3 held-out target datasets. Source is Roleplaying; targets include Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, and Sandbagging. Activations are averaged over assistant-response tokens from Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct; GPT-4o labels responses honest (0), ambiguous (-1, removed), or deceptive (1). Activations are standardized using source statistics, and PCA produces 100 source PCs. A target-supervised greedy oracle selects 8–15 PCs by repeatedly adding the PC with the greatest target-AUROC improvement and nearly matches target-trained probes. Ranking PCs by source- or target-probe standardized coefficients does not recover the transferable subspace. An LLM judge (GPT-5-mini) rates PC directions for likely OOD usefulness on a 1–10 scale; 6 is the maximum observed score. The 19 PCs receiving 6 in both scoring runs are interp-selected, without target data; this improves transfer on all 3 targets and closes 78% and 25% of the gap between the full-representation baseline and greedy oracle on two targets. The remaining 81 PCs form the interp-ablated control, but no causal inference-time ablation validation was performed. Other controls include selecting top PCs by source variance. Key metrics are AUROC with 5-fold target CV and 95% CIs. Glossary definitions introduce no contradictions.

Summary: The paper examines whether selecting subspaces of language-model representations improves out-of-distribution deception detection. It compares probes (classifiers detecting a property) trained on full representations versus selected directions. One selection method uses target labels without fitting probe weights on the target data; another uses natural-language interpretations without target data. Small target-guided subspaces nearly match target-trained probes. Selection by source weights, target-class separation, or explained variance does not recover the same transferable subspaces. Interpretation-based selection improves over the full-representation baseline on all targets, but recovery varies sharply. The study uses one model and one source dataset. Interpretations are descriptive, not causal. Glossary heading appears, but no glossary content is provided in this part.

It compares source-trained logistic-regression probes on full standardized activations with probes using selected directions. One target-label-guided method selects directions without fitting probe weights on target data; interpretation-based selection uses natural-language direction descriptions without target data. Small target-guided subspaces nearly match target-trained probes, while source-weight, target-class-separation, and explained-variance rankings do not recover the same transferable subspaces. Interpretation-based selection improves over the full-representation baseline on all targets, but recovery varies. The study uses one model (E6/Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct), layer-15 residual-stream activations averaged over assistant-response tokens, and one source dataset (V8/Roleplaying); targets are C2R, W6, and J9. Labels are -1 ambiguous, 0 honest, and 1 deceptive; ambiguous examples are removed. Standardization uses source statistics for source and targets. N4D retains the leading 100 source PCs. All classifiers are logistic regression with stated λ=10. B8Q is the full-representation source-trained baseline; Y4 ranks PCs by explained variance; H2 is target-guided greedy selection with source-fitted probe weights and 5-fold CV, treated as a transfer upper bound rather than unbiased OOD evaluation. T6 and M9 provide source- and target-PCA coefficient rankings; X4 is absolute coefficient times Q7 standard deviation. C7 judges direction interpretations (P2/GPT-5-mini); L2 selects directions reaching maximum OOD rating in both runs, and A7 uses the complement. Decoder alignment uses SAE resource `andyrdt/saes-llama-3.1-8b-instruct`; Spearman ρ and Jaccard overlap D3 are reported. Interpretations are descriptive, not causal. final_notes: Abstract/setup: Study evaluates linear probes for Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct on held-out deception datasets, training from Roleplaying deception scenarios and testing on Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, and Sandbagging. Layer-15 residual activations; source PCA top 100 PCs; labels honest=0, ambiguous=-1, deceptive=1, with ambiguous removed; source standardization applied to targets. Full-representation source-trained AUROC: Confirm .874, Report .706, Sandbagging .606. Target-trained top-100 AUROC: Report .950, Confirm .936, Sandbagging .869. Greedy target-guided selection improves baseline by about .22/.23 on Report/Sandbagging; full-dataset greedy reported k=13 Report, k=7 Confirm, k=14 Sandbagging, with oracle AUROC .929 Report and .832 Sandbagging. Interpretation-based selection uses GPT-5-mini PC scores (maximum 6); 19 PCs score 6 in both runs. Interp-selected results: Report .706 to .881 (78% of baseline-to-greedy gap), Sandbagging .606 to .662 (25% toward .832); beats baseline and controls on all targets. Source-probe coefficient ranking transfers poorly; target-probe ranking does well on Report but worse than greedy on Confirm and below random on Sandbagging. Appendix C claims lower PCs have stronger decoder alignment (Spearman rho -0.857 best feature, -0.917 top-10 mean). Appendix D: Jaccard overlap greedy/target-PCA = .182 Report, .077 Confirm, .167 Sandbagging; all under one-fifth. Table 2 lists source weights (15 PCs), greedy selections (Report 13, Confirm 7, Sandbagging 15 PCs), and target separability rankings (15 each); Sandbagging table count conflicts with earlier k=14. Appendix E Tables 3–4 give LLM OOD interpretability scores. Table 3: PC62, PC57 score 6 for Report+Sandbagging; PC9 score 3 for Report+Sandbagging; PC81 score 3 for Confirm+Sandbagging; PC86 score 6 for Confirm+Sandbagging. Table 4: PC7=3, PC8=4, PC11=3, PC12=3, PC4=6. Explanations characterize high-scoring PCs as moderately general deception-related strategies but noisy and surface/wording-dependent, while low scores are domain-specific or brittle.

Abstract: Study evaluates linear probes for Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct on 3 held-out deception-detection datasets. Claim: projecting activations onto a small subset of PCs from the training distribution enables cross-domain transfer nearly matching probes trained directly on each test distribution. PC interpretations are used to select transferable PCs: an LLM judge scores PCs based on whether their most/least activating examples imply a transferable deception direction. Summary: The paper examines whether selecting subspaces of language-model representations improves out-of-distribution deception detection. It compares probes (classifiers detecting a property) trained on full representations versus selected directions. One selection method uses target labels without fitting probe weights on the target data; another uses natural-language interpretations without target data. Small target-guided subspaces nearly match target-trained probes. Selection by source weights, target-class separation, or explained variance does not recover the same transferable subspaces. Interpretations are descriptive, not causal. Glossary heading appears, but no glossary content is provided in this part.

Section 4.3: Source-PCA probe ranks source PCs by weights from a source-trained probe; target-PCA probe ranks PCs by weights from a target-trained probe. Both train probes on source data projected onto top-k PCs in the source-PCA basis. Greedy full-target selection sets k=13 Report, 7 Confirm, 14 Sandbagging; these differ slightly from prior CV averages (15, 8, 14). Source-PCA transfers about as well as full-representation baseline. Target-PCA performs well on Report, worse than greedy on Confirm, and below random on Sandbagging. Neither hypothesis recovers greedy performance.

Section 4.4/5: Interpretability-selected subspace uses 19 PCs. Report: baseline 0.706, interpretability 0.881, greedy 0.929. Confirm baseline 0.874; methods similar/near ceiling. Sandbagging: baseline 0.606, interpretability 0.662, greedy 0.832. Recovery is partial, especially Sandbagging. Section 6 claim that small subset nearly matches target-trained probes conflicts with the Sandbagging gap.

Appendix C: Lower PCs show stronger decoder alignment; Spearman rho is -0.857 for best-matching SAE feature and -0.917 for mean top 10.

Appendix D: Reported greedy/target-PCA Jaccards are .182, .077, .167, but listed sets imply .167, .100, .154. Table lists 15 Sandbagging greedy PCs despite earlier k=14. Table’s target separability ranking appears to correspond to target-PCA. Dataset counts and Appendix B prompt have no noted conflicts.

Appendix E: Tables 3–4 provide LLM-judge OOD interpretability scores for PCs. Table 3 lists PC62, PC57, PC9 (Report + Sandbagging) and PC81, PC86 (Confirm + Sandbagging), with scores 6, 6, 3, 3, 6. Table 4 lists PC7, PC8, PC11, PC12, PC4 with scores 3, 4, 3, 3, 6. Explanations repeatedly qualify transferability as noisy, surface-cue-dependent, and context-dependent. No clear internal contradiction found in this part.

Abstract: Study evaluates linear probes on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct for deception detection, focusing on generalization across 3 held-out OOD datasets. Projecting activations onto a small subset of PCs from the training distribution enables cross-domain transfer nearly matching probes trained directly on test distributions. An LLM judge scores PCs based on whether their most/least activating examples imply a transferable deception direction; probing highest-scoring PCs closes the baseline-to-oracle gap by 78% on Insider Trading Report and 25% on Sandbagging. Heavily weighted source-probe directions may encode source-specific surface features, while transferable directions encode the contrast more abstractly. Main conclusion: OOD probe robustness is largely determined by subspace selection.

Introduction: Linear probes may learn spurious correlations despite linear representation of concepts. Study uses source-domain PCA basis for deception probes on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, training on Roleplaying deception scenarios and evaluating on held-out Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, and Sandbagging. Contributions: (1) target-supervised greedy search finds a small transferable subspace of 8–15 source PCs where source-trained probes nearly match target-trained probes; (2) source- and target-side PC weight rankings fail to outperform the full-representation baseline; (3) an LLM judge partially recovers the transferable subspace without target data by selecting PCs likely to encode behavioral contrast rather than surface patterns.

Experiments: Source-trained full-representation baseline AUROC: Confirm 0.874, Report 0.706, Sandbagging 0.606. Target-trained probes within top-100 source-PC subspace (5-fold CV) achieve 0.936 / 0.950 / 0.869 across Report / Confirm / Sandbagging (order implied by target listing), showing the subspace contains sufficient target information. Greedy target-guided PC selection trains source probes on subsets, using target folds for selection and held-out target folds for evaluation; it stops when no candidate improves AUROC >0.001. Average selected PCs: Report 15, Confirm 8, Sandbagging 14. This is an upper bound, not unbiased OOD estimate. Greedy improves baseline by 0.22 (Report) and 0.23 (Sandbagging), nearly reaching target-trained performance; variance-top-k control matches greedy only on Confirm and lags on harder tasks. Section 4.3 tests whether greedy PCs are individually target-discriminative or simply heavily weighted by source probe. Rankings use absolute standardized coefficients (absolute coefficient × PC standard deviation) from probes trained on source-PCA projections.

Section 4.3: Source-PCA probe ranks source PCs by weights from a source-trained probe; target-PCA probe ranks PCs by weights from a target-trained probe. Both then train probes on source data projected onto top-k PCs in the source-PCA basis. Greedy full-target (not CV) selection sets k=13 Report, 7 Confirm, 14 Sandbagging; these differ slightly from prior CV averages (15, 8, 14). Source-PCA probe transfers about as well as the full-representation baseline. Target-PCA performs well on Report, worse than greedy on Confirm, and below random on Sandbagging. Thus neither hypothesis recovers greedy performance.

Section 4.4: For each top-100 source PC, 8 most/least activating source examples are interpreted by an LLM. OOD generalizability scored 1–10; no score exceeded 6, so 6 is the maximum observed. PCs scoring 6 in both runs yield 19 PCs. Five PCs occurred in greedy selections for more than one target; 3/5 received maximum OOD score. Only 1 of the top 5 source-PCA-selected PCs did. Greedy-selected interpretations describe abstractions surviving domain shifts.

H2-selected directions differ from source/target classification directions. X4 is standardized coefficient magnitude. Interpretations assign OOD score R5; scores noisy.

The paper studies OOD deception detection using linear logistic-regression probes trained on one source dataset and evaluated on 3 held-out target datasets. It investigates selecting principal components (PCs), or directions in a source activation basis, as a transferable subspace. A target-supervised greedy search selects 8–15 PCs and nearly matches probes trained on target data. Ranking PCs by source- or target-probe weights does not recover the transferable subspace. An LLM judge selects 19 PCs receiving the maximum observed score in both runs, without target data; this improves transfer on all 3 targets and closes 78% and 25% of the gap between the full-representation baseline and the greedy oracle on two targets.

Abstract claims: The study examines Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct linear probes for deception detection across 3 held-out OOD datasets. Projecting activations onto a small subset of principal components (PCs) from the training distribution enables cross-domain transfer nearly matching probes trained directly on each test distribution. PC interpretations identify transferable PCs: an LLM judge scores each PC based on whether its most/least activating examples imply a transferable deception direction; probing on highest-scoring PCs closes the baseline-to-oracle gap by 78% on Insider Trading Report and 25% on Sandbagging. Heavily weighted directions in source probes induce deceptive responses via source-specific surface features, while genuinely transferable directions encode the contrast more abstractly and are capturable by natural-language descriptions. Main conclusion: OOD probe robustness is largely determined by subspace selection.

Setup: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct E6 layer-15 residual-stream activations, averaged over assistant-response tokens. Experiments: W6 transfer is good, C2R moderate, J9 poor; target-trained probes in the retained 100-dimensional source-Q7 subspace separate deceptive/honest responses on every target, showing relevant information exists while source-trained directions fail to transfer. Greedy target-guided subset search adds source-Q7 directions using source-fitted weights and target F3; target labels guide selection but not fitting. final_notes: Section 4.3: Source-PCA probe ranks source PCs by weights from a source-trained probe; target-PCA ranks PCs by weights from a target-trained probe. Both train source probes on top-k PCs in the source-PCA basis. Greedy full-target selection sets k=13 Report, 7 Confirm, 14 Sandbagging, differing from prior CV averages (15, 8, 14). Source-PCA transfers about as well as full-representation baseline. Target-PCA performs well on Report, worse than greedy on Confirm, and below random on Sandbagging; neither matches greedy. Section 4.4: No OOD score above 6 among top-100 source PCs; 19 PCs scored 6 in both runs. Five PCs occurred in greedy selections for more than one target; 3/5 got maximum OOD score versus 1/5 of top source-PCA PCs. Section 4.5: Interpretability-selected subspace uses 19 PCs; outperforms baseline and source-variance control on all targets and beats interp-ablated on all. Report: baseline .706, interp .881, greedy .929 (78% gap); Confirm baseline .874, little headroom; Sandbagging baseline .606, interp .662, greedy .832 (25% gap). Section 5/6: limitations and conclusion; interpretability is descriptive, not causal. Appendix C: lower PCs show stronger decoder alignment; Spearman rho -0.857 (best SAE feature) and -0.917 (mean top 10). Appendix D: Jaccard overlaps between greedy and target-PCA are .182 Report, .077 Confirm, .167 Sandbagging; it incorrectly says methods agree on more than half and target separability matches most greedy choices. Appendix E: Table 3 lists five PCs selected for likely transferability: PC62, PC57, PC9 for Report+Sandbagging (scores 6, 6, 3), and PC81, PC86 for Confirm+Sandbagging (scores 3, 6). Table 4 lists PC7, PC8, PC11, PC12, PC4 with OOD scores 3, 4, 3, 3, 6. All listed scores are at most 6, consistent with earlier top-100 score claim; the five multiply selected PCs include three score-6 PCs, consistent with the 3/5 maximum-score note.

Abstract: Study evaluates linear probes on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct for deception detection, focusing on generalization across 3 held-out OOD datasets. Projecting activations onto a small subset of PCs from the training distribution enables cross-domain transfer nearly matching probes trained directly on test distributions. An LLM judge scores PCs based on whether their most/least activating examples imply a transferable deception direction; probing highest-scoring PCs closes the baseline-to-oracle gap by 78% on Insider Trading Report and 25% on Sandbagging. Heavily weighted source-probe directions may encode source-specific surface features, while transferable directions encode the contrast more abstractly. Main conclusion: OOD probe robustness is largely determined by subspace selection.

Abstract: Study evaluates linear probes on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct for deception detection, focusing on generalization across 3 held-out OOD datasets. Projecting activations onto a small subset of PCs from the training distribution enables cross-domain transfer nearly matching probes trained directly on test distributions. An LLM judge scores PCs based on whether their most/least activating examples imply a transferable deception direction; probing highest-scoring PCs closes the baseline-to-oracle gap by 78% on Insider Trading Report and 25% on Sandbagging. Heavily weighted source-probe directions may encode source-specific surface features, while transferable directions encode the contrast more abstractly. Setup: Roleplaying is source; targets are Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, and Sandbagging. Experiments: Source-trained full-representation baseline AUROC: Confirm 0.874, Report 0.706, Sandbagging 0.606. final_notes: The paper studies OOD deception detection using linear logistic-regression probes trained on Roleplaying and evaluated on Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, and Sandbagging. The paper studies OOD deception detection using linear logistic-regression probes trained on one source dataset and evaluated on 3 held-out target datasets. It investigates selecting principal components (PCs), or directions in a source activation basis, as a transferable subspace. A target-supervised greedy search selects 8–15 PCs and nearly matches probes trained on target data. Ranking PCs by source- or target-probe weights does not recover the transferable subspace. An LLM judge selects 19 PCs receiving the maximum observed score in both runs, without target data; this improves transfer on all 3 targets and closes 78% and 25% of the gap between the full-representation baseline and the greedy oracle on two targets.

The paper studies OOD deception detection using linear logistic-regression probes trained on one source dataset and evaluated on 3 held-out target datasets. Activations are averaged over assistant-response tokens from Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct; GPT-4o labels responses honest (0), ambiguous (-1, removed), or deceptive (1). Activations are standardized using source statistics, and PCA produces 100 source PCs. A target-supervised greedy oracle selects 8–15 PCs by repeatedly adding the PC with the greatest target-AUROC improvement and nearly matches target-trained probes. Ranking PCs by source- or target-probe standardized coefficients does not recover the transferable subspace. An LLM judge (GPT-5-mini) rates PC directions for likely OOD usefulness on a 1–10 scale; 6 is the maximum observed score. The 19 PCs receiving 6 in both scoring runs are interp-selected, without target data; this improves transfer on all 3 targets and closes 78% and 25% of the gap between the full-representation baseline and greedy oracle on two targets. The remaining 81 PCs form the interp-ablated control, but no causal inference-time ablation validation was performed. Other controls include selecting top PCs by source variance. Key metrics are AUROC with 5-fold target CV and 95% CIs. Glossary definitions introduce no contradictions.

Summary: The paper examines whether selecting subspaces of language-model representations improves out-of-distribution deception detection. It compares probes (classifiers detecting a property) trained on full representations versus selected directions. One selection method uses target labels without fitting probe weights on the target data; another uses natural-language interpretations without target data. Small target-guided subspaces nearly match target-trained probes. Selection by source weights, target-class separation, or explained variance does not recover the same transferable subspaces. Interpretation-based selection improves over the full-representation baseline on all targets, but recovery varies sharply. The study uses one model and one source dataset. Interpretations are descriptive, not causal. Glossary heading appears, but no glossary content is provided in this part.

The paper studies whether selecting subspaces of language-model residual-stream representations improves OOD deception detection. It compares source-trained logistic-regression probes on full standardized activations with probes using selected directions. One target-label-guided method selects directions without fitting probe weights on target data; interpretation-based selection uses natural-language direction descriptions without target data. Small target-guided subspaces nearly match target-trained probes, while source-weight, target-class-separation, and explained-variance rankings do not recover the same transferable subspaces. Interpretation-based selection improves over the full-representation baseline on all targets, but recovery varies. The study uses one model (E6/Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct), layer-15 residual-stream activations averaged over assistant-response tokens, and one source dataset (V8/Roleplaying); targets are C2R, W6, and J9. Labels are -1 ambiguous, 0 honest, and 1 deceptive; ambiguous examples are removed. Standardization uses source statistics for source and targets. N4D retains the leading 100 source PCs. All classifiers are logistic regression with stated λ=10. B8Q is the full-representation source-trained baseline; Y4 ranks PCs by explained variance; H2 is target-guided greedy selection with source-fitted probe weights and 5-fold CV, treated as a transfer upper bound rather than unbiased OOD evaluation. Decoder alignment uses SAE resource `andyrdt/saes-llama-3.1-8b-instruct`; Spearman ρ and Jaccard overlap D3 are reported. Interpretations are descriptive, not causal. Study evaluates linear probes on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct for deception detection, focusing on generalization across three held-out OOD datasets. Source domain is Roleplaying; targets are Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, and Sandbagging. Layer-15 residual activations, averaged over assistant-response tokens; labels honest 0, ambiguous -1, deceptive 1, with ambiguous removed. PCA retains top 100 PCs; logistic regression lambda=10. Full source-trained AUROC: Confirm 0.874, Report 0.706, Sandbagging 0.606. Target-trained probes in source-PC subspace: Report 0.936, Confirm 0.950, Sandbagging 0.869. Interpretability selection improves Report 0.706→0.881 and Sandbagging 0.606→0.662; CV greedy selection averages 15/8/14 PCs for Report/Confirm/Sandbagging. Conclusion: sparse PC subspaces may isolate transferable behavioral structure.

Appendix C claims lower PCs have stronger decoder alignment: Spearman rho -0.857 for best SAE feature and -0.917 for mean top 10. Appendix D lists greedy and target-separability PC sets. It claims Jaccard overlaps 0.182 (Report), 0.077 (Confirm), 0.167 (Sandbagging), but direct calculation from the listed sets gives 0.167 (4/24), 0.100 (2/20), and 0.154 (4/26), respectively. The listed overlaps are all under one-fifth.

Appendix E: Table 3 interpretable transferability-selected PCs: PC62, PC57 (Report + Sandbagging), scores 6; PC9 (Report + Sandbagging), score 3; PC81 (Confirm + Sandbagging), score 3; PC86 (Confirm + Sandbagging), score 6. Table 4 lists PCs and OOD scores: PC7=3, PC8=4, PC11=3, PC12=3, PC4=6. Interpretations generally describe denial/admission, hedging, defensive or stylistic cues as potentially transferable but noisy, surface-dependent, and brittle; no explicit contradiction found.

Abstract: Study evaluates linear probes on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct for deception detection, focusing on generalization across 3 held-out OOD datasets. Projecting activations onto a small subset of PCs from the training distribution enables cross-domain transfer nearly matching probes trained directly on test distributions. An LLM judge scores PCs based on whether their most/least activating examples imply a transferable deception direction; probing highest-scoring PCs closes the baseline-to-oracle gap by 78% on Insider Trading Report and 25% on Sandbagging. Heavily weighted source-probe directions may encode source-specific surface features, while transferable directions encode the contrast more abstractly. Main conclusion: OOD probe robustness is largely determined by subspace selection.

The paper studies whether selecting subspaces of language-model residual-stream representations improves OOD deception detection. It compares source-trained logistic-regression probes on full standardized activations with probes using selected directions. One target-label-guided method selects directions without fitting probe weights on target data; interpretation-based selection uses natural-language direction descriptions without target data. final_notes:
Section 4.3: Source-PCA probe ranks source-basis PCs by source-probe weights; target-PCA ranks them by target-probe weights, but both train source probes on selected top-k source-basis PCs. Full-dataset greedy sets use k=13 Report, 7 Confirm, 14 Sandbagging, differing from CV values. Both hypotheses fail: source-PCA ranking transfers about like the full-representation baseline; target-PCA ranking does well on Report but worse than greedy on Confirm and below-random on Sandbagging.

Section 4.4: LLM interpretation of top-100 source PCs found no PC above 6/10 OOD; six was treated as maximum. Nineteen PCs scored 6 in both runs. Five PCs appeared in greedy selections for more than one target; 3/5 received maximum OOD, versus 1/5 top source-PCA PCs.

Section 4.5: Interpretation-selected 19-PC probe outperforms baseline and source-variance control on all targets and beats the 81-PC ablation across all targets. It closes 78% of baseline-to-greedy gap on Report (0.706→0.881 vs greedy 0.929) and 25% on Sandbagging (0.606→0.662 vs greedy 0.832). Confirm baseline is 0.874 and methods are similar.

Appendix C reports negative Spearman correlations between PC rank and decoder alignment: rho=-0.857 for best SAE feature and -0.917 for mean top 10.

Appendix D Table 2 lists source-weight, greedy, and target-separability PC sets. Its stated Jaccard values conflict with the listed sets: Report 4/24=.167, Confirm 2/20=.100, Sandbagging 4/25=.160, rather than .182, .077, and .167.

Appendix E: Tables 3–4 list interpreted PCs with OOD scores 3–6. The maximum listed score is 6, consistent with the earlier statement that no PC exceeded 6; listed PCs include PC62, PC57, PC9, PC81, PC86, PC7, PC8, PC11, PC12, and PC4.

Abstract: Studies Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct linear probes for deception detection across 3 held-out OOD datasets. Projecting activations onto a small subset of training-distribution PCs enables cross-domain transfer nearly matching probes trained directly on test distributions. PC interpretations identify transferable PCs. An LLM judge recovered all five repeatedly transferable PCs from most/least activating examples; probing on highest-scoring PCs closed the baseline-to-oracle gap by 78% on Insider Trading Report and 25% on Sandbagging. Heavily weighted source-probe directions appear source-specific and surface-level, while transferable directions encode the contrast more abstractly and are describable in natural language. Main conclusion: OOD robustness is largely determined by subspace selection.

The paper studies OOD deception detection using linear logistic-regression probes trained on one source dataset and evaluated on 3 held-out target datasets. It investigates selecting principal components (PCs), or directions in a source activation basis, as a transferable subspace. A target-supervised greedy search selects 8–15 PCs and nearly matches probes trained on target data. Ranking PCs by source- or target-probe weights does not recover the transferable subspace. An LLM judge selects 19 PCs receiving the maximum observed score in both runs, without target data; this improves transfer on all 3 targets and closes 78% and 25% of the gap between the full-representation baseline and the greedy oracle on two targets.

The paper studies OOD deception detection using linear logistic-regression probes trained on one source dataset and evaluated on 3 held-out target datasets. Source is Roleplaying; targets include Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, and Sandbagging. Activations are averaged over assistant-response tokens from Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct; GPT-4o labels responses honest (0), ambiguous (-1, removed), or deceptive (1). Activations are standardized using source statistics, and PCA produces 100 source PCs. A target-supervised greedy oracle selects 8–15 PCs by repeatedly adding the PC with the greatest target-AUROC improvement and nearly matches target-trained probes. Ranking PCs by source- or target-probe standardized coefficients does not recover the transferable subspace. An LLM judge (GPT-5-mini) rates PC directions for likely OOD usefulness on a 1–10 scale; 6 is the maximum observed score. The 19 PCs receiving 6 in both scoring runs are interp-selected, without target data; this improves transfer on all 3 targets and closes 78% and 25% of the gap between the full-representation baseline and greedy oracle on two targets. The remaining 81 PCs form the interp-ablated control, but no causal inference-time ablation validation was performed. Other controls include selecting top PCs by source variance. Key metrics are AUROC with 5-fold target CV and 95% CIs. Glossary definitions introduce no contradictions.

The paper studies whether selecting subspaces of language-model representations improves OOD deception detection. It compares probes trained on full representations versus selected directions. One selection method uses target labels without fitting probe weights on target data; another uses natural-language interpretations to recover repeatedly transferable directions without target data. Small target-guided subspaces nearly match target-trained probes. Selection by source weights, target-class separation, or explained variance does not recover the same transferable subspaces. Interpretation-based selection improves over the full-representation baseline on all targets, but recovery varies sharply. The study uses one model and one source dataset. Interpretations are descriptive, not causal.

The paper studies whether selecting subspaces of language-model residual-stream representations improves OOD deception detection. It compares full-representation source-trained probes with selected-direction probes. All classifiers are logistic regression (lambda=10); activations come from layer 15 of Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (E6), averaged over assistant-response tokens and standardized using source statistics. V8/Roleplaying is the sole source dataset; targets are C2R, W6, and J9. Labels are -1 ambiguous, 0 honest, 1 deceptive; ambiguous cases are removed. Decoder alignment is measured with SAE/U9 features from andyrdt/saes-llama-3.1-8b-instruct, with Spearman rho for component-index relationships. D3 is Jaccard overlap. Abstract: Study evaluates linear probes on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct for deception detection, focusing on generalization across 3 held-out OOD datasets. Projecting activations onto a small subset of PCs from the training distribution enables cross-domain transfer nearly matching probes trained directly on test distributions. An LLM judge scores PCs based on whether their most/least activating examples imply a transferable deception direction; probing highest-scoring PCs closes the baseline-to-oracle gap by 78% on Insider Trading Report and 25% on Sandbagging. Heavily weighted source-probe directions may encode source-specific surface features, while transferable directions encode the contrast more abstractly. Main conclusion: OOD probe robustness is largely determined by subspace selection.

Experiments: Source-trained full-representation baseline AUROC: Confirm 0.874, Report 0.706, Sandbagging 0.606. Target-trained probes within top-100 source-PC subspace (5-fold CV) achieve 0.936 / 0.950 / 0.869 across Report / Confirm / Sandbagging (order implied by target listing), showing the subspace contains sufficient target information. Greedy target-guided PC selection trains source probes on subsets, using target folds for selection and held-out target folds for evaluation; it stops when no candidate improves AUROC >0.001. Average selected PCs: Report 15, Confirm 8, Sandbagging 14. This is an upper bound, not unbiased OOD estimate. Greedy improves baseline by 0.22 (Report) and 0.23 (Sandbagging), nearly reaching target-trained performance; variance-top-k control matches greedy only on Confirm and lags on harder tasks. Section 4.3 tests whether greedy PCs are individually target-discriminative or simply heavily weighted by source probe. Rankings use absolute standardized coefficients (absolute coefficient × PC standard deviation) from probes trained on source-PCA projections.

Section 4.3: Source-PCA probe ranks source PCs by weights from a source-trained probe; target-PCA probe ranks PCs by weights from a target-trained probe. Both then train probes on source data projected onto top-k PCs in the source-PCA basis. Greedy full-target (not CV) selection sets k=13 Report, 7 Confirm, 14 Sandbagging; these differ slightly from prior CV averages (15, 8, 14). Source-PCA probe transfers about as well as the full-representation baseline. Target-PCA performs well on Report, worse than greedy on Confirm, and below random on Sandbagging. Thus neither hypothesis recovers greedy performance.

Section 4.4: For each top-100 source PC, 8 most/least activating source examples are interpreted by an LLM. OOD generalizability scored 1–10; no score exceeded 6, so 6 is the maximum observed. PCs scoring 6 in both runs yield 19 PCs. Five PCs occurred in greedy selections for more than one target; 3/5 received maximum OOD score. Only 1 of the top 5 source-PCA-selected PCs did. Greedy-selected interpretations describe abstractions surviving domain shifts.

The paper studies OOD deception detection using linear logistic-regression probes trained on one source dataset and evaluated on 3 held-out target datasets. It investigates selecting principal components (PCs), or directions in a source activation basis, as a transferable subspace. The paper introduces dropout for reducing overfitting in large neural networks. During training, units and their connections are randomly dropped, sampling exponentially many thinned networks and preventing excessive co-adaptation. At test time, the paper says their averaged predictions can be approximated with one unthinned network using smaller weights. It claims significant reductions in overfitting, major improvements over other regularization methods, and state-of-the-art results on many supervised tasks in vision, speech recognition, document classification, and computational biology. Introduction: deep nets are expressive but can overfit limited data; mentioned regularization methods include early stopping, L1/L2 penalties, and soft weight sharing. No internal contradictions identified so far.

The paper introduces dropout as a way to approximate an equally weighted geometric mean of predictions from exponentially many learned, parameter-sharing models, approaching Bayesian performance with less computation. Model averaging generally improves performance, but separately training many large networks is computationally and practically infeasible. Dropout addresses this by randomly removing hidden and visible units and their connections during training, thereby combining many architectures efficiently and reducing overfitting. Each unit is retained independently with probability p; p may be selected by validation or set to 0.5, while input retention is usually closer to 1. At test time, all units are present and outgoing weights are multiplied by p; the figure states this gives the same output as the expected training-time output. Earlier notes also record that test-time averaged predictions are approximated using one unthinned network with smaller weights, consistent with this description. No internal contradictions identified.

Dropout samples a thinned network by independently removing units; a network with n units corresponds to 2^n possible thinned networks sharing O(n^2) or fewer parameters. A new thinned network is sampled for each training case, so each individual model is rarely trained. At test time, instead of averaging exponentially many models, use one full network with each unit’s outgoing weights multiplied by its training retention probability p; this makes each hidden unit’s expected training-time output equal its test-time output and approximates model averaging. The paper claims this yields significantly lower generalization error than other regularizers across many classification problems. Dropout can also be applied to graphical models, and the paper introduces and evaluates a dropout Restricted Boltzmann Machine against standard RBMs. Structure: motivation (Sec. 2), prior work (Sec. 3), formal model (Sec. 4), training algorithm (Sec. 5), experiments (Sec. 6), analysis/hyperparameters (Sec. 7), dropout RBM (Sec. 8), marginalizing dropout (Sec. 9), practical guide (Appendix A). Feed-forward dropout uses independent Bernoulli masks during training and test-time weight scaling W_test=pW. Training uses SGD on each sampled thinned network, with mini-batch gradients averaged; momentum, decaying learning rates, and L2 decay are useful. Max-norm regularization constrains each hidden unit’s incoming weight vector to ||w||2≤c via projection; c is selected on validation data. Dropout combined with max-norm, large decaying learning rates, and high momentum improves over dropout alone.

For pretrained networks, pretraining is unchanged; pretrained weights are scaled by 1/p before dropout finetuning so expected dropout output matches pretraining. Smaller finetuning learning rates preserve pretrained information and can improve final generalization error.

Motivation: dropout is analogized to sexual reproduction, breaking co-adapted gene sets and selecting robust, mixable features. Replica codes and large co-adaptations are described as inferior to multiple smaller co-adaptations.

Related work: Denoising autoencoders add input noise and reconstruct clean inputs. Dropout extends noise to hidden layers, supervised learning, and other neuron architectures such as Boltzmann Machines. DAE noise is typically 5%, whereas dropout often uses 20% input-unit dropout and 50% hidden-unit dropout; test-time weight scaling enables higher noise. Deterministic counterparts can be obtained by marginalizing dropout in simple cases; prior work studied related marginalization, input-only models, or adversarial unit dropping.

Model: Standard feed-forward layers use z^(l+1)=W^(l+1)y^(l)+b^(l+1), y=f(z). Dropout samples independent Bernoulli(p) masks r^(l), forms thinned outputs y-tilde^(l)=r^(l)*y^(l), and feeds these forward; backpropagation occurs through the sampled subnetwork. At test time W_test^(l)=pW^(l), and the resulting network is used without dropout. Section 5 begins learning procedure.

errors.claim: “For every hidden unit, expected output under the training deletion distribution equals actual test-time output under the prescribed reduced weights.”
errors.evidence: The same section states that “Any activation \(f\) is admissible,” including the sigmoid \(f(x)=1/(1+\exp(-x))\), and defines training output as \(y_i^{(l+1)}=f(\mathbf w_i^{(l+1)}(\mathbf r^{(l)}*\mathbf y^{(l)})+b_i^{(l+1)})\), whereas test-time output uses \(f(p\mathbf w_i^{(l+1)}\mathbf y^{(l)}+b_i^{(l+1)})\).
errors.explanation: For a nonlinear activation such as the sigmoid, generally \(E[f(z)]\ne f(E[z])\). Weight scaling makes the test-time preactivation equal to the expected training preactivation, but does not make the expected training output equal to the test-time output.

errors.claim: “Bayesian neural nets outperform QX2 on Z7P, while QX2 substantially improves standard neural nets and exceeds every other method.”
errors.evidence: Table 8 reports Neural Network with QX2 at 567 C4Y bits and Bayesian Neural Network at 623; the text states that higher C4Y values are preferred.
errors.explanation: Because higher C4Y is better, the Bayesian neural network outperforms QX2, so QX2 does not exceed every other listed method.

errors.claim: “P(h_j=1\mid r_j,\mathbf v)=\mathbf1(r_j=1)\,\sigma(b_j+\sum_iW_{ij}v_i)” and “P(v_i=1\mid\mathbf h)=\sigma(a_i+\sum_jW_{ij}h_j)”
errors.evidence: The ordinary U2L joint distribution is defined as “\(\mathbf v^\top\mathbf W\mathbf h+\mathbf a^\top\mathbf h+\mathbf b^\top\mathbf v\).” Thus \(a\) is the hidden-unit bias and \(b\) is the visible-unit bias.
errors.explanation: The conditional equations swap the bias vectors: the hidden conditional should use \(a_j\), while the visible conditional should use \(b_i\), assuming the preceding joint distribution. As written, they are inconsistent with the model definition.

Introduction: posterior-weighted averaging over parameter settings is ideal with unlimited computation; QX2 is a cheaper construction approximating an equally weighted geometric mean of exponentially many learned, parameter-sharing models. An n-unit network represents 2^n thinned networks while retaining O(n^2) or fewer shared parameters; a new member is sampled/trained for each training presentation, so each member is rarely trained. Dropout addresses overfitting from spurious co-adaptations; alternatives include early stopping, soft weight sharing, and L1/L2 penalties. Model combination often improves performance but separately training/inferencing many large nets is expensive. T6R (weight scaling) uses one unthinned network; X9M (Monte-Carlo model averaging) averages sampled members’ predictions. T6R is claimed to outperform other regularizers across varied classification tasks. The construction extends to graphical models, including U2L (RBMs), yielding B8T (Dropout RBM). Figure 1 contrasts a standard two-hidden-layer net with a QX2-thinned net. Paper map: §2 motivation; §3 previous work; §4 formal model; §5 training; §6 experiments; §7 network properties/hyperparameters; §8 B8T; §9 marginalization; Appendix A practical guidance.

§2 Motivation: Sexual reproduction can break successful co-adapted gene sets, while asexual reproduction preserves them, yet advanced organisms mostly evolved sexually. Livnat et al. (2010) is invoked to argue selection may favor gene mix-ability/robustness over individual fitness. QX2-trained hidden units face randomly selected partners, favoring independently useful robust features rather than reliance on other units; units in a layer still learn different functions. Replicating units is said to be a poor robustness solution, analogous to replica codes for noisy channels. Ten five-person conspiracies may have a havoc-producing advantage over one fifty-person conspiracy under non-stationarity, though ample rehearsal and unchanged conditions can make the larger conspiracy work. Complex co-adaptations may fit training data yet generalize worse than multiple simpler co-adaptations.

errors.explanation: For a nonlinear activation such as the sigmoid, generally \(E[f(z)]\ne f(E[z])\). Weight scaling makes the test-time preactivation equal to the expected training preactivation, but does not make the expected training output equal to the test-time output.

steps.notes_before:
Paper: “Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting,” JMLR 15 (2014), pp. 1929–1958. Abstract/introduction: dropout (called QX2 here) randomly removes units/connections during training, reduces co-adaptation and overfitting, samples exponentially many thinned networks, and uses a single unthinned network with reduced weights to approximate averaged predictions. Claims improvements across vision, speech, document classification, and computational biology. It approximates an equally weighted geometric mean of many learned, parameter-sharing models; each presentation samples/trains a new thinned member. T6R is weight scaling; X9M is Monte-Carlo model averaging. T6R is claimed to outperform other regularizers. Extensions include graphical models/RBMs (U2L, B8T).

§2 motivation: QX2-trained hidden units face randomly selected partners, favoring independently useful robust features rather than reliance on other units; units in a layer still learn different functions. Complex co-adaptations may fit training data yet generalize worse.

§3 related work: Hidden-state noise gives QX2 a regularization interpretation, extending denoising autoencoders (S2H), with hidden-layer corruption, model averaging, supervised/unsupervised use, and applicability to architectures such as Boltzmann Machines. Best noise levels reported: S2H input 5%; QX2 input removal 20%; QX2 hidden removal 50%. Test-time T6R permits higher noise than usually best for S2H. Analytical marginalization yields deterministic regularizers; prior work studied blankout noise without hidden layers, marginalized denoising autoencoders, and accelerated QX2.

§4 model: Hidden/output vectors and standard feed-forward equations are defined; QX2 independently gates each layer’s outputs with Bernoulli retention probability \(p\), including possible visible and hidden unit removal. At inference all units remain and weights are scaled to \(pW\). The text claims expected training output equals test output for every hidden unit, but this conflicts with allowing nonlinear activations (e.g. sigmoid): scaling matches expected preactivation, not generally expected activation.

errors.claim: “P(h_j=1\mid r_j,\mathbf v)=\mathbf1(r_j=1)\,\sigma(b_j+\sum_iW_{ij}v_i)” and “P(v_i=1\mid\mathbf h)=\sigma(a_i+\sum_jW_{ij}h_j)”
errors.evidence: The ordinary U2L joint distribution is defined as “\(\mathbf v^\top\mathbf W\mathbf h+\mathbf a^\top\mathbf h+\mathbf b^\top\mathbf v\).” Thus \(a\) is the hidden-unit bias and \(b\) is the visible-unit bias.
errors.explanation: The conditional equations swap the bias vectors: the hidden conditional should use \(a_j\), while the visible conditional should use \(b_i\), assuming the preceding joint distribution. As written, they are inconsistent with the model definition.

errors.claim: “For every hidden unit, expected output under the training deletion distribution equals actual test-time output under the prescribed reduced weights.”
errors.evidence: The training equations define \(y_i^{(l+1)}=f(\mathbf w_i^{(l+1)}(\mathbf r^{(l)}*\mathbf y^{(l)})+b_i^{(l+1)})\), while inference uses \(\mathbf W_{\mathrm{test}}^{(l)}=p\mathbf W^{(l)}\), giving \(f(p\mathbf w_i^{(l+1)}\mathbf y^{(l)}+b_i^{(l+1)})\). For the explicitly allowed nonlinear sigmoid \(f\), generally \(E[f(\mathbf w_i(\mathbf r*\mathbf y)+b_i)]\ne f(p\mathbf w_i\mathbf y+b_i)\).
errors.explanation: Weight scaling matches the expected preactivation, not generally the expected post-activation output. Thus the universal equality claimed is inconsistent with the stated nonlinear computation (unless restricted to linear activations or described as an approximation).

errors.claim: “QX2 substantially improves standard neural nets and exceeds every other method.”
errors.evidence: The same section states that “Bayesian neural nets outperform QX2 on Z7P,” and Table 8 reports Bayesian Neural Network = 623 versus Neural Network with QX2 = 567, with higher C4Y preferred.
errors.explanation: The claim that QX2 exceeds every other method contradicts both the preceding statement and Table 8, where the Bayesian neural network scores higher.

errors.claim: The prose comparison lists the “8-layer net” pre-QX2 error as 20.5%.
errors.location: This part, Table 7 and accompanying prose comparison
errors.evidence: Table 7 lists “G6W-pretrained NN (8 layers) (Mohamed et al., 2010)” at 20.7%, while the prose comparison gives the 8-layer net a pre-QX2 error of 20.5%.

errors.claim: “For every hidden unit, expected output under the training deletion distribution equals actual test-time output under the prescribed reduced weights.”
errors.evidence: The training equations define \(y_i^{(l+1)}=f(\mathbf w_i^{(l+1)}(\mathbf r^{(l)}*\mathbf y^{(l)})+b_i^{(l+1)})\), while inference uses \(\mathbf W_{\mathrm{test}}^{(l)}=p\mathbf W^{(l)}\), giving \(f(p\mathbf w_i^{(l+1)}\mathbf y^{(l)}+b_i^{(l+1)})\). For the explicitly allowed nonlinear sigmoid \(f\), generally \(E[f(\mathbf w_i(\mathbf r*\mathbf y)+b_i)]\ne f(p\mathbf w_i\mathbf y+b_i)\).
errors.explanation: Weight scaling matches the expected preactivation, not generally the expected post-activation output. Thus the universal equality claimed is inconsistent with the stated nonlinear computation (unless restricted to linear activations or described as an approximation).

final_notes: Section 8 defines Dropout RBMs as mixtures of weight-sharing RBMs under hidden masks r, with hidden retention probability p. The joint RBM distribution is exp(v^TWh+a^Th+b^Tv), so a denotes hidden biases and b visible biases; stated conditional equations incorrectly swap these biases. Given a mask, dropped hidden units are zero and retained hidden conditionals factorize. Learning samples a new mask per mini-batch and uses CD-1. On MNIST 256-hidden-unit RBMs, p=0.5 produces coarser features and apparently fewer dead units than standard RBMs. Figure 13 claims much sparser hidden representations without an added sparsity regularizer, without numerical sparsity data. Section 9: marginalized dropout for linear regression gives ||y-pXw||²+p(1-p)||Γw||², Γ=(diag(XᵀX))^{1/2}; with w~=pw, ||y-Xw~||²+((1-p)/p)||Γw~||², so lower p increases regularization. Logistic marginalization is approximate and claimed to improve training time/generalization over Monte Carlo dropout; assumptions weaken with added layers. Section 10: inverted-dropout Bernoulli multiplier has mean 1, variance (1-p)/p; moment-matched Gaussian performs slightly better in Table 10 (MNIST 0.95±0.04 vs 1.08±0.04%; CIFAR-10 12.5±0.1 vs 12.6±0.1%). Section 11 claims dropout reduces overfitting, improves applications, and achieves state-of-the-art on several datasets; training typically takes 2–3 times longer. Appendix A recommends layer size at least n/p; hidden p=.5–.8, input p≈.8; smaller p requires larger n and can underfit. Appendix B: MNIST 60k train/10k test, 10k validation then reunited for final 1m updates. Figure 4 uses hidden p=.5, input p=.8, momentum .95, max-norm c=2; larger 2-layer networks improve (4096: 1.01%; 8192: .95%), while 3-layer versions and stronger dropout do not beat 2-layer networks. SVHN has ~600k train and 26k test, with 6000 validation. Another SVHN/speech setup uses input p=.8, hidden p=.5, max-norm c=4, momentum .95, learning rate .1 with decay; DBN dropout finetuning works best around .01 and max-norm adds no improvement. The paper studies dropout to reduce overfitting and approximate model combination without training many separate networks. Dropout randomly removes hidden or visible units and their connections; each unit is retained independently with probability p (often 0.5 for hidden units, closer to 1 for inputs). A network with n units yields 2^n possible thinned networks sharing parameters, so parameter count remains O(n^2) or less. A new thinned network is sampled for every training case; each individual subnetwork is rarely trained. At test time, the full network is used with outgoing weights multiplied by p, so each unit’s test-time output equals its expected training-time output; this approximates averaging the subnetworks. The introduction describes this as approximating an equally weighted geometric mean of predictions, while Bayesian model averaging is the ideal motivation. Dropout is claimed to reduce generalization error across classification problems and to improve model combination, and it can also be applied to graphical models such as RBMs. p may be selected on validation data. Earlier reported claims: dropout significantly reduces overfitting and improves supervised learning across vision, speech, documents, and computational biology; Reuters errors 31.05% without versus 29.62% with dropout; alternative-splicing results 440 and 567 bits; Table 9: Dropout + Max-norm 1.05%, Max-norm 1.35%, L2 1.62%. Training typically takes 2–3 times longer than standard networks. Later sections: motivation, related work, model, training, experiments, network properties/hyperparameters, Dropout RBMs, marginalizing dropout, and practical hyperparameter guidance.

Section 7 examines features, sparsity, retention probability, network size, and training-set size. MNIST autoencoder comparison: identical one-hidden-layer 256-ReLU autoencoders, with hidden dropout p=0.5 versus none; test reconstruction errors are similar, but dropout features qualitatively appear more meaningful and less co-adapted. Dropout is claimed to break co-adaptations. Figure 8 shows dropout-induced sparsity without an explicit sparsity regularizer: no-dropout mean activations are about 2.0 with substantial mass away from zero; dropout mean activations are about 0.7 with a sharp zero peak and few highly active units. Figure 9 varies retention probability. With fixed architecture 784-2048-2048-2048-10 and no input dropout, small p causes few active units and high training error/underfitting; error decreases as p rises, is flat for p=0.4–0.8, then increases near p=1. In the second setting, pn (expected retained units per layer) is fixed, so smaller p means a larger network; expected retained count is constant but test-network size differs. No exact numerical errors are given for Figures 7–9.

For linear regression with elementwise Bernoulli(p) input masks, the expected objective is ||y-pXw||² + p(1-p)||Γw||², Γ=(diag(XᵀX))^{1/2}, equivalent to ridge with feature-dependent costs. Summary: The paper studies reducing overfitting in large neural networks without training many separate networks. Dropout randomly removes units and connections during training, sampling smaller networks that share weights; at test time, a full network with scaled weights approximates their combined predictions. Reported improvements cover image, speech, text, and alternative-splicing tasks. The paper compares dropout with other regularizers and Bayesian neural networks, and examines learned features, sparsity, dropout rates, network size, training-set size, and test-time averaging. Dropout RBMs learn qualitatively different features and sparser representations. For linear regression, marginalizing dropout yields a modified ridge-regression objective. Preliminary experiments compare Bernoulli dropout with multiplicative Gaussian noise. Limitation: dropout networks typically take 2–3 times longer to train than standard networks with the same architecture.

errors.claim: “For every hidden unit, expected output under training-time deletion equals actual test-time output under the prescribed reduced weights.”
errors.location: This part, opening paragraph of Section 4
errors.evidence: The same section defines training output as \(f(\mathbf w\, (\mathbf r*\mathbf y)+b)\), while test output uses \(f(p\mathbf w\mathbf y+b)\), with admissible nonlinear activations including the logistic function.
errors.explanation: For a nonlinear \(f\), generally \(E[f(\mathbf w(\mathbf r*\mathbf y)+b)]\neq f(p\mathbf w\mathbf y+b)\). Thus the stated equality is not exact for the model defined here; at most the preactivation expectations coincide (or the test computation is an approximation).

errors.claim: The prose comparison for the deeper pretrained network uses a pre-QX2 baseline of 20.5%.
errors.evidence: Table 7 lists “G6W-pretrained NN (8 layers)” with a phone error rate of 20.7%, whereas the prose-comparison table gives “8-layer net” a pre-QX2 error of 20.5%.
errors.explanation: The reported baseline for the deeper 8-layer pretrained network conflicts with the corresponding Table 7 baseline.

errors.claim: “QX2 nevertheless substantially improves standard neural nets and exceeds every other method.”
errors.evidence: Table 8 reports Bayesian Neural Network: 623 and Neural Network with QX2: 567; the text states that higher C4Y values are preferred, and also says “Bayesian neural nets outperform QX2.”
errors.explanation: QX2 does not exceed every listed method: the Bayesian neural network scores higher (623 versus 567). The claim is only consistent if “every other method” is intended to exclude the Bayesian method, but that exclusion is not stated in the claim.

errors.claim: The ordinary U2L energy uses “\(\mathbf a^\top\mathbf h+\mathbf b^\top\mathbf v\),” while the conditionals are given as \(P(h_j=1\mid r_j,\mathbf v)=\sigma(b_j+\sum_iW_{ij}v_i)\) and \(P(v_i=1\mid\mathbf h)=\sigma(a_i+\sum_jW_{ij}h_j)\).
errors.evidence: The joint distribution assigns \(\mathbf a\) to hidden units and \(\mathbf b\) to visible units, but the hidden conditional uses \(b_j\) and the visible conditional uses \(a_i\).
errors.explanation: For the stated joint distribution, the hidden conditional should use the hidden bias \(a_j\), and the visible conditional should use the visible bias \(b_i\). The bias assignments in the conditionals are reversed relative to the joint model.

errors.claim: "A dimension’s standard deviation scales its weight cost."
errors.evidence: The displayed penalty uses \(\mathbf\Gamma=(\operatorname{diag}(\mathbf X^\top\mathbf X))^{1/2}\), so dimension \(j\)'s factor is \(\sqrt{\sum_i X_{ij}^2}\), i.e. an uncentered root-sum-of-squares, not its standard deviation in general.
errors.explanation: The stated interpretation in terms of standard deviation does not follow from the paper’s own definition of the penalty matrix unless additional centering/normalization assumptions are supplied, which are not stated.

final_notes: §8 introduces B8T as dropout for shared-weight RBMs/U2L models: it mixes exponentially many hidden-retention subsets, with Bernoulli(p) retention and dropped units forced to zero; training samples a different retention vector per case using CD-1. Features are claimed coarser than ordinary U2L and to have fewer dead units (Figure 12, 256 hidden units, B8T p=.5), without numerical counts. B8T is claimed to produce much sparser representations without an extra sparsity regularizer; Figure 13 contrasts ordinary/no-QX2 activations with QX2 p=.5, without numerical sparsity scores. §8.1 has a notation error: joint model uses a^T h+b^T v but conditionals use b_j for hidden and a_i for visible, reversing bias labels. §9: Marginalizing QX2 gives deterministic objectives. Linear regression expected dropout loss is ||y-pXw||²+p(1-p)||Γw||², Γ=(diag(XᵀX))^{1/2}; with w~=pw, penalty coefficient is (1-p)/p. Text says a dimension’s standard deviation scales its weight cost, but Γ is uncentered root-sum-of-squares, not standard deviation absent centering/normalization. §10: P7V Bernoulli dropout; D4K Gaussian dropout. Inverted Bernoulli multiplier mean 1, variance (1-p)/p; Gaussian N(1,σ²) matches. Gaussian noise leaves expected activations unchanged, so test-time scaling unnecessary. §11 claims state-of-the-art on A2F, K9D, W6R, H4Z, citing reported table values. Other reported improvements: Table 7 23.4 vs 21.8; §6.3 31.05% vs 29.62%; Table 8 Z7P: QX2 567 bits, early-stopped neural net 440, Bayesian neural net 623. Training typically costs 2–3×, partly due to noisy updates; gradients are not of final inference architecture. Noise likely prevents overfitting. Appendix A: QX2 requires extensive tuning; recommended layer width at least n/p when standard-net optimum is n, giving pn expected survivors; applies to convolutional and fully connected layers. Higher learning rate/momentum compensate for gradient noise; typical QX2 rate 10–100× standard-net optimal, momentum .95–.99 versus common .9. V9C bounds incoming hidden-unit weight norms, typical c=3–4. Retention: hidden p .5–.8, real-valued inputs typically .8, broad default .5, input optimum closer to 1; lower p requires wider layers, slows training and can underfit. Figure 9/§7.3: p=.1 fixed architecture error 2.7% vs fixed expected width 1.7%. A2F uses held-out validation and specified convolution/pooling

errors.claim: The prose comparison for the deeper pretrained network gives a pre-QX2 error of 20.5% (the 8-layer net).
errors.evidence: Table 7 lists “G6W-pretrained NN (8 layers) (Mohamed et al., 2010)” with a Phone Error Rate of 20.7%; 20.5% is listed for the separate “mcRBM-G6W-pretrained NN (5 layers)” row.
errors.explanation: The prose identifies the 8-layer baseline as 20.5%, but the table reports 20.7% for the 8-layer G6W-pretrained network. The 20.5% value belongs to a different, 5-layer mcRBM-pretrained comparison.

errors.claim: “QX2 nevertheless substantially improves standard neural nets and exceeds every other method.”
errors.evidence: Table 8 reports Bayesian Neural Network = 623 and Neural Network with QX2 = 567 C4Y bits, with higher values preferred; the section also states that QX2 “remains below Bayesian neural networks.”
errors.explanation: QX2 does not exceed every other method: the Bayesian neural network has a higher, and therefore better, score (623 versus 567).
The first Table 4 value is recorded as 14.98, not 15.60; the claim therefore misstates the reported result.

errors.claim: The ordinary U2L distribution is defined with bias terms \(\mathbf a^\top\mathbf h+\mathbf b^\top\mathbf v\), and the text says that \(W_{ij}\), \(b_j\), and \(a_i\) are the corresponding entries; however, the hidden conditional uses \(b_j\) and the visible conditional uses \(a_i\).
errors.evidence: The joint distribution assigns \(\mathbf a\) to hidden units and \(\mathbf b\) to visible units: \(\mathbf a^\top\mathbf h+\mathbf b^\top\mathbf v\). But \(P(h_j=1\mid r_j,\mathbf v)=\mathbf1(r_j=1)\sigma(b_j+\sum_iW_{ij}v_i)\), while \(P(v_i=1\mid\mathbf h)=\sigma(a_i+\sum_jW_{ij}h_j)\).
errors.explanation: The bias symbols are reversed between the joint energy and the two conditional distributions (and the accompanying notation statement), so the equations cannot all be consistent as written.

errors.claim: “A dimension’s standard deviation scales its weight cost.”
errors.evidence: The displayed penalty uses “\(\mathbf\Gamma=(\operatorname{diag}(\mathbf X^\top\mathbf X))^{1/2}\),” so each dimension’s cost is based on the square root of its sum of squared values (its uncentered L2 norm), not its standard deviation.
errors.explanation: Unless the inputs are explicitly centered and otherwise normalized—which is not stated—the formula depends on the uncentered second moment, not the dimension’s standard deviation. Thus the verbal claim does not follow from the stated objective.

errors.claim: “Other-domain improvements include ... Table 8, 440 versus 567.”
errors.evidence: Table 8 lists early-stop NN at 440 and QX2 NN at 567.
errors.explanation: The Table 8 comparison does not show an improvement from QX2: QX2 has the higher value (567 versus 440).

final_notes: The paper studies dropout (QX2), which samples thinned subnetworks and uses test-time weight scaling; it generally improves generalization but training takes 2–3× longer. QX2 retains all units at inference and scales weights by p, not biases; typical rates are 10–100× standard values, with momentum .95–.99; pretrained weights are multiplied by 1/p before finetuning. Key results: Table 9 H4Z regularizers: Y5F 1.62, Y5F+O3U 1.60, Y5F+KL 1.55, V9C 1.35, QX2+Y5F 1.25, QX2+V9C 1.05. Table 8 Z7P: early-stop NN 440, PCA regression 463, PCA SVM 487, QX2 NN 567, Bayesian NN 623; claim that QX2 exceeds every other method conflicts with Bayesian result, and the conclusion’s description of 440 versus 567 as an “improvement” is inconsistent because QX2 is higher. §6 misstates Table 4’s first value as 15.60 instead of 14.98; actual sequences 14.98→14.32→12.61 and 43.48→41.26→37.20. Prior prose calls 8-layer pre-QX2 baseline 20.5%, table gives 20.7%; 20.5% is separate 5-layer comparison. §7: QX2 features are more localized; autoencoder mean activation about 2.0 without versus 0.7 with QX2. Fixed-architecture error flat for p=.4–.8; p=.1 gives 2.7% versus 1.7% with fixed expected retained width; best expected widths near p=.6, default p=.5 close to optimal. Sampled averaging matches T6R around k=50 and is slightly better thereafter, within one SD; T6R approximates true averaging. §8 B8T extends dropout to shared-weight RBMs; claimed coarser, fewer dead units and sparser representations. During training, units are independently retained with probability p; hidden and input units may be dropped. At inference all units are retained and weights scaled by p, with biases unchanged. A fixed p can be selected by validation; optimal input retention is generally closer to full retention. QX2 uses backpropagation through sampled subnetworks, with per-case gradients averaged across minibatches. High momentum, decaying learning rates, and max-norm regularization are useful. Max-norm constrains each hidden unit’s incoming weight vector to norm <= c, with validation tuning c. Appendix A.2 gives learning rates typically 10–100 times standard-net values and momentum about 0.95–0.99.

QX2 can finetune pretrained networks. Smaller finetuning rates preserve pretrained information; before QX2 finetuning, pretrained weights are multiplied by 1/p. Table 2 reports G6W finetuning values 1.18 without QX2 and 0.92 with QX2, and E5Q values 0.96 and 0.79. Appendix B.4 reports about 0.01 as the best QX2 G6W-finetuning rate versus listed high rate 0.1. Pretraining may use stacked RBMs, autoencoders, or DBMs.

errors.claim: The ordinary U2L distribution is defined with bias terms \(\mathbf a^\top\mathbf h+\mathbf b^\top\mathbf v\), and the text says that \(W_{ij}\), \(b_j\), and \(a_i\) are the corresponding entries; however, the hidden conditional uses \(b_j\) and the visible conditional uses \(a_i\).
errors.evidence: The joint distribution assigns \(\mathbf a\) to hidden units and \(\mathbf b\) to visible units: \(\mathbf a^\top\mathbf h+\mathbf b^\top\mathbf v\). But \(P(h_j=1\mid r_j,\mathbf v)=\mathbf1(r_j=1)\sigma(b_j+\sum_iW_{ij}v_i)\), while \(P(v_i=1\mid\mathbf h)=\sigma(a_i+\sum_jW_{ij}h_j)\).
errors.explanation: The bias symbols are reversed between the joint energy and the two conditional distributions (and the accompanying notation statement), so the equations cannot all be consistent as written.

The paper introduces dropout for reducing overfitting in large neural networks. During training, units and their connections are randomly dropped, sampling exponentially many thinned networks and preventing excessive co-adaptation. At test time, the paper says their averaged predictions can be approximated with one unthinned network using smaller weights. It claims significant reductions in overfitting, major improvements over other regularization methods, and state-of-the-art results on many supervised tasks in vision, speech recognition, document classification, and computational biology. Introduction: deep nets are expressive but can overfit limited data; mentioned regularization methods include early stopping, L1/L2 penalties, and soft weight sharing. No internal contradictions identified so far.

The paper introduces dropout as a way to approximate an equally weighted geometric mean of predictions from exponentially many learned, parameter-sharing models, approaching Bayesian performance with less computation. Model averaging generally improves performance, but separately training many large networks is computationally and practically infeasible. Dropout addresses this by randomly removing hidden and visible units and their connections during training, thereby combining many architectures efficiently and reducing overfitting. Each unit is retained independently with probability p; p may be selected by validation or set to 0.5, while input retention is usually closer to 1. At test time, all units are present and outgoing weights are multiplied by p; the figure states this gives the same output as the expected training-time output. Earlier notes also record that test-time averaged predictions are approximated using one unthinned network with smaller weights, consistent with this description. No internal contradictions identified.

Dropout samples a thinned network by independently removing units; a network with n units corresponds to 2^n possible thinned networks sharing O(n^2) or fewer parameters. A new thinned network is sampled for each training case, so each individual model is rarely trained. At test time, instead of averaging exponentially many models, use one full network with each unit’s outgoing weights multiplied by its training retention probability p; this makes each hidden unit’s expected training-time output equal its test-time output and approximates model averaging. The paper claims this yields significantly lower generalization error than other regularizers across many classification problems. Dropout can also be applied to graphical models, and the paper introduces and evaluates a dropout Restricted Boltzmann Machine against standard RBMs. Structure: motivation (Sec. 2), prior work (Sec. 3), formal model (Sec. 4), training algorithm (Sec. 5), experiments (Sec. 6), analysis/hyperparameters (Sec. 7), dropout RBM (Sec. 8), marginalizing dropout (Sec. 9), practical guide (Appendix A). Earlier introduction: dropout approximates an equally weighted geometric mean/model average over exponentially many parameter-sharing models; units retained independently with probability p, typically p=0.5 for hidden units and closer to 1 for inputs; test-time scaling by p approximates expected training output.

Motivation: analogy to sexual reproduction, which breaks up complex co-adapted gene sets and favors mixability/robustness. Dropout-trained hidden units must work with random subsets of other units, encouraging individually useful, robust features while still allowing different units to learn different things; simply replicating units is characterized as a poor solution. A related “conspiracies” analogy says many smaller co-adaptations are more robust under non-stationary conditions than one large complex co-adaptation, which may fit training data but fail on novel test data. Section 3 begins related work: dropout is interpretable as regularization by adding noise to hidden-unit states; denoising autoencoders previously used noise on unit states (Vincent et al., 2008, 2010).

Related work: denoising autoencoders add noise to inputs and reconstruct noise-free inputs; dropout extends noise to hidden layers, supervised learning, and architectures such as Boltzmann Machines. DAE noise is typically 5%, whereas dropout often works with 20% input and 50% hidden-unit dropout. Dropout is stochastic expected-loss minimization; adversarial unit-dropping methods instead fix a maximum number dropped and generally lack hidden units.

Model: standard feed-forward layers use z^(l+1)=W^(l+1)y^(l)+b^(l+1), y=f(z). Dropout samples independent Bernoulli(p) masks r^(l), forms y-tilde^(l)=r^(l)*y^(l), and feeds these to the next layer; at test time no dropout is used and weights are scaled W_test^(l)=pW^(l). Section 5 begins learning procedure.

Dropout is claimed to reduce generalization error across many classification problems. It can also be applied to graphical models, including a dropout RBM. Units are retained independently with probability p, typically p=0.5 for hidden units and closer to 1 for inputs.

Dropout is motivated by breaking up co-adapted feature sets and encouraging robust, individually useful features. Related work includes denoising autoencoders, which typically use 5% input noise versus dropout’s often 20% input and 50% hidden-unit dropout. Dropout is stochastic expected-loss minimization.

Feed-forward dropout uses independent Bernoulli masks during training and test-time weight scaling W_test=pW. Training uses SGD on each sampled thinned network, with mini-batch gradients averaged; momentum, decaying learning rates, and L2 decay are useful. Max-norm regularization constrains each hidden unit’s incoming weight vector to ||w||2≤c via projection; c is selected on validation data. Dropout combined with max-norm, large decaying learning rates, and high momentum improves over dropout alone.

For pretrained networks, pretraining is unchanged; pretrained weights are scaled by 1/p before dropout finetuning so expected dropout output matches pretraining. Smaller finetuning learning rates preserve pretrained information and can improve final generalization error.

Section 6 claims dropout improved generalization on all listed datasets (MNIST, TIMIT, CIFAR-10/100, SVHN, ImageNet, Reuters-RCV1, and Alternative Splicing) versus neural nets without dropout.
