errors.explanation: QX2 does not achieve the reported best result on A2F or W6R, so the blanket state-of-the-art claim contradicts the paper’s own results.

final_notes: Paper: “Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting,” JMLR 15 (2014), pp. 1929–1958. Dropout (QX2) randomly removes units/connections during training, reduces co-adaptation/overfitting, samples exponentially many thinned networks, and uses one unthinned network with reduced weights to approximate averaged predictions. Best noise: input dropout 20% (retention .8), hidden dropout 50% (retention .5); ordinary input noise 5%. Expected training output matches test output for hidden units despite nonlinear caveat. Gains improve with momentum, decaying learning rates, and V9C max-norm; pretrained weights are multiplied by 1/p before QX2 fine-tuning. Results: H4Z 0.79% with E5Q+QX2 vs 0.96% without. A2F: max pooling 3.95, QX2 FC 3.02, stochastic pooling 2.80, QX2 all layers 2.55, L8J 2.47. J3V QX2 12.61 vs L8J 11.68; W6R QX2 37.20 vs L8J 38.57. K9D QX2 top-1/top-5 37.5/17.0. N8Q: 6-layer NN 23.4, QX2 21.8; best QX2 19.7. M5X 31.05 without vs 29.62 with QX2. Z7P Table 8: QX2 NN 567, Bayesian NN 623; text inconsistently says QX2 exceeds every method and Bayesian outperforms QX2. Table 9 H4Z: Y5F 1.62, +O3U 1.60, +KL 1.55, V9C 1.35, QX2+Y5F 1.25, QX2+V9C 1.05. §7: QX2 features localized and activations sparser (about 0.7 vs 2.0); H4Z best retention near .6, default .5. §8 B8T: mixture of shared-weight subnetworks; displayed conditionals swap a/b relative to joint model (parameter-label inconsistency). §9 marginalization: deterministic noise-marginalized models avoid random bits and permit marginalized-loss gradients. Linear QX2 regression marginalizes to squared loss plus p(1-p)||Γw||², or with w~=pw, ridge penalty (1-p)/p||Γw~||². Approximate marginalization reportedly outperforms Monte-Carlo QX2 for logistic regression; closed forms difficult for logistic/deep nets. §10 Gaussian dropout (D4K) and Bernoulli dropout (P7V) can match first two moments; Gaussian highest entropy, Bernoulli lowest. Table 10: H4Z P7V 1.08±.04, D4K .95±.04; J3V P7V 12.6±.1, D4K 12.5±.1. §11 conclusion claims QX2 is state of the art on A2F, K9D, W6R, H4Z, conflicting with A2F and W6R comparisons. Training typically 2–3 times as long; noise marginalization gives an expectation-equivalent regularizer; accelerating QX2 is future work. Appendix B: H4Z uses 10,000 validation images.

Introduction: posterior-weighted averaging over parameter settings is ideal with unlimited computation; QX2 is a cheaper construction approximating an equally weighted geometric mean of exponentially many learned, parameter-sharing models. An n-unit network represents 2^n thinned networks while retaining O(n^2) or fewer shared parameters; a new member is sampled/trained for each training presentation, so each member is rarely trained. Dropout addresses overfitting from spurious co-adaptations; alternatives include early stopping, soft weight sharing, and L1/L2 penalties. Model combination often improves performance but separately training/inferencing many large nets is expensive. T6R (weight scaling) uses one unthinned network; X9M (Monte-Carlo model averaging) averages sampled members’ predictions. T6R is claimed to outperform other regularizers across varied classification tasks. The construction extends to graphical models, including U2L (RBMs), yielding B8T (Dropout RBM). Figure 1 contrasts a standard two-hidden-layer net with a QX2-thinned net. §2 Motivation: Sexual reproduction can break successful co-adapted gene sets, while asexual reproduction preserves them, yet advanced organisms mostly evolved sexually. Livnat et al. (2010) is invoked to argue selection may favor gene mix-ability/robustness over individual fitness. QX2-trained hidden units face randomly selected partners, favoring independently useful robust features rather than reliance on other units; units in a layer still learn different functions. Replicating units is said to be a poor robustness solution, analogous to replica codes for noisy channels. Ten five-person conspiracies may have a havoc-producing advantage over one fifty-person conspiracy under non-stationarity, though ample rehearsal and unchanged conditions can make the larger conspiracy work. Complex co-adaptations may fit training data yet generalize worse than multiple simpler co-adaptations.

errors.claim: The ordinary U2L is defined with parameters θ = {W, a, b} and energy terms "a^T h + b^T v," while the conditionals state "P(h_j=1|r_j,v) = 1(r_j=1) σ(b_j + Σ_i W_ij v_i)" and "P(v_i=1|h) = σ(a_i + Σ_j W_ij h_j)."
errors.evidence: The joint distribution assigns a to hidden units and b to visible units: "a^T h + b^T v." For that joint distribution, the hidden conditional should use a_j and the visible conditional should use b_i, opposite to the displayed conditionals.
errors.explanation: The bias vectors are interchanged between the joint U2L distribution and both conditional-distribution equations. Unless the parameter definitions are reversed, these equations cannot describe the same model.

grade.reason: None of the reported review errors mention or contradict the paper's ReLU vs maxout MNIST error claim (0.95 vs 0.94), so the planted error was not identified.

errors.claim: “Goodfellow et al. (2013) worsened error to 0.94% by replacing ReLUs with maxout units.”
errors.evidence: The preceding network reaches 0.95%, while the maxout result is 0.94% (also recorded in the notes as Table 2: maxout 0.94%).
errors.explanation: An error of 0.94% is lower, not higher, than 0.95%, so replacing ReLUs with maxout improved the reported error rather than worsened it.

errors.claim: “Similarly, for an 8-layer network, error falls from 20.5% to 19.7%.”
errors.evidence: Table 7 reports “DBN-pretrained NN (8 layers) (Mohamed et al., 2010)” at 20.7%, while 20.5% is reported for the “mcRBM-DBN-pretrained NN (5 layers).”
errors.explanation: The prose assigns the 20.5% error to the 8-layer DBN-pretrained network, but the table assigns 20.7% to that network and 20.5% to a different 5-layer model.

errors.claim: "Dropout substantially improves standard neural networks and outperforms every other method listed" and "Dropout outperforms the other listed methods."
errors.location: This part, discussion and claims under Table 8
errors.evidence: Table 8 reports Bayesian Neural Network = 623 bits and Neural Network with dropout = 567 bits; the text also states, "Bayesian networks perform better than dropout."
errors.explanation: Because higher Code Quality is better, the Bayesian Neural Network outperforms dropout, so dropout does not outperform every other listed method.

errors.claim: The hidden conditional is \(P(h_j=1\mid r_j,v)=\mathbf1(r_j=1)\sigma\left(b_j+\sum_i W_{ij}v_i\right)\), and the visible conditional is \(P(v_i=1\mid h)=\sigma\left(a_i+\sum_jW_{ij}h_j\right)\).
errors.evidence: The RBM distribution is defined with \(a^\top h+b^\top v\), so \(a\) is the hidden-unit bias and \(b\) is the visible-unit bias.
errors.explanation: The conditional equations swap the bias vectors relative to the model definition: the hidden conditional should use \(a_j\), while the visible conditional should use \(b_i\). Thus the claim that the visible conditional is the same as in the defined RBM is inconsistent with the preceding distribution.

The paper studies reducing overfitting in large neural networks without training many separate networks. Dropout randomly removes units/connections during training, sampling smaller networks that share weights; at test time, a full network with scaled weights approximates their combined predictions. Reported improvements cover image, speech, text, and alternative-splicing tasks. The paper compares dropout with other regularizers and Bayesian neural networks, and examines learned features, sparsity, dropout rates, network size, training-set size, and test-time averaging. Dropout RBMs learn qualitatively different features and sparser representations. For linear regression, marginalizing dropout yields a modified ridge-regression objective. Preliminary experiments compare Bernoulli dropout with multiplicative Gaussian noise. Limitation: dropout networks typically take 2–3 times longer to train than standard networks with the same architecture.

Section 5: Dropout uses mini-batch SGD with momentum, annealed learning rates, L2 decay, and especially max-norm constraints. Max-norm bounds each hidden unit’s incoming weight vector by c; validation selects c. Combining dropout, max-norm, large decaying learning rates, and high momentum is claimed to improve results. Table 9 evidence: Dropout + L2 1.25% versus Dropout + Max-norm 1.05%; Max-norm without dropout 1.35% versus L2 1.62%.

For pretrained networks (RBMs, autoencoders, DBMs), dropout can be used during finetuning without changing pretraining. Pretrained weights are multiplied by 1/p so expected dropout outputs match pretraining outputs. Larger finetuning learning rates may erase pretrained information; smaller rates seem to preserve it and improve final generalization. Table 2: dropout finetuning improves pretrained MNIST DBN error 1.18% to 0.92% and DBM error 0.96% to 0.79%.

grade.reason: The reviewer's first reported error directly points out that Table 2 shows 0.95% for the ReLU network and 0.94% for maxout, so the paper's claim that replacing ReLUs with maxout worsened error is incorrect.

errors.claim: “For every hidden unit, expected output under training-time deletion equals actual test-time output under the prescribed reduced weights.”
errors.location: This part, opening paragraph of Section 4
errors.evidence: The same section defines training output as \(f(\mathbf w\, (\mathbf r*\mathbf y)+b)\), while test output uses \(f(p\mathbf w\mathbf y+b)\), with admissible nonlinear activations including the logistic function.
errors.explanation: For a nonlinear \(f\), generally \(E[f(\mathbf w(\mathbf r*\mathbf y)+b)]\neq f(p\mathbf w\mathbf y+b)\). Thus the stated equality is not exact for the model defined here; at most the preactivation expectations coincide (or the test computation is an approximation).

errors.claim: The prose comparison for the deeper pretrained network reports a pre-QX2 error of 20.5%.
errors.evidence: Table 7 lists “G6W-pretrained NN (8 layers) (Mohamed et al., 2010)” with a phone error rate of 20.7%; 20.5% appears only for the separate “mcRBM-G6W-pretrained NN (5 layers)” row.
errors.explanation: The prose assigns the 20.5% error to the 8-layer pretrained baseline, but the corresponding table entry is 20.7%. The 20.5% value belongs to a different 5-layer mcRBM-pretrained model.

errors.claim: “QX2 nevertheless substantially improves standard neural nets and exceeds every other method.” / “QX2 exceeds all other listed methods.”
errors.location: This part, Section 6.4 claims and evidence
errors.evidence: The section states that “Bayesian neural nets outperform QX2,” and Table 8 reports Bayesian Neural Network: 623 versus Neural Network with QX2: 567.
errors.explanation: QX2 does not exceed every other listed method: the Bayesian Neural Network has a higher C4Y score (623), while higher scores are preferred. The claim is also inconsistent with the section’s opening statement that QX2 remains below Bayesian neural networks.

errors.evidence: Earlier notes for Table 4 record J3V as “14.98→14.32→12.61” and W6R as “43.48→41.26→37.20.”
errors.explanation: The first Table 4 baseline is given as 15.60 here but was reported earlier as 14.98. The W6R baseline of 43.48 agrees, but the J3V value conflicts.

errors.claim: The ordinary U2L energy uses \(\mathbf a^\top\mathbf h+\mathbf b^\top\mathbf v\), but the conditional equations state \(P(h_j=1\mid r_j,\mathbf v)=\mathbf1(r_j=1)\sigma(b_j+\sum_iW_{ij}v_i)\) and \(P(v_i=1\mid\mathbf h)=\sigma(a_i+\sum_jW_{ij}h_j)\).
errors.evidence: The joint distribution defines \(\mathbf a\) as the hidden-bias vector and \(\mathbf b\) as the visible-bias vector through \(\mathbf a^\top\mathbf h+\mathbf b^\top\mathbf v\). Therefore the hidden conditional should use \(a_j\), and the visible conditional should use \(b_i\), not vice versa.
errors.explanation: The conditional equations swap the roles of the hidden and visible biases relative to the preceding joint distribution, so the model specification is internally inconsistent.

errors.claim: “A dimension’s standard deviation scales its weight cost.”
errors.evidence: The displayed penalty uses \(\mathbf\Gamma=(\operatorname{diag}(\mathbf X^\top\mathbf X))^{1/2}\), so the cost for dimension \(j\) is proportional to \(\sqrt{\sum_i X_{ij}^2}\), not its standard deviation. The section only states that \(\mathbf X\) contains real-valued data and does not assume each dimension is centered.
errors.explanation: Without a zero-mean assumption, the square root of the sum of squares is an RMS/norm quantity that includes the dimension’s mean, whereas standard deviation subtracts the mean. Thus the verbal claim does not follow from, and can conflict with, the stated penalty formula.

errors.claim: “QX2 methods attain state of the art on A2F, K9D, W6R and H4Z.”
errors.evidence: Table 3 reports A2F at 2.55 for QX2, while L8J achieves 2.47.
errors.explanation: Because lower error is better, the reported L8J result outperforms QX2 on A2F, so QX2 cannot be described as attaining state of the art there based on the paper’s own table.

errors.claim: The ordinary U2L energy uses \(\mathbf a^\top\mathbf h+\mathbf b^\top\mathbf v\), but the conditional equations state \(P(h_j=1\mid r_j,\mathbf v)=\mathbf1(r_j=1)\sigma(b_j+\sum_iW_{ij}v_i)\) and \(P(v_i=1\mid\mathbf h)=\sigma(a_i+\sum_jW_{ij}h_j)\).
errors.evidence: The joint distribution defines \(\mathbf a\) as the hidden-bias vector and \(\mathbf b\) as the visible-bias vector through \(\mathbf a^\top\mathbf h+\mathbf b^\top\mathbf v\). Therefore the hidden conditional should use \(a_j\), and the visible conditional should use \(b_i\), not vice versa.
errors.explanation: The conditional equations swap the roles of the hidden and visible biases relative to the preceding joint distribution, so the model specification is internally inconsistent.

errors.claim: “A dimension’s standard deviation scales its weight cost.”
errors.evidence: The displayed penalty uses \(\mathbf\Gamma=(\operatorname{diag}(\mathbf X^\top\mathbf X))^{1/2}\), so the cost for dimension \(j\) is proportional to \(\sqrt{\sum_i X_{ij}^2}\), not its standard deviation. The section only states that \(\mathbf X\) contains real-valued data and does not assume each dimension is centered.
errors.explanation: Without a zero-mean assumption, the square root of the sum of squares is an RMS/norm quantity that includes the dimension’s mean, whereas standard deviation subtracts the mean. Thus the verbal claim does not follow from, and can conflict with, the stated penalty formula.

errors.claim: The conditional distributions are given as \(P(h_j=1\mid r_j,v)=\mathbf{1}(r_j=1)\sigma(b_j+\sum_i W_{ij}v_i)\) and \(P(v_i=1\mid h)=\sigma(a_i+\sum_j W_{ij}h_j)\).

The paper introduces dropout for reducing overfitting in large neural networks. During training, units and their connections are randomly dropped, sampling exponentially many thinned networks and preventing excessive co-adaptation. At test time, the paper says their averaged predictions can be approximated with one unthinned network using smaller weights. It claims significant reductions in overfitting, major improvements over other regularization methods, and state-of-the-art results on many supervised tasks in vision, speech recognition, document classification, and computational biology. Introduction: deep nets are expressive but can overfit limited data; mentioned regularization methods include early stopping, L1/L2 penalties, and soft weight sharing. No internal contradictions identified so far.

The paper introduces dropout as a way to approximate an equally weighted geometric mean of predictions from exponentially many learned, parameter-sharing models, approaching Bayesian performance with less computation. Model averaging generally improves performance, but separately training many large networks is computationally and practically infeasible. Dropout addresses this by randomly removing hidden and visible units and their connections during training, thereby combining many architectures efficiently and reducing overfitting. Each unit is retained independently with probability p; p may be selected by validation or set to 0.5, while input retention is usually closer to 1. At test time, all units are present and outgoing weights are multiplied by p; the figure states this gives the same output as the expected training-time output. Earlier notes also record that test-time averaged predictions are approximated using one unthinned network with smaller weights, consistent with this description. No internal contradictions identified.

Dropout samples a thinned network by independently removing units; a network with n units corresponds to 2^n possible thinned networks sharing O(n^2) or fewer parameters. A new thinned network is sampled for each training case, so each individual model is rarely trained. At test time, instead of averaging exponentially many models, use one full network with each unit’s outgoing weights multiplied by its training retention probability p; this makes each hidden unit’s expected training-time output equal its test-time output and approximates model averaging. The paper claims this yields significantly lower generalization error than other regularizers across many classification problems. Dropout can also be applied to graphical models, and the paper introduces and evaluates a dropout Restricted Boltzmann Machine against standard RBMs. Structure: motivation (Sec. 2), prior work (Sec. 3), formal model (Sec. 4), training algorithm (Sec. 5), experiments (Sec. 6), analysis/hyperparameters (Sec. 7), dropout RBM (Sec. 8), marginalizing dropout (Sec. 9), practical guide (Appendix A). Earlier introduction: dropout approximates an equally weighted geometric mean/model average over exponentially many parameter-sharing models; units retained independently with probability p, typically p=0.5 for hidden units and closer to 1 for inputs; test-time scaling by p approximates expected training output.

Motivation: analogy to sexual reproduction, which breaks up complex co-adapted gene sets and favors mixability/robustness. Dropout-trained hidden units must work with random subsets of other units, encouraging individually useful, robust features while still allowing different units to learn different things; simply replicating units is characterized as a poor solution. A related “conspiracies” analogy says many smaller co-adaptations are more robust under non-stationary conditions than one large complex co-adaptation, which may fit training data but fail on novel test data. Section 3 begins related work: dropout is interpretable as regularization by adding noise to hidden-unit states; denoising autoencoders previously used noise on unit states (Vincent et al., 2008, 2010).

Model: standard feed-forward layers use z^(l+1)=W^(l+1)y^(l)+b^(l+1), y=f(z). Dropout samples independent Bernoulli(p) masks r^(l), forms y-tilde^(l)=r^(l)*y^(l), and feeds these to the next layer; at test time no dropout is used and weights are scaled W_test^(l)=pW^(l). Dropout is motivated by breaking up co-adapted feature sets and encouraging robust, individually useful features. Related work includes denoising autoencoders, which typically use 5% input noise versus dropout’s often 20% input and 50% hidden-unit dropout. Dropout is stochastic expected-loss minimization.

Feed-forward dropout uses independent Bernoulli masks during training and test-time weight scaling W_test=pW. Training uses SGD on each sampled thinned network, with mini-batch gradients averaged; momentum, decaying learning rates, and L2 decay are useful. Max-norm regularization constrains each hidden unit’s incoming weight vector to ||w||2≤c via projection; c is selected on validation data. Dropout combined with max-norm, large decaying learning rates, and high momentum improves over dropout alone.

For pretrained networks, pretraining is unchanged; pretrained weights are scaled by 1/p before dropout finetuning so expected dropout output matches pretraining. Smaller finetuning learning rates preserve pretrained information and can improve final generalization error.

Section 6 claims dropout improved generalization on all listed datasets (MNIST, TIMIT, CIFAR-10/100, SVHN, ImageNet, Reuters-RCV1, and Alternative Splicing) versus neural nets without dropout.

grade.reason: The third reported error directly identifies the planted claim about Bayesian nets vs dropout and points out Table 8 shows Bayesian (623) > dropout (567) despite the text claiming the opposite.

errors.claim: “For every hidden unit, expected output under the training deletion distribution equals actual test-time output under the prescribed reduced weights.”
errors.evidence: The same section states that “Any activation \(f\) is admissible,” including the sigmoid \(f(x)=1/(1+\exp(-x))\), and defines training output as \(y_i^{(l+1)}=f(\mathbf w_i^{(l+1)}(\mathbf r^{(l)}*\mathbf y^{(l)})+b_i^{(l+1)})\), whereas test-time output uses \(f(p\mathbf w_i^{(l+1)}\mathbf y^{(l)}+b_i^{(l+1)})\).
errors.explanation: For a nonlinear activation such as the sigmoid, generally \(E[f(z)]\ne f(E[z])\). Weight scaling makes the test-time preactivation equal to the expected training preactivation, but does not make the expected training output equal to the test-time output.

errors.claim: “Bayesian neural nets underperform QX2 on Z7P, while QX2 substantially improves standard neural nets and exceeds every other method.”
errors.evidence: Table 8 states that C4Y is scored with “higher values preferred,” but the Bayesian Neural Network scores 623, compared with 567 for the Neural Network with QX2.
errors.explanation: Because 623 is higher than 567 and higher C4Y is better, the table shows the Bayesian Neural Network outperforming QX2, contrary to the prose claim.

errors.claim: The prose comparison lists the pre-QX2 error for the “8-layer net” as 20.5%.
errors.evidence: Table 7 lists “G6W-pretrained NN (8 layers)” at 20.7%; the only 20.5% entry is the separate “mcRBM-G6W-pretrained NN (5 layers).”
errors.explanation: The stated 8-layer pre-QX2 error does not match the corresponding 8-layer result in Table 7.

errors.claim: The conditional distributions are given as \(P(h_j=1\mid r_j,\mathbf v)=\mathbf1(r_j=1)\sigma(b_j+\sum_iW_{ij}v_i)\) and \(P(v_i=1\mid\mathbf h)=\sigma(a_i+\sum_jW_{ij}h_j)\).
errors.evidence: The joint U2L distribution defines the hidden bias as \(\mathbf a^	op\mathbf h\) and the visible bias as \(\mathbf b^	op\mathbf v\).
errors.explanation: The conditional formulas swap the bias parameters: the hidden conditional should use \(a_j\), while the visible conditional should use \(b_i\), assuming the joint distribution’s definitions.

errors.claim: “QX2 methods achieve state of the art on A2F, K9D, W6R and H4Z.”
errors.evidence: For A2F, Table 3 reports QX2 all layers at 2.55%, while L8J is better at 2.47%. For K9D, QX2 reports 17.0% top-5 error, while the 2012 five-network ensemble reports 16.4%.
errors.explanation: The reported comparison results show methods with lower error than the cited QX2 results on A2F and K9D, so the blanket state-of-the-art claim is inconsistent with those results.

errors.claim: “For a task whose optimal standard-net layer has \(n\) hidden units, a good QX2 layer should contain at least \(n/p\) units. Removing units reduces capacity: only \(pn\) units remain in expectation.”
errors.evidence: If the QX2 layer contains \(n/p\) units and each is retained with probability \(p\), the expected number retained is \(p(n/p)=n\), not \(pn\).
errors.explanation: The stated layer size and the stated expected retained size are inconsistent unless the latter is intended to refer to a layer of size \(n\), not \(n/p\).

final_notes: Paper: “Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting,” JMLR 15 (2014), pp. 1929–1958. Dropout (QX2) randomly removes units/connections, reduces co-adaptation and overfitting, samples exponentially many thinned networks, and uses one unthinned network with reduced weights (T6R) to approximate averaged predictions (X9M). Best noise levels: S2H input 5%, QX2 input removal 20% (retention .8), hidden removal 50% (retention .5). Test scaling matches expected preactivation, not generally expected activation. Gains improve with momentum, decaying learning rates, and V9C max-norm constraints; pretrained weights are multiplied by 1/p before QX2 finetuning. Results: H4Z standard NN 1.60% to best pretrained QX2 0.79%. A2F Table 3: ConvNet+pooling 3.95%, QX2 fully connected 3.02%, QX2 all layers 2.55%, L8J 2.47%, human 2.0%. J3V/W6R QX2 all layers 12.61%/37.20%, L8J 11.68%/38.57%. K9D ConvNet+QX2 37.5/17.0 top-1/top-5; 2012 five-net ensemble 16.4% top-5. N8Q Table 7: 6-layer NN 23.4, QX2 21.8, pretrained 4-layer 22.7, 6-layer 22.4, 8-layer 20.7, mcRBM 5-layer 20.5, pretrained 4-layer+QX2 19.7, 8-layer+QX2 19.7; prose says 8-layer pre-QX2 20.5, conflicting with table’s 20.7. Text classification: without QX2 31.05%, with 29.62%. Z7P Table 8: QX2 567 C4Y, Bayesian NN 623; higher C4Y preferred, contradicting prose that QX2 exceeds every method. H4Z regularizers: Y5F 1.62%, Y5F+O3U 1.60%, Y5F+KL 1.55%, V9C 1.35%, QX2+Y5F 1.25%, QX2+V9C 1.05%. QX2 features detect localized edges/strokes/spots; no-QX2 features appear co-adapted. QX2 autoencoder activations mean about 0.7 versus 2.0 without QX2. Fixed-architecture error is high at low retention, lowest/flat for p=.4–.8, rises near p=1; best retention near .6, default p=.5 near optimal. X9M matches T6R around k=50 and is slightly better thereafter within one SD. B8T is a mixture of exponentially many shared-weight U2L models with hidden retention vector r; CD-1 samples a different r per case. B8T features are coarser than ordinary U2L, with few dead units relative to U2L. Without additional sparsity regularization, B8T learns much sparser representations than U2L, with activations near zero and few highly active units. Gaussian dropout D4K uses multipliers N(1,sigma²), sigma²=(1-p)/p matching Bernoulli inverted dropout’s mean. Appendix settings: G6W windows

Introduction: posterior-weighted averaging over parameter settings is ideal with unlimited computation; QX2 is a cheaper construction approximating an equally weighted geometric mean of exponentially many learned, parameter-sharing models. An n-unit network represents 2^n thinned networks while retaining O(n^2) or fewer shared parameters; a new member is sampled/trained for each training presentation, so each member is rarely trained. Dropout addresses overfitting from spurious co-adaptations; alternatives include early stopping, soft weight sharing, and L1/L2 penalties. Model combination often improves performance but separately training/inferencing many large nets is expensive. T6R (weight scaling) uses one unthinned network; X9M (Monte-Carlo model averaging) averages sampled members’ predictions. T6R is claimed to outperform other regularizers across varied classification tasks. The construction extends to graphical models, including U2L (RBMs), yielding B8T (Dropout RBM). Figure 1 contrasts a standard two-hidden-layer net with a QX2-thinned net. (2010) is invoked to argue selection may favor gene mix-ability/robustness over individual fitness. QX2-trained hidden units face randomly selected partners, favoring independently useful robust features rather than reliance on other units; units in a layer still learn different functions. Replicating units is said to be a poor robustness solution, analogous to replica codes for noisy channels. Ten five-person conspiracies may have a havoc-producing advantage over one fifty-person conspiracy under non-stationarity, though ample rehearsal and unchanged conditions can make the larger conspiracy work. Complex co-adaptations may fit training data yet generalize worse than multiple simpler co-adaptations.

Abstract/introduction: dropout (called QX2 here) randomly removes units/connections during training, reduces co-adaptation and overfitting, samples exponentially many thinned networks, and uses a single unthinned network with reduced weights to approximate averaged predictions. Claims improvements across vision, speech, document classification, and computational biology. It approximates an equally weighted geometric mean of many learned, parameter-sharing models; each presentation samples/trains a new thinned member. T6R is weight scaling; X9M is Monte-Carlo model averaging. T6R is claimed to outperform other regularizers. Extensions include graphical models/RBMs (U2L, B8T).

§2 motivation: QX2-trained hidden units face randomly selected partners, favoring independently useful robust features rather than reliance on other units; units in a layer still learn different functions. Complex co-adaptations may fit training data yet generalize worse.

§3 related work: Hidden-state noise gives QX2 a regularization interpretation, extending denoising autoencoders (S2H), with hidden-layer corruption, model averaging, supervised/unsupervised use, and applicability to architectures such as Boltzmann Machines. Best noise levels reported: S2H input 5%; QX2 input removal 20%; QX2 hidden removal 50%. Test-time T6R permits higher noise than usually best for S2H. Analytical marginalization yields deterministic regularizers; prior work studied blankout noise without hidden layers, marginalized denoising autoencoders, and accelerated QX2.

§4 model: Hidden/output vectors and standard feed-forward equations are defined; QX2 independently gates each layer’s outputs with Bernoulli retention probability \(p\), including possible visible and hidden unit removal. At inference all units remain and weights are scaled to \(pW\). The text claims expected training output equals test output for every hidden unit, but this conflicts with allowing nonlinear activations (e.g. sigmoid): scaling matches expected preactivation, not generally expected activation.

errors.claim: “Bayesian neural nets underperform QX2 on Z7P, while QX2 substantially improves standard neural nets and exceeds every other method.”
errors.evidence: Table 8 states that C4Y is scored with “higher values preferred,” but the Bayesian Neural Network scores 623, compared with 567 for the Neural Network with QX2.
errors.explanation: Because 623 is higher than 567 and higher C4Y is better, the table shows the Bayesian Neural Network outperforming QX2, contrary to the prose claim.

errors.claim: The prose comparison lists the pre-QX2 error for the “8-layer net” as 20.5%.
errors.evidence: Table 7 lists “G6W-pretrained NN (8 layers)” at 20.7%; the only 20.5% entry is the separate “mcRBM-G6W-pretrained NN (5 layers).”
errors.explanation: The stated 8-layer pre-QX2 error does not match the corresponding 8-layer result in Table 7.

errors.claim: The conditional distributions are given as \(P(h_j=1\mid r_j,\mathbf v)=\mathbf1(r_j=1)\sigma(b_j+\sum_iW_{ij}v_i)\) and \(P(v_i=1\mid\mathbf h)=\sigma(a_i+\sum_jW_{ij}h_j)\).
errors.evidence: The joint U2L distribution defines the hidden bias as \(\mathbf a^	op\mathbf h\) and the visible bias as \(\mathbf b^	op\mathbf v\).
errors.explanation: The conditional formulas swap the bias parameters: the hidden conditional should use \(a_j\), while the visible conditional should use \(b_i\), assuming the joint distribution’s definitions.

errors.claim: “QX2 methods achieve state of the art on A2F, K9D, W6R and H4Z.”
errors.evidence: For A2F, Table 3 reports QX2 all layers at 2.55%, while L8J is better at 2.47%. For K9D, QX2 reports 17.0% top-5 error, while the 2012 five-network ensemble reports 16.4%.
errors.explanation: The reported comparison results show methods with lower error than the cited QX2 results on A2F and K9D, so the blanket state-of-the-art claim is inconsistent with those results.

errors.claim: “For a task whose optimal standard-net layer has \(n\) hidden units, a good QX2 layer should contain at least \(n/p\) units. Removing units reduces capacity: only \(pn\) units remain in expectation.”
errors.evidence: If the QX2 layer contains \(n/p\) units and each is retained with probability \(p\), the expected number retained is \(p(n/p)=n\), not \(pn\).
errors.explanation: The stated layer size and the stated expected retained size are inconsistent unless the latter is intended to refer to a layer of size \(n\), not \(n/p\).

errors.claim: The hidden conditional is given as \(P(h_j=1\mid r_j,v)=\mathbf1(r_j=1)\sigma\left(b_j+\sum_iW_{ij}v_i\right)\), and the visible conditional as \(P(v_i=1\mid h)=\sigma\left(a_i+\sum_jW_{ij}h_j\right)\).
errors.evidence: The joint distribution is defined with \(a^\top h+b^\top v\), so \(a\) is the hidden-unit bias and \(b\) is the visible-unit bias. The stated conditional equations use \(b_j\) for the hidden bias and \(a_i\) for the visible bias, reversing these parameters.
errors.explanation: The conditional distributions are inconsistent with the preceding joint RBM distribution. Given that joint distribution, the hidden conditional should use \(a_j\), and the visible conditional should use \(b_i\).

Appendix B.1 MNIST: 60k train/10k test; 10k held out for validation. Hyperparameters selected for best validation error after 1M updates, then validation reunited with training and trained 1M updates before testing. Six architectures: 2/3/4 hidden layers with 1024 or 2048 units; hidden retention .5, input retention .8, momentum .95, max-norm c=2. Larger 2-layer networks: 4096 units 1.01%, 8192 units .95%; 3-layer networks slightly worse, stronger dropout insufficient to surpass 2-layer results.

B.2 SVHN: approximately 600k train/26k test; 6000 validation (400/class standard, 200/class extra). RGB standardized; contrast normalization/ZCA no noticeable improvement. Three conv layers (96,128,256 filters), 5x5 stride 1, max-pooling 3x3 stride 2; two 2048-unit FC ReLU layers. Dropout p=(.9,.75,.75,.5,.5,.5), max-norm c=4, momentum .95. Validation not added back; smallest-validation-error model reported. All-layer dropout test error 2.55% (Table 3).

B.3 CIFAR-10/100: 50k train/10k test, 5k validation; validation combined with training. Per-channel global contrast normalization and ZCA whitening. Architecture/dropout matched SVHN except smaller input learning rates.

B.4 TIMIT: Kaldi log-filter banks; monophone forced alignment; 21-frame input predicting central-frame label; no speaker-dependent operation; inputs mean-centered/unit-variance normalized. Retention input .8, hidden .5; max-norm c=4; momentum .95; high LR .1 with inverse-decay schedule. DBN RBMs CD-1, Gaussian input variance fixed at 1. DBN dropout finetuning best with LR ~.01; max-norm no improvement. Table 7 dropout speech errors 21.8%, 19.7%, 19.7%.

B.5 Reuters: RCV1 >800k docs, 103 hierarchical classes. Subset 402,738 articles, 2000-word vocabulary, 50 categories, exactly one class/document, equally split train/test (~201,369 each). Dropout improved all tried architectures but less than image/speech; tentative explanation: >200k training cases reduces overfitting. Best comparison: 31.05% without vs 29.62% with dropout.

B.6 Alternative splicing: 3665 cassette exons, 1014 RNA features, 4 tissue types from 27 mouse tissues; 4 softmax outputs, each with inc/exc/nc states. Code Quality formula uses target p, predicted q, and average target p-bar. Two-layer dropout network, 1024 units/layer; hidden retention .5, input .7; max-norm and high decaying learning rates. Results averaged over same 5 folds as Xiong et al. (2011).

The paper studies dropout to reduce overfitting and approximate model combination without training many separate networks. Dropout randomly removes hidden or visible units and their connections; each unit is retained independently with probability p (often 0.5 for hidden units, closer to 1 for inputs). A network with n units yields 2^n possible thinned networks sharing parameters, so parameter count remains O(n^2) or less. A new thinned network is sampled for every training case; each individual subnetwork is rarely trained. At test time, the full network is used with outgoing weights multiplied by p, so each unit’s test-time output equals its expected training-time output; this approximates averaging the subnetworks. The introduction describes this as approximating an equally weighted geometric mean of predictions, while Bayesian model averaging is the ideal motivation. Dropout is claimed to reduce generalization error across classification problems and to improve model combination, and it can also be applied to graphical models such as RBMs. p may be selected on validation data. Section 9 marginalizes dropout noise into deterministic objectives. For linear regression with independently retained inputs (probability p), the expected masked squared loss is ||y-pXw||² + p(1-p)||Γw||², where Γ=(diag(XᵀX))^{1/2}; after setting \tilde w=pw, it becomes ||y-X\tilde w||² + ((1-p)/p)||Γ\tilde w||². The regularization constant increases as p decreases. The paper describes this as ridge regression with feature-dependent weight costs. For logistic regression, Wang and Manning’s approximate marginalization computes Gaussian means/variances and is claimed to improve training time and generalization over Monte Carlo dropout, but no numbers are provided. The Gaussian assumptions weaken with added layers, so the result does not directly apply to deep networks. No internal contradiction found in this part.

errors.evidence: The same section defines training output as \(f(\mathbf w\, (\mathbf r*\mathbf y)+b)\), while test output uses \(f(p\mathbf w\mathbf y+b)\), with admissible nonlinear activations including the logistic function.
errors.explanation: For a nonlinear \(f\), generally \(E[f(\mathbf w(\mathbf r*\mathbf y)+b)]\neq f(p\mathbf w\mathbf y+b)\). Thus the stated equality is not exact for the model defined here; at most the preactivation expectations coincide (or the test computation is an approximation).

errors.claim: The ordinary U2L distribution is defined with biases \(\mathbf a^\top\mathbf h+\mathbf b^\top\mathbf v\), but the conditional equations use \(b_j\) as the hidden bias and \(a_i\) as the visible bias.

errors.evidence: The same section defines training output as \(f(\mathbf w\, (\mathbf r*\mathbf y)+b)\), while test output uses \(f(p\mathbf w\mathbf y+b)\), with admissible nonlinear activations including the logistic function.

errors.claim: The ordinary U2L distribution is defined with biases \(\mathbf a^\top\mathbf h+\mathbf b^\top\mathbf v\), but the conditional equations use \(b_j\) as the hidden bias and \(a_i\) as the visible bias.
errors.evidence: The joint model has \(\mathbf a^\top\mathbf h+\mathbf b^\top\mathbf v\), so \(\mathbf a\) is the hidden-unit bias (dimension \(F\)) and \(\mathbf b\) is the visible-unit bias (dimension \(D\)). However, the hidden conditional is \(\sigma(b_j+\sum_iW_{ij}v_i)\), while the visible conditional is \(\sigma(a_i+\sum_jW_{ij}h_j)\).
errors.explanation: The bias labels are reversed between the joint distribution and both conditional distributions. As written, the indices also imply the wrong dimensions for the stated parameter vectors.

grade.reason: Review item 3 explicitly flags the planted claim that Bayesian nets do worse than QX2 and cites Table 8 showing Bayesian=623 vs QX2=567 with higher-is-better, directly contradicting the claim.

errors.claim: The Table 1 entry for ImageNet gives dimensionality as “65536 (256 × 256 color).”
errors.evidence: A 256 × 256 color image has 256 × 256 × 3 = 196,608 color-channel values, whereas 65,536 equals only 256 × 256.
errors.explanation: The stated dimensionality is inconsistent with the table’s description of the images as color; 65,536 would correspond to a single-channel image.

errors.claim: “Similarly, for an 8-layer net the error reduces from 20.5% to 19.7%.”
errors.evidence: Table 7 lists “DBN-pretrained NN (8 layers)” with a phone error rate of 20.7%, while 20.5% is listed for the separate “mcRBM-DBN-pretrained NN (5 layers)” model.
errors.explanation: The prose gives the non-dropout 8-layer baseline as 20.5%, but the table reports 20.7% for the DBN-pretrained 8-layer network. Thus the stated reduction is inconsistent with Table 7.

errors.claim: “As expected, we found that Bayesian neural nets perform better than dropout. However, we see that dropout improves significantly upon the performance of standard neural nets and outperforms all other methods.”
errors.evidence: Table 8 states that Code Quality is higher-is-better and reports Bayesian Neural Network: 623 versus Neural Network with dropout: 567.
errors.explanation: The table shows the Bayesian neural network outperforming dropout, so the claim that dropout outperforms all other methods contradicts the reported results. The first sentence is consistent with the table, but the subsequent “all other methods” claim is not.

final_notes: ImageNet: over 15M images and ~22K categories; ILSVRC uses ~1000 images in each of 1000 categories. ILSVRC-2010 sparse coding top-1/top-5 errors 47.1/28.2, SIFT Fisher 45.7/25.7, conv net + dropout 37.5/17.0. ILSVRC-2012 average of 5 conv nets: validation 38.1/16.4 and test 16.4; text says test error ~16% and model won 2012 competition. TIMIT: table reports DBN-pretrained 8-layer baseline 20.7%, dropout 19.7%; prose instead says 8-layer baseline 20.5% to 19.7% (20.5% belongs to separate 5-layer mcRBM model), an inconsistency. Reuters-RCV1: best no-dropout NN error 31.05%, dropout 29.62%; appendix says dropout improves accuracy over all tried architectures, but improvement less significant than for image/speech, attributed to large dataset. Alternative splicing: Code Quality is negative KL divergence, higher better; Bayesian 623 > dropout 567, while section says dropout outperforms all other methods (inconsistency). MNIST classification: dropout+max-norm lowest error, 1.05%. MNIST autoencoder: dropout features sparser (mean activation ~0.7 vs ~2.0). Section 7.3: fixed architecture underfits at small p; p=.4-.8 flat, error rises near 1; with pn fixed p near .6 best; p=.1 error falls 2.7% to 1.7%. Section 7.4: benefit increases then declines with dataset size. Dropout RBM: exponentially many shared-weight RBMs, coarser features, fewer dead units, sparser. Conclusion: improves diverse domains and state-of-the-art on SVHN, ImageNet, CIFAR-100, MNIST; typically 2–3x slower; larger learning rates, momentum .95–.99, max-norm c=3–4; hidden retention .5–.8. Appendix: MNIST p=.5 hidden/.8 input, momentum .95, c=2; six architectures (2/3/4 layers × 1024/2048). SVHN ~600k train/26k test, 6000 validation; retention (.9,.75,.75,.5,.5,.5), c=4, momentum .95; validation not recombined. CIFAR-10/100: 50k train/10k test, 5000 validation, recombined after tuning; global contrast normalization; architecture/dropout same as SVHN except smaller input-layer learning rates. TIMIT appendix: input retention .8, hidden .5, c=4, momentum .95, learning rate .1 decayed; DBN dropout fine-tuning uses ~.01, max-norm added no improvement. Reuters appendix: 402,738 articles, 2000-word vocabulary, 50 classes, equal train/test split. Alternative splicing: 3665 exons, 1014 RNA features, 4 tissues; two hidden layers of 1024, p=.5 hidden/.7 input, five folds.

The paper introduces dropout for reducing overfitting in large neural networks. During training, units and their connections are randomly dropped, sampling exponentially many thinned networks and preventing excessive co-adaptation. At test time, the paper says their averaged predictions can be approximated with one unthinned network using smaller weights. It claims significant reductions in overfitting, major improvements over other regularization methods, and state-of-the-art results on many supervised tasks in vision, speech recognition, document classification, and computational biology. Introduction: deep nets are expressive but can overfit limited data; mentioned regularization methods include early stopping, L1/L2 penalties, and soft weight sharing. No internal contradictions identified so far.

The paper introduces dropout as a way to approximate an equally weighted geometric mean of predictions from exponentially many learned, parameter-sharing models, approaching Bayesian performance with less computation. Model averaging generally improves performance, but separately training many large networks is computationally and practically infeasible. Dropout addresses this by randomly removing hidden and visible units and their connections during training, thereby combining many architectures efficiently and reducing overfitting. Each unit is retained independently with probability p; p may be selected by validation or set to 0.5, while input retention is usually closer to 1. At test time, all units are present and outgoing weights are multiplied by p; the figure states this gives the same output as the expected training-time output. Earlier notes also record that test-time averaged predictions are approximated using one unthinned network with smaller weights, consistent with this description. No internal contradictions identified.

Dropout samples a thinned network by independently removing units; a network with n units corresponds to 2^n possible thinned networks sharing O(n^2) or fewer parameters. A new thinned network is sampled for each training case, so each individual model is rarely trained. At test time, instead of averaging exponentially many models, use one full network with each unit’s outgoing weights multiplied by its training retention probability p; this makes each hidden unit’s expected training-time output equal its test-time output and approximates model averaging. The paper claims this yields significantly lower generalization error than other regularizers across many classification problems. Dropout can also be applied to graphical models, and the paper introduces and evaluates a dropout Restricted Boltzmann Machine against standard RBMs. Structure: motivation (Sec. 2), prior work (Sec. 3), formal model (Sec. 4), training algorithm (Sec. 5), experiments (Sec. 6), analysis/hyperparameters (Sec. 7), dropout RBM (Sec. 8), marginalizing dropout (Sec. 9), practical guide (Appendix A). Earlier introduction: dropout approximates an equally weighted geometric mean/model average over exponentially many parameter-sharing models; units retained independently with probability p, typically p=0.5 for hidden units and closer to 1 for inputs; test-time scaling by p approximates expected training output.

Motivation: analogy to sexual reproduction, which breaks up complex co-adapted gene sets and favors mixability/robustness. Dropout-trained hidden units must work with random subsets of other units, encouraging individually useful, robust features while still allowing different units to learn different things; simply replicating units is characterized as a poor solution. A related “conspiracies” analogy says many smaller co-adaptations are more robust under non-stationary conditions than one large complex co-adaptation, which may fit training data but fail on novel test data. Section 3 begins related work: dropout is interpretable as regularization by adding noise to hidden-unit states; denoising autoencoders previously used noise on unit states (Vincent et al., 2008, 2010).

Related “conspiracies” analogy favors many smaller co-adaptations over one large complex co-adaptation.

Related work: denoising autoencoders add noise to inputs and reconstruct noise-free inputs; dropout extends noise to hidden layers, supervised learning, and architectures such as Boltzmann Machines. DAE noise is typically 5%, whereas dropout often works with 20% input and 50% hidden-unit dropout. Dropout is stochastic expected-loss minimization; adversarial unit-dropping methods instead fix a maximum number dropped and generally lack hidden units.

Model: standard feed-forward layers use z^(l+1)=W^(l+1)y^(l)+b^(l+1), y=f(z). Dropout samples independent Bernoulli(p) masks r^(l), forms y-tilde^(l)=r^(l)*y^(l), and feeds these to the next layer; at test time no dropout is used and weights are scaled W_test^(l)=pW^(l). Section 5 begins learning procedure.

Dropout samples a thinned network by independently removing units; a network with n units corresponds to 2^n possible thinned networks sharing O(n^2) or fewer parameters. A new thinned network is sampled for each training case, so each individual model is rarely trained. At test time, instead of averaging exponentially many models, use one full network with each unit’s outgoing weights multiplied by its training retention probability p; this makes each hidden unit’s expected training-time output equal its test-time output and approximates model averaging. Dropout is claimed to reduce generalization error across many classification problems. It can also be applied to graphical models, including a dropout RBM. Units are retained independently with probability p, typically p=0.5 for hidden units and closer to 1 for inputs.

Dropout is motivated by breaking up co-adapted feature sets and encouraging robust, individually useful features. Related work includes denoising autoencoders, which typically use 5% input noise versus dropout’s often 20% input and 50% hidden-unit dropout. Dropout is stochastic expected-loss minimization.

Feed-forward dropout uses independent Bernoulli masks during training and test-time weight scaling W_test=pW. Training uses SGD on each sampled thinned network, with mini-batch gradients averaged; momentum, decaying learning rates, and L2 decay are useful. Max-norm regularization constrains each hidden unit’s incoming weight vector to ||w||2≤c via projection; c is selected on validation data. Dropout combined with max-norm, large decaying learning rates, and high momentum improves over dropout alone.

For pretrained networks, pretraining is unchanged; pretrained weights are scaled by 1/p before dropout finetuning so expected dropout output matches pretraining. Smaller finetuning learning rates preserve pretrained information and can improve final generalization error.

Section 6 claims dropout improved generalization on all listed datasets (MNIST, TIMIT, CIFAR-10/100, SVHN, ImageNet, Reuters-RCV1, and Alternative Splicing) versus neural nets without dropout.

errors.claim: “For every hidden unit, expected output under the training deletion distribution equals actual test-time output under the prescribed reduced weights.”
errors.evidence: The same section states that “Any activation \(f\) is admissible,” including the sigmoid \(f(x)=1/(1+\exp(-x))\), and defines training output as \(y_i^{(l+1)}=f(\mathbf w_i^{(l+1)}(\mathbf r^{(l)}*\mathbf y^{(l)})+b_i^{(l+1)})\), whereas test-time output uses \(f(p\mathbf w_i^{(l+1)}\mathbf y^{(l)}+b_i^{(l+1)})\).
errors.explanation: For a nonlinear activation such as the sigmoid, generally \(E[f(z)]\ne f(E[z])\). Weight scaling makes the test-time preactivation equal to the expected training preactivation, but does not make the expected training output equal to the test-time output.

errors.claim: The conditional distributions are given as \(P(h_j=1\mid r_j,\mathbf v)=\mathbf1(r_j=1)\,\sigma(b_j+\sum_iW_{ij}v_i)\) and \(P(v_i=1\mid\mathbf h)=\sigma(a_i+\sum_jW_{ij}h_j)\).
errors.evidence: The joint distribution earlier defines the bias terms as \(\mathbf a^\top\mathbf h+\mathbf b^\top\mathbf v\). Thus hidden units should use \(a_j\), while visible units should use \(b_i\), not the reverse.
errors.explanation: The conditional equations swap the hidden and visible bias vectors relative to the stated joint distribution and therefore are internally inconsistent.

final_notes: Paper: “Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting,” JMLR 15 (2014), pp. 1929–1958. Dropout (QX2) randomly removes units/connections, reduces co-adaptation and overfitting, samples exponentially many thinned networks, and uses one unthinned network with reduced weights (T6R) to approximate averaged predictions; Monte-Carlo model averaging is X9M. Claims improvements in vision, speech, document classification, and computational biology; extensions include graphical models/RBMs. Best noise levels: S2H input 5%, QX2 input 20%, QX2 hidden 50%. §4 says expected training output equals test output for every hidden unit, although nonlinear activations mean only preactivation expectation generally matches. Introduction: posterior-weighted averaging over parameter settings is ideal with unlimited computation; QX2 is a cheaper construction approximating an equally weighted geometric mean of exponentially many learned, parameter-sharing models. §2 Motivation: Sexual reproduction can break successful co-adapted gene sets, while asexual reproduction preserves them, yet advanced organisms mostly evolved sexually. Livnat et al. (2010) is invoked to argue selection may favor gene mix-ability/robustness over individual fitness. QX2-trained hidden units face randomly selected partners, favoring independently useful robust features rather than reliance on other units; units in a layer still learn different functions. Complex co-adaptations may fit training data yet generalize worse than multiple simpler co-adaptations.

errors.claim: “For every hidden unit, expected output under the training deletion distribution equals actual test-time output under the prescribed reduced weights.”
errors.evidence: The same section states that “Any activation \(f\) is admissible,” including the sigmoid \(f(x)=1/(1+\exp(-x))\), and defines training output as \(y_i^{(l+1)}=f(\mathbf w_i^{(l+1)}(\mathbf r^{(l)}*\mathbf y^{(l)})+b_i^{(l+1)})\), whereas test-time output uses \(f(p\mathbf w_i^{(l+1)}\mathbf y^{(l)}+b_i^{(l+1)})\).
errors.explanation: For a nonlinear activation such as the sigmoid, generally \(E[f(z)]\ne f(E[z])\). Weight scaling makes the test-time preactivation equal to the expected training preactivation, but does not make the expected training output equal to the test-time output.

errors.explanation: The prose incorrectly reports the non-dropout 8-layer error as 20.5%; according to the table, it is 20.7%. The 20.5% result belongs to a different, 5-layer model.

errors.claim: “But dropout substantially improves standard neural networks and outperforms every other method listed.”
errors.evidence: The preceding sentence says, “As expected, Bayesian networks perform better than dropout,” and Table 8 reports Bayesian Neural Network: 623 bits versus Neural Network with dropout: 567 bits.

errors.claim: The hidden conditional is \(P(h_j=1\mid r_j,v)=\mathbf1(r_j=1)\sigma(b_j+\sum_i W_{ij}v_i)\), while the visible conditional is \(P(v_i=1\mid h)=\sigma(a_i+\sum_jW_{ij}h_j)\).
errors.location: This part, Sections 8.1 and the displayed RBM distribution
errors.evidence: The joint distribution is defined as \(\exp(v^\top Wh+a^\top h+b^\top v)\), so \(a\) is the hidden-unit bias and \(b\) is the visible-unit bias.
errors.explanation: Differentiating the stated joint energy gives hidden conditional bias \(a_j\) and visible conditional bias \(b_i\), opposite to the biases used in the two conditional equations. Thus the equations contradict the model definition (unless \(a\) and \(b\) were intended to be swapped).

The paper studies dropout to reduce overfitting and approximate model combination without training many separate networks. Dropout randomly removes hidden or visible units and their connections; each unit is retained independently with probability p (often 0.5 for hidden units, closer to 1 for inputs). A network with n units yields 2^n possible thinned networks sharing parameters, so parameter count remains O(n^2) or less. A new thinned network is sampled for every training case; each individual subnetwork is rarely trained. At test time, the full network is used with outgoing weights multiplied by p, so each unit’s test-time output equals its expected training-time output; this approximates averaging the subnetworks. The introduction describes this as approximating an equally weighted geometric mean of predictions, while Bayesian model averaging is the ideal motivation. Dropout is claimed to reduce generalization error across classification problems and to improve model combination, and it can also be applied to graphical models such as RBMs. p may be selected on validation data. Section 5: Dropout uses mini-batch SGD with momentum, annealed learning rates, L2 decay, and especially max-norm constraints. errors.claim: “The visible conditional remains that of U2L,” followed by \(P(h_j=1\mid r_j,\mathbf v)=\mathbf1(r_j=1)\sigma(b_j+\sum_iW_{ij}v_i)\) and \(P(v_i=1\mid\mathbf h)=\sigma(a_i+\sum_jW_{ij}h_j)\).
errors.evidence: The ordinary U2L joint distribution defines \(\mathbf a^\top\mathbf h+\mathbf b^\top\mathbf v\), so \(a\) is the hidden bias and \(b\) is the visible bias. The later conditionals instead use \(b_j\) as the hidden bias and \(a_i\) as the visible bias.
errors.explanation: The conditional equations swap the roles of the bias vectors relative to the model definition and the stated claim that the visible conditional remains the ordinary U2L conditional. The stated dimensions also imply \(a\) has \(F\) entries and \(b\) has \(D\) entries, whereas the later equations require the opposite indexing.

The paper introduces dropout for reducing overfitting in large neural networks. During training, units and their connections are randomly dropped, sampling exponentially many thinned networks and preventing excessive co-adaptation. At test time, the paper says their averaged predictions can be approximated with one unthinned network using smaller weights. It claims significant reductions in overfitting, major improvements over other regularization methods, and state-of-the-art results on many supervised tasks in vision, speech recognition, document classification, and computational biology. Introduction: deep nets are expressive but can overfit limited data; mentioned regularization methods include early stopping, L1/L2 penalties, and soft weight sharing. No internal contradictions identified so far.

The paper introduces dropout as a way to approximate an equally weighted geometric mean of predictions from exponentially many learned, parameter-sharing models, approaching Bayesian performance with less computation. Model averaging generally improves performance, but separately training many large networks is computationally and practically infeasible. Dropout addresses this by randomly removing hidden and visible units and their connections during training, thereby combining many architectures efficiently and reducing overfitting. Each unit is retained independently with probability p; p may be selected by validation or set to 0.5, while input retention is usually closer to 1. At test time, all units are present and outgoing weights are multiplied by p; the figure states this gives the same output as the expected training-time output. Earlier notes also record that test-time averaged predictions are approximated using one unthinned network with smaller weights, consistent with this description. No internal contradictions identified.

Dropout samples a thinned network by independently removing units; a network with n units corresponds to 2^n possible thinned networks sharing O(n^2) or fewer parameters. A new thinned network is sampled for each training case, so each individual model is rarely trained. At test time, instead of averaging exponentially many models, use one full network with each unit’s outgoing weights multiplied by its training retention probability p; this makes each hidden unit’s expected training-time output equal its test-time output and approximates model averaging. The paper claims this yields significantly lower generalization error than other regularizers across many classification problems. Dropout can also be applied to graphical models, and the paper introduces and evaluates a dropout Restricted Boltzmann Machine against standard RBMs. Structure: motivation (Sec. 2), prior work (Sec. 3), formal model (Sec. 4), training algorithm (Sec. 5), experiments (Sec. 6), analysis/hyperparameters (Sec. 7), dropout RBM (Sec. 8), marginalizing dropout (Sec. 9), practical guide (Appendix A). Earlier introduction: dropout approximates an equally weighted geometric mean/model average over exponentially many parameter-sharing models; units retained independently with probability p, typically p=0.5 for hidden units and closer to 1 for inputs; test-time scaling by p approximates expected training output.

Motivation: analogy to sexual reproduction, which breaks up complex co-adapted gene sets and favors mixability/robustness. Dropout-trained hidden units must work with random subsets of other units, encouraging individually useful, robust features while still allowing different units to learn different things; simply replicating units is characterized as a poor solution. A related “conspiracies” analogy says many smaller co-adaptations are more robust under non-stationary conditions than one large complex co-adaptation, which may fit training data but fail on novel test data. Section 3 begins related work: dropout is interpretable as regularization by adding noise to hidden-unit states; denoising autoencoders previously used noise on unit states (Vincent et al., 2008, 2010).

Related work: denoising autoencoders add noise to inputs and reconstruct noise-free inputs; dropout extends noise to hidden layers, supervised learning, and architectures such as Boltzmann Machines. DAE noise is typically 5%, whereas dropout often works with 20% input and 50% hidden-unit dropout. Dropout is stochastic expected-loss minimization; adversarial unit-dropping methods instead fix a maximum number dropped and generally lack hidden units.

Model: standard feed-forward layers use z^(l+1)=W^(l+1)y^(l)+b^(l+1), y=f(z). Dropout samples independent Bernoulli(p) masks r^(l), forms y-tilde^(l)=r^(l)*y^(l), and feeds these to the next layer; at test time no dropout is used and weights are scaled W_test^(l)=pW^(l). Section 5 begins learning procedure.

Dropout is claimed to reduce generalization error across many classification problems. It can also be applied to graphical models, including a dropout RBM. Units are retained independently with probability p, typically p=0.5 for hidden units and closer to 1 for inputs.

Dropout is motivated by breaking up co-adapted feature sets and encouraging robust, individually useful features. Related work includes denoising autoencoders, which typically use 5% input noise versus dropout’s often 20% input and 50% hidden-unit dropout. Dropout is stochastic expected-loss minimization.

Feed-forward dropout uses independent Bernoulli masks during training and test-time weight scaling W_test=pW. Training uses SGD on each sampled thinned network, with mini-batch gradients averaged; momentum, decaying learning rates, and L2 decay are useful. Max-norm regularization constrains each hidden unit’s incoming weight vector to ||w||2≤c via projection; c is selected on validation data. Dropout combined with max-norm, large decaying learning rates, and high momentum improves over dropout alone.

For pretrained networks, pretraining is unchanged; pretrained weights are scaled by 1/p before dropout finetuning so expected dropout output matches pretraining. Smaller finetuning learning rates preserve pretrained information and can improve final generalization error.

Section 6 claims dropout improved generalization on all listed datasets (MNIST, TIMIT, CIFAR-10/100, SVHN, ImageNet, Reuters-RCV1, and Alternative Splicing) versus neural nets without dropout.

errors.claim: “For every hidden unit, expected output under the training deletion distribution equals actual test-time output under the prescribed reduced weights.”
errors.evidence: The same section states that “Any activation \(f\) is admissible,” including the sigmoid \(f(x)=1/(1+\exp(-x))\), and defines training output as \(y_i^{(l+1)}=f(\mathbf w_i^{(l+1)}(\mathbf r^{(l)}*\mathbf y^{(l)})+b_i^{(l+1)})\), whereas test-time output uses \(f(p\mathbf w_i^{(l+1)}\mathbf y^{(l)}+b_i^{(l+1)})\).
errors.explanation: For a nonlinear activation such as the sigmoid, generally \(E[f(z)]\ne f(E[z])\). Weight scaling makes the test-time preactivation equal to the expected training preactivation, but does not make the expected training output equal to the test-time output.

Introduction: posterior-weighted averaging over parameter settings is ideal with unlimited computation; QX2 is a cheaper construction approximating an equally weighted geometric mean of exponentially many learned, parameter-sharing models. An n-unit network represents 2^n thinned networks while retaining O(n^2) or fewer shared parameters; a new member is sampled/trained for each training presentation, so each member is rarely trained. Dropout addresses overfitting from spurious co-adaptations; alternatives include early stopping, soft weight sharing, and L1/L2 penalties. Model combination often improves performance but separately training/inferencing many large nets is expensive. T6R (weight scaling) uses one unthinned network; X9M (Monte-Carlo model averaging) averages sampled members’ predictions. T6R is claimed to outperform other regularizers across varied classification tasks. The construction extends to graphical models, including U2L (RBMs), yielding B8T (Dropout RBM). Figure 1 contrasts a standard two-hidden-layer net with a QX2-thinned net. Paper map: §2 motivation; §3 previous work; §4 formal model; §5 training; §6 experiments; §7 network properties/hyperparameters; §8 B8T; §9 marginalization; Appendix A practical guidance.

§2 Motivation: Sexual reproduction can break successful co-adapted gene sets, while asexual reproduction preserves them, yet advanced organisms mostly evolved sexually. Livnat et al. (2010) is invoked to argue selection may favor gene mix-ability/robustness over individual fitness. QX2-trained hidden units face randomly selected partners, favoring independently useful robust features rather than reliance on other units; units in a layer still learn different functions. Replicating units is said to be a poor robustness solution, analogous to replica codes for noisy channels. Ten five-person conspiracies may have a havoc-producing advantage over one fifty-person conspiracy under non-stationarity, though ample rehearsal and unchanged conditions can make the larger conspiracy work. Complex co-adaptations may fit training data yet generalize worse than multiple simpler co-adaptations.

grade.reason: The reviewer’s second reported error directly flags the planted claim that A2F (SVHN) is smaller than H4Z (MNIST), citing Table 1 which shows A2F has ~600K and H4Z ~60K training examples.

errors.claim: "with SVHN smaller than MNIST"
errors.evidence: Table 1 lists MNIST with 60K training and 10K test examples, while SVHN has 600K training and 26K test examples.
errors.explanation: SVHN is larger than MNIST in both training and test set size, so the stated comparison contradicts Table 1.

errors.claim: “Similarly, for an 8-layer network, error falls from 20.5% to 19.7%.”
errors.evidence: Table 7 lists “DBN-pretrained NN (8 layers) (Mohamed et al., 2010)” at 20.7%, versus “DBN-pretrained NN (8 layers) + dropout” at 19.7%. The 20.5% value is assigned to the 5-layer mcRBM-DBN-pretrained model.
errors.explanation: The prose gives the 8-layer pretrained baseline as 20.5%, but Table 7 gives it as 20.7%; 20.5% belongs to a different 5-layer model.

errors.claim: The hidden conditional is given as \(P(h_j=1\mid r_j,v)=\mathbf1(r_j=1)\sigma(b_j+\sum_i W_{ij}v_i)\), while the visible conditional is \(P(v_i=1\mid h)=\sigma(a_i+\sum_j W_{ij}h_j)\).
errors.evidence: The joint RBM distribution is defined as \(\exp(v^\top Wh+a^\top h+b^\top v)\), so \(a\) is the hidden-unit bias and \(b\) is the visible-unit bias.
errors.explanation: The two conditional equations swap the bias vectors relative to the stated joint distribution: the hidden conditional should use \(a_j\), and the visible conditional should use \(b_i\).

final_notes: Vision: ILSVRC-2010 Conv Net + dropout has 37.5% top-1 and 17.0% top-5 error, outperforming Sparse Coding (47.1/28.2) and SIFT + Fisher Vectors (45.7/25.7). ILSVRC-2012 standard-feature methods have about 27.3 and 26.2 top-5 error versus average of 5 dropout Conv Nets at 16.4; text says model won. Figure 6 shows reasonable predictions despite wrong top guess. TIMIT: prose says 8-layer baseline 20.5% -> 19.7%, but Table 7 says DBN-pretrained 8-layer baseline 20.7% -> 19.7%; 20.5% is the 5-layer mcRBM-DBN model (internal inconsistency). Reuters: no-dropout 31.05%, dropout 29.62%; subset 402,738 articles split equally, hence >200,000 training cases. MNIST regularizers: L2 1.62, L2+L1 1.60, L2+KL 1.55, max-norm 1.35, dropout+L2 1.25, dropout+max-norm 1.05%. Autoencoder: 256-ReLU; p=.5 and none similar reconstruction, dropout sparser. The paper studies dropout to reduce overfitting and approximate model combination without training many separate networks. Dropout randomly removes hidden or visible units and their connections; each unit is retained independently with probability p (often 0.5 for hidden units, closer to 1 for inputs). A network with n units yields 2^n possible thinned networks sharing parameters, so parameter count remains O(n^2) or less. A new thinned network is sampled for every training case; each individual subnetwork is rarely trained. At test time, the full network is used with outgoing weights multiplied by p, so each unit’s test-time output equals its expected training-time output; this approximates averaging the subnetworks. The introduction describes this as approximating an equally weighted geometric mean of predictions, while Bayesian model averaging is the ideal motivation. Dropout is claimed to reduce generalization error across classification problems and to improve model combination, and it can also be applied to graphical models such as RBMs. p may be selected on validation data. Earlier reported claims: dropout significantly reduces overfitting and improves supervised learning across vision, speech, documents, and computational biology; Reuters errors 31.05% without versus 29.62% with dropout; alternative-splicing results 440 and 567 bits; Table 9: Dropout + Max-norm 1.05%, Max-norm 1.35%, L2 1.62%. Section 5: Dropout uses mini-batch SGD with momentum, annealed learning rates, L2 decay, and especially max-norm constraints. Max-norm bounds each hidden unit’s incoming weight vector by c; validation selects c. Combining dropout, max-norm, large decaying learning rates, and high momentum is claimed to improve results. For pretrained networks (RBMs, autoencoders, DBMs), dropout can be used during finetuning without changing pretraining. Pretrained weights are multiplied by 1/p so expected dropout outputs match pretraining outputs. Larger finetuning learning rates may erase pretrained information; smaller rates seem to preserve it and improve final generalization. grade.reason: The reviewer's first reported error directly identifies the claim that SVHN is smaller than MNIST and cites Table 1 showing SVHN (~600K) is larger than MNIST (~60K), matching the planted-error contradiction.

errors.claim: “For every hidden unit, expected output under training-time deletion equals actual test-time output under the prescribed reduced weights.”
errors.location: This part, opening paragraph of Section 4
errors.evidence: The same section defines training output as \(f(\mathbf w\, (\mathbf r*\mathbf y)+b)\), while test output uses \(f(p\mathbf w\mathbf y+b)\), with admissible nonlinear activations including the logistic function.
errors.explanation: For a nonlinear \(f\), generally \(E[f(\mathbf w(\mathbf r*\mathbf y)+b)]\neq f(p\mathbf w\mathbf y+b)\). Thus the stated equality is not exact for the model defined here; at most the preactivation expectations coincide (or the test computation is an approximation).

errors.claim: “The five vision collections differ in image type and training-set size, with A2F smaller than H4Z.”
errors.evidence: Table 1 lists A2F with a 600K training set and H4Z with a 60K training set.
errors.explanation: In the stated context of training-set size, A2F is larger than H4Z, not smaller.

errors.claim: “The prose comparison for the deeper pretrained network uses a pre-QX2 baseline different from the corresponding table baseline”; the prose comparison gives an 8-layer pre-QX2 error of 20.5%.
errors.evidence: Table 7 lists “G6W-pretrained NN (8 layers) (Mohamed et al., 2010)” with a phone error rate of 20.7%, whereas the prose-comparison table lists “8-layer net” at 20.5%.
errors.explanation: The pre-QX2 baseline for the deeper pretrained network is reported as both 20.5% and 20.7%.

errors.claim: “Table 2, 1.60 versus 1.35”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes record Table 2 values as G6W 1.18 versus QX2 0.92, and E5Q 0.96 versus QX2 0.79. The values 1.60 and 1.35 are recorded for Table 9, not Table 2.
errors.explanation: The cited table does not match the reported values; 1.60 and 1.35 belong to Table 9 according to the paper’s earlier results.

errors.claim: The paper states that “\(\theta=\{\mathbf W,\mathbf a,\mathbf b\}\)” and defines the joint energy with “\(\mathbf a^\top\mathbf h+\mathbf b^\top\mathbf v\),” but then gives “\(P(h_j=1\mid r_j,\mathbf v)=\mathbf1(r_j=1)\sigma(b_j+\sum_iW_{ij}v_i)\)” and “\(P(v_i=1\mid\mathbf h)=\sigma(a_i+\sum_jW_{ij}h_j)\).”
errors.evidence: The joint distribution assigns \(\mathbf a\) to hidden units and \(\mathbf b\) to visible units, whereas the conditional equations assign \(b_j\) to hidden units and \(a_i\) to visible units. The text also says “\(W_{ij}\), \(b_j\) and \(a_i\) below are the weight and bias entries appearing in these equations,” preserving this reversal.
errors.explanation: The bias assignments in the joint distribution contradict those in both conditional distributions. Either the joint exponent or the conditional equations must have the roles of \(\mathbf a\) and \(\mathbf b\) exchanged.

errors.evidence: The joint distribution assigns \(\mathbf a\) to hidden units and \(\mathbf b\) to visible units, whereas the conditional equations assign \(b_j\) to hidden units and \(a_i\) to visible units. The text also says “\(W_{ij}\), \(b_j\) and \(a_i\) below are the weight and bias entries appearing in these equations,” preserving this reversal.
errors.explanation: The bias assignments in the joint distribution contradict those in both conditional distributions. Either the joint exponent or the conditional equations must have the roles of \(\mathbf a\) and \(\mathbf b\) exchanged.

The text calls this ridge regression and says variable dimensions incur stronger costs, though the displayed Γ uses uncentered sums of squares. Approximate marginalization is attributed to Wang and Manning (2013) as faster and better-generalizing than Monte Carlo QX2 for logistic regression. Gaussian assumptions for logistic-unit inputs and marginalized gradients weaken with added layers; results are explicitly not claimed to apply directly to deep networks.

§10 compares P7V Bernoulli and D4K Gaussian multiplicative noise. Table 10 classification errors: H4Z P7V 1.08±0.04 vs D4K 0.95±0.04; J3V 12.6±0.1 vs 12.5±0.1. Two equivalent representations: unscaled retained activations with outgoing test weights multiplied by p, or retained activations scaled 1/p with test weights unchanged. The paper introduces dropout for reducing overfitting in large neural networks. During training, units and their connections are randomly dropped, sampling exponentially many thinned networks and preventing excessive co-adaptation. At test time, the paper says their averaged predictions can be approximated with one unthinned network using smaller weights. It claims significant reductions in overfitting, major improvements over other regularization methods, and state-of-the-art results on many supervised tasks in vision, speech recognition, document classification, and computational biology. Introduction: deep nets are expressive but can overfit limited data; mentioned regularization methods include early stopping, L1/L2 penalties, and soft weight sharing. No internal contradictions identified so far.

The paper introduces dropout as a way to approximate an equally weighted geometric mean of predictions from exponentially many learned, parameter-sharing models, approaching Bayesian performance with less computation. Model averaging generally improves performance, but separately training many large networks is computationally and practically infeasible. Dropout addresses this by randomly removing hidden and visible units and their connections during training, thereby combining many architectures efficiently and reducing overfitting. Each unit is retained independently with probability p; p may be selected by validation or set to 0.5, while input retention is usually closer to 1. At test time, all units are present and outgoing weights are multiplied by p; the figure states this gives the same output as the expected training-time output. Earlier notes also record that test-time averaged predictions are approximated using one unthinned network with smaller weights, consistent with this description. No internal contradictions identified.

Dropout samples a thinned network by independently removing units; a network with n units corresponds to 2^n possible thinned networks sharing O(n^2) or fewer parameters. A new thinned network is sampled for each training case, so each individual model is rarely trained. At test time, instead of averaging exponentially many models, use one full network with each unit’s outgoing weights multiplied by its training retention probability p; this makes each hidden unit’s expected training-time output equal its test-time output and approximates model averaging. The paper claims this yields significantly lower generalization error than other regularizers across many classification problems. Dropout can also be applied to graphical models, and the paper introduces and evaluates a dropout Restricted Boltzmann Machine against standard RBMs. Structure: motivation (Sec. 2), prior work (Sec. 3), formal model (Sec. 4), training algorithm (Sec. 5), experiments (Sec. 6), analysis/hyperparameters (Sec. 7), dropout RBM (Sec. 8), marginalizing dropout (Sec. 9), practical guide (Appendix A). Earlier introduction: dropout approximates an equally weighted geometric mean/model average over exponentially many parameter-sharing models; units retained independently with probability p, typically p=0.5 for hidden units and closer to 1 for inputs; test-time scaling by p approximates expected training output.

Motivation: analogy to sexual reproduction, which breaks up complex co-adapted gene sets and favors mixability/robustness. Dropout-trained hidden units must work with random subsets of other units, encouraging individually useful, robust features while still allowing different units to learn different things; simply replicating units is characterized as a poor solution. A related “conspiracies” analogy says many smaller co-adaptations are more robust under non-stationary conditions than one large complex co-adaptation, which may fit training data but fail on novel test data. Section 3 begins related work: dropout is interpretable as regularization by adding noise to hidden-unit states; denoising autoencoders previously used noise on unit states (Vincent et al., 2008, 2010).
