Related work: denoising autoencoders add noise to inputs and reconstruct noise-free inputs; dropout extends noise to hidden layers, supervised learning, and architectures such as Boltzmann Machines. DAE noise is typically 5%, whereas dropout often works with 20% input and 50% hidden-unit dropout. Model: standard feed-forward layers use z^(l+1)=W^(l+1)y^(l)+b^(l+1), y=f(z). Dropout samples independent Bernoulli(p) masks r^(l), forms y-tilde^(l)=r^(l)*y^(l), and feeds these to the next layer; at test time no dropout is used and weights are scaled W_test^(l)=pW^(l). Section 5 begins learning procedure.

Dropout is motivated by breaking up co-adapted feature sets and encouraging robust, individually useful features. Related work includes denoising autoencoders, which typically use 5% input noise versus dropout’s often 20% input and 50% hidden-unit dropout. Dropout is stochastic expected-loss minimization.

Feed-forward dropout uses independent Bernoulli masks during training and test-time weight scaling W_test=pW. Training uses SGD on each sampled thinned network, with mini-batch gradients averaged; momentum, decaying learning rates, and L2 decay are useful. Max-norm regularization constrains each hidden unit’s incoming weight vector to ||w||2≤c via projection; c is selected on validation data. Dropout combined with max-norm, large decaying learning rates, and high momentum improves over dropout alone.

For pretrained networks, pretraining is unchanged; pretrained weights are scaled by 1/p before dropout finetuning so expected dropout output matches pretraining. Smaller finetuning learning rates preserve pretrained information and can improve final generalization error.

Section 6 claims dropout improved generalization on all listed datasets (MNIST, TIMIT, CIFAR-10/100, SVHN, ImageNet, Reuters-RCV1, and Alternative Splicing) versus neural nets without dropout.

errors.claim: “For every hidden unit, expected output under the training deletion distribution equals actual test-time output under the prescribed reduced weights.”
errors.evidence: The same section states that “Any activation \(f\) is admissible,” including the sigmoid \(f(x)=1/(1+\exp(-x))\), and defines training output as \(y_i^{(l+1)}=f(\mathbf w_i^{(l+1)}(\mathbf r^{(l)}*\mathbf y^{(l)})+b_i^{(l+1)})\), whereas test-time output uses \(f(p\mathbf w_i^{(l+1)}\mathbf y^{(l)}+b_i^{(l+1)})\).
errors.explanation: For a nonlinear activation such as the sigmoid, generally \(E[f(z)]\ne f(E[z])\). Weight scaling makes the test-time preactivation equal to the expected training preactivation, but does not make the expected training output equal to the test-time output.

errors.claim: “P(h_j=1\mid r_j,\mathbf v)=\mathbf1(r_j=1)\,\sigma(b_j+\sum_iW_{ij}v_i)” and “P(v_i=1\mid\mathbf h)=\sigma(a_i+\sum_jW_{ij}h_j)”

Introduction: posterior-weighted averaging over parameter settings is ideal with unlimited computation; QX2 is a cheaper construction approximating an equally weighted geometric mean of exponentially many learned, parameter-sharing models. An n-unit network represents 2^n thinned networks while retaining O(n^2) or fewer shared parameters; a new member is sampled/trained for each training presentation, so each member is rarely trained. Dropout addresses overfitting from spurious co-adaptations; alternatives include early stopping, soft weight sharing, and L1/L2 penalties. Model combination often improves performance but separately training/inferencing many large nets is expensive. T6R (weight scaling) uses one unthinned network; X9M (Monte-Carlo model averaging) averages sampled members’ predictions. T6R is claimed to outperform other regularizers across varied classification tasks. The construction extends to graphical models, including U2L (RBMs), yielding B8T (Dropout RBM). §2 Motivation: Sexual reproduction can break successful co-adapted gene sets, while asexual reproduction preserves them, yet advanced organisms mostly evolved sexually. Livnat et al. (2010) is invoked to argue selection may favor gene mix-ability/robustness over individual fitness. QX2-trained hidden units face randomly selected partners, favoring independently useful robust features rather than reliance on other units; units in a layer still learn different functions. Replicating units is said to be a poor robustness solution, analogous to replica codes for noisy channels. Ten five-person conspiracies may have a havoc-producing advantage over one fifty-person conspiracy under non-stationarity, though ample rehearsal and unchanged conditions can make the larger conspiracy work. Complex co-adaptations may fit training data yet generalize worse than multiple simpler co-adaptations.

final_notes: Section 8 defines Dropout RBMs as mixtures of weight-sharing RBMs under hidden masks r, with hidden retention probability p. The joint RBM distribution is exp(v^T W h + a^T h + b^T v), so a denotes hidden biases and b visible biases. The stated conditional equations incorrectly swap these biases: hidden conditional uses b_j and visible conditional uses a_i, conflicting with the joint distribution. Given a mask, dropped hidden units are constrained to zero; retained hidden conditionals factorize. Learning samples a new mask per mini-batch and uses CD-1. On MNIST 256-hidden-unit RBMs, dropout p=0.5 produces qualitatively coarser features and apparently fewer dead units than standard RBMs. Figure 13 claims dropout produces much sparser hidden representations without an added sparsity regularizer, but gives no numerical sparsity measure. Section 9: marginalized dropout linear regression yields ||y-pXw||²+p(1-p)||Γw||²; with w~=pw, ||y-Xw~||²+((1-p)/p)||Γw~||², so lower p increases regularization. Logistic marginalization is approximate and claimed to improve training time/generalization over Monte Carlo dropout. Section 10: inverted dropout has mean 1 and variance (1-p)/p; Gaussian noise matches moments. Table 10: Gaussian slightly outperforms Bernoulli (MNIST 0.95 vs 1.08%; CIFAR-10 12.5 vs 12.6%). Section 11 repeats benefits, image results, qualitative RBM sparsity/features, 2–3× training cost, and modified L2 regularization. Appendix A: expected retained units pn; use at least n/p units; high learning rates, momentum .95–.99, max-norm typically 3–4; hidden p=.5–.8 and input p=.8 for real-valued patches/speech; lower p can underfit. Appendix B MNIST: 60k/10k train/test, 10k validation, 1m updates before and after reunification. Figure 4: 2–4 layers, 1024/2048 units; hidden p=.5, input p=.8, momentum .95, c=2. Table 2: 4096 gives 1.01%, 8192 .95%; 3-layer versions slightly worse. Current Appendix B.4 setup: input p=.8, hidden p=.5, max-norm c=4, momentum .95, high learning rate .1 with decay epsilon_0(1+t/T)^-1. Gaussian RBM input variance fixed at 1; CD-1 pretraining. DBN dropout finetuning reportedly works best with smaller learning rate ~.01; max-norm adds no improvement. Reported speech dropout results: 21.8%, 19.7%, 19.7%. The paper studies reducing overfitting in large neural networks without training many separate networks. Dropout randomly removes units/connections during training, sampling smaller networks that share weights; at test time, a full network with scaled weights approximates their combined predictions. Reported improvements cover image, speech, text, and alternative-splicing tasks. The paper compares dropout with other regularizers and Bayesian neural networks, and examines learned features, sparsity, dropout rates, network size, training-set size, and test-time averaging. Dropout RBMs learn qualitatively different features and sparser representations. For linear regression, marginalizing dropout yields a modified ridge-regression objective. Preliminary experiments compare Bernoulli dropout with multiplicative Gaussian noise. Limitation: dropout networks typically take 2–3 times longer to train than standard networks with the same architecture.

The abstract claims dropout significantly reduces overfitting and improves supervised learning in vision, speech recognition, document classification, and computational biology, with state-of-the-art results on many benchmarks. Reported improvements include MNIST, speech/TIMIT, text/Reuters-RCV1, image datasets (CIFAR, SVHN, ImageNet/ILSVRC), and alternative-splicing tasks. Specific reported results include Reuters error rates of 31.05% without dropout versus 29.62% with dropout, alternative-splicing results of 440 and 567 bits, and Table 9 results where Dropout + Max-norm gives 1.05%, versus 1.35% for Max-norm and 1.62% for L2. Dropout improves over other regularizers and is described as preventing excessive co-adaptation. Limitations and definitions from earlier parts remain: training typically takes 2–3 times longer than standard networks; p is retention probability; test-time weights are pW; there are 2^n possible thinned networks, with expected pn retained units and shared parameter count O(n^2).

The paper studies dropout to reduce overfitting and approximate model combination without training many separate networks. Dropout randomly removes hidden or visible units and their connections; each unit is retained independently with probability p (often 0.5 for hidden units, closer to 1 for inputs). A network with n units yields 2^n possible thinned networks sharing parameters, so parameter count remains O(n^2) or less. A new thinned network is sampled for every training case; each individual subnetwork is rarely trained. At test time, the full network is used with outgoing weights multiplied by p, so each unit’s test-time output equals its expected training-time output; this approximates averaging the subnetworks. The introduction describes this as approximating an equally weighted geometric mean of predictions, while Bayesian model averaging is the ideal motivation. Dropout is claimed to reduce generalization error across classification problems and to improve model combination, and it can also be applied to graphical models such as RBMs. p may be selected on validation data. Training typically takes 2–3 times longer than standard networks. Section 5: Dropout uses mini-batch SGD with momentum, annealed learning rates, L2 decay, and especially max-norm constraints. Max-norm bounds each hidden unit’s incoming weight vector by c; validation selects c. Combining dropout, max-norm, large decaying learning rates, and high momentum is claimed to improve results. For pretrained networks (RBMs, autoencoders, DBMs), dropout can be used during finetuning without changing pretraining. Pretrained weights are multiplied by 1/p so expected dropout outputs match pretraining outputs. Larger finetuning learning rates may erase pretrained information; smaller rates seem to preserve it and improve final generalization. Section 7 examines features, sparsity, retention probability, network size, and training-set size. MNIST autoencoder comparison: identical one-hidden-layer 256-ReLU autoencoders, with hidden dropout p=0.5 versus none; test reconstruction errors are similar, but dropout features qualitatively appear more meaningful and less co-adapted. Dropout is claimed to break co-adaptations. Figure 8 shows dropout-induced sparsity without an explicit sparsity regularizer: no-dropout mean activations are about 2.0 with substantial mass away from zero; dropout mean activations are about 0.7 with a sharp zero peak and few highly active units. Figure 9 varies retention probability. With fixed architecture 784-2048-2048-2048-10 and no input dropout, small p causes few active units and high training error/underfitting; error decreases as p rises, is flat for p=0.4–0.8, then increases near p=1. In the second setting, pn (expected retained units per layer) is fixed, so smaller p means a larger network; expected retained count is constant but test-network size differs. No exact numerical errors are given for Figures 7–9.

With fixed architecture and no input dropout, small p causes few active units and high training error/underfitting; error is flat for p=0.4–0.8 and rises near p=1. Figure 9b has lower low-p error: at p=0.1, error decreases from 2.7% (fixed architecture) to 1.7% (fixed expected size). p near 0.6 performs best; default p=0.5 is close to optimal.

Section 7.4 varies MNIST training size (100, 500, 1K, 5K, 10K, 50K) using architecture 784-1024-1024-2048-10, hidden p=0.5 and input p=0.8. Figure 10 claims no dropout improvement at 100/500 cases; dropout’s gain first increases and then declines with data size, suggesting a sweet spot.

Section 7.5 compares Monte-Carlo dropout model averaging with weight scaling. At about k=50 sampled networks, MC averaging matches weight scaling; beyond that it is slightly better but within one standard deviation, so weight scaling is a fairly good approximation.

steps.notes_before: Section 8 defines Dropout RBMs as mixtures of weight-sharing RBMs under hidden masks \(r\), with hidden retention probability \(p\). The joint RBM distribution is exp(v^T W h + a^T h + b^T v), so a denotes hidden biases and b visible biases. The stated conditional equations incorrectly swap these biases: hidden conditional uses b_j and visible conditional uses a_i, conflicting with the joint distribution. Given a mask, dropped hidden units are constrained to zero; retained hidden conditionals factorize. Learning samples a new mask per mini-batch and uses CD-1. Section 9 derives marginalized dropout. For linear regression with elementwise Bernoulli(p) input masks, the expected objective is ||y-pXw||² + p(1-p)||Γw||², Γ=(diag(XᵀX))^{1/2}, equivalent to ridge with feature-dependent costs. With \tilde w=pw, it is ||y-X\tilde w||² + ((1-p)/p)||Γ\tilde w||²; lower p increases regularization. For logistic regression, Wang and Manning’s marginalization is approximate, using Gaussian means/variances, and is claimed to improve training time and generalization over Monte Carlo dropout. Assumptions weaken with added layers, so the result does not directly apply to deep networks. No internal inconsistency found in Section 9.

Section 10 compares Bernoulli and Gaussian multiplicative noise. In the inverted-dropout convention, Bernoulli multiplier is 1/p with probability p and 0 otherwise, with mean 1 and variance (1-p)/p. Gaussian multiplier has mean 1 and variance sigma²=(1-p)/p, matching the first two moments; expected activation is unchanged, so no test-time weight scaling is needed. Table 10 reports slightly lower error for Gaussian than Bernoulli: MNIST 0.95±0.04 vs 1.08±0.04%; CIFAR-10 12.5±0.1 vs 12.6±0.1%, averaged over 10 seeds. No internal inconsistency found in Section 10.

errors.claim: “For every hidden unit, expected output under training-time deletion equals actual test-time output under the prescribed reduced weights.”
errors.location: This part, opening paragraph of Section 4
errors.evidence: The same section defines training output as \(f(\mathbf w\, (\mathbf r*\mathbf y)+b)\), while test output uses \(f(p\mathbf w\mathbf y+b)\), with admissible nonlinear activations including the logistic function.
errors.explanation: For a nonlinear \(f\), generally \(E[f(\mathbf w(\mathbf r*\mathbf y)+b)]\neq f(p\mathbf w\mathbf y+b)\). Thus the stated equality is not exact for the model defined here; at most the preactivation expectations coincide (or the test computation is an approximation).

errors.claim: The prose comparison for the deeper pretrained network uses a pre-QX2 baseline of 20.5%.
errors.evidence: Table 7 lists “G6W-pretrained NN (8 layers)” with a phone error rate of 20.7%, whereas the prose-comparison table gives “8-layer net” a pre-QX2 error of 20.5%.
errors.explanation: The reported baseline for the deeper 8-layer pretrained network conflicts with the corresponding Table 7 baseline.

errors.claim: “QX2 nevertheless substantially improves standard neural nets and exceeds every other method.”
errors.evidence: Table 8 reports Bayesian Neural Network: 623 and Neural Network with QX2: 567; the text states that higher C4Y values are preferred, and also says “Bayesian neural nets outperform QX2.”
errors.explanation: QX2 does not exceed every listed method: the Bayesian neural network scores higher (623 versus 567). The claim is only consistent if “every other method” is intended to exclude the Bayesian method, but that exclusion is not stated in the claim.

errors.claim: The ordinary U2L energy uses “\(\mathbf a^\top\mathbf h+\mathbf b^\top\mathbf v\),” while the conditionals are given as \(P(h_j=1\mid r_j,\mathbf v)=\sigma(b_j+\sum_iW_{ij}v_i)\) and \(P(v_i=1\mid\mathbf h)=\sigma(a_i+\sum_jW_{ij}h_j)\).
errors.evidence: The joint distribution assigns \(\mathbf a\) to hidden units and \(\mathbf b\) to visible units, but the hidden conditional uses \(b_j\) and the visible conditional uses \(a_i\).
errors.explanation: For the stated joint distribution, the hidden conditional should use the hidden bias \(a_j\), and the visible conditional should use the visible bias \(b_i\). The bias assignments in the conditionals are reversed relative to the joint model.

errors.claim: "A dimension’s standard deviation scales its weight cost."
errors.evidence: The displayed penalty uses \(\mathbf\Gamma=(\operatorname{diag}(\mathbf X^\top\mathbf X))^{1/2}\), so dimension \(j\)'s factor is \(\sqrt{\sum_i X_{ij}^2}\), i.e. an uncentered root-sum-of-squares, not its standard deviation in general.
errors.explanation: The stated interpretation in terms of standard deviation does not follow from the paper’s own definition of the penalty matrix unless additional centering/normalization assumptions are supplied, which are not stated.

The paper introduces dropout for reducing overfitting in large neural networks. During training, units and their connections are randomly dropped, sampling exponentially many thinned networks and preventing excessive co-adaptation. At test time, the paper says their averaged predictions can be approximated with one unthinned network using smaller weights. It claims significant reductions in overfitting, major improvements over other regularization methods, and state-of-the-art results on many supervised tasks in vision, speech recognition, document classification, and computational biology. Introduction: deep nets are expressive but can overfit limited data; mentioned regularization methods include early stopping, L1/L2 penalties, and soft weight sharing. No internal contradictions identified so far.

The paper introduces dropout as a way to approximate an equally weighted geometric mean of predictions from exponentially many learned, parameter-sharing models, approaching Bayesian performance with less computation. Model averaging generally improves performance, but separately training many large networks is computationally and practically infeasible. Dropout addresses this by randomly removing hidden and visible units and their connections during training, thereby combining many architectures efficiently and reducing overfitting. Each unit is retained independently with probability p; p may be selected by validation or set to 0.5, while input retention is usually closer to 1. At test time, all units are present and outgoing weights are multiplied by p; the figure states this gives the same output as the expected training-time output. Earlier notes also record that test-time averaged predictions are approximated using one unthinned network with smaller weights, consistent with this description. No internal contradictions identified.

Dropout samples a thinned network by independently removing units; a network with n units corresponds to 2^n possible thinned networks sharing O(n^2) or fewer parameters. A new thinned network is sampled for each training case, so each individual model is rarely trained. At test time, instead of averaging exponentially many models, use one full network with each unit’s outgoing weights multiplied by its training retention probability p; this makes each hidden unit’s expected training-time output equal its test-time output and approximates model averaging. The paper claims this yields significantly lower generalization error than other regularizers across many classification problems. Dropout can also be applied to graphical models, and the paper introduces and evaluates a dropout Restricted Boltzmann Machine against standard RBMs. Structure: motivation (Sec. 2), prior work (Sec. 3), formal model (Sec. 4), training algorithm (Sec. 5), experiments (Sec. 6), analysis/hyperparameters (Sec. 7), dropout RBM (Sec. 8), marginalizing dropout (Sec. 9), practical guide (Appendix A). Earlier introduction: dropout approximates an equally weighted geometric mean/model average over exponentially many parameter-sharing models; units retained independently with probability p, typically p=0.5 for hidden units and closer to 1 for inputs; test-time scaling by p approximates expected training output.

Motivation: analogy to sexual reproduction, which breaks up complex co-adapted gene sets and favors mixability/robustness. Dropout-trained hidden units must work with random subsets of other units, encouraging individually useful, robust features while still allowing different units to learn different things; simply replicating units is characterized as a poor solution. A related “conspiracies” analogy says many smaller co-adaptations are more robust under non-stationary conditions than one large complex co-adaptation, which may fit training data but fail on novel test data. Section 3 begins related work: dropout is interpretable as regularization by adding noise to hidden-unit states; denoising autoencoders previously used noise on unit states (Vincent et al., 2008, 2010).

Related work: denoising autoencoders add noise to inputs and reconstruct noise-free inputs; dropout extends noise to hidden layers, supervised learning, and architectures such as Boltzmann Machines. DAE noise is typically 5%, whereas dropout often works with 20% input and 50% hidden-unit dropout. Dropout is stochastic expected-loss minimization; adversarial unit-dropping methods instead fix a maximum number dropped and generally lack hidden units.

Model: standard feed-forward layers use z^(l+1)=W^(l+1)y^(l)+b^(l+1), y=f(z). Dropout samples independent Bernoulli(p) masks r^(l), forms y-tilde^(l)=r^(l)*y^(l), and feeds these to the next layer; at test time no dropout is used and weights are scaled W_test^(l)=pW^(l). Section 5 begins learning procedure.

Dropout is claimed to reduce generalization error across many classification problems. It can also be applied to graphical models, including a dropout RBM. Units are retained independently with probability p, typically p=0.5 for hidden units and closer to 1 for inputs.

Dropout is motivated by breaking up co-adapted feature sets and encouraging robust, individually useful features. Related work includes denoising autoencoders, which typically use 5% input noise versus dropout’s often 20% input and 50% hidden-unit dropout. Dropout is stochastic expected-loss minimization.

Feed-forward dropout uses independent Bernoulli masks during training and test-time weight scaling W_test=pW. Training uses SGD on each sampled thinned network, with mini-batch gradients averaged; momentum, decaying learning rates, and L2 decay are useful. Max-norm regularization constrains each hidden unit’s incoming weight vector to ||w||2≤c via projection; c is selected on validation data. Dropout combined with max-norm, large decaying learning rates, and high momentum improves over dropout alone.

For pretrained networks, pretraining is unchanged; pretrained weights are scaled by 1/p before dropout finetuning so expected dropout output matches pretraining. Smaller finetuning learning rates preserve pretrained information and can improve final generalization error.

Section 6 claims dropout improved generalization on all listed datasets (MNIST, TIMIT, CIFAR-10/100, SVHN, ImageNet, Reuters-RCV1, and Alternative Splicing) versus neural nets without dropout.

errors.claim: “For every hidden unit, expected output under the training deletion distribution equals actual test-time output under the prescribed reduced weights.”
errors.evidence: The same section states that “Any activation \(f\) is admissible,” including the sigmoid \(f(x)=1/(1+\exp(-x))\), and defines training output as \(y_i^{(l+1)}=f(\mathbf w_i^{(l+1)}(\mathbf r^{(l)}*\mathbf y^{(l)})+b_i^{(l+1)})\), whereas test-time output uses \(f(p\mathbf w_i^{(l+1)}\mathbf y^{(l)}+b_i^{(l+1)})\).
errors.explanation: For a nonlinear activation such as the sigmoid, generally \(E[f(z)]\ne f(E[z])\). Weight scaling makes the test-time preactivation equal to the expected training preactivation, but does not make the expected training output equal to the test-time output.

errors.claim: “P(h_j=1\mid r_j,\mathbf v)=\mathbf1(r_j=1)\,\sigma(b_j+\sum_iW_{ij}v_i)” and “P(v_i=1\mid\mathbf h)=\sigma(a_i+\sum_jW_{ij}h_j)”

Introduction: posterior-weighted averaging over parameter settings is ideal with unlimited computation; QX2 is a cheaper construction approximating an equally weighted geometric mean of exponentially many learned, parameter-sharing models. An n-unit network represents 2^n thinned networks while retaining O(n^2) or fewer shared parameters; a new member is sampled/trained for each training presentation, so each member is rarely trained. Dropout addresses overfitting from spurious co-adaptations; alternatives include early stopping, soft weight sharing, and L1/L2 penalties. Model combination often improves performance but separately training/inferencing many large nets is expensive. T6R (weight scaling) uses one unthinned network; X9M (Monte-Carlo model averaging) averages sampled members’ predictions. T6R is claimed to outperform other regularizers across varied classification tasks. The construction extends to graphical models, including U2L (RBMs), yielding B8T (Dropout RBM). Figure 1 contrasts a standard two-hidden-layer net with a QX2-thinned net. Paper map: §2 motivation; §3 previous work; §4 formal model; §5 training; §6 experiments; §7 network properties/hyperparameters; §8 B8T; §9 marginalization; Appendix A practical guidance.

§2 Motivation: Sexual reproduction can break successful co-adapted gene sets, while asexual reproduction preserves them, yet advanced organisms mostly evolved sexually. Livnat et al. (2010) is invoked to argue selection may favor gene mix-ability/robustness over individual fitness. QX2-trained hidden units face randomly selected partners, favoring independently useful robust features rather than reliance on other units; units in a layer still learn different functions. Replicating units is said to be a poor robustness solution, analogous to replica codes for noisy channels. Ten five-person conspiracies may have a havoc-producing advantage over one fifty-person conspiracy under non-stationarity, though ample rehearsal and unchanged conditions can make the larger conspiracy work. Complex co-adaptations may fit training data yet generalize worse than multiple simpler co-adaptations.

errors.claim: “Similarly, for an 8-layer network, error falls from 20.5% to 19.7%.”
errors.evidence: Table 7 lists “DBN-pretrained NN (8 layers) (Mohamed et al., 2010)” at 20.7%, while 20.5% is assigned to the “mcRBM-DBN-pretrained NN (5 layers)” row.
errors.explanation: The prose gives the 8-layer pretrained baseline as 20.5%, but the table gives it as 20.7% and assigns 20.5% to a different 5-layer model.

errors.claim: “Convolutional networks with dropout reach about 16% test error” and “The ILSVRC-2012 test comparison is about 26% versus about 16%.”
errors.evidence: The notes record Table 6 as reporting ILSVRC-2012 validation errors: standard-feature rows at 27.3% and 26.2% top-5 error, and the average of five dropout Conv Nets at 16.4% top-5 error.
errors.explanation: The claims characterize these results as test errors, whereas Table 6 is described as reporting validation errors.

errors.claim: “But dropout substantially improves standard neural networks and outperforms every other method listed.”
errors.evidence: The same paragraph states, “As expected, Bayesian networks perform better than dropout,” and Table 8 reports Bayesian Neural Network = 623 bits versus dropout = 567 bits; higher Code Quality is better.
errors.explanation: Dropout cannot outperform every method listed because the Bayesian Neural Network has a higher Code Quality score (623 vs. 567). The later claims-and-evidence bullet repeats this incorrect assertion.

errors.claim: The hidden conditional is given by \(P(h_j=1\mid r_j,v)=\mathbf1(r_j=1)\sigma(b_j+\sum_i W_{ij}v_i)\), and the visible conditional by \(P(v_i=1\mid h)=\sigma(a_i+\sum_j W_{ij}h_j)\).
errors.evidence: The RBM distribution is defined as “\(\exp(v^\top Wh+a^\top h+b^\top v)\)”, so \(a\) is the hidden-unit bias and \(b\) is the visible-unit bias.
errors.explanation: The conditional formulas interchange the bias vectors: the hidden conditional should use \(a_j\), while the visible conditional should use \(b_i\), given the stated joint distribution.

errors.claim: “The assumptions become successively weaker as layers are added. The results therefore apply directly to networks of arbitrary depth.”
errors.evidence: The immediately preceding sentence states that “the assumptions become successively weaker as layers are added,” while the subsection summary says: “The result does not directly extend to deep networks.”
errors.explanation: The claim that the results apply directly to networks of arbitrary depth contradicts the stated limitation that the results do not directly extend to deep networks.

final_notes: Section 8 defines Dropout RBMs as mixtures of weight-sharing RBMs under hidden masks r, with hidden retention probability p. The joint RBM distribution is exp(v^TWh+a^Th+b^Tv), so a denotes hidden biases and b visible biases. The stated conditional equations incorrectly swap these biases: hidden conditional uses b_j and visible conditional uses a_i, conflicting with the joint distribution. Given a mask, dropped hidden units are constrained to zero; retained hidden conditionals factorize. Learning samples a new mask per mini-batch and uses CD-1. On MNIST 256-hidden-unit RBMs, dropout p=0.5 produces qualitatively coarser features and apparently fewer dead units than standard RBMs. Figure 13 claims dropout produces much sparser hidden representations without an added sparsity regularizer, but gives no numerical sparsity measure. Section 9: expected masked-input squared loss is ||y-pXw||²+p(1-p)||Γw||², Γ=(diag(XᵀX))^{1/2}; with w~=pw, penalty coefficient is (1-p)/p, increasing as p decreases. Logistic marginalization is approximate, based on Gaussian assumptions, and may improve training/generalization. Assumptions weaken with added layers and do not directly extend to deep networks, contradicting an earlier claim of direct applicability to arbitrary-depth networks. Section 10: inverted Bernoulli multiplier has mean 1 and variance (1-p)/p; matched Gaussian is N(1,(1-p)/p), requiring no test-time scaling. Table 10: Gaussian slightly outperforms Bernoulli (MNIST 0.95±0.04% vs 1.08±0.04%; CIFAR-10 12.5±0.1% vs 12.6±0.1%). Section 11 conclusion claims training typically takes 2–3 times longer, without timing table. Appendix A recommends layer size at least n/p; learning rates 10–100 times standard optimum, momentum 0.95–0.99, max-norm c=3–4, hidden p=0.5–0.8, and input p=0.8 for real-valued image patches/speech frames. Smaller p requires larger n and may risk underfitting; larger p may insufficiently prevent overfitting. Appendix B: MNIST held out 10,000 of 60,000 training images for validation, selected hyperparameters at 1m updates, then reunited data and trained 1m updates. Figure 4 has six architectures (2–4 hidden layers, 1024/2048 units), hidden p=.5, input p=.8, momentum .95, max-norm c=2. Larger 2-layer networks: Table 2 errors 1.01% (4096) and .95% (8192); 3-layer versions slightly worse and stronger dropout did not beat. Speech setup in B.4: input p=.8,

The paper studies dropout to reduce overfitting and approximate model combination without training many separate networks. Dropout randomly removes hidden or visible units and their connections; each unit is retained independently with probability p (often 0.5 for hidden units, closer to 1 for inputs). A network with n units yields 2^n possible thinned networks sharing parameters, so parameter count remains O(n^2) or less. A new thinned network is sampled for every training case; each individual subnetwork is rarely trained. At test time, the full network is used with outgoing weights multiplied by p, so each unit’s test-time output equals its expected training-time output; this approximates averaging the subnetworks. The introduction describes this as approximating an equally weighted geometric mean of predictions, while Bayesian model averaging is the ideal motivation. Dropout is claimed to reduce generalization error across classification problems and to improve model combination, and it can also be applied to graphical models such as RBMs. p may be selected on validation data. errors.claim: “For every hidden unit, expected output under training-time deletion equals actual test-time output under the prescribed reduced weights.”
errors.location: This part, opening paragraph of Section 4
errors.evidence: The same section defines training output as \(f(\mathbf w\, (\mathbf r*\mathbf y)+b)\), while test output uses \(f(p\mathbf w\mathbf y+b)\), with admissible nonlinear activations including the logistic function.
errors.explanation: For a nonlinear \(f\), generally \(E[f(\mathbf w(\mathbf r*\mathbf y)+b)]\neq f(p\mathbf w\mathbf y+b)\). Thus the stated equality is not exact for the model defined here; at most the preactivation expectations coincide (or the test computation is an approximation).

errors.claim: The ordinary U2L energy uses “\(\mathbf a^\top\mathbf h+\mathbf b^\top\mathbf v\),” while the conditionals are given as \(P(h_j=1\mid r_j,\mathbf v)=\sigma(b_j+\sum_iW_{ij}v_i)\) and \(P(v_i=1\mid\mathbf h)=\sigma(a_i+\sum_jW_{ij}h_j)\).
errors.evidence: The joint distribution assigns \(\mathbf a\) to hidden units and \(\mathbf b\) to visible units, but the hidden conditional uses \(b_j\) and the visible conditional uses \(a_i\).
errors.explanation: For the stated joint distribution, the hidden conditional should use the hidden bias \(a_j\), and the visible conditional should use the visible bias \(b_i\). The bias assignments in the conditionals are reversed relative to the joint model.

errors.claim: “The assumptions become successively weaker as layers are added. The results therefore apply directly to networks of arbitrary depth.”

Dropout removes randomly selected units and connections during training, effectively training many smaller parameter-sharing networks; at test time, a complete network with reduced weights approximates averaged predictions. errors.claim: “For every hidden unit, expected output under training-time deletion equals actual test-time output under the prescribed reduced weights.”
errors.location: This part, opening paragraph of Section 4
errors.evidence: The same section defines training output as \(f(\mathbf w\, (\mathbf r*\mathbf y)+b)\), while test output uses \(f(p\mathbf w\mathbf y+b)\), with admissible nonlinear activations including the logistic function.
errors.explanation: For a nonlinear \(f\), generally \(E[f(\mathbf w(\mathbf r*\mathbf y)+b)]\neq f(p\mathbf w\mathbf y+b)\). Thus the stated equality is not exact for the model defined here; at most the preactivation expectations coincide (or the test computation is an approximation).

The paper introduces dropout for reducing overfitting in large neural networks. During training, units and their connections are randomly dropped, sampling exponentially many thinned networks and preventing excessive co-adaptation. At test time, the paper says their averaged predictions can be approximated with one unthinned network using smaller weights. It claims significant reductions in overfitting, major improvements over other regularization methods, and state-of-the-art results on many supervised tasks in vision, speech recognition, document classification, and computational biology. Introduction: deep nets are expressive but can overfit limited data; mentioned regularization methods include early stopping, L1/L2 penalties, and soft weight sharing. No internal contradictions identified so far.

The paper introduces dropout as a way to approximate an equally weighted geometric mean of predictions from exponentially many learned, parameter-sharing models, approaching Bayesian performance with less computation. Model averaging generally improves performance, but separately training many large networks is computationally and practically infeasible. Dropout addresses this by randomly removing hidden and visible units and their connections during training, thereby combining many architectures efficiently and reducing overfitting. Each unit is retained independently with probability p; p may be selected by validation or set to 0.5, while input retention is usually closer to 1. At test time, all units are present and outgoing weights are multiplied by p; the figure states this gives the same output as the expected training-time output. Earlier notes also record that test-time averaged predictions are approximated using one unthinned network with smaller weights, consistent with this description. No internal contradictions identified.

Dropout samples a thinned network by independently removing units; a network with n units corresponds to 2^n possible thinned networks sharing O(n^2) or fewer parameters. A new thinned network is sampled for each training case, so each individual model is rarely trained. At test time, instead of averaging exponentially many models, use one full network with each unit’s outgoing weights multiplied by its training retention probability p; this makes each hidden unit’s expected training-time output equal its test-time output and approximates model averaging. The paper claims this yields significantly lower generalization error than other regularizers across many classification problems. Dropout can also be applied to graphical models, and the paper introduces and evaluates a dropout Restricted Boltzmann Machine against standard RBMs. Structure: motivation (Sec. 2), prior work (Sec. 3), formal model (Sec. 4), training algorithm (Sec. 5), experiments (Sec. 6), analysis/hyperparameters (Sec. 7), dropout RBM (Sec. 8), marginalizing dropout (Sec. 9), practical guide (Appendix A). Earlier introduction: dropout approximates an equally weighted geometric mean/model average over exponentially many parameter-sharing models; units retained independently with probability p, typically p=0.5 for hidden units and closer to 1 for inputs; test-time scaling by p approximates expected training output.

Motivation: analogy to sexual reproduction, which breaks up complex co-adapted gene sets and favors mixability/robustness. Dropout-trained hidden units must work with random subsets of other units, encouraging individually useful, robust features while still allowing different units to learn different things; simply replicating units is characterized as a poor solution. A related “conspiracies” analogy says many smaller co-adaptations are more robust under non-stationary conditions than one large complex co-adaptation, which may fit training data but fail on novel test data. Section 3 begins related work: dropout is interpretable as regularization by adding noise to hidden-unit states; denoising autoencoders previously used noise on unit states (Vincent et al., 2008, 2010).

Dropout can also be applied to graphical models, and the paper introduces and evaluates a dropout RBM against standard RBMs. Earlier introduction: dropout approximates an equally weighted geometric mean/model average over exponentially many parameter-sharing models; units are retained independently with probability p, typically p=0.5 for hidden units and closer to 1 for inputs; test-time scaling by p approximates expected training output.

Motivation: analogy to sexual reproduction, which breaks up complex co-adapted gene sets and favors mixability/robustness. Dropout-trained hidden units must work with random subsets of other units, encouraging individually useful, robust features. Related “conspiracies” analogy favors many smaller co-adaptations over one large complex co-adaptation.

Related work: denoising autoencoders add noise to inputs and reconstruct noise-free inputs; dropout extends noise to hidden layers, supervised learning, and architectures such as Boltzmann Machines. DAE noise is typically 5%, whereas dropout often works with 20% input and 50% hidden-unit dropout. Dropout is stochastic expected-loss minimization; adversarial unit-dropping methods instead fix a maximum number dropped and generally lack hidden units.

Model: standard feed-forward layers use z^(l+1)=W^(l+1)y^(l)+b^(l+1), y=f(z). Dropout samples independent Bernoulli(p) masks r^(l), forms y-tilde^(l)=r^(l)*y^(l), and feeds these to the next layer; at test time no dropout is used and weights are scaled W_test^(l)=pW^(l). Section 5 begins learning procedure.

Dropout samples a thinned network by independently removing units; a network with n units corresponds to 2^n possible thinned networks sharing O(n^2) or fewer parameters. A new thinned network is sampled for each training case, so each individual model is rarely trained. At test time, instead of averaging exponentially many models, use one full network with each unit’s outgoing weights multiplied by its training retention probability p; this makes each hidden unit’s expected training-time output equal its test-time output and approximates model averaging. Dropout is claimed to reduce generalization error across many classification problems. It can also be applied to graphical models, including a dropout RBM. Units are retained independently with probability p, typically p=0.5 for hidden units and closer to 1 for inputs.

Dropout is motivated by breaking up co-adapted feature sets and encouraging robust, individually useful features. Related work includes denoising autoencoders, which typically use 5% input noise versus dropout’s often 20% input and 50% hidden-unit dropout. Dropout is stochastic expected-loss minimization.

Feed-forward dropout uses independent Bernoulli masks during training and test-time weight scaling W_test=pW. Training uses SGD on each sampled thinned network, with mini-batch gradients averaged; momentum, decaying learning rates, and L2 decay are useful. Max-norm regularization constrains each hidden unit’s incoming weight vector to ||w||2≤c via projection; c is selected on validation data. Dropout combined with max-norm, large decaying learning rates, and high momentum improves over dropout alone.

For pretrained networks, pretraining is unchanged; pretrained weights are scaled by 1/p before dropout finetuning so expected dropout output matches pretraining. Smaller finetuning learning rates preserve pretrained information and can improve final generalization error.

Section 6 claims dropout improved generalization on all listed datasets (MNIST, TIMIT, CIFAR-10/100, SVHN, ImageNet, Reuters-RCV1, and Alternative Splicing) versus neural nets without dropout.

grade.reason: The fifth reported error explicitly flags the sentence claiming weight scaling always matches or outperforms Monte-Carlo averaging and cites the preceding statement that Monte-Carlo becomes slightly better after ~50 samples, directly contradicting the planted claim.

errors.claim: “For every hidden unit, expected output under the training deletion distribution equals actual test-time output under the prescribed reduced weights.”
errors.evidence: The same section states that “Any activation \(f\) is admissible,” including the sigmoid \(f(x)=1/(1+\exp(-x))\), and defines training output as \(y_i^{(l+1)}=f(\mathbf w_i^{(l+1)}(\mathbf r^{(l)}*\mathbf y^{(l)})+b_i^{(l+1)})\), whereas test-time output uses \(f(p\mathbf w_i^{(l+1)}\mathbf y^{(l)}+b_i^{(l+1)})\).
errors.explanation: For a nonlinear activation such as the sigmoid, generally \(E[f(z)]\ne f(E[z])\). Weight scaling makes the test-time preactivation equal to the expected training preactivation, but does not make the expected training output equal to the test-time output.

errors.claim: “Bayesian neural nets outperform QX2 on Z7P, while QX2 substantially improves standard neural nets and exceeds every other method.”
errors.evidence: Table 8 reports Neural Network with QX2 at 567 C4Y bits and Bayesian Neural Network at 623; the text states that higher C4Y values are preferred.
errors.explanation: Because higher C4Y is better, the Bayesian neural network outperforms QX2, so QX2 does not exceed every other listed method.

errors.claim: “X9M matches T6R after sufficiently many samples and then performs slightly better, within one standard deviation; T6R always matches or outperforms X9M for the tested model.”
errors.evidence: The first clause says X9M performs slightly better than T6R after sufficiently many samples, whereas the second says T6R always matches or outperforms X9M.
errors.explanation: These claims contradict each other regarding whether X9M ever outperforms T6R.

errors.claim: The conditional distributions are given as \(P(h_j=1\mid r_j,\mathbf v)=\mathbf1(r_j=1)\sigma(b_j+\sum_iW_{ij}v_i)\) and \(P(v_i=1\mid\mathbf h)=\sigma(a_i+\sum_jW_{ij}h_j)\).
errors.evidence: The joint exponent is \(\mathbf v^\top\mathbf W\mathbf h+\mathbf a^\top\mathbf h+\mathbf b^\top\mathbf v\), so \(a\) is the hidden-unit bias and \(b\) is the visible-unit bias.
errors.explanation: The conditional formulas use the biases in the opposite roles from the joint distribution: the hidden conditional should use \(a_j\), while the visible conditional should use \(b_i\).

errors.claim: The text says each training case in every mini-batch receives a different \(\mathbf r\), while §8.1 defines \(\mathbf r\) as independently sampled with retention probability \(p\).
errors.evidence: This is consistent with the stated independent sampling distribution \(P(\mathbf r;p)=\prod_jp^{r_j}(1-p)^{1-r_j}\); no contradiction is established.
errors.explanation: No internal error is reportable here; the per-case sampling statement is compatible with the model definition.

Introduction: posterior-weighted averaging over parameter settings is ideal with unlimited computation; QX2 is a cheaper construction approximating an equally weighted geometric mean of exponentially many learned, parameter-sharing models. An n-unit network represents 2^n thinned networks while retaining O(n^2) or fewer shared parameters; a new member is sampled/trained for each training presentation, so each member is rarely trained. Dropout addresses overfitting from spurious co-adaptations; alternatives include early stopping, soft weight sharing, and L1/L2 penalties. Model combination often improves performance but separately training/inferencing many large nets is expensive. T6R (weight scaling) uses one unthinned network; X9M (Monte-Carlo model averaging) averages sampled members’ predictions. T6R is claimed to outperform other regularizers across varied classification tasks. The construction extends to graphical models, including U2L (RBMs), yielding B8T (Dropout RBM). §2 Motivation: Sexual reproduction can break successful co-adapted gene sets, while asexual reproduction preserves them, yet advanced organisms mostly evolved sexually. Livnat et al. (2010) is invoked to argue selection may favor gene mix-ability/robustness over individual fitness. QX2-trained hidden units face randomly selected partners, favoring independently useful robust features rather than reliance on other units; units in a layer still learn different functions. Replicating units is said to be a poor robustness solution, analogous to replica codes for noisy channels. Ten five-person conspiracies may have a havoc-producing advantage over one fifty-person conspiracy under non-stationarity, though ample rehearsal and unchanged conditions can make the larger conspiracy work. Complex co-adaptations may fit training data yet generalize worse than multiple simpler co-adaptations.

errors.claim: “For every hidden unit, expected output under the training deletion distribution equals actual test-time output under the prescribed reduced weights.”
errors.evidence: The same section states that “Any activation \(f\) is admissible,” including the sigmoid \(f(x)=1/(1+\exp(-x))\), and defines training output as \(y_i^{(l+1)}=f(\mathbf w_i^{(l+1)}(\mathbf r^{(l)}*\mathbf y^{(l)})+b_i^{(l+1)})\), whereas test-time output uses \(f(p\mathbf w_i^{(l+1)}\mathbf y^{(l)}+b_i^{(l+1)})\).
errors.explanation: For a nonlinear activation such as the sigmoid, generally \(E[f(z)]\ne f(E[z])\). Weight scaling makes the test-time preactivation equal to the expected training preactivation, but does not make the expected training output equal to the test-time output.

grade.reason: Reviewer item 3 points out the direct contradiction between the claim that T6R always matches or outperforms X9M and the earlier statement that X9M becomes slightly better after ~50 samples, which is the planted error.

errors.claim: “Similarly, for an 8-layer network, error falls from 20.5% to 19.7%.”
errors.evidence: Table 7 lists “DBN-pretrained NN (8 layers) (Mohamed et al., 2010)” at 20.7%, while 20.5% is assigned to the “mcRBM-DBN-pretrained NN (5 layers)” row.

errors.claim: “Convolutional networks with dropout reach about 16% test error” and “The ILSVRC-2012 test comparison is about 26% versus about 16%.”
errors.evidence: The notes record Table 6 as reporting ILSVRC-2012 validation errors: standard-feature rows at 27.3% and 26.2% top-5 error, and the average of five dropout Conv Nets at 16.4% top-5 error.
errors.explanation: The claims characterize these results as test errors, whereas Table 6 is described as reporting validation errors.

errors.claim: “But dropout substantially improves standard neural networks and outperforms every other method listed.”
errors.evidence: The same paragraph states, “As expected, Bayesian networks perform better than dropout,” and Table 8 reports Bayesian Neural Network = 623 bits versus dropout = 567 bits; higher Code Quality is better.
errors.explanation: Dropout cannot outperform every method listed because the Bayesian Neural Network has a higher Code Quality score (623 vs. 567). The later claims-and-evidence bullet repeats this incorrect assertion.

errors.claim: “This shows that weight scaling always matches or outperforms Monte-Carlo averaging for the tested model.”
errors.evidence: The preceding sentence states: “Beyond that, it is slightly better, but well within one standard deviation,” referring to Monte-Carlo averaging after about \(k=50\).
errors.explanation: The claim that weight scaling always matches or outperforms Monte-Carlo averaging contradicts the statement that Monte-Carlo averaging is slightly better at larger sample counts, even if the difference is within one standard deviation.

errors.claim: The conditional distributions are given as \(P(h_j=1\mid r_j,v)=\mathbf1(r_j=1)\sigma(b_j+\sum_iW_{ij}v_i)\) and \(P(v_i=1\mid h)=\sigma(a_i+\sum_jW_{ij}h_j)\).
errors.evidence: The RBM energy/distribution is defined with \(a^\top h+b^\top v\), so \(a\) is the hidden-unit bias and \(b\) is the visible-unit bias.
errors.explanation: The conditional equations use the biases in the opposite roles: the hidden conditional should use \(a_j\), while the visible conditional should use \(b_i\).

errors.claim: “The selected all-layer-dropout network reaches 2.55% error” (Appendix B.2).
errors.location: This part, Appendix B.2; compared with earlier notes
errors.evidence: Earlier notes record the paper’s reported SVHN result as 2.47% (Section 11 conclusion).

The paper studies reducing overfitting in large neural networks without training many separate networks. Dropout randomly removes units/connections during training, sampling smaller networks that share weights; at test time, a full network with scaled weights approximates their combined predictions. Reported improvements cover image, speech, text, and alternative-splicing tasks. The paper compares dropout with other regularizers and Bayesian neural networks, and examines learned features, sparsity, dropout rates, network size, training-set size, and test-time averaging. Dropout RBMs learn qualitatively different features and sparser representations. For linear regression, marginalizing dropout yields a modified ridge-regression objective. Preliminary experiments compare Bernoulli dropout with multiplicative Gaussian noise. Limitation: dropout networks typically take 2–3 times longer to train than standard networks with the same architecture.

The abstract claims dropout significantly reduces overfitting and improves supervised learning in vision, speech recognition, document classification, and computational biology, with state-of-the-art results on many benchmarks. Dropout improves over other regularizers and is described as preventing excessive co-adaptation. Limitations and definitions from earlier parts remain: training typically takes 2–3 times longer than standard networks; p is retention probability; test-time weights are pW; there are 2^n possible thinned networks, with expected pn retained units and shared parameter count O(n^2).

The paper studies dropout to reduce overfitting and approximate model combination without training many separate networks. Dropout randomly removes hidden or visible units and their connections; each unit is retained independently with probability p (often 0.5 for hidden units, closer to 1 for inputs). A network with n units yields 2^n possible thinned networks sharing parameters, so parameter count remains O(n^2) or less. A new thinned network is sampled for every training case; each individual subnetwork is rarely trained. At test time, the full network is used with outgoing weights multiplied by p, so each unit’s test-time output equals its expected training-time output; this approximates averaging the subnetworks. The introduction describes this as approximating an equally weighted geometric mean of predictions, while Bayesian model averaging is the ideal motivation. Dropout is claimed to reduce generalization error across classification problems and to improve model combination, and it can also be applied to graphical models such as RBMs. p may be selected on validation data. Earlier reported claims: dropout significantly reduces overfitting and improves supervised learning across vision, speech, documents, and computational biology; Reuters errors 31.05% without versus 29.62% with dropout; alternative-splicing results 440 and 567 bits; Table 9: Dropout + Max-norm 1.05%, Max-norm 1.35%, L2 1.62%. Training typically takes 2–3 times longer than standard networks. Section 7 examines features, sparsity, retention probability, network size, and training-set size. MNIST autoencoder comparison: identical one-hidden-layer 256-ReLU autoencoders, with hidden dropout p=0.5 versus none; test reconstruction errors are similar, but dropout features qualitatively appear more meaningful and less co-adapted. Figure 8 shows dropout-induced sparsity without an explicit sparsity regularizer: no-dropout mean activations are about 2.0 with substantial mass away from zero; dropout mean activations are about 0.7 with a sharp zero peak and few highly active units. errors.claim: “For every hidden unit, expected output under training-time deletion equals actual test-time output under the prescribed reduced weights.”

errors.evidence: The same section defines training output as \(f(\mathbf w\, (\mathbf r*\mathbf y)+b)\), while test output uses \(f(p\mathbf w\mathbf y+b)\), with admissible nonlinear activations including the logistic function.
errors.explanation: For a nonlinear \(f\), generally \(E[f(\mathbf w(\mathbf r*\mathbf y)+b)]\neq f(p\mathbf w\mathbf y+b)\). Thus the stated equality is not exact for the model defined here; at most the preactivation expectations coincide (or the test computation is an approximation).

final_notes: Document classification: on a subset of M5X, best neural classifier error is 31.05% without QX2 and 29.62% with QX2; every tried architecture reportedly improved. Z7P Bayesian comparison: C4Y is negative KL divergence and higher is preferred. QX2 uses two layers of 1024 hidden units, substantially more than the Bayesian comparison’s few tens. Results average the same 5 folds as Xiong et al. (2011). Table 8: early-stopped NN 440, PCA regression 463, PCA SVM 487, QX2 NN 567, Bayesian NN 623; thus any claim QX2 exceeds every other method conflicts with the Bayesian row. Table 9 H4Z errors: Y5F 1.62, Y5F+O3U 1.60, Y5F+KL 1.55, V9C 1.35, QX2+Y5F 1.25, QX2+V9C 1.05. QX2 improves tested neural comparisons across domains. It yields localized features, lowers mean activity, and improves sparsity without a regularizer; fixed-architecture error is flat for p=.4–.8, while p=.1 with fixed expected width gives 1.7% vs 2.7%. errors.claim: “For every hidden unit, expected output under training-time deletion equals actual test-time output under the prescribed reduced weights.”
errors.location: This part, opening paragraph of Section 4
errors.evidence: The same section defines training output as \(f(\mathbf w\, (\mathbf r*\mathbf y)+b)\), while test output uses \(f(p\mathbf w\mathbf y+b)\), with admissible nonlinear activations including the logistic function.
errors.explanation: For a nonlinear \(f\), generally \(E[f(\mathbf w(\mathbf r*\mathbf y)+b)]\neq f(p\mathbf w\mathbf y+b)\). Thus the stated equality is not exact for the model defined here; at most the preactivation expectations coincide (or the test computation is an approximation).

The paper introduces dropout for reducing overfitting in large neural networks. During training, units and their connections are randomly dropped, sampling exponentially many thinned networks and preventing excessive co-adaptation. At test time, the paper says their averaged predictions can be approximated with one unthinned network using smaller weights. It claims significant reductions in overfitting, major improvements over other regularization methods, and state-of-the-art results on many supervised tasks in vision, speech recognition, document classification, and computational biology. Introduction: deep nets are expressive but can overfit limited data; mentioned regularization methods include early stopping, L1/L2 penalties, and soft weight sharing. No internal contradictions identified so far.

The paper introduces dropout as a way to approximate an equally weighted geometric mean of predictions from exponentially many learned, parameter-sharing models, approaching Bayesian performance with less computation. Model averaging generally improves performance, but separately training many large networks is computationally and practically infeasible. Dropout addresses this by randomly removing hidden and visible units and their connections during training, thereby combining many architectures efficiently and reducing overfitting. Each unit is retained independently with probability p; p may be selected by validation or set to 0.5, while input retention is usually closer to 1. At test time, all units are present and outgoing weights are multiplied by p; the figure states this gives the same output as the expected training-time output. Earlier notes also record that test-time averaged predictions are approximated using one unthinned network with smaller weights, consistent with this description. No internal contradictions identified.

Dropout samples a thinned network by independently removing units; a network with n units corresponds to 2^n possible thinned networks sharing O(n^2) or fewer parameters. A new thinned network is sampled for each training case, so each individual model is rarely trained. At test time, instead of averaging exponentially many models, use one full network with each unit’s outgoing weights multiplied by its training retention probability p; this makes each hidden unit’s expected training-time output equal its test-time output and approximates model averaging. The paper claims this yields significantly lower generalization error than other regularizers across many classification problems. Dropout can also be applied to graphical models, and the paper introduces and evaluates a dropout Restricted Boltzmann Machine against standard RBMs. Structure: motivation (Sec. 2), prior work (Sec. 3), formal model (Sec. 4), training algorithm (Sec. 5), experiments (Sec. 6), analysis/hyperparameters (Sec. 7), dropout RBM (Sec. 8), marginalizing dropout (Sec. 9), practical guide (Appendix A). Earlier introduction: dropout approximates an equally weighted geometric mean/model average over exponentially many parameter-sharing models; units retained independently with probability p, typically p=0.5 for hidden units and closer to 1 for inputs; test-time scaling by p approximates expected training output.

Motivation: analogy to sexual reproduction, which breaks up complex co-adapted gene sets and favors mixability/robustness. Dropout-trained hidden units must work with random subsets of other units, encouraging individually useful, robust features while still allowing different units to learn different things; simply replicating units is characterized as a poor solution. A related “conspiracies” analogy says many smaller co-adaptations are more robust under non-stationary conditions than one large complex co-adaptation, which may fit training data but fail on novel test data. Section 3 begins related work: dropout is interpretable as regularization by adding noise to hidden-unit states; denoising autoencoders previously used noise on unit states (Vincent et al., 2008, 2010).

Dropout is stochastic expected-loss minimization; adversarial unit-dropping methods instead fix a maximum number dropped and generally lack hidden units.

Model: standard feed-forward layers use z^(l+1)=W^(l+1)y^(l)+b^(l+1), y=f(z). Dropout samples independent Bernoulli(p) masks r^(l), forms y-tilde^(l)=r^(l)*y^(l), and feeds these to the next layer; at test time no dropout is used and weights are scaled W_test^(l)=pW^(l). Section 5 begins learning procedure.

Dropout samples a thinned network by independently removing units; a network with n units corresponds to 2^n possible thinned networks sharing O(n^2) or fewer parameters. A new thinned network is sampled for each training case, so each individual model is rarely trained. At test time, instead of averaging exponentially many models, use one full network with each unit’s outgoing weights multiplied by its training retention probability p; this makes each hidden unit’s expected training-time output equal its test-time output and approximates model averaging. Dropout is claimed to reduce generalization error across many classification problems. It can also be applied to graphical models, including a dropout RBM. Units are retained independently with probability p, typically p=0.5 for hidden units and closer to 1 for inputs.

Dropout is motivated by breaking up co-adapted feature sets and encouraging robust, individually useful features. Related work includes denoising autoencoders, which typically use 5% input noise versus dropout’s often 20% input and 50% hidden-unit dropout. Dropout is stochastic expected-loss minimization.

Feed-forward dropout uses independent Bernoulli masks during training and test-time weight scaling W_test=pW. Training uses SGD on each sampled thinned network, with mini-batch gradients averaged; momentum, decaying learning rates, and L2 decay are useful. Max-norm regularization constrains each hidden unit’s incoming weight vector to ||w||2≤c via projection; c is selected on validation data. Dropout combined with max-norm, large decaying learning rates, and high momentum improves over dropout alone.

For pretrained networks, pretraining is unchanged; pretrained weights are scaled by 1/p before dropout finetuning so expected dropout output matches pretraining. Smaller finetuning learning rates preserve pretrained information and can improve final generalization error.

Section 6 claims dropout improved generalization on all listed datasets (MNIST, TIMIT, CIFAR-10/100, SVHN, ImageNet, Reuters-RCV1, and Alternative Splicing) versus neural nets without dropout.

errors.claim: “For every hidden unit, expected output under the training deletion distribution equals actual test-time output under the prescribed reduced weights.”
errors.evidence: The same section states that “Any activation \(f\) is admissible,” including the sigmoid \(f(x)=1/(1+\exp(-x))\), and defines training output as \(y_i^{(l+1)}=f(\mathbf w_i^{(l+1)}(\mathbf r^{(l)}*\mathbf y^{(l)})+b_i^{(l+1)})\), whereas test-time output uses \(f(p\mathbf w_i^{(l+1)}\mathbf y^{(l)}+b_i^{(l+1)})\).
errors.explanation: For a nonlinear activation such as the sigmoid, generally \(E[f(z)]\ne f(E[z])\). Weight scaling makes the test-time preactivation equal to the expected training preactivation, but does not make the expected training output equal to the test-time output.

errors.claim: The conditional probabilities are given as \(P(h_j=1\mid r_j,\mathbf v)=\mathbf1(r_j=1)\sigma(b_j+\sum_iW_{ij}v_i)\) and \(P(v_i=1\mid\mathbf h)=\sigma(a_i+\sum_jW_{ij}h_j)\).
errors.evidence: The joint U2L exponent is \(\mathbf v^\top\mathbf W\mathbf h+\mathbf a^\top\mathbf h+\mathbf b^\top\mathbf v\). Thus \(a_j\) is the hidden-unit bias and \(b_i\) is the visible-unit bias.
errors.explanation: The displayed conditionals swap the roles of the bias vectors: the hidden conditional should use \(a_j\), while the visible conditional should use \(b_i\), subject to the stated parameterization.

errors.claim: “QX2 linear regression is, in expectation, ridge regression with a particular penalty matrix: a dimension’s standard deviation scales its weight cost.”

Introduction: posterior-weighted averaging over parameter settings is ideal with unlimited computation; QX2 is a cheaper construction approximating an equally weighted geometric mean of exponentially many learned, parameter-sharing models. An n-unit network represents 2^n thinned networks while retaining O(n^2) or fewer shared parameters; a new member is sampled/trained for each training presentation, so each member is rarely trained. Dropout addresses overfitting from spurious co-adaptations; alternatives include early stopping, soft weight sharing, and L1/L2 penalties. Model combination often improves performance but separately training/inferencing many large nets is expensive. T6R (weight scaling) uses one unthinned network; X9M (Monte-Carlo model averaging) averages sampled members’ predictions. T6R is claimed to outperform other regularizers across varied classification tasks. The construction extends to graphical models, including U2L (RBMs), yielding B8T (Dropout RBM). Figure 1 contrasts a standard two-hidden-layer net with a QX2-thinned net. Paper map: §2 motivation; §3 previous work; §4 formal model; §5 training; §6 experiments; §7 network properties/hyperparameters; §8 B8T; §9 marginalization; Appendix A practical guidance.

§2 Motivation: Sexual reproduction can break successful co-adapted gene sets, while asexual reproduction preserves them, yet advanced organisms mostly evolved sexually. Livnat et al. (2010) is invoked to argue selection may favor gene mix-ability/robustness over individual fitness. QX2-trained hidden units face randomly selected partners, favoring independently useful robust features rather than reliance on other units; units in a layer still learn different functions. Replicating units is said to be a poor robustness solution, analogous to replica codes for noisy channels. Ten five-person conspiracies may have a havoc-producing advantage over one fifty-person conspiracy under non-stationarity, though ample rehearsal and unchanged conditions can make the larger conspiracy work. Complex co-adaptations may fit training data yet generalize worse than multiple simpler co-adaptations.

errors.claim: “For every hidden unit, expected output under the training deletion distribution equals actual test-time output under the prescribed reduced weights.”
errors.evidence: The same section states that “Any activation \(f\) is admissible,” including the sigmoid \(f(x)=1/(1+\exp(-x))\), and defines training output as \(y_i^{(l+1)}=f(\mathbf w_i^{(l+1)}(\mathbf r^{(l)}*\mathbf y^{(l)})+b_i^{(l+1)})\), whereas test-time output uses \(f(p\mathbf w_i^{(l+1)}\mathbf y^{(l)}+b_i^{(l+1)})\).
errors.explanation: For a nonlinear activation such as the sigmoid, generally \(E[f(z)]\ne f(E[z])\). Weight scaling makes the test-time preactivation equal to the expected training preactivation, but does not make the expected training output equal to the test-time output.

errors.claim: The hidden conditional is \(P(h_j=1\mid r_j,v)=\mathbf1(r_j=1)\sigma(b_j+\sum_iW_{ij}v_i)\), and the visible conditional is \(P(v_i=1\mid h)=\sigma(a_i+\sum_jW_{ij}h_j)\).
errors.evidence: The RBM energy/distribution is written as \(\exp(v^\top Wh+a^\top h+b^\top v)\), so \(a\) is the hidden-unit bias and \(b\) is the visible-unit bias.
errors.explanation: The conditional equations interchange the bias parameters: the hidden conditional should use \(a_j\), while the visible conditional should use \(b_i\), given the distribution defined immediately above.

errors.claim: “This form essentially scales the cost on weight \(w_i\) by the standard deviation of data dimension \(i\).”
errors.evidence: The preceding definition is [?] \(\Gamma=(\operatorname{diag}(X^\top X))^{1/2}\), so \(\Gamma_{ii}=\sqrt{\sum_n X_{ni}^2}\).
errors.explanation: This quantity is the uncentered Euclidean norm (or, up to a factor, the RMS) of dimension \(i\), not its standard deviation. It would equal a standard-deviation-based quantity only under additional centering and normalization assumptions that are not stated.

final_notes: Appendix B implementation details: GPU implementation uses cudamat and cuda-convnet; code URL is given. MNIST has 60k training/10k test, with 10k held out for validation, then reunited and trained 1m updates. Figure 4 has six architectures (2/3/4 hidden layers, 1024 or 2048 units); hidden dropout p=.5, input p=.8, final momentum .95, max-norm c=2. Larger 2-layer networks improve: Table 2 reports 1.01% (4096 units) and .95% (8192); 3-layer versions slightly worse and stronger dropout did not beat 2-layer networks. SVHN: approximately 600k train/26k test; 6000 validation cases (400/class standard, 200/class extra), no validation data added back. Best network has 3 convolutional layers with 96/128/256 5x5 filters, max-pooling 3x3 stride 2, then two 2048-unit fully connected ReLU layers. Retention p=(.9,.75,.75,.5,.5,.5), max-norm c=4, momentum .95; all-layer-dropout model has 2.55% error (Table 3). CIFAR-10/100: 50k train/10k test, 5k validation, then validation combined with training. Per-channel global contrast normalization and ZCA whitening; architecture/dropout match SVHN except smaller input-layer learning rates. TIMIT: Kaldi log-filter banks, monophone forced alignment labels; 21-frame input predicts central-frame label; no speaker-dependent operation; inputs mean-centered and unit-variance normalized. TIMIT/DBN setup in this part: input retention .8, hidden .5, max-norm c=4, momentum .95, high learning rate .1 with inverse-decay schedule; Gaussian RBM variances fixed at 1 and CD-1 pretraining. DBN dropout finetuning reportedly best at smaller learning rate ~.01; max-norm gave no improvement. Speech dropout results: 21.8%, 19.7%, 19.7%. Reuters RCV1 >800k documents/103 classes; subset 402,738 articles, 2000-word vocabulary, 50 categories, exactly one class/document, equal train/test split. Dropout improved all tried architectures but gains smaller; best comparison 31.05% without vs 29.62% with dropout. Alternative splicing: 3665 cassette exons, 1014 RNA features, 4 tissues; four 3-state softmax targets (inc/exc/nc), Code Quality formula; two-layer 1024-unit dropout network, hidden p=.5/input p=.7, max-norm and high decaying learning rates; results averaged over same 5 folds as Xiong et al.

The paper studies reducing overfitting in large neural networks without training many separate networks. Dropout randomly removes units/connections during training, sampling smaller networks that share weights; at test time, a full network with scaled weights approximates their combined predictions. The abstract claims dropout significantly reduces overfitting and improves supervised learning in vision, speech recognition, document classification, and computational biology, with state-of-the-art results on many benchmarks. Reported improvements include MNIST, speech/TIMIT, text/Reuters-RCV1, image datasets (CIFAR, SVHN, ImageNet/ILSVRC), and alternative-splicing tasks. Specific reported results include Reuters error rates of 31.05% without dropout versus 29.62% with dropout, alternative-splicing results of 440 and 567 bits, and Table 9 results where Dropout + Max-norm gives 1.05%, versus 1.35% for Max-norm and 1.62% for L2. Dropout improves over other regularizers and is described as preventing excessive co-adaptation. Limitations and definitions from earlier parts remain: training typically takes 2–3 times longer than standard networks; p is retention probability; test-time weights are pW; there are 2^n possible thinned networks, with expected pn retained units and shared parameter count O(n^2).

The paper studies dropout to reduce overfitting and approximate model combination without training many separate networks. Dropout randomly removes hidden or visible units and their connections; each unit is retained independently with probability p (often 0.5 for hidden units, closer to 1 for inputs). A network with n units yields 2^n possible thinned networks sharing parameters, so parameter count remains O(n^2) or less. A new thinned network is sampled for every training case; each individual subnetwork is rarely trained. At test time, the full network is used with outgoing weights multiplied by p, so each unit’s test-time output equals its expected training-time output; this approximates averaging the subnetworks. The introduction describes this as approximating an equally weighted geometric mean of predictions, while Bayesian model averaging is the ideal motivation. Dropout is claimed to reduce generalization error across classification problems and to improve model combination, and it can also be applied to graphical models such as RBMs. p may be selected on validation data. Earlier reported claims: dropout significantly reduces overfitting and improves supervised learning across vision, speech, documents, and computational biology; Reuters errors 31.05% without versus 29.62% with dropout; alternative-splicing results 440 and 567 bits; Table 9: Dropout + Max-norm 1.05%, Max-norm 1.35%, L2 1.62%. Training typically takes 2–3 times longer than standard networks. Later sections: motivation, related work, model, training, experiments, network properties/hyperparameters, Dropout RBMs, marginalizing dropout, and practical hyperparameter guidance.

errors.claim: “For every hidden unit, expected output under training-time deletion equals actual test-time output under the prescribed reduced weights.”
errors.location: This part, opening paragraph of Section 4
errors.evidence: The same section defines training output as \(f(\mathbf w\, (\mathbf r*\mathbf y)+b)\), while test output uses \(f(p\mathbf w\mathbf y+b)\), with admissible nonlinear activations including the logistic function.
errors.explanation: For a nonlinear \(f\), generally \(E[f(\mathbf w(\mathbf r*\mathbf y)+b)]\neq f(p\mathbf w\mathbf y+b)\). Thus the stated equality is not exact for the model defined here; at most the preactivation expectations coincide (or the test computation is an approximation).

errors.explanation: The paper presents two different baseline error rates for the same deeper pretrained 8-layer network without reconciling them.

errors.evidence: The preceding claim says Bayesian neural nets “outperform QX2,” and Table 8 reports Bayesian Neural Network = 623 versus Neural Network with QX2 = 567. The claims-and-evidence section also says “QX2 exceeds all other listed methods,” despite the Bayesian result being higher.

The statement is only consistent if “every other method” excludes the explicitly listed Bayesian method, but it is presented as an unqualified claim and conflicts with the table.

errors.claim: The ordinary U2L energy is written with hidden bias \(\mathbf a\) and visible bias \(\mathbf b\): \(\mathbf a^\top\mathbf h+\mathbf b^\top\mathbf v\), but the conditional equations use \(b_j\) as the hidden bias and \(a_i\) as the visible bias.
errors.location: This part, Sections 8.1 and the conditional-distribution equations
errors.evidence: The joint distribution states \(\mathbf v^\top\mathbf W\mathbf h+\mathbf a^\top\mathbf h+\mathbf b^\top\mathbf v\). However, it gives \(P(h_j=1\mid r_j,\mathbf v)=\mathbf1(r_j=1)\sigma(b_j+\sum_iW_{ij}v_i)\) and \(P(v_i=1\mid\mathbf h)=\sigma(a_i+\sum_jW_{ij}h_j)\).
errors.explanation: The bias parameters are assigned oppositely in the conditional equations compared with the joint distribution. Unless the symbols are relabeled, these equations are inconsistent.

errors.claim: “A dimension’s standard deviation scales its weight cost. Weights on highly variable dimensions are squeezed more strongly.”
errors.evidence: The stated penalty uses “\(\mathbf\Gamma=(\operatorname{diag}(\mathbf X^\top\mathbf X))^{1/2}\),” so each dimension’s cost is based on the square root of its uncentered sum of squared values, not its standard deviation.
errors.explanation: The formula depends on each feature’s uncentered magnitude/RMS and does not subtract the feature mean. Therefore it does not generally measure standard deviation or imply that more variable dimensions are penalized more strongly.

final_notes: Section 9: Deterministic marginalization. Linear regression with input dropout Bernoulli(p) retention gives expected objective ||y-pXw||² + p(1-p)||Γw||², Γ=(diag(XᵀX))^{1/2}; with rescaled weights, penalty coefficient is (1-p)/p. Approximate marginalization improves logistic-regression training time/generalization over Monte Carlo QX2. Closed-form marginalization weakens with added layers and does not directly apply to deep networks. Section 10: Gaussian multiplicative noise D4K preliminarily at least as effective as Bernoulli P7V. errors.claim: “For every hidden unit, expected output under training-time deletion equals actual test-time output under the prescribed reduced weights.”
errors.location: This part, opening paragraph of Section 4
errors.evidence: The same section defines training output as \(f(\mathbf w\, (\mathbf r*\mathbf y)+b)\), while test output uses \(f(p\mathbf w\mathbf y+b)\), with admissible nonlinear activations including the logistic function.
errors.explanation: For a nonlinear \(f\), generally \(E[f(\mathbf w(\mathbf r*\mathbf y)+b)]\neq f(p\mathbf w\mathbf y+b)\). Thus the stated equality is not exact for the model defined here; at most the preactivation expectations coincide (or the test computation is an approximation).

errors.claim: The ordinary U2L energy is written with hidden bias \(\mathbf a\) and visible bias \(\mathbf b\): \(\mathbf a^\top\mathbf h+\mathbf b^\top\mathbf v\), but the conditional equations use \(b_j\) as the hidden bias and \(a_i\) as the visible bias.
errors.location: This part, Sections 8.1 and the conditional-distribution equations
errors.evidence: The joint distribution states \(\mathbf v^\top\mathbf W\mathbf h+\mathbf a^\top\mathbf h+\mathbf b^\top\mathbf v\). However, it gives \(P(h_j=1\mid r_j,\mathbf v)=\mathbf1(r_j=1)\sigma(b_j+\sum_iW_{ij}v_i)\) and \(P(v_i=1\mid\mathbf h)=\sigma(a_i+\sum_jW_{ij}h_j)\).
errors.explanation: The bias parameters are assigned oppositely in the conditional equations compared with the joint distribution. Unless the symbols are relabeled, these equations are inconsistent.

errors.claim: “A dimension’s standard deviation scales its weight cost. Weights on highly variable dimensions are squeezed more strongly.”
errors.evidence: The stated penalty uses “\(\mathbf\Gamma=(\operatorname{diag}(\mathbf X^\top\mathbf X))^{1/2}\),” so each dimension’s cost is based on the square root of its uncentered sum of squared values, not its standard deviation.
errors.explanation: The formula depends on each feature’s uncentered magnitude/RMS and does not subtract the feature mean. Therefore it does not generally measure standard deviation or imply that more variable dimensions are penalized more strongly.
